m1-overview: purpose this module introduces the role of data analytics in modern business, the four analytics types, the crisp-dm methodology, and ethical considerations. learning objectives understand the role of data analytics in modern business differentiate between analytics types and their applications apply the crisp-dm methodology to structure projects recognize ethical considerations in data handling practice through case studies and worked examples module flow 5 sections 1 landscape 2 types 3 crisp-dm 4 ethics 5 recap guiding principle analytics helps businesses move from opinions to evidence-based decisions.
m1-role: key idea analytics helps businesses move from opinions to evidence-based decisions. five ways analytics creates value value how evidence-based decisions replace opinions with data-backed evidence kpi tracking monitor key performance indicators over time early detection identify drops, spikes, and risks quickly planning support targets, forecasting, resource allocation accountability link actions to measurable outcomes visual — from opinions to evidence business value flow 1 opinions 2 analytics 3 evidence-based decisions example a simple weekly report showing total leads, appointments booked, and website traffic (with basic totals and trends) is descriptive analytics in action. role of analytics opinions vs evidence in business decisions ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice decide on gut feel opinion drives the budget call back decisions with data evidence replaces opinion check results once in a while no kpi tracked over time track kpis over time weekly leads, bookings, traffic spot problems after the damage drops and spikes found late set up early detection drops, spikes, risks flagged fast result: debates, no accountability result: measurable, defensible choices mistake opinions settle the debate and nobody can verify it. best practice link every action to a measurable outcome. value flow opinions to analytics to evidence-based decisions. three fixes to apply 1 use evidence ask what data supports the decision. 2 track kpis monitor the same metrics over time. 3 detect early watch for drops and spikes before they grow.
m1-landscape: definition data analytics is the process of collecting, transforming, and organizing data to conclude, make predictions, and drive informed decision-making. what the landscape includes methods and tools used across industries and roles expectations and how organizations measure success with data variations based on company size, tools, culture, and data quality links between business needs and analytics approaches visual — landscape layers from data to decisions data methods insights decisions understanding the landscape helps pick the right type of analysis for a problem. evolution analytics progressed from manual reporting to structured decision systems. growth in digital systems created more data and more opportunities. analytics landscape the landscape: pick the right analysis first ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice start with a favourite tool method chosen before the problem start from the business need link need to analytics approach copy another firm's approach ignores company size and culture fit method to your context size, tools, culture, data quality skip data quality questions weak data, shaky conclusions follow data to decisions data, methods, insights, decisions result: right tool, wrong problem result: analysis that drives action mistake methods drift away from the business need. best practice understand the landscape to pick the right type. rule of thumb need first, method second, decision last. three fixes to apply 1 start with need name the business question before choosing a tool. 2 fit your context check size, tools, culture and data quality. 3 end in a decision every analysis feeds one clear decision.
m1-outline: five sections this module covers the landscape, analytics types, crisp-dm, ethics, and key takeaways. section breakdown section topics 1. landscape evolution, careers, industry use, maturity model 2. types descriptive, diagnostic, predictive, prescriptive 3. crisp-dm business understanding → deployment 4. ethics gdpr, privacy principles, bias, responsible use 5. recap core ideas and key takeaways module flow 1 descriptive 2 probability 3 inference 4 tests 5 recap
m1-evolution: overview analytics progressed from manual reporting to structured decision systems across five stages. the five stages analytics evolution 1 basic 2 standardized 3 diagnostic 4 predictive 5 prescriptive key drivers growth in digital systems created more data and more opportunities importance increased because businesses compete on speed and quality of decisions governance and ethical handling became more critical as data volume increased recap analytics evolved from reporting to decision support and optimization. ethics becomes more important as data usage grows. analytics evolution analytics maturity: do not skip the stages ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice jump straight to predictive spreadsheet data, no shared kpis build stages in order basic, standardized, diagnostic... ignore governance as data grows more data, more ethical risk add governance as volume grows ethics matures with data use stop at reporting forever slow decisions, low trust move reporting to decision support then to optimization result: advanced tools on weak base result: trusted, scalable analytics mistake fancy models built on unreliable numbers. best practice each stage rests on the one before it. rule of thumb reporting, then why, then next, then what to do. three fixes to apply 1 order the stages fix reporting before you forecast. 2 grow governance raise controls as data use grows. 3 keep moving aim from reports toward decision support.
m1-stage1: characteristics data in spreadsheets, manual reports, inconsistent definitions. what it looks like data is mostly in spreadsheets or basic systems reports are manual and repeated every month/week focus is on totals and simple comparisons definitions vary across teams (same metric, different values) high effort, lower trust, slow decision-making example sample a simple weekly report showing total leads, appointments booked, and website traffic (with basic totals and trends). basic reporting flow spreadsheets manual reports inconsistent kpis stage 1: basic reporting basic reporting: same metric, different values ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice rebuild the report by hand repeated every week or month automate the repeated report spreadsheets to a system each team defines its own kpi same metric, different values agree on one kpi definition written once, used everywhere stop at totals simple comparisons only add trends to totals leads, bookings, traffic over time result: high effort, low trust result: faster, consistent reporting mistake slow decisions because nobody trusts the numbers. best practice move toward stage 2: standardized reporting. test do two teams get the same number for one metric? three fixes to apply 1 automate stop rebuilding the same report by hand. 2 one definition write kpi definitions down and share them. 3 add trends show change over time, not only totals.
m1-stage2: characteristics agreed kpi definitions, repeatable reports, one source of truth. what changes teams agree on kpi definitions used across the business reporting becomes repeatable and more consistent trend tracking becomes regular (month-over-month, year-over-year) stakeholders expect "one source of truth" for core metrics faster operational decisions become possible example sample a weekly dashboard using the same fixed kpis and format (e.g., leads, conversion rate, cac) across all campaigns so results are consistently comparable. standardized kpi dashboard leads 1,240 conversion 3.2% cac $42 stage 2: standardized standardized reporting: one source of truth ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice change kpi formats each week results not comparable fix kpis and format leads, conversion rate, cac skip month-over-month views no trend tracking track mom and yoy regularly trend tracking becomes routine keep several versions of metrics stakeholders argue over numbers publish one source of truth core metrics defined once result: reports no one can compare result: faster operational decisions mistake time goes to reconciling, not deciding. best practice same kpis across all campaigns, every week. rule of thumb same kpi, same format, same definition, every time. three fixes to apply 1 fix the kpis use the same set across all campaigns. 2 track trends compare month-over-month and year-over-year. 3 one source define core metrics in one place.
m1-stage3: characteristics going beyond "what" to "why" using segmentation and root-cause thinking. what changes teams go beyond "what happened" to "why it happened." analysis uses segmentation (region, product, customer type) root-cause thinking becomes part of regular reviews teams act on drivers, not only on totals decision-making improves because causes are clearer example sample after a drop in leads, analyze channel performance and landing page conversion to identify the cause (e.g., higher cpc + lower form completion rate). diagnostic drill-down leads dropped higher cpc lower form rate stage 3: diagnostic diagnostic: go from what to why ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice report the drop and stop leads dropped, no reason given ask why it happened check channel and landing page look only at totals no region or product slices segment the data region, product, customer type guess one cause and act root cause never tested trace the driver chain higher cpc + lower form rate result: fixes aimed at the wrong thing result: clear causes, better decisions mistake teams act on totals, not on drivers. best practice act on drivers, not only on totals. rule of thumb segment first, then find the driver, then act. three fixes to apply 1 ask why follow every drop with a drill-down. 2 segment slice by region, product and customer type. 3 find the driver name the cause before you propose a fix.
m1-stage4: characteristics forecasting what is likely to happen next to support planning. what changes businesses start forecasting what is likely to happen next predictions support planning (inventory, staffing, budget) outputs include forecasts or risk scores (e.g., churn risk) validation becomes important to avoid misleading predictions monitoring remains necessary because reality can change example sample use past lead and conversion trends to forecast next month's appointments and expected revenue from current campaigns. forecast with confidence band today forecast stage 4: predictive predictive: forecasts need validation ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice publish a forecast unchecked no validation before planning validate before planning compare forecast with actuals show one confident number hides the uncertainty show a confidence band forecast range, not one point set it and forget it reality changes, model does not monitor continuously re-check as reality changes result: misleading plans and budgets result: forecasts people can plan on mistake inventory and staffing built on a bad forecast. best practice use for inventory, staffing and budget planning. rule of thumb forecast = estimate with a range, checked against actuals. three fixes to apply 1 validate test forecasts against what really happened. 2 show a range give a band, not a single number. 3 monitor re-check as conditions change.
m1-stage5: characteristics recommending actions under constraints to reach the best outcome. what changes businesses use analytics to recommend actions under constraints examples include optimizing budgets or recommending next steps requires strong data quality, clear objectives, and business buy-in recommendations must be measurable and realistic to implement ethical and governance controls become even more important example sample based on forecasted roi, recommend shifting 20% budget from low-performing keywords to high-converting campaigns and adjusting bids/timing to hit the target bookings. optimization under constraints low roi reallocate budget high roi increase budget target hit stage 5: prescriptive prescriptive: advice needs constraints ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice recommend without goals no clear objective to optimize set a clear objective hit the target bookings ignore budget and capacity advice cannot be implemented respect constraints shift 20% budget, keep the cap build on unclean data optimizing the wrong numbers require strong data quality then measure the outcome result: recommendations no one uses result: measurable, realistic actions mistake unrealistic advice loses business buy-in. best practice low roi down, high roi up, target hit. rule of thumb goal + constraints + clean data = usable advice. three fixes to apply 1 set the goal define the objective before you optimize. 2 add constraints include budget, time and capacity. 3 measure results track whether the action worked.
m1-careers: key checks career paths and opportunities ✓ communicate explain findings in plain business terms. ✓ learn ethics know privacy and bias basics. ✓ widen scope take on higher-impact decisions. overview analytics careers exist in nearly every function. growth comes from bigger scope and higher-impact decisions. five common roles role focus data analyst define kpis, explore data, communicate findings, track results bi / reporting analyst consistent kpi reporting, dashboards, metric definitions product analyst user behavior, funnels, cohorts, product decisions marketing analyst campaign performance, cost efficiency, attribution operations analyst service levels, delays, bottlenecks, process improvement skill note communication skill matters as much as technical skills. ethics knowledge is increasingly required. analytics careers analytics careers: skills beyond the tools ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice train on technical skills only findings never explained well practice communication communicate findings clearly ignore ethics knowledge increasingly required learn ethics and privacy part of the job now stay in one narrow scope growth stalls grow scope and impact bigger decisions, more growth result: great analysis, no impact result: skills that advance a career mistake insights fail if nobody understands them. best practice communication matters as much as technical skill. rule of thumb technical skill + clear voice + ethics = growth. three fixes to apply 1 communicate explain findings in plain business terms. 2 learn ethics know privacy and bias basics. 3 widen scope take on higher-impact decisions.
m1-types-overview: overview four analytics types answer different questions. choosing the right type prevents wrong conclusions. the four types analytics ladder 1 descriptive 2 diagnostic 3 predictive 4 prescriptive quick reference type question output descriptive what happened? reports, dashboards, kpi scorecards diagnostic why did it happen? driver tables, root cause summaries predictive what will happen? forecast charts, risk scores prescriptive what should we do? action plan + expected impact + trade-offs rule use the simplest type that answers the business need reliably. types of analytics four types: match the type to the question ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice forecast when asked what happened over-engineered answer descriptive for what happened reports, dashboards, scorecards report totals when asked why descriptive cannot explain causes diagnostic for why driver tables, root causes use any type, any question wrong type, wrong conclusion predictive or prescriptive: next forecasts, action plans result: wrong conclusions result: answers that fit the question mistake right data, wrong analytics type for the question. best practice what, why, next, do: one type each. rule use the simplest type that answers the need reliably. three fixes to apply 1 name the question is it what, why, next or do? 2 pick the type map question to analytics type. 3 keep it simple choose the simplest type that works.
m1-descriptive: definition descriptive analytics summarizes historical data using totals, averages, and trends. key characteristics answers: "what happened?" and "what is happening now?" focuses on reliable measurement and clear kpis does not attempt to prove causes outputs: reports, dashboards, kpi scorecards example — sales trend sample measure monthly revenue over the last 12 months, compare current vs previous month and vs same month last year, identify highest and lowest months, break down by region and product category. monthly revenue trend 12-month revenue trend + summary table descriptive analytics descriptive: summarize, do not claim causes ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice report revenue with no comparison one month, no context compare vs last month and year month-over-month, year-over-year say the trend proves why descriptive shows what only break down by region and product find highest and lowest months use vague kpis numbers differ between teams define clear kpis reliable, consistent measurement result: numbers without meaning result: clear picture of what happened mistake a total alone cannot say good or bad. best practice 12-month trend plus a summary table. rule of thumb descriptive says what, not why. three fixes to apply 1 add comparisons show vs prior month and prior year. 2 break it down split by region and product category. 3 define kpis use the same definition every time.
m1-diagnostic: definition diagnostic analytics investigates reasons behind changes in performance. key characteristics answers: "why did it happen?" using comparisons and segmentation looks for drivers by slicing data by time, region, product, or customer group tests multiple explanations before concluding outputs: driver tables, root cause summaries, prioritized issues example — conversion drop sample observe conversion decreased from 2.6% to 2.4%, segment by device (mobile fell, desktop stable), segment by landing page (one page shows higher bounce rate), compare before/after a site change, conclude the likely driver and recommend a test/fix. conversion drop by device 2.0% mobile 2.8% desktop mobile is the driver diagnostic analytics diagnostic: test several explanations ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice blame the first cause you see single explanation, untested test multiple explanations device, page, timing look at the overall rate only conversion 2.6% to 2.4% segment the drop mobile fell, desktop stable skip before/after checks no comparison to site change compare before and after around the site change result: confident but wrong reasons result: likely driver found mistake fix aimed at the wrong driver. best practice mobile is the driver: recommend a test or fix. rule of thumb slice, compare, then conclude the driver. three fixes to apply 1 test alternatives list several possible causes first. 2 segment slice by device, page and customer group. 3 compare check before vs after a change.
m1-predictive: definition predictive analytics uses historical patterns to estimate future outcomes. key characteristics answers: "what will happen?" or "what is likely to happen?" outputs include forecasts or probability scores predictions must be validated to avoid misleading planning decisions outputs: forecast charts, risk scores, probability rankings example — demand forecast sample use past sales to estimate next month's demand, identify seasonality (peak and low periods), produce a forecast range instead of a single number when possible, use forecast for inventory and staffing planning, track forecast vs actual to improve future predictions. demand forecast with range today forecast range predictive analytics predictive: a forecast is a likelihood ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice present one number as certain prediction treated as fact give a forecast range not a single number ignore seasonality peaks and lows missed identify peaks and lows seasonality built in never compare forecast to actual model never improves track forecast vs actual improve future predictions result: plans broken by surprises result: realistic, improving forecasts mistake misleading inventory and staffing decisions. best practice plan inventory and staffing using the range. rule of thumb predictions are probabilities, not guarantees. three fixes to apply 1 use a range show best, worst and expected cases. 2 find seasonality mark peak and low periods. 3 track accuracy compare forecast with actuals.
m1-prescriptive: definition prescriptive analytics recommends actions to reach the best outcome. key characteristics answers: "what should we do?" under constraints (budget, time, capacity) uses rules, scenarios, or optimization logic recommendations must be practical to implement outputs: action plan + expected impact + trade-offs example — marketing budget sample goal: maximize conversions within a fixed budget. compare channel performance and diminishing returns. allocate more budget to high-performing channels within constraints. recommend stopping or reducing low-performing segments. track results and adjust allocation based on outcomes. budget optimization low roi reduce budget high roi increase budget maximize conversions prescriptive analytics prescriptive: recommend within limits ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice advise with no budget limit ignores time and capacity state goal and constraints maximize conversions, fixed budget spread budget evenly low roi keeps its share shift to high-roi channels reduce low-performing segments recommend and walk away no tracking of results track results and adjust reallocate based on outcomes result: plans that cannot be done result: practical, measurable plan mistake no feasibility check, so no trust. best practice action plan, expected impact and trade-offs. rule of thumb goal + constraints = a recommendation to trust. three fixes to apply 1 state limits list budget, time and capacity. 2 shift spend move budget toward high roi. 3 track and adjust review outcomes, then reallocate.
m1-misuse: key checks common misuse of analytics types ✓ confirm first quantify the problem before explaining it. ✓ test causes check alternative drivers before concluding. ✓ state likelihood present predictions as probabilities. critical using the wrong analytics type or misinterpreting outputs leads to bad decisions. five common misuses misuse why it's wrong treating a descriptive trend as proof of cause descriptive shows what, not why claiming reasons without testing alternative drivers diagnostic requires testing multiple explanations treating a prediction as certainty rather than likelihood predictions are probabilistic, not guaranteed giving prescriptive advice without constraints or feasibility recommendations must be practical ignoring ethics/privacy when segmenting people-level data responsibility increases with granularity rule start descriptive to confirm the problem exists and quantify it. move to diagnostic to find the most likely drivers. use predictive to plan for future demand or risk. use prescriptive when you have clear goals and constraints. misuse of analytics misuse: the wrong type, the wrong decision ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice treat a trend as proof of cause descriptive shows what, not why descriptive to confirm the problem quantify it first claim a reason, test no others diagnostic needs alternatives diagnostic to find likely drivers test several explanations treat a prediction as certain predictions are probabilistic predict to plan, prescribe to act needs clear goals and limits result: bad decisions, lost trust result: each type used correctly mistake also: advice with no constraints, ethics ignored. best practice responsibility grows with people-level granularity. rule of thumb describe, diagnose, predict, then prescribe. three fixes to apply 1 confirm first quantify the problem before explaining it. 2 test causes check alternative drivers before concluding. 3 state likelihood present predictions as probabilities.
m1-crispdm-overview: definition crisp-dm is a standard process to structure analytics projects end-to-end. why it matters ensures alignment between business goals and data work reduces wasted effort by defining phases and expected outputs is iterative: you revisit phases as you learn more fits descriptive, diagnostic, predictive, and prescriptive projects the 6 phases crisp-dm flow 1 business 2 data u. 3 data p. 4 modeling 5 evaluate 6 deploy recap crisp-dm structures analytics projects reliably. each phase has clear goals and outputs. evaluation prevents misleading conclusions. deployment ensures the work is used and measured. crisp-dm overview crisp-dm: structure beats ad-hoc work ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice dive into data with no plan work not tied to business goals align goals before data work business understanding first skip defined outputs per phase wasted effort define phases and outputs six phases, clear deliverables treat the project as one pass never revisit earlier phases iterate as you learn revisit phases when needed result: busy work, unused results result: reliable, reusable projects mistake findings that nobody can act on. best practice evaluation prevents misleading conclusions. rule of thumb business, data, prep, model, evaluate, deploy. three fixes to apply 1 start with goals tie every task to a business goal. 2 define outputs name what each phase delivers. 3 iterate loop back as you learn.
m1-crispdm-phases: key checks 6 phases detail ✓ define kpi write formula, scope and decision first. ✓ check data test duplicates, missing values, joins. ✓ deploy assign an owner and monitor impact. overview each phase has a clear purpose and produces specific outputs. phase 1: business understanding define the problem clearly in business terms identify kpis and success criteria for "what good looks like" decide scope (timeframe, audience, segments, boundaries) list constraints (privacy, time, budget, access) define the decision that will be made from the analysis phase 2: data understanding identify what data sources exist and what they contain clarify definitions of fields and metrics check coverage (time range, missingness, duplicates) confirm data is fit for the kpi and segmentation needed document limitations before heavy analysis starts phase 3: data preparation common issues: duplicates inflate totals, missing values distort trends, inconsistent labels split categories, incorrect joins create false spikes/drops, wrong data types produce calculation errors phase 4: modeling apply methods to answer the question choose the simplest valid approach that meets business needs document assumptions used while modeling and interpreting results keep outputs aligned to kpis and decisions defined in phase 1 phase 5: evaluation confirm results answer the original business objective and kpi validate logic: results should be plausible and consistent check sensitivity: do results change wildly if assumptions shift? identify bias or unfair impact risks when analyzing people-level data get stakeholder review so interpretation matches real business context phase 6: deployment deliver results so they can be used repeatedly outputs may be a report, dashboard, or decision playbook define how often results are reviewed and by whom define ownership for maintenance and updates set up monitoring to track whether actions worked crisp-dm phases six phases: skip one and it shows later ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice jump to modeling no kpi or decision defined define kpi and decision first success criteria, scope, constraints join tables without checks incorrect joins create false spikes check coverage and duplicates missing values, labels, data types stop at findings no owner, no monitoring evaluate, then deploy with owner stakeholder review, monitoring result: duplicates, false spikes result: results used and trusted mistake bad prep inflates totals and distorts trends. best practice each phase produces an output for the next. rule of thumb decide, check data, model, validate, deploy. three fixes to apply 1 define kpi write formula, scope and decision first. 2 check data test duplicates, missing values, joins. 3 deploy assign an owner and monitor impact.
m1-crispdm-example: scenario improve customer retention with churn kpi. phase-by-phase walkthrough phase what happens business "improve customer retention" with churn kpi data subscription history and customer activity records prep clean dates, define churn event, remove duplicates modeling identify churn drivers by segment and time evaluation validate with stakeholders and confirm data coverage deployment deliver recurring retention report and action plan retention project flow 1 business 2 data u. 3 data p. 4 modeling 5 evaluate 6 deploy key insight each phase produces artifacts that feed the next. evaluation and deployment ensure the work creates value. crisp-dm example retention project: skipping phases costs you ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice build churn models at once churn event never defined start with churn kpi improve customer retention use raw subscription history dates messy, duplicates in clean dates, remove duplicates define the churn event send findings once no recurring retention report validate, then deliver a report recurring report plus action plan result: churn numbers nobody trusts result: retention work that sticks mistake insights are forgotten. no impact proven. best practice each phase feeds the next. rule of thumb business, data, prep, model, evaluate, deploy. three fixes to apply 1 define churn fix the event and kpi first. 2 clean first fix dates and remove duplicates. 3 deliver ship a recurring report and action plan.
m1-crispdm-vs-random: why structure matters crisp-dm prevents common mistakes by forcing clarity at every phase. side-by-side comparison crisp-dm random analysis starts with business goals starts with data documents assumptions leaves them unstated validates data quality trusts data blindly produces reusable outputs produces one-off charts includes deployment often stops at findings two approaches crisp-dm structured, repeatable, documented random analysis ad-hoc, one-off, undocumented crisp-dm vs random crisp-dm vs random analysis ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice start with the data no business goal in mind start with business goals know the question first leave assumptions unstated nobody can check the logic document assumptions visible and reviewable trust data blindly no quality validation validate data quality then produce reusable outputs result: one-off charts, no reuse result: structured, repeatable work mistake often stops at findings, never deployed. best practice includes deployment so results get used. test could someone else repeat this analysis tomorrow? three fixes to apply 1 goal first begin with the business question. 2 write assumptions document them where others can see. 3 validate data check quality before charting.
m1-crispdm-pitfalls: key checks common crisp-dm pitfalls ✓ define kpis add formula, timeframe and filters. ✓ run data qa validate before you present. ✓ plan deploy name an owner and a review cadence. critical these three pitfalls derail analytics projects. 1. vague kpis kpi must have formula, timeframe, and filters vague kpi causes conflicting numbers across teams misaligned kpi leads to wrong "success" evaluation fix by documenting kpi definition in phase 1 reuse the same kpi definition in evaluation and deployment 2. skipping data qa skipping qa leads to wrong conclusions from bad data missing values can hide important segments duplicates inflate totals and distort trends incorrect joins create false spikes or drops always validate before producing final insights 3. no deployment plan without deployment, analysis is not reused stakeholders forget findings without a recurring deliverable no monitoring means you can't prove impact lack of ownership means dashboards become outdated deployment turns analysis into business value prevention crisp-dm prevents these by forcing kpi definition early, validating data first, requiring preparation and qa, including evaluation, and planning deployment. crisp-dm pitfalls three pitfalls that derail projects ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice vague kpi with no formula conflicting numbers across teams kpi: formula, timeframe, filters documented in phase 1 skip data qa duplicates inflate, joins mislead validate before final insights duplicates, missing values, joins no deployment plan findings forgotten, dashboards stale plan deployment and ownership recurring deliverable, monitoring result: wrong success, no impact result: trusted kpis, proven impact mistake missing values can hide key segments. best practice reuse the same kpi in evaluation and deployment. check formula, timeframe, filters, owner, monitoring. three fixes to apply 1 define kpis add formula, timeframe and filters. 2 run data qa validate before you present. 3 plan deploy name an owner and a review cadence.
m1-ethics-overview: key checks ethics in analytics ✓ protect data get consent and limit exposure. ✓ check fairness look for groups that may be harmed. ✓ be transparent state limits and assumptions. definition ethics means using data in ways that are fair, safe, and appropriate. why it matters as analytics becomes more powerful, responsibility increases data can harm people if misused or exposed ethics ensures fairness and appropriate use privacy ensures compliance and trust key ethical risks risk example privacy violations exposing personal data without consent bias unfair targeting or exclusion of groups misuse of insights using predictions to harm or discriminate standard ethics is a required professional standard, not an optional extra. ethical analytics requires transparency about limitations and assumptions. ethics in analytics ethics: a standard, not an extra ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice expose personal data no consent obtained protect privacy compliance and trust target or exclude groups unfairly bias goes unchecked check fairness review who may be excluded hide limits and assumptions predictions used to harm state limits and assumptions be transparent result: harm to people, lost trust result: fair, safe, appropriate use mistake data can hurt people if misused or exposed. best practice responsibility grows as analytics gets stronger. rule of thumb fair, safe and appropriate use is required. three fixes to apply 1 protect data get consent and limit exposure. 2 check fairness look for groups that may be harmed. 3 be transparent state limits and assumptions.
m1-gdpr: definition gdpr is a privacy regulation focused on protecting personal data rights. core principles lawful, transparent handling of personal data purpose limitation: use data only for stated reasons data minimization: collect only what is needed accountability: organizations must demonstrate compliance visual — gdpr flow gdpr principles 1 collect 2 use 3 store 4 protect important gdpr applies to any organization handling personal data of eu residents, regardless of where the organization is located. gdpr fundamentals gdpr: collect less, use it only as stated ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice collect everything just in case breaks data minimization collect only what is needed data minimization reuse data for a new purpose breaks purpose limitation use data only for stated reasons purpose limitation assume eu rules do not apply applies to eu residents anywhere treat eu resident data as covered wherever your company is result: compliance risk result: lawful, accountable handling mistake cannot show how data was handled. best practice be able to demonstrate compliance. rule of thumb collect, use, store, protect: lawful and transparent. three fixes to apply 1 minimize collect only what the task needs. 2 limit purpose use data only for stated reasons. 3 be accountable keep records that prove compliance.
m1-privacy: key checks data privacy principles ✓ aggregate show groups, not people, when possible. ✓ set retention delete data once it is no longer needed. ✓ limit access apply access controls to sensitive data. overview five principles guide responsible data collection, use, and storage. principles principle what it means minimization collect only necessary data purpose limitation use data only for the intended purpose accuracy keep data accurate and up to date security secure data with access controls retention retain data only as long as needed personal data examples direct identifiers: name, email, phone number indirect identifiers: device ids, ip address, location patterns sensitive data: health or financial details risk combining datasets can create identification risk. aggregation reduces risk compared to individual-level display. data privacy principles privacy: show aggregates, keep less ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice show individual-level rows names, emails, phone numbers aggregate where possible lower risk than individual rows keep data forever no retention limit set a retention period keep data only as long as needed combine datasets freely creates identification risk use access controls security and accuracy upheld result: identification and exposure risk result: lower risk, kept trust mistake health or financial details leak. best practice minimization and purpose limitation guide use. rule of thumb collect only what is needed, use it as intended. three fixes to apply 1 aggregate show groups, not people, when possible. 2 set retention delete data once it is no longer needed. 3 limit access apply access controls to sensitive data.
m1-bias: key checks bias in data collection ✓ widen the sample include groups that left or are missing. ✓ review surveys check who answered and who did not. ✓ question labels test whether success is defined fairly. definition bias occurs when data does not represent reality fairly. common bias types bias type example survey bias only certain groups respond, skewing results selection bias dataset includes only active users, ignoring churned users label bias "success" defined in a way that reflects older unfair practices geographic bias some regions have missing or delayed data tool/process bias inconsistent data entry by different teams impact bias leads to unfair or incorrect conclusions. historical bias can repeat unfair past decisions. measurement bias occurs when proxies don't reflect true concepts. bias in data bias: when data misrepresents reality ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice analyze only active users churned users ignored include churned users avoid selection bias trust survey responses as is only some groups respond check who responded survey bias review reuse a past definition of success repeats old unfair practice redefine success and labels question historical bias result: unfair or incorrect conclusions result: representative, fairer analysis mistake proxies may not reflect the true concept. best practice check coverage, regions and data entry. check who is missing from this data and why? three fixes to apply 1 widen the sample include groups that left or are missing. 2 review surveys check who answered and who did not. 3 question labels test whether success is defined fairly.
m1-responsible: purpose five questions to ask before any analysis involving people-level data. checklist do we have a valid reason and permission to use this data? are we using the minimum data necessary for the objective? are metrics and methods explained without hiding limitations? could outputs harm individuals or unfairly target groups? are access controls and security applied appropriately? visual responsible use cycle 1 collect 2 use 3 store 4 protect definition responsible use means analyzing data with privacy, fairness, and transparency. show only what is necessary for decision-making. avoid exposing individual identities when not needed. document assumptions and limitations clearly. add safeguards: permissions, aggregation, and review processes. responsible usage responsible use: five questions first ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice use people data without permission no valid reason documented confirm a valid reason documented consent, owner: legal pull every column available more than the goal needs use the minimum data necessary show only what decisions need hide limitations in the report methods left unexplained explain methods and limits add permissions and review result: harm, exposure, no safeguards result: privacy, fairness, transparency mistake no check on whether outputs target groups unfairly. best practice turn each principle into a yes or no with owner. check reason, minimum data, limits, harm, access controls. three fixes to apply 1 get permission confirm a valid reason and consent. 2 use minimum data aggregate and avoid identities. 3 document limits record assumptions and safeguards.
m1-recap: module flow 1 descriptive 2 probability 3 inference 4 tests 5 practice the five key takeaways analytics landscape evolved from reporting to decision support and optimization. types of analytics define the question: what/why/next/do. crisp-dm structures projects reliably with clear phases and outputs. ethics and privacy protect people and build trust in analytics. practical exercises connect concepts to real business scenarios. carry-forward rules use the simplest analytics type that answers the business need. always define kpis before analysis. validate data quality before drawing conclusions. consider ethical implications at every stage. plan deployment to turn analysis into business value. next module module 2 explores data types and sources — the foundation for choosing the right analysis methods.
m2-overview: purpose data classification determines which analysis methods are valid. wrong classification → wrong conclusions. module flow roadmap 1 structure 2 scales 3 temporal 4 sources four dimensions of classification dimension question example structure how organized? structured, semi, unstructured measurement what math is valid? nominal, ordinal, interval, ratio temporal how does time factor? cross-sectional, time series, panel source where from? primary/secondary, internal/external guiding principle classify first, analyze second. the classification dictates what operations are meaningful. data types and sources classify first, analyze second ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice run stats before checking type wrong classification classify before choosing a method type decides valid math classify on one dimension only structure, scale, time, source label all four dimensions sales table: structured, ratio... skip the source question unknown bias and quality ask where data came from primary or secondary, internal result: invalid methods, wrong results result: valid, defensible analysis mistake classification decides which operations are valid. best practice every dataset has a value on all four dimensions. rule of thumb classify first. the type sets what operations are valid. three fixes to apply 1 check the type name the type before any calculation. 2 use 4 dimensions structure, scale, time, source. 3 trace the source ask who collected it and why.
m2-classification-framework: overview four independent dimensions. a dataset has a value on each. visual — 4 dimensions classification dimensions structure organized? measurement math valid? temporal time factor? source where from? each dimension is independent — a dataset has a value on all four. example: a sales table is structured · ratio · panel · internal. quick reference matrix dimension options key question structure structured / semi / unstructured can sql query it directly? measurement nominal / ordinal / interval / ratio can i average it? temporal cross-sectional / time series / panel does time matter? source primary/secondary · internal/external who collected it? common mistake treating ordinal data as interval (e.g., averaging likert scores without caution). classification framework four dimensions, four questions ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice average likert scores freely ordinal treated as interval ask: can i average it? check measurement scale call a table just structured ignores scale and time label all four dimensions structured, ratio, panel, internal skip the key question can i average it? never asked ask: does time matter? pick cross-sectional, series, panel result: meaningless averages result: right method for each dataset mistake one label hides three other dimensions. best practice each dimension is independent. check sql? average? time? who collected it? three fixes to apply 1 ask four questions one per dimension for every dataset. 2 check the scale before you average anything. 3 check time decide if time matters to the method.
m2-why-matters: key idea statistical operations are only valid for certain data types. misclassification = invalid results. examples data wrong operation correct approach nominal (colors) mean of color codes mode / frequency table ordinal (satisfaction) mean of likert scale median / mode / ordinal regression interval (temperature °c) ratio: "20°c is twice 10°c" differences are valid, ratios are not time series simple random sample assumption autocorrelation-aware methods decision impact 1 wrong type invalid stats 2 wrong analysis bad conclusions 3 wrong decisions costly errors bottom line always verify data type before applying any statistical method. why classification matters wrong type: invalid stats, costly decisions ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice mean of color codes nominal treated as numbers mode or frequency table for nominal categories mean of a likert scale ordinal treated as interval median, mode, ordinal regression for ordinal data say 20c is twice 10c ratio on interval data use differences, not ratios valid for interval data result: invalid stats, costly errors result: valid methods, sound decisions mistake wrong analysis leads to bad conclusions. best practice time series: use methods aware of autocorrelation. rule of thumb verify the data type before any statistical method. three fixes to apply 1 use mode count categories, do not average them. 2 use median rank ordered data with median. 3 use differences subtract interval values, skip ratios.
m2-structure-overview: overview three levels of organization, each with trade-offs on storage, query cost, and analytic flexibility. visual comparison structured → semi → unstructured structured rows & columns sql-ready semi-structured json, xml, key-value parse then query unstructured text, image, audio nlp/cv pipeline trade-off: flexibility ↑, query cost ↑, schema clarity ↓ decision table type schema query cost analytics example structured fixed low direct sql/bi sales table semi flexible medium parse then query json api response unstructured none high nlp / cv pipeline customer reviews rule structured is easiest but rigid. unstructured is richest but expensive to process. data structure types structure: match the pipeline to the data ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice query json like a sql table parse step skipped structured: direct sql or bi sales table, fixed schema expect sql on raw reviews needs an nlp pipeline semi: parse, then query json api response pick on flexibility alone query cost ignored unstructured: nlp or cv pipeline customer reviews result: failed queries, high cost result: right tool at right cost mistake unstructured is rich but expensive. best practice flexibility up, query cost up, schema clarity down. rule of thumb structured is easy but rigid. unstructured is rich, costly. three fixes to apply 1 use sql query structured tables directly. 2 parse first flatten semi-structured data before analysis. 3 budget effort plan nlp or cv for unstructured data.
m2-structured: definition data organized in rows and columns with a fixed schema. queried directly by sql. sql syntax -- structured table query select region, avg(order_value) as avg_order from sales where order_date >= '2024-01-01' group by region order by avg_order desc; schema example order_id customer_id region order_value order_date 1001 c-201 north 100 2024-01-15 1002 c-205 south 200 2024-01-16 1003 c-203 east 300 2024-01-16 visual rows & columns id name value 1 alice 100 2 bob 200 every row follows the same schema. strength easy to store, query, and validate. best for transactional data and bi dashboards. structured data structured data: rows, columns, fixed schema ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice skip schema validation rows that break the schema validate against the schema every row follows the same shape pull rows with no filter all dates, all regions where order_date >= '2024-01-01' filter in sql average without grouping one mean hides regions group by region, order by avg compare segments result: dirty rows, misleading averages result: easy, trusted bi queries mistake rigid schema needs checks. do not trust blindly. best practice best for transactional data and dashboards. rule of thumb select, filter, group, then order the result. three fixes to apply 1 validate check every row against the schema. 2 filter limit by date in the where clause. 3 group aggregate per segment with group by.
m2-semi: definition no rigid table schema, but contains tags or markers that separate elements. examples: json, xml, yaml, email headers. json syntax { "order_id" : 1001 , "customer" : { "name" : "alice" , "id" : "c-201" }, "items" : [ { "product" : "laptop" , "price" : 1200 }, { "product" : "mouse" , "price" : 25 } ], "total" : 1225 } parsing in python import json with open ( 'order.json' ) as f: data = json. load (f) # access nested fields customer_name = data[ 'customer' ][ 'name' ] items = data[ 'items' ] # flatten to table import pandas as pd df = pd. json_normalize (data, record_path= 'items' , meta=[ 'order_id' ]) visual — tree structure json as tree order customer items total laptop mouse watch out nested structures need flattening before tabular analysis. use json_normalize or equivalent. semi-structured data semi-structured: flatten before you analyze ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice load nested json as a table customer and items nested parse with json.load then access nested fields index fields by hand data['items'] breaks on change use json_normalize record_path='items', meta order_id ignore the order and items total counted once per order keep order_id as a link items tie back to the order result: errors and lost nested detail result: clean flat table, linked rows mistake nested structures resist tabular analysis. best practice use json_normalize or an equivalent. rule of thumb parse, flatten, then use tabular analysis. three fixes to apply 1 parse load json into python objects first. 2 flatten use json_normalize for nested items. 3 keep keys carry order_id into each item row.
m2-unstructured: definition no predefined schema. requires nlp, cv, or audio pipelines to extract features. examples & extraction # text — sentiment analysis from transformers import pipeline sentiment = pipeline ( "sentiment-analysis" ) sentiment( "the product arrived late but quality was great." ) # → [{'label': 'positive', 'score': 0.98}] # image — classification from transformers import pipeline classifier = pipeline ( "image-classification" ) classifier( "product.jpg" ) # audio — speech-to-text import whisper model = whisper. load_model ( "base" ) result = model. transcribe ( "call.wav" ) visual — pipelines unstructured → features text reviews, emails image photos, scans audio calls, recordings feature extraction turns unstructured into structured vectors. business value unstructured data holds rich signals (sentiment, intent, defects) not captured in tables. unstructured data unstructured: extract features first ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice query reviews with sql no schema to query use nlp, cv or audio pipelines extract features trust one sentiment score mixed review scored positive 0.98 check scores against examples late but great quality review ignore images and calls rich signals left unused turn files into structured vectors text, image, audio result: signals missed or misread result: sentiment, intent and defects mistake tables do not capture sentiment or defects. best practice feature extraction makes data usable. rule of thumb unstructured in, features out, then analyze. three fixes to apply 1 pick a pipeline match nlp, cv or speech to the file type. 2 spot check read samples against model scores. 3 structure it convert outputs into vectors or columns.
m2-scales-overview: overview four levels of measurement. each allows progressively more mathematical operations. progression nominal → ordinal → interval → ratio 1 nominal 2 ordinal 3 interval 4 ratio what operations are valid? scale order? equal gaps? true zero? valid stats nominal no no no mode, frequency ordinal yes no no median, mode, percentiles interval yes yes no mean, sd, correlation ratio yes yes yes all stats + ratios critical averaging nominal or ordinal data can produce meaningless numbers. always check the scale first. measurement scales scales: check before you calculate ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice average nominal codes mean of device ids nominal: mode and frequency count the categories average ordinal ranks gaps are not equal ordinal: median and percentiles order, not distance use ratios on interval data no true zero interval: mean, sd. ratio: all true zero allows ratios result: meaningless numbers result: valid statistics for each scale mistake wrong scale, wrong math. always check first. best practice each scale allows more operations than the last. rule of thumb order? equal gaps? true zero? then pick the stat. three fixes to apply 1 nominal use mode and frequency tables. 2 ordinal use median and percentiles. 3 interval / ratio mean and sd; ratios need true zero.
m2-nominal: definition categories with no order. labels or names only. examples colors: red, blue, green device: mobile, desktop, tablet region: north, south, east, west syntax # frequency table (valid) df[ 'device' ]. value_counts () # mode (valid) df[ 'device' ]. mode () # encoding for ml pd. get_dummies (df[ 'device' ]) visual device frequency mobile 6 desktop 3 tablet 1 invalid mean of device codes. "mobile" + "desktop" ÷ 2 makes no sense. nominal scale nominal: labels have no order or mean ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice mean of device codes mobile plus desktop divided by 2 df['device'].value_counts() frequency table treat codes 1,2,3 as quantities order that does not exist df['device'].mode() most common category skip the frequency table counts never shown pd.get_dummies(df['device']) encode for ml result: averages that mean nothing result: valid counts and encodings mistake codes are only names. do no math on them. best practice mobile 6, desktop 3, tablet 1. rule of thumb nominal: count it, never average it. three fixes to apply 1 count use value_counts for categories. 2 use the mode report the most common label. 3 one-hot encode use get_dummies for models.
m2-ordinal: definition categories with a meaningful order, but gaps between ranks are not necessarily equal. examples satisfaction: very unsatisfied → unsatisfied → neutral → satisfied → very satisfied education: high school → bachelor → master → phd priority: low → medium → high → critical syntax # ordinal encoding (preserves order) from sklearn.preprocessing import ordinalencoder enc = ordinalencoder (categories=[[ 'low' , 'medium' , 'high' , 'critical' ]]) df[ 'priority_encoded' ] = enc. fit_transform (df[[ 'priority' ]]) # median is valid df[ 'satisfaction_rank' ]. median () visual ordinal satisfaction very unsat unsat neutral sat very sat order exists, but gap between ranks is not equal. caution mean of ordinal data is technically invalid because gaps are unequal. use median or ordinal regression. ordinal scale ordinal: rank order, unequal gaps ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice mean of satisfaction ranks gaps are not equal report the median rank df['satisfaction_rank'].median() assume equal rank gaps neutral to sat equals sat to very sat percentiles or ordinal regression respect order only encode priority alphabetically high before low ordinalencoder with set order low, medium, high, critical result: technically invalid averages result: valid ordered comparisons mistake order exists but distance does not. best practice order preserved without pretending equal gaps. rule of thumb ordinal: median and mode, not mean. three fixes to apply 1 use median report the middle rank, not the mean. 2 use ordinal models use ordinal regression or percentiles. 3 set the order pass categories in order to the encoder.
m2-interval: definition ordered with equal gaps between values, but no true zero. ratios are not meaningful. examples temperature in celsius or fahrenheit (0 is arbitrary) iq scores calendar years customer satisfaction scores on a 1–10 scale (debatable) syntax # differences are valid temp_diff = df[ 'temp_day2' ] - df[ 'temp_day1' ] # mean and sd are valid df[ 'temperature' ]. mean (), df[ 'temperature' ]. std () # invalid: "20°c is twice as hot as 10°c" # 0°c is not absolute zero — it's the freezing point of water visual interval scale: equal gaps, no true zero 0°c 10°c 20°c 30°c equal gaps, but 0°c is not "no temperature". valid differences, mean, sd, correlation. invalid: ratios ("twice as hot"). interval scale interval: differences yes, ratios no ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice say 20c is twice as hot as 10c 0c is not zero heat use differences temp_day2 minus temp_day1 compute ratios of temperatures arbitrary zero point use mean, sd, correlation all valid on interval data treat calendar years as ratio zero year is arbitrary switch to kelvin for ratios true zero needed result: false ratio claims result: valid comparisons mistake equal gaps but no true zero. best practice say 10 degrees warmer, not twice as hot. rule of thumb interval: subtract, do not divide. three fixes to apply 1 subtract report differences between values. 2 use mean and sd both are valid on interval data. 3 need a true zero use kelvin or ratio data for ratios.
m2-ratio: definition ordered, equal gaps, and a true zero. ratios are meaningful. examples revenue, profit, cost height, weight, age number of orders, clicks, conversions kelvin temperature (true zero) syntax # all operations valid df[ 'revenue' ]. mean () df[ 'revenue' ]. std () df[ 'revenue' ] / df[ 'cost' ] # ratio valid # "revenue is 2x cost" is meaningful visual ratio scale: true zero, ratios valid $0 $100 $200 $300 $0 means no money. $200 is twice $100. most business metrics revenue, profit, clicks, orders are ratio scales — most statistical methods are valid. ratio scale ratio: true zero, ratios allowed ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice skip ratio metrics revenue and cost kept apart compute revenue / cost ratio is meaningful avoid ratio claims revenue is 2x cost is valid say $200 is twice $100 $0 means no money assume every metric is ratio scores may not be confirm a true zero first revenue, clicks, orders result: insights left on the table result: all statistics are valid mistake most business metrics allow every method. best practice mean, sd and ratios all work. test does zero mean none? then ratios are valid. three fixes to apply 1 use ratios divide revenue by cost. ratios are meaningful. 2 claim multiples say twice or half only with a true zero. 3 test zero ask whether 0 means none.
m2-temporal-overview: overview how a dataset relates to time. wrong choice → wrong analytical method. visual comparison three temporal shapes cross-sectional one snapshot time series same variable over time panel same entities over time quick reference type structure example cross-sectional one row per entity, one time point survey of 100 customers today time series one variable, many time points daily sales for 3 years panel many entities × many time points monthly revenue for 50 stores over 2 years method matters time series has autocorrelation — simple random sample assumptions break. temporal classification time shapes: pick the right method ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice treat time series as random sample autocorrelation ignored use time-aware methods for one variable over time call a one-day survey a trend cross-sectional snapshot only use a snapshot for comparisons 100 customers today ignore the store dimension panel data pooled blindly use panel methods 50 stores over 2 years result: wrong analytical method result: method fits the data shape mistake simple random sample assumptions break. best practice ask how the dataset relates to time. rule of thumb one time, one series, or many entities over time. three fixes to apply 1 spot autocorrelation do not assume independent observations. 2 snapshot not trend one time point shows no change. 3 use panel methods handle entity and time together.
m2-cross-sectional: definition data observed at a single point in time. one row per entity. example customer_id age income spend c-001 28 50k 1200 c-002 35 75k 2100 c-003 42 90k 1800 syntax # summary stats across entities df[[ 'age' , 'income' , 'spend' ]]. describe () # correlation at one time point df[[ 'income' , 'spend' ]]. corr () visual one snapshot — entity vs value a b c d each dot is one entity at the same point in time. typical methods descriptive stats, correlation, cross-sectional regression. cross-sectional data cross-sectional: one snapshot, no trend ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice claim growth from one snapshot no earlier time point describe the snapshot df.describe() across entities read correlation as causation income and spend only correlate at one time point income vs spend, carefully mix collection dates rows from different times keep one point in time one row per entity result: false trends and causes result: valid snapshot insights mistake snapshot cannot show change over time. best practice use descriptive stats and cross-sectional regression. rule of thumb one row per entity at one moment in time. three fixes to apply 1 describe summarize with describe() across entities. 2 correlate carefully report links, not causes. state limits. 3 one time point collect all rows at the same moment.
m2-time-series: definition a sequence of values for one variable at successive time points. example date sales visitors 2024-01-01 1000 5000 2024-01-02 1200 5500 2024-01-03 900 4800 syntax # set time index df[ 'date' ] = pd. to_datetime (df[ 'date' ]) df. set_index ( 'date' , inplace= true ) # rolling average df[ 'sales_7d' ] = df[ 'sales' ]. rolling ( 7 ). mean () # lag for autocorrelation df[ 'sales_lag1' ] = df[ 'sales' ]. shift ( 1 ) visual sales over time consecutive points are correlated (autocorrelation). key assumption time series data is not independent. standard tests assuming random sampling are invalid. time series data time series: values are not independent ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice run tests assuming random sampling autocorrelation ignored use time-aware methods lag and arima-type models leave date as plain text no time index pd.to_datetime, set_index real time index judge noisy daily sales 1000, 1200, 900 jump around smooth with rolling(7).mean() 7-day average result: invalid tests and conclusions result: valid, readable trends mistake consecutive points are correlated. best practice use shift(1) to check lag correlation. rule of thumb time series data is not independent. three fixes to apply 1 use time methods account for autocorrelation. 2 set a date index convert dates, then index by date. 3 smooth noise use a rolling average to see the trend.
m2-panel: definition multiple entities tracked over multiple time periods. combines cross-sectional and time series. example store_id month revenue visitors store-01 2024-01 50k 2000 store-01 2024-02 55k 2200 store-02 2024-01 80k 3500 store-02 2024-02 82k 3400 syntax # panel regression with entity fixed effects from linearmodels import panelols df_panel = df. set_index ([ 'store_id' , 'month' ]) model = panelols (df_panel[ 'revenue' ], df_panel[[ 'visitors' ]], entity_effects= true ) results = model. fit () visual multiple entities over time each line = one store; captures both entity and time variation. power panel data can control for unobserved entity-level differences (fixed effects). panel data panel data: track entities over time ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice pool all stores into one line entity differences lost index by store_id and month entity plus time ignore time and compare stores treated as cross-section use both dimensions cross-section and time series ignore hidden store traits unobserved differences add entity fixed effects panelols entity_effects=true result: mixed-up store and time effects result: controls for entity differences mistake store-01 and store-02 differ at baseline. best practice captures entity and time variation. rule of thumb many entities x many time points = panel. three fixes to apply 1 set a dual index index by store_id and month. 2 use both axes keep entity and time in the model. 3 add fixed effects control stable store differences.
m2-sources-overview: overview where data comes from affects quality, cost, and bias. two dimensions source classification primary you collect it secondary someone else collected it internal from within your org external from outside your org trade-offs type pros cons primary control over quality, fit for purpose expensive, time-consuming secondary fast, often cheap, large scale may not fit your question, unknown bias internal relevant, accessible, context-rich may be siloed, inconsistent definitions external benchmarks, market context coverage gaps, format issues data sources overview sources: know where data came from ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice treat secondary data as a fit may not fit your question weigh primary: control vs cost expensive, time-consuming assume internal data is consistent silos, different definitions check internal definitions relevant, context-rich skip bias checks on external data coverage gaps, format issues use external for benchmarks validate coverage and format result: hidden bias and poor fit result: sources matched to the question mistake source affects quality, cost and bias. best practice know who collected it and where it lives. rule of thumb ask who collected it and from where. three fixes to apply 1 weigh trade-offs compare cost, speed and fit. 2 check definitions align fields across internal silos. 3 validate external check coverage before use.
m2-primary: definition data collected first-hand for the specific question at hand. methods surveys — structured questionnaires experiments — a/b tests, clinical trials interviews — qualitative depth observations — user behavior tracking syntax — survey data in python # load survey responses import pandas as pd survey = pd. read_csv ( 'survey_responses.csv' ) # check response distribution survey[ 'satisfaction' ]. value_counts () # cross-tab: segment × satisfaction pd. crosstab (survey[ 'segment' ], survey[ 'satisfaction' ]) visual primary collection flow design collect clean analyze best for new questions, niche segments, experimental designs. primary data sources primary data: collect it for your question ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice start surveying without a design questions do not fit the goal design, then collect surveys, a/b tests, interviews skip the response distribution value_counts never checked check distributions survey['satisfaction'].value_counts() ignore segments no crosstab by segment cross-tab by segment pd.crosstab(segment, rating) result: costly data that fits poorly result: fit-for-purpose, clean data mistake expensive and slow to redo. best practice best for new questions and niche segments. rule of thumb design, collect, clean, then analyze. three fixes to apply 1 design first write the question before the survey. 2 check responses review the distribution of answers. 3 cross-tab compare answers across segments.
m2-secondary: definition data collected by someone else for a different purpose, reused for your analysis. examples government statistics (census, labor data) industry reports (gartner, forrester) public apis (weather, financial) research datasets (kaggle, uci) internal data warehouses syntax — api data import requests import pandas as pd # example: public economic data url = "https://api.example.com/gdp?country=us" response = requests. get (url) data = response. json () df = pd. dataframe (data) visual secondary reuse flow original different purpose your reuse new question analyze + caveats always ask who collected it, why, and what population does it represent? secondary data sources secondary data: ask who collected it and why ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice use public data without context different original purpose ask who collected it and why source, purpose, date assume it matches your population unknown bias check the population what group it represents pull from an api unchecked response.json() straight to table analyze with caveats document limits found result: conclusions on the wrong people result: reuse with eyes open mistake reused data carries hidden limits. best practice fast and cheap, if the fit is checked. always ask who collected it, why, and which population? three fixes to apply 1 ask who and why learn the original purpose. 2 check population confirm it covers your group. 3 add caveats state limits beside results.
m2-internal: definition data generated within your organization through normal operations. examples crm — customer records, interactions erp — orders, inventory, finance web logs — clicks, sessions, funnels support tickets — complaints, resolutions syntax — join internal tables -- join crm + orders select c.segment, avg(o.order_value) as avg_order from crm.customers c join sales.orders o using (customer_id) where o.order_date >= '2024-01-01' group by c.segment; visual internal data ecosystem crm orders web logs unified analytics warehouse best for operational insights, customer analytics, performance monitoring. internal data sources internal data: join silos with care ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice join crm and orders blindly keys and definitions differ join on customer_id using (customer_id) keep crm, orders, logs apart siloed views unify in a warehouse crm, orders, web logs trust inconsistent definitions same metric, different values align definitions first one meaning per metric result: duplicates, false spikes result: reliable operational insight mistake siloed data gives partial answers. best practice good for customer analytics and monitoring. rule of thumb join on a shared key after aligning definitions. three fixes to apply 1 join on keys use a shared id such as customer_id. 2 unify sources land crm, orders and logs in one place. 3 align definitions agree one meaning per metric.
m2-external: definition data from outside your organization — government, vendors, public datasets. examples government: census, economic indicators market research: industry trends web scraping: competitor prices, reviews apis: weather, social media syntax — web scraping import requests from bs4 import beautifulsoup import pandas as pd # scrape competitor prices (example) response = requests. get ( "https://competitor.com/products" ) soup = beautifulsoup (response.text, 'html.parser' ) products = soup. find_all ( 'div' , class_= 'product' ) visual external data integration gov data apis scraping reports merge with internal data watch out coverage gaps, different definitions, and terms of service. always validate before merging. external data sources external data: validate before you merge ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice scrape competitor pages blindly terms of service ignored check terms of service first scraping, apis, vendors merge straight into internal data definitions do not match map definitions before merging gov data, reports, apis assume coverage is complete gaps in region or period test coverage and format validate, then merge result: legal risk, bad merges result: trusted benchmarks and context mistake format and definition gaps skew results. best practice always validate before merging. rule of thumb check terms, check coverage, then merge. three fixes to apply 1 check terms read terms of service before scraping. 2 map definitions match fields before you merge. 3 test coverage look for gaps and format issues.
m2-summary-table: key checks data classification summary ✓ read the row find the type, then its tools. ✓ heed watch-outs each type has one key caution. ✓ match tools use the tools listed for the type. dimension type tells tools watch out structure structured rows & columns sql, pandas rigid schema semi tags / keys json parser nesting, flatten unstructured no schema nlp, cv expensive processing measurement nominal categories mode, frequency don't average ordinal ordered categories median, percentiles unequal gaps interval equal gaps, no zero mean, sd no ratios ratio equal gaps + zero all stats none temporal cross-sectional one snapshot descriptive, corr no time dynamics time series one variable, many times rolling, arima autocorrelation panel many entities × times fixed effects complex models source primary you collect it surveys, experiments cost, time secondary already collected apis, datasets fit, bias rule classify first. the type dictates what operations are valid. classification summary classification summary: match tool to type ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice mean on nominal categories do not average nominal: mode and frequency count the categories mean on ordinal ranks gaps are unequal ordinal: median and percentiles respect unequal gaps standard tests on time series autocorrelation breaks them time series: rolling, arima panel: fixed effects result: wrong tools, wrong answers result: the right tool per type mistake ratios on interval data fail too. best practice pair each type with its watch-out. rule of thumb classify first. the type dictates valid operations. three fixes to apply 1 read the row find the type, then its tools. 2 heed watch-outs each type has one key caution. 3 match tools use the tools listed for the type.
m2-checklist: use in every new dataset 5 steps to classify correctly. step-by-step # 1. structure # can sql query it directly? → structured # does it have tags/keys? → semi # is it raw text/image/audio? → unstructured # 2. measurement # categories with no order? → nominal # ordered categories? → ordinal # equal gaps, no true zero? → interval # equal gaps + true zero? → ratio # 3. temporal # one snapshot? → cross-sectional # one variable over time? → time series # many entities over time? → panel # 4. source # you collected it? → primary # someone else collected it? → secondary # 5. validate # check assumptions before analysis checklist flow 1 structure 2 scales 3 temporal 4 source 5 validate most common error skipping step 2 → averaging ordinal data or treating nominal codes as numbers. classification checklist classification checklist: do step 2 ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice skip the measurement step scale never identified run five steps on every dataset structure, scale, time, source, validate treat nominal codes as numbers average region codes ask: category, order, gaps, zero nominal to ratio jump to analysis assumptions never validated validate assumptions first check before you analyze result: averaging ordinal data result: correct classification each time mistake the most common error in new datasets. best practice structure, scales, temporal, source, validate. rule of thumb five steps, every new dataset, no skipping. three fixes to apply 1 run all 5 steps never skip the scale step. 2 ask the scale categories, order, gaps, zero. 3 validate check assumptions before you analyze.
m3-overview: purpose spreadsheets are the most widely used analytics tool in business. this module turns them from a notepad into a repeatable analysis workflow. the four-step workflow clean → calculate → summarize → visualize 1 1 · clean trim · value · power query 2 2 · calculate if · sumifs · xlookup 3 3 · summarize pivottable · stats 4 4 · visualize charts · formatting golden rules one row per record, one column per field , with a single header row (tidy data). keep raw data on its own sheet ; never overwrite it. build everything else with formulas. use tables / named ranges so formulas grow with the data. put assumptions in labeled cells , not buried in formulas. excel vs sheets core formulas are shared. excel adds power query and power pivot; sheets adds query, arrayformula, importrange, and easy sharing.
m3-shortcuts: key checks speed shortcuts ✓ jump fast ctrl + arrow to reach the edge of your data. ✓ paste values ctrl + shift + v keeps numbers stable. ✓ f4 locks press f4 to cycle the $ reference types. why keyboard-first analysts finish the same work in half the time. windows / mac shown. action windows mac jump to edge of data ctrl + arrow ⌘ + arrow select whole region ctrl + shift + arrow ⌘ + ⇧ + arrow select current region ctrl + a ⌘ + a toggle $ reference f4 ⌘ + t fill down / right ctrl + d / r ⌘ + d / r insert table ctrl + t ⌘ + t auto-sum alt + = ⌘ + ⇧ + t paste values only ctrl + shift + v ⌘ + ⇧ + v find / replace ctrl + f / h ⌘ + f / ⌘ + ⇧ + h show formulas ctrl + ` ⌘ + ` habit always paste values when copying results out of formulas so they do not break when the source moves. speed shortcuts shortcuts: paste values, not formulas ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice mouse-drag to select a region slow on long columns ctrl + shift + arrow selects the region in one keystroke plain paste of formula results links break if the source moves ctrl + shift + v values only frozen results survive moves retype totals by hand skips alt + = auto-sum alt + = for total one key sums the block result: slow work, broken links result: half the time, stable data mistake hours lost to scrolling and fragile pasted cells. best practice keyboard first, paste values when copying results out. habit copy results out of formulas as values, not as links. three fixes to apply 1 jump fast ctrl + arrow to reach the edge of your data. 2 paste values ctrl + shift + v keeps numbers stable. 3 f4 locks press f4 to cycle the $ reference types.
m3-refs: definition a reference tells a formula where to look. the $ sign locks the row or column when you copy the formula. type looks like when copied… relative a2 both row and column shift absolute $a$2 never moves (rates, targets) mixed $a2 or a$2 locks column or row only structured sales[amount] grows with the table syntax — commission using a locked rate ' rate lives in f1. lock it so copying down keeps pointing at f1 =b2 * $f$1 ' multiplication table: lock column of row-heads and row of col-heads = $a2 * b$1 what happens when you drag down without $ with $f$1 row 2: =b2*f1 ✓ row 3: =b3*f2 ✗ (f2 empty) row 4: =b4*f3 ✗ row 2: =b2*$f$1 ✓ row 3: =b3*$f$1 ✓ row 4: =b4*$f$1 ✓ press f4 while editing to cycle through the four reference types. most common bug forgetting to lock the lookup range or the rate cell. if results look right in row 2 but wrong below it, check the $ signs first. cell references references: forgetting to lock the $ ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice =b3*f2 after dragging down rate cell f1 slid to f2, f3 =b2*$f$1 absolute lock on the rate cell rate typed into every formula hard-coded 0.08 in many cells rate lives in one cell f1 change it once, all update times table, nothing locked =a2*b1 shifts both ways =$a2*b$1 mixed refs lock row heads and col heads result: right in row 2, wrong below result: every row points correctly mistake only the first row is correct; the rest drift. best practice press f4 while editing to cycle the four types. test: drag it row 2 right but row 3 wrong? check the $ signs first. three fixes to apply 1 use f4 cycles relative, absolute and mixed references. 2 lock the rate $f$1 never moves when you copy down. 3 use tables sales[amount] grows with the table.
