m3-logic: goal create labels, flags, and tiers automatically from rules. syntax ' simple flag = if (d2>= 1000 , "large" , "standard" ) ' several conditions at once = if ( and (d2>= 1000 , e2= "north" ), "priority" , "normal" ) = if ( or (f2= "refund" , f2= "chargeback" ), "review" , "ok" ) ' tiers — ifs reads top to bottom, first true wins = ifs (d2>= 5000 , "gold" , d2>= 1000 , "silver" , true , "bronze" ) ifs tier logic order value ≥ 5,000 → gold ≥ 1,000 → silver otherwise → bronze order matters: put the strictest rule first. watch out always end ifs with true, "default" , otherwise unmatched rows return #n/a. if / ifs / and / or ifs: tier order and the missing default ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice ifs with silver rule first d2>=1000 catches 5000 as silver strictest rule first d2>=5000 gold, then silver no true default at the end unmatched rows return #n/a end with true, bronze every row gets a label nested ifs for every combo hard to read and audit and / or inside if if(and(d2>=1000,e2=north)) result: wrong tiers and #n/a rows result: every row tiered correctly mistake order decides which rule wins, first true only. best practice strictest first, always end with a true default. rule of thumb ifs reads top to bottom; first true wins. three fixes to apply 1 order rules put the strictest test at the top. 2 add default finish with true and a default label. 3 combine tests use and / or instead of deep nesting.
m3-sumifs: key checks sumifs / countifs / averageifs ✓ match sizes all ranges must be the same size. ✓ use operators >1000 or >= with cell references and &. ✓ pick the tool sumifs fixed layout; pivot for exploring. goal total, count, or average only the rows that meet your conditions. faster than filtering by hand and always up to date. syntax (sum range first, then pairs of range + criteria) = sumifs (sales[amount], sales[region], "north" , sales[month], "jan" ) = countifs (sales[region], "north" , sales[amount], ">1000" ) = averageifs (sales[amount], sales[segment], "smb" ) ' criteria from cells and operators = sumifs (sales[amount], sales[date], ">=" & h1, sales[date], "<=" & h2) example result region jan sales orders > 1,000 avg order north 2,020 1 505 east 1,180 1 394 south 990 0 330 sumifs vs pivot use sumifs inside dashboards and templates (fixed layout). use a pivottable for exploration (flexible layout). gotcha all ranges must be the same size, and text criteria are not case sensitive. wildcards work: "n*" . sumifs / countifs sumifs: ranges that do not line up ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice ranges of different sizes d:d with b2:b100 breaks the pair same-size ranges, or table refs sales[amount], sales[region] filter by hand, then add up stale the moment data changes =sumifs(...,region,east) always up to date wrong argument order sum range must come first sum range first, then pairs range + criteria, repeated result: errors or stale totals result: live, correct conditional totals mistake mismatched ranges give errors or wrong sums. best practice use sumifs in dashboards, a pivottable to explore. syntax check sum range first, then pairs of range + criteria. three fixes to apply 1 match sizes all ranges must be the same size. 2 use operators >1000 or >= with cell references and &. 3 pick the tool sumifs fixed layout; pivot for exploring.
m3-text: key checks text functions ✓ trim first removes extra spaces that break matches. ✓ split codes left, mid or textsplit to pull parts. ✓ standardize proper or lower for one consistent case. goal split, join, and standardize text so it can be grouped and matched. need formula result first 3 chars =left(a2,3) "c-2" from "c-201" middle chars =mid(a2,3,3) "201" split by delimiter =textsplit(a2,"-") / sheets =split(a2,"-") "c" | "201" replace =substitute(a2,"-","") "c201" join with separator =textjoin(", ",true,a2:c2) "ann, ny, gold" standardize case =proper(trim(a2)) "alice wong" find position =search("@",a2) 6 email domain =mid(a2,search("@",a2)+1,99) "acme.com" tip wrap in trim() first. hidden spaces are the number-one reason lookups return #n/a. text functions text: hidden spaces break lookups ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice lookup on untrimmed text alice wong with a trailing space wrap in trim() first =proper(trim(a2)) retype names by hand kim, ana to ana kim left / mid / textjoin split the code, rebuild the name mixed case left as is groups split by capitalization proper or lower everywhere one case so groups collapse result: #n/a and split groups result: clean keys that match mistake hidden spaces are the top cause of #n/a lookups. best practice trim, then split or join, then standardize case. tip wrap in trim() before any lookup or match. three fixes to apply 1 trim first removes extra spaces that break matches. 2 split codes left, mid or textsplit to pull parts. 3 standardize proper or lower for one consistent case.
m3-dates: key idea dates are numbers (days since 1900 in excel). that is why you can subtract them. if a date is left-aligned, it is text and must be converted first. need formula year / month / weekday =year(a2) · =month(a2) · =weekday(a2,2) month start / end =eomonth(a2,-1)+1 · =eomonth(a2,0) month label for grouping =text(a2,"yyyy-mm") days between =b2-a2 · =datedif(a2,b2,"d") working days =networkdays(a2,b2,holidays) add months =edate(a2,3) quarter ="q"&roundup(month(a2)/3,0) date → grouping keys 2024-03-22 2024-03 q1 friday create helper columns once, then pivot by month or quarter. date functions dates: text that looks like a date ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice left-aligned date left as text subtraction and sorting fail convert text to real dates dates are numbers, so b2-a2 works group by typing months manual labels drift helper column text(a2,yyyy-mm) pivot by month or quarter count calendar days for work includes weekends and holidays networkdays(a2,b2,holidays) working days only result: wrong gaps, messy grouping result: reliable durations and groups mistake if it is left-aligned it is text, not a date. best practice convert once, add helper columns, then pivot. key idea dates are numbers; text must be converted first. three fixes to apply 1 check alignment left-aligned means text, convert it. 2 add helpers month, quarter, weekday keys once. 3 use eomonth eomonth finds month start and end.
m3-dynamic: definition one formula returns many cells that "spill" into neighbors and resize automatically. available in excel 365 and google sheets. syntax ' rows that match = filter (sales[[orderid]:[amount]], sales[region]= "north" , "none" ) ' distinct list for a dropdown or summary = unique (sales[region]) ' sort descending by amount = sort (sales[amount], 1 , - 1 ) ' top 5 orders — combine them = take ( sortby (sales, sales[amount], - 1 ), 5 ) ' live summary table: region list + totals beside it = sumifs (sales[amount], sales[region], f2# ) spill range =unique(...) east south type one formula → results spill down automatically add new region → list grows #spill! means something is blocking the spill area. clear the cells below the formula. dynamic arrays spill: blocked cells and hand lists ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice data typed under a formula spill area blocked: #spill! clear cells below the formula spill range must be empty region list typed by hand new region never appears =unique(sales[region]) list grows with new regions copy a formula per row one formula could spill filter, sort, take together take(sortby(...),5) top 5 result: #spill! and stale lists result: self-resizing live results mistake something in the spill range stops the result. best practice one formula, many cells, resizing automatically. remember reference a spill with f2# so totals follow the list. three fixes to apply 1 clear spill empty the cells below the formula. 2 use unique drives dropdowns and summaries. 3 reference f2# sumifs beside a spilled list.

m3-condfmt: goal let color do the scanning: spot duplicates, outliers, overdue items, and patterns instantly. visual — heatmap of monthly sales color scale (low → high) east north south jan feb mar 1,180 1,510 1,720 2,020 1,450 1,600 990 2,360 1,300 darker = higher. south jumped in feb; north peaked in jan. useful rules use rule highlight duplicates built-in "duplicate values" or formula =countif($a:$a,$a2)>1 overdue =and($c2<today(), $d2<>"done") outliers =abs(b2-average(b:b))>3*stdev.s(b:b) whole row by status apply to $a$2:$h$500 with =$f2="at risk" accessibility do not rely on red vs green only. add icons, bold, or text labels. conditional formatting color rules: red vs green only ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice red and green as the only signal colour-blind readers miss it add icons, bold or text labels do not rely on color rule on one cell only row status not highlighted whole row by status $a$2:$h$500 with =$f2=at risk eyeball duplicates and outliers missed in a long column countif($a:$a,$a2)>1 rule duplicates light up instantly result: hidden signals, poor access result: patterns spotted at a glance mistake color alone is not an accessible signal. best practice let color scan for you, with a text backup. accessibility never rely on red vs green alone; add a label. three fixes to apply 1 color scale darker means higher for heatmaps. 2 row rules anchor the column: $f2 across the row. 3 add labels icons or bold support color.
m3-powerquery: definition a recorded, repeatable cleaning pipeline. build the steps once; click refresh when new data arrives. where data → get data → from file / database / web , then edit in the power query editor. applied steps pipeline 1 source 2 promote headers 3 change types 4 trim & remove dupes 5 merge 6 load common transforms unpivot columns : turn jan, feb, mar columns into month + value rows. split column by delimiter · fill down for merged-cell exports. merge queries : a no-formula lookup (join) between two tables. append queries : stack monthly files into one table. why it matters repeatability. a recorded pipeline is auditable and saves you re-cleaning the same export every month. power query power query: re-cleaning by hand every month ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice manually clean each export extra header row, text dates recorded applied steps click refresh for new data paste months below each other layout changes break it append queries stack monthly files in one table vlookup chains between tables heavy and hard to audit merge queries no-formula lookup (join) result: slow, error-prone, unrepeatable result: repeatable, auditable pipeline mistake same cleaning redone every single month. best practice build the steps once, refresh when data arrives. why it matters repeatability: a recorded pipeline is auditable. three fixes to apply 1 record steps promote headers, change types, trim. 2 append files stack sales_jan, feb, mar together. 3 unpivot turn month columns into rows.
m3-charts: rule start with the question, then pick the chart. one message per chart. question → chart trend over time line compare categories bar / column relationship scatter distribution histogram / box part-to-whole with ≤ 5 slices → stacked bar (avoid 3-d and busy pies). always: clear title with the takeaway · labeled axes · start bars at zero. quick checklist title states the insight: "south overtook north in feb", not "sales by region". remove gridlines, legends, and decoration that do not help. sort bars by value unless there is a natural order (months). highlight one series in color; mute the rest in gray. choosing a chart charts: pick the chart after the question ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice busy 3-d pie with many slices hard to compare shares line for trend, bar to compare match chart to question title says sales by region names the data, not the insight title: south overtook north in feb the takeaway is the title unsorted bars, bars not from zero misleading, hard to rank sort by value, start at zero highlight one series in color result: unclear, misleading chart result: one clear message per chart mistake decoration hides the one message. best practice question first, then chart, one message each. rule start with the question, then pick the chart. three fixes to apply 1 match chart trend line, compare bar, relationship scatter. 2 title insight state the takeaway, not the data. 3 cut clutter remove gridlines and extra legends.

m3-gs-import: key checks importrange & live data ✓ raw tab import once, reference the tab. ✓ check access allow access once, only for approved sheets. ✓ filter it wrap with query to pull needed columns. goal pull data from other sheets, csvs, or web tables so reports refresh themselves. m3-recap: module flow 1 clean 2 formulas 3 pivot 4 charts 5 audit the five lines clean first : trim, convert types, standardize dates and labels. lock references and keep assumptions in labeled cells. lookups + conditional totals (xlookup, sumifs) beat manual copy-paste. pivottables explore; formulas power repeatable dashboards. one message per chart , with a takeaway title. before you send any workbook totals tie back to the raw data (spot-check 3 numbers). no hard-coded numbers inside formulas. no error values; blanks handled on purpose. sheet names, units, and date ranges are labeled. a short "notes" tab explains sources and definitions. next module module 5 builds on this by moving from spreadsheets to larger analysis tools.

m4-central: definition a single value that represents the "typical" data point. when to use it use it when summarizing a typical value for a numeric column. pick by data shape: mean for symmetric data, median for skewed data, mode for categories. avoid or switch when you report one number alone: it hides the spread. pair it with sd or iqr. business example reporting the typical order value in a monthly review. three measures at a glance one outlier drags the mean past the median 100 200 300 400 1000 median 300 mean 400 1000 pulls the mean up no mode every value appears once syntax — python import pandas as pd s = pd. series ([ 100 , 200 , 300 , 400 , 1000 ]) s. mean () # 400.0 s. median () # 300.0 s. mode () # all values appear once here which to pick measure best for watch out mean symmetric data outliers median skewed data ignores extremes mode categories multiple modes central tendency center: mean on skewed data ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice mean of 100,200,300,400,1000 400 is above 4 of 5 values median on skewed data 300 is the typical order mean for category data device has no average mode for categories most frequent device report center alone spread not shown show mean and median gap signals skew result: center that is not typical result: a center that fits the data mistake the 1000 outlier pulls the mean away from typical. best practice pick the measure that fits the data shape. which to pick mean symmetric; median skewed; mode categories. three fixes to apply 1 symmetric use the mean when there are no outliers. 2 skewed use the median for skewed values. 3 categories use the mode for most common.
m4-mean: definition mean = sum of values ÷ number of values. when to use it use it when the data is numeric, roughly symmetric and free of extreme outliers, or when totals matter (mean x count = total). avoid or switch when the data is skewed or has outliers (use the median), or the values are categories. business example average daily sales used to forecast a month's revenue. formula x̄ = (x₁ + x₂ + ... + xₙ) / n live example worked order values: 100, 200, 300, 400, 1000 mean = (100+200+300+400+1000) / 5 = 2000 / 5 = 400 see it svg chart 100 200 300 400 1000 mean 400 median 300 outlier drags mean up # ascii chart ████ 100 ████████ 200 ████████████ 300 ████████████████ 400 ████████████████████████ 1000 ← outlier mean = 400 (pulled up by the outlier) beware the 1000 outlier inflates the mean — it's higher than 4 of the 5 values. always check the median. mean mean: the outlier inflates the average ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice report mean 400 as typical higher than 4 of 5 values compare to median 300 gap exposes the outlier skip the median check outlier goes unnoticed always check the median before trusting the mean quote aov as one number hides the 1000 order show mean and median together typical customer is clearer result: overstated typical spend result: honest average mistake 2000 / 5 = 400, but most orders are 300 or less. best practice mean = sum / n, then test it against the median. formula mean = sum of values / n check median alongside. three fixes to apply 1 see the tail plot values to spot the outlier. 2 compare mean 400 vs median 300 shows a pull. 3 report both give typical spend as well.
m4-median: definition the middle value after sorting. 50th percentile. when to use it use it when the data is skewed or has outliers, such as salaries, prices or response times. avoid or switch when you need totals: median x count does not equal the sum. business example the typical salary in a department that includes one executive. live example — same values worked sorted: 100, 200, 300 , 400, 1000 median = 300 (middle of 5 values) mean = 400, median = 300 → outlier raised the mean. visual — mean vs median outlier shifts mean, not median 100 200 300 400 1000 median 300 mean 400 syntax # python df[ 'order_value' ]. median () # sql select percentile_cont( 0.5 ) within group (order by order_value) from sales; business framing typical customer spends ~300, not 400. when reporting aov, show the median too. median median: report typical, not inflated ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice aov reported as the mean 400 vip order lifts it sort, then take the middle 100,200,300,400,1000 gives 300 median ignored typical spend ~300 hidden show median with aov typical customer ~300 unsorted values wrong middle picked median() or percentile_cont(0.5) pandas and sql result: aov overstated result: typical value reported mistake mean 400 vs median 300: outlier raised the mean. best practice median resists the outlier; the mean does not. business framing typical customer spends ~300, not 400. three fixes to apply 1 sort first middle of the ordered values. 2 add to aov report median next to the mean. 3 use sql percentile_cont(0.5) in sql.
m4-mode: definition most frequent value. great for categories. when to use it use it when the data is categorical or discrete and you want the most common value. avoid or switch when the data is continuous with few repeats, or has several peaks that one mode would hide. business example the most common shirt size, to decide what to stock. live example — device # 10 orders — device column mobile, mobile, desktop, mobile, tablet, desktop, mobile, mobile, desktop, mobile # counts mobile: ██████ 6 desktop: ███ 3 tablet: █ 1 mode = mobile see it device frequency 6 mobile 3 desktop 1 tablet mode syntax # python df[ 'device' ]. mode () # or counts (more informative) df[ 'device' ]. value_counts () next step most orders come from mobile users. check if mobile also has lower conversion or higher return rate. mode mode: a count says more than one winner ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice mode on a numeric column rarely repeats exactly value_counts() for categories mobile 6, desktop 3, tablet 1 report only mobile 6 of 10, ignores the rest show the full counts shares of each device stop at the mode no follow-up question ask the next question does mobile convert less? result: thin view of categories result: mode with context mistake a single label hides the distribution. best practice mode names the leader, counts tell the story. next step after the mode, compare its conversion or returns. three fixes to apply 1 use counts value_counts gives more detail. 2 categories mode fits labels, not measurements. 3 follow up compare the top group on outcomes.
m4-range: definition range = max − min. when to use it use it when a quick check of the minimum and maximum, for example to spot impossible values during data validation. avoid or switch when outliers are present, because one extreme value sets the range. use iqr or sd instead. business example checking that ages in a customer file run from 18 to 95, not 0 to 999. live example worked delivery times: 20, 22, 25, 30, 120 (minutes) range = 120 − 20 = 100 # delivery times ██ 20 ██ 22 ███ 25 ███ 30 ████████████████████ 120 ← outlier range = 100 min — inflated by outlier range is unstable 20 25 30 120 range = 100 typical spread ≈ 10 syntax max(x) - min(x) not stable range is sensitive to a single outlier. pair it with iqr or standard deviation. range range: one outlier sets the spread ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice delivery range 120 - 20 = 100 outlier 120 sets it alone pair range with iqr or sd spread of the middle 50% range as the only spread typical spread is about 10 use range as a sanity check min to max at a glance compare ranges across days one bad trip dominates check the outlier itself is 120 an incident? result: spread looks far too wide result: realistic view of spread mistake range is not stable; one value controls it. best practice range for a quick look, iqr or sd for truth. not stable range = max - min and is sensitive to one outlier. three fixes to apply 1 pair it show iqr or sd beside the range. 2 look at max investigate the extreme value. 3 quick check use range only to sanity check.
m4-stddev: definition standard deviation = √variance. spread in the same units as the data. when to use it use it when comparing variability between numeric groups on the same scale, or as an input to z-scores and confidence intervals. avoid or switch when the data is heavily skewed (use iqr), or the groups use different units or scales (use the coefficient of variation). business example which delivery route has the more consistent delivery times. formula sd = √[ σ(xᵢ − x̄)² / (n − 1) ] # small sd → consistent # large sd → variable live examples # all identical → sd = 0 10, 10, 10, 10, 10 mean = 10, sd = 0 → perfect consistency # some variation → sd > 0 8, 10, 12, 10, 10 mean = 10, sd ≈ 1.41 → some noise see it — same mean, different sd two processes with mean = 10 process a — consistent process b — inconsistent (same average) syntax # python (sample sd, ddof=1 default) df[ 'order_value' ]. std () # sql select stddev_samp(order_value) from sales; use it in dashboards track mean and sd together. "average improving but variability worsening" is a real risk signal. standard deviation sd: same mean, very different process ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice track only the average mean 10 for both a and b track mean and sd together sd = 0 means identical values population sd on a sample divides by n, not n-1 sample sd with n - 1 df.std() or stddev_samp ignore sd of 0 versus 1.41 consistency never reviewed read sd in data units sd 1.41 on mean 10 result: variability goes unseen result: risk signals caught early mistake average improving while variability worsens. best practice mean tells the level, sd tells the stability. formula sd = sqrt(sum sq / (n-1)) same units as data. three fixes to apply 1 pair them dashboard mean and sd together. 2 use n - 1 sample sd is the default in pandas. 3 compare sd smaller means more consistent.
m4-iqr: definition iqr = q3 − q1 (middle 50% spread). outlier rule: < q1−1.5·iqr or > q3+1.5·iqr. when to use it use it when the data is skewed, you want a resistant measure of spread, or you want to flag outliers with the 1.5 x iqr rule and compare groups with boxplots. avoid or switch when the sample is very small, because quartiles are unstable. business example comparing order values across regions with side-by-side boxplots. see it — boxplot boxplot of order values iqr = 200 min 100 q1 200 median 300 q3 400 1000 upper fence 700 outlier live example worked sorted: 100, 200, 300, 400, 1000 q1 ≈ 200, q3 ≈ 400 → iqr ≈ 200 upper fence ≈ 400 + 1.5×200 = 700 → 1000 is an outlier ascii boxplot ┌──────┐ ├─────┤ │ ├─────┤ ● └──────┘ 100 200 300 400 1000 min q1 med q3 max outlier iqr = q3 − q1 = 400 − 200 = 200 syntax # python q1, q3 = df[ 'order_value' ]. quantile ([ 0.25 , 0.75 ]) iqr = q3 - q1 outliers = df[(df.order_value < q1 - 1.5*iqr) | (df.order_value > q3 + 1.5*iqr)] business action separate vip orders from typical ones so the average doesn't mislead. iqr and boxplot iqr: spot outliers with fences ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice eyeball the 1000 order no rule, subjective call fence q3 + 1.5 x iqr 400 + 300 = 700, so 1000 flagged mean of all orders vip lifts the average separate vip from typical report each segment delete outliers silently information lost q1 = 200, q3 = 400, iqr = 200 middle 50 percent spread result: distorted averages result: clear, defensible outliers mistake outliers mix with typical orders. best practice flag with a rule, then segment, not delete. outlier rule below q1-1.5*iqr or above q3+1.5*iqr. three fixes to apply 1 compute iqr q3 minus q1 using quantile(). 2 set fences 1.5 x iqr beyond each quartile. 3 segment separate vip orders from typical.
m4-percentiles: definition the value below which x% of data falls. p50 = median. when to use it use it when setting thresholds and service levels, ranking, or answering how the slowest or highest 10% behave. avoid or switch when the sample is tiny, because extreme percentiles are unreliable. business example a target that 95% of support tickets are answered within a set time (p95). see it — sla at p90 delivery time distribution p50 = 30 min p90 = 45 min p99 = 70 min syntax # python — common percentiles df[ 'delivery_min' ]. quantile ([ 0.5 , 0.9 , 0.99 ]) # sql select percentile_cont( 0.9 ) within group (order by delivery_min) from orders; why it matters mean = 40 but p90 = 70 → customers still experience late orders. set slas around p90, not the mean. percentiles percentiles: sla on the mean hides late orders ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice sla set on mean 40 min many orders are later set the sla around p90 covers 9 of 10 orders report p50 only median misses the tail track p50, p90 and p99 30, 45, 70 min in the example ignore p99 of 70 min worst waits never seen quantile([0.5,0.9,0.99]) or percentile_cont in sql result: customers still get late orders result: slas customers actually feel mistake mean 40 but p90 70: the tail is hidden. best practice percentiles show position, not just the average. why it matters p50 = median; p90 and p99 expose the long tail. three fixes to apply 1 use p90 anchor slas to p90, not the mean. 2 report several p50, p90 and p99 together. 3 code it quantile() in python or sql.
m4-skewness: definition asymmetry of a distribution. right-skew = long tail right. left-skew = long tail left. when to use it use it when deciding between mean and median, whether to transform a variable (for example log), and whether a normal-based test is reasonable. avoid or switch when the sample is small, because skewness estimates are noisy. look at a histogram too. business example revenue per customer is right-skewed, so report the median or use a log scale. see it right-skewed order values (typical) mode median mean long right tail (vips) mode < median < mean → report the median most customers small, few customers huge. mean gets pulled to the right. live example worked most customers spend 100–500. a few spend 10,000+. mean pulled up by vip spenders. median stays near typical customer spend. syntax # python — skewness coefficient from scipy.stats import skew skew (df[ 'order_value' ]) # > 0 → right-skewed (typical for order values) # ~ 0 → symmetric # < 0 → left-skewed when mean lies right-skewed data: report median. segment vips separately instead of letting them distort the typical customer view. mistake vs best practice: skewness skew: the mean lies on long tails ✗ common mistake ✗ mean reported for order value vips spending 10,000+ pull it ✗ skew coefficient never checked shape assumed symmetric ✗ vips mixed into typical view distorts the main customer result: mean misstates typical spend ✓ best practice ✓ report the median stays near typical spend ✓ scipy skew(): above 0 is right check shape numerically ✓ segment vips separately typical view stays clean result: a truthful typical customer mistake: mode < median < mean on right-skewed data. when mean lies right skew: median, with vips segmented out. best practice: right-skewed: report the median. three fixes to apply 1 check skew skew() above 0 means right tail. 2 use median resists the long right tail. 3 split vips report them as their own segment.
m4-kurtosis: definition tail heaviness — how prone the distribution is to extreme values. when to use it use it when checking for heavy tails and extreme events that raise risk. avoid or switch when you read it alone or with a small sample. confirm with a histogram or boxplot. business example daily transaction spikes that a normal model would under-predict. see it — normal vs fat tails kurtosis comparison fatter tail fatter tail normal (kurtosis 0) high kurtosis (rare big spikes) high kurtosis → more "rare big spikes" than the normal curve predicts. live example worked product returns show rare massive spikes during supplier or shipping issues. average return rate looks stable while spikes disrupt operations. syntax # python — excess kurtosis (normal = 0) from scipy.stats import kurtosis kurtosis (df[ 'returns' ]) # > 0 → fat tails, more outliers than normal # < 0 → thin tails, fewer extremes business action high kurtosis signals need for incident response planning — use percentile thresholds and monitoring alerts. mistake vs best practice: kurtosis kurtosis: stable average, rare spikes ✗ common mistake ✗ watch only average return rate looks stable ✗ assume a normal curve underpredicts rare extremes ✗ no plan for spikes supplier issues hit unprepared result: surprised by big spikes ✓ best practice ✓ kurtosis() above 0 means fat tails more outliers than normal ✓ use percentile thresholds high percentiles catch spikes ✓ monitoring alerts, incident plan prepare for the rare event result: ready for extreme events mistake: average hides rare, massive events. reading excess kurtosis: above 0 is fat tails, normal = 0. best practice: high kurtosis calls for incident response. three fixes to apply 1 measure it kurtosis() in scipy, normal is 0. 2 use percentiles set thresholds on the tail. 3 alert monitor and plan for the spikes.
m4-histogram: purpose visualize distribution shape — spot skew, modes, and outliers at a glance. when to use it use it when a first look at one numeric variable: shape, peaks, spread and outliers. avoid or switch when the bins are too few or too many, or you need to compare groups (use boxplots or overlaid densities). business example seeing whether customer ages have one peak or two before choosing a statistic. three shapes side by side normal · right-skew · bimodal normal right-skew bimodal ascii reading # normal-ish ▁▄█▄▁ most values near center # right-skewed (order values) ███▆▄▂▁ many small, few large # bimodal (two customer groups) ▆█▂▂█▆ two peaks → likely two segments syntax # python df[ 'order_value' ]. hist (bins= 30 ) # or seaborn for nicer defaults import seaborn as sns sns. histplot (df, x= 'order_value' , bins= 30 ) histogram reading histogram: shape before summary ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice report one mean for bimodal data two peaks, two segments two peaks mean two groups split customers, then analyze default bin count shape washed out or noisy hist(bins=30) or histplot choose bins deliberately skip the plot entirely skew and outliers missed plot first, then summarize normal, right-skew, bimodal result: a mean describing no one result: the right summary per shape mistake the average lands between the two peaks. best practice read the shape, then pick the statistic. check normal: mean. skew: median. bimodal: segment. three fixes to apply 1 plot first see the shape at a glance. 2 tune bins try 30 bins and compare them. 3 split peaks bimodal usually means two segments.
m4-desc-summary: key checks descriptive summary table ✓ pair up mean with sd, median with iqr. ✓ read limits check the watch out column. ✓ add n state sample size with every number. metric tells good for watch out mean average symmetric metrics outliers median typical skewed metrics ignores extremes mode most common categories multiple modes sd variability consistency skew sensitivity iqr middle spread skew / outliers needs quartiles range min to max quick sanity check single-outlier dominated percentile position in dist. slas, segments interpretation depends on context rule never report center without spread. when to use it use it when at the start of every analysis and at the top of a report, to show count, centre, spread and range together. avoid or switch when you rely on the table alone. add a chart so shape and outliers are visible. business example pasting df.describe() into a data-quality check. descriptive summary summary: never report center alone ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice mean only in the report no spread, no n center plus spread mean or median with sd or iqr same stat for every metric mean on skewed metrics match stat to shape median and iqr for skew range as the whole story single outlier dominates range as sanity check only percentiles for slas result: misleading summary result: balanced, honest summary mistake center without spread says little. best practice choose each metric by its strength and its limit. rule never report center without spread. three fixes to apply 1 pair up mean with sd, median with iqr. 2 read limits check the watch out column. 3 add n state sample size with every number.
m4-prob-basic: definition likelihood from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). when to use it use it when estimating how likely an outcome is from counts: favourable outcomes divided by total outcomes. avoid or switch when the sample is small, so the estimate is unstable. say how many records it is based on. business example the share of customers who churned last quarter. estimate from frequency p(event) = # favorable outcomes / # total outcomes p(convert) = conversions / visitors live example — conversion worked 10,000 visitors, 300 conversions → p = 0.03 (3%) see it probability scale 0 (never) 0.5 1 (certain) p = 0.03 syntax # direct calculation p = conversions / visitors # 300/10000 = 0.03 # or with pandas df[ 'converted' ]. mean () # if converted is 0/1 basic probability probability: rate vs raw count ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice report 300 conversions alone no denominator p = conversions / visitors 300 / 10,000 = 0.03 write 3 as the probability must be 0 to 1 probability between 0 and 1 0.03 is 3 percent compare counts across sites different traffic sizes mean of a 0/1 column df.converted.mean() result: counts that cannot compare result: comparable rates mistake without visitors, 300 means nothing. best practice favorable over total, always from 0 to 1. formula p(event) = favorable / total outcomes. three fixes to apply 1 divide count over total gives a rate. 2 stay in 0 to 1 0 is impossible, 1 is certain. 3 use pandas mean of a 0/1 column is p.
m4-prob-rules: core rules # complement p(not a) = 1 − p(a) # addition (mutually exclusive) p(a or b) = p(a) + p(b) # general addition (overlap) p(a or b) = p(a) + p(b) − p(a and b) # multiplication (independent) p(a and b) = p(a) × p(b) visual — venn logic overlap vs mutually exclusive a b ∩ overlap: subtract p(a∩b) a b no overlap: add ask first are a and b independent? mutually exclusive? getting this wrong flips the math. when to use it use it when combining events: complement for 'at least one', addition for 'a or b', multiplication for 'a and b'. avoid or switch when you multiply probabilities without checking that the events are independent. business example the chance that at least one of three emails is opened. probability rules rules: adding when events overlap ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice p(a)+p(b) when a and b overlap overlap counted twice subtract p(a and b) general addition rule multiply dependent events assumes independence multiply only if independent p(a) x p(b) skip the complement hard route for not-a p(not a) = 1 - p(a) retention from churn result: probabilities above the truth result: correct combined probability mistake wrong assumption flips the math. best practice ask first: independent or mutually exclusive? ask first independent? mutually exclusive? then choose. three fixes to apply 1 check overlap overlap means subtract the intersection. 2 check independence only then multiply the two. 3 use complement 1 minus p is often quicker.
m4-conditional: definition p(a|b) = probability of a given b has occurred. when to use it use it when the probability depends on a condition or segment, such as the churn rate given no login in 30 days. avoid or switch when you confuse p(a given b) with p(b given a). business example churn probability among customers who contacted support twice. formula p(a | b) = p(a and b) / p(b) live example — conversion by device device visitors conversions p(convert|device) mobile 6,000 120 2.0% desktop 4,000 180 4.5% see it conversion rate by device 2.0% mobile 4.5% desktop syntax # python — conditional conversion p_mobile = df[df.device== 'mobile' ][ 'converted' ]. mean () p_desktop = df[df.device== 'desktop' ][ 'converted' ]. mean () # or as a cross-tab rate pd. crosstab (df.device, df.converted, normalize= 'index' ) insight strong device effect → prioritize mobile ux fixes and a/b the mobile checkout. conditional probability conditional: one blended rate hides segments ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice overall conversion 3 percent blends mobile and desktop p(convert|device) mobile 120/6,000 = 2.0% treat p(a|b) as p(b|a) directions swapped p(a and b) / p(b) divide by the condition same fix for all devices ignores the device effect prioritize mobile ux fixes a/b the mobile checkout result: segment gaps stay invisible result: segment-level insight mistake mobile 2.0% vs desktop 4.5% is lost in the blend. best practice condition on the segment before deciding. formula p(a|b) = p(a and b) divided by p(b). three fixes to apply 1 segment compute the rate per device group. 2 crosstab normalize=index gives row rates. 3 act strong effect means test the weak segment.
m4-bayes: definition update beliefs with evidence. posterior ∝ likelihood × prior. formula p(cause | evidence) = p(evidence | cause) × p(cause) / p(evidence) see it — fraud alert scenario bayes update flow prior fraud = 1% likelihood alert | fraud = 90% posterior fraud | alert = ? with a 5% false positive rate, most alerts are not fraud. live calculation # given p_fraud = 0.01 # prior p_alert_if_fraud = 0.90 # sensitivity p_alert_if_not = 0.05 # false positive # total alert probability p_alert = 0.90 * 0.01 + 0.05 * 0.99 = 0.009 + 0.0495 = 0.0585 # bayes p_fraud_given_alert = ( 0.90 * 0.01 ) / 0.0585 ≈ 0.154 # ~15% # business: don't auto-block on a single alert base-rate trap when events are rare, high sensitivity still yields many false positives. bayes' theorem bayes: the base-rate trap ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice alert means 90% fraud confuses sensitivity with p posterior about 0.154 0.009 / 0.0585 ignore the 1% prior fraud is rare include the prior 0.01 evidence times the prior auto-block on one alert false positives blocked review, do not auto-block combine more signals result: most blocked users are innocent result: sensible fraud decisions mistake 5% false positives swamp a 1% base rate. best practice about 15% of alerts are real fraud. formula p(c|e) = p(e|c) x p(c) divided by p(e). three fixes to apply 1 state prior start with the base rate of the rare event. 2 total alerts true plus false alerts give p(e). 3 act carefully one alert is not proof.
m4-binomial: definition successes in n independent trials, each with probability p. when to use it use it when a fixed number of independent trials, each with two outcomes and the same chance of success. avoid or switch when the success chance changes between trials, or trials affect each other. business example how many of 100 website visitors will convert if the rate is 3%. see it — distribution shapes binomial: n=1000, p=0.03 e[x] = 30 conversions live numbers worked n = 1,000 visitors · p = 0.03 expected conversions = n × p = 30 actuals will vary around 30 due to randomness. syntax # simulate one experiment import numpy as np np.random. binomial (n= 1000 , p= 0.03 ) # → e.g. 32 # simulate 10,000 experiments to see distribution sims = np.random. binomial ( 1000 , 0.03 , size= 10000 ) why it matters larger n → smaller relative noise → tighter conversion-rate estimates. binomial distribution binomial: expecting exactly the average ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice expect exactly 30 conversions every run should hit n x p e[x] = n x p = 30 a center, not a guarantee panic at 32 or 27 normal randomness simulate 10,000 experiments np.random.binomial(1000, 0.03) small n, tight conclusions noise dominates larger n narrows the noise tighter rate estimates result: false alarms from noise result: realistic expectations mistake actuals vary around 30 by chance. best practice expect a spread around n x p. formula expected successes = n x p for n independent trials. three fixes to apply 1 compute e[x] 1,000 visitors x 0.03 = 30 expected. 2 simulate see the range of outcomes by running it. 3 grow n more trials, less relative noise.
m4-poisson: definition number of rare events in a fixed interval. parameter λ = average rate. when to use it use it when counting independent events in a fixed interval at a steady average rate. avoid or switch when counts are more spread out than the mean (overdispersed) or the rate changes through the interval. business example calls arriving per hour at a help desk. see it — tickets per hour poisson with λ = 12 tickets/hour λ = 12 tickets/hour live example worked average λ = 12 tickets/hour. some hours 8, some 15, some 20 — all normal variation. use this to plan staffing buffers. syntax # poisson probability in python from scipy.stats import poisson poisson. pmf ( 20 , mu= 12 ) # p(exactly 20 tickets) poisson. cdf ( 20 , mu= 12 ) # p(≤ 20 tickets) special cause sudden spikes far beyond poisson range → treat as incident, not normal variation. poisson distribution poisson: variation vs a real incident ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice staff exactly to the average 12 some hours hit 15 or 20 staffing buffer above lambda plan for 15 to 20 per hour treat 8 or 15 as alarming normal variation poisson.pmf and cdf probability of 20 or fewer treat a huge spike as noise incident missed far beyond range is an incident special cause, not variation result: understaffed or false alarms result: staffing that fits reality mistake averages ignore the natural hourly swings. best practice know normal swing, then spot real incidents. special cause a spike far beyond poisson range is an incident. three fixes to apply 1 use lambda average rate, here 12 per hour. 2 add buffer plan above the average for natural swings. 3 escalate treat extreme spikes as incidents.
m4-normal: definition bell-shaped curve defined by μ (mean) and σ (sd). when to use it use it when continuous, roughly symmetric, bell-shaped data, for z-scores, the 68-95-99.7 rule and control limits. avoid or switch when the data is skewed, heavy-tailed or bounded, such as waiting times. business example flagging unusually heavy parcels with z-scores. see it normal with μ = 30, σ = 5 μ−3σ μ−2σ μ−σ μ μ+σ μ+2σ μ+3σ 15 20 25 30 35 40 45 68% 95% within ±2σ · 99.7% within ±3σ 45 min = incident empirical rule (68–95–99.7) # delivery times — μ=30, σ=5 ▼ ▁▄███▄▁ ▁▄█████████▄▁ ▄███████████████████▄ ▄████████████████████████████▄ ───────────────────────────────────── 15 20 25 30 35 40 45 μ−2σ μ−σ μ μ+σ μ+2σ μ+3σ 68% within ±1σ 95% within ±2σ 99.7% within ±3σ 45 min is 3σ above → rare, likely incident syntax # python — z-score and probability from scipy.stats import norm mu, sigma = 30 , 5 z = ( 45 - mu) / sigma # 3.0 prob = 1 - norm. cdf ( 45 , mu, sigma) # p(x > 45) check first don't assume normality — look at the histogram. right-skewed metrics (order value) are not normal. normal distribution normal: assuming a bell curve ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice assume normality without a look data may be skewed plot a histogram first check the shape before using ignore the 68-95-99.7 rule no sense of rare z = (45 - 30) / 5 = 3.0 rare, likely an incident treat 45 min as ordinary it is 3 sigma above norm.cdf for p(x > 45) 1 - norm.cdf(45, 30, 5) result: wrong rarity and false claims result: valid probabilities mistake normal models fail on skewed data. best practice check normality, then use z-scores. empirical rule 68% within 1 sigma, 95% in 2, 99.7% in 3. three fixes to apply 1 look first histogram before any normal claim. 2 use z z = (x - mu) / sigma per value. 3 flag 3 sigma beyond 3 sigma is rare.
m4-clt: definition sample means approach a normal distribution as n grows — even when the raw data isn't normal. when to use it use it when justifying normal-based confidence intervals and tests for sample means when the sample is reasonably large (about 30 is a common rough guide). avoid or switch when the sample is tiny and the data very skewed, or you want to describe individual values rather than means. business example building a confidence interval for average order value. see it — narrowing spread distribution of sample mean as n grows true value n = 30 n = 200 n = 1,000 se = σ/√n shrinks live example worked individual order values are right-skewed. average of 30 orders → still noisy. average of 1,000 orders → very stable. simulation in python import numpy as np # right-skewed "population" population = np.random. exponential (scale= 100 , size= 100000 ) # distribution of sample means, various n for n in [ 10 , 30 , 100 , 1000 ]: means = [np.random. choice (population, n). mean () for _ in range ( 500 )] print (n, np. std (means)) why it matters this is why a/b tests on means work — even when the underlying metric is skewed, sample means are near-normal for reasonable n. central limit theorem clt: trusting a small sample mean ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice average of 30 orders as stable still noisy average of 1,000 orders very stable fear skewed data for a/b means raw data need not be normal sample means near normal even for skewed metrics ignore se = sigma / root n precision unknown simulate with exponential data watch the spread shrink result: shaky estimates from small n result: reliable mean-based tests mistake small samples give noisy means. best practice larger n, narrower spread, normal-looking means. why a/b works sample means near-normal for reasonable n. three fixes to apply 1 raise n spread falls as n grows. 2 use se se = sigma over root n. smaller means tighter. 3 simulate test it on skewed data.
m4-prob-summary: match the question to a distribution match the question to a distribution what is measured? check assumptions before choosing yes / no binomial successes out of a fixed number of trials. event count poisson events in an interval at an assumed rate. measurement normal continuous measurements if shape fits. these are starting candidates. validate independence, stability and distribution assumptions. expand diagram when to use it use it when choosing a distribution: yes/no counts suggest binomial, event counts per interval suggest poisson, measurements suggest normal. avoid or switch when you pick a distribution by habit without checking the assumptions. business example matching each business question in this module to its distribution. concept business use example complement retention from churn 1 − 5% churn = 95% stay conditional p(a|b) segment-level rates conversion by device bayes diagnosis fraud given alert binomial success counts conversions out of visitors poisson event rate tickets per hour normal measurement variation delivery time variation clt why a/b works sample means converge
m4-pop-sample: definition population: everyone you care about. sample: the subset you observed. when to use it use it when you cannot measure everyone, so you sample and infer. define the population first and sample randomly. avoid or switch when the sample is a convenience sample treated as representative. business example surveying 400 customers to estimate satisfaction for 20,000. see it sample from population population — all visitors sample — this week's traffic n = ? always ask "is my sample representative?" — campaign traffic differs from organic. sample across weeks and segments. population vs sample sample: is it representative ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice generalize from campaign traffic differs from organic ask: is my sample representative always question it use only this week's data one slice of time sample across weeks cover time variation skip asking who is missing bias unnoticed sample across segments include organic and paid result: conclusions do not transfer result: sample reflects the population mistake the sample is not the whole population. best practice sample to match the population you care about. always ask is my sample representative of everyone i care about? three fixes to apply 1 define name the population first. 2 spread out sample weeks and segments. 3 state n report the size of the sample.
m4-sampling-dist: definition distribution of a statistic (mean, rate) across many independent samples. when to use it use it when understanding how a statistic such as the mean varies from sample to sample. it is the basis for standard errors and confidence intervals. avoid or switch when you confuse the spread of the data with the spread of the sampling distribution. business example explaining why a bigger sample gives a more precise average. see it — variability shrinks with n sampling distribution of the mean true value n = 30 n = 200 n = 1,000 se = σ/√n shrinks live example worked true conversion = 3%. sample 1 (n=1,000) shows 2.6%. sample 2 (n=1,000) shows 3.4%. variation ≠ change in truth — it's noise. standard error formula se = σ / √n # larger n → smaller se → tighter cis # halve se → need 4× the sample sampling distributions sampling: noise read as a real change ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice sample 2.6% vs 3.4% as a shift true rate stays 3% treat 2.6 and 3.4 as noise both samples n = 1,000 ignore standard error spread unknown se = sigma / root n quantifies the spread small n for tight results wide sampling spread quadruple n to halve se tighter cis result: chasing random variation result: noise separated from change mistake variation is not a change in truth. best practice know the se before you react to a change. se formula se = sigma / root n; halve se needs 4x sample. three fixes to apply 1 expect noise samples differ by chance. 2 compute se use sigma over root n. 3 plan n 4x the data halves the se.
m4-ci: definition a range of plausible values for a parameter, with a stated confidence level. when to use it use it when reporting an estimate with its uncertainty, so decisions consider the plausible range. avoid or switch when you read one interval as a 95% chance that this particular interval contains the truth. it describes the method. business example average order value of 52 with a margin, not just 52. see it — narrow vs wide ci comparison 250 275 300 325 350 estimate n = 20 wide → need more data n = 500 formula ci = x̄ ± t* × se se = s / √n syntax from scipy import stats import numpy as np def mean_ci (values, conf= 0.95 ): x = np. asarray (values, dtype=float) n = len (x) m, se = x. mean (), stats. sem (x) h = se * stats.t. ppf (( 1 +conf)/ 2 , n- 1 ) return m-h, m, m+h mean_ci ([ 100 , 200 , 300 , 400 , 1000 ]) plain english "we estimate the average is 300, typically between 290–310." wide ci → need more data. confidence intervals ci: a single number without a range ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice report the estimate alone no sense of uncertainty ci = x-bar +/- t* x se se = s / root n ignore a wide interval at n = 20 shaky estimate wide interval means need more data compare n = 20 and n = 500 call 95% a 95% chance misread meaning say plausible range with a stated confidence level result: false precision result: estimates with honest range mistake a point estimate hides how uncertain it is. best practice always give estimate plus interval. formula ci = mean +/- t* x se se = s / sqrt(n). three fixes to apply 1 use t* small samples need the t value. 2 read width wide means collect more data. 3 write plain state the range in plain words.
m4-ht: purpose decide if an observed difference is real or noise. when to use it use it when deciding whether an observed difference is larger than chance would explain, with the question set before you look at the data. avoid or switch when you run many tests and report only the significant ones, or treat statistical significance as practical importance. business example testing whether a new checkout page changes conversion. 5-step framework testing flow 1 1. h₀ / h₁ 2 2. choose α 3 3. statistic 4 4. p-value 5 5. decide live a/b hypotheses worked h₀: conversion rate is the same. h₁: conversion rate is different (or higher). choose α = 0.05 before looking. syntax — t-test and z-test # one-sample t-test from scipy.stats import ttest_1samp t, p = ttest_1samp (deliveries, popmean= 30 ) # two-proportion z-test (a/b) from statsmodels.stats.proportion import proportions_ztest stat, p = proportions_ztest ([ 300 , 330 ], [ 10000 , 10000 ]) hypothesis testing hypotheses: choosing the rules after ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice pick alpha after seeing the data rigged threshold choose alpha = 0.05 first before results no h0 or h1 stated unclear question h0: rates are the same h1: they differ skip the test, eyeball it real or noise unknown run the matching test ttest_1samp or proportions_ztest result: unreliable conclusions result: defensible decisions mistake decisions must be set before looking. best practice follow the five steps in order. 5 steps h0 and h1, alpha, statistic, p-value, decide. three fixes to apply 1 state h0 h1 write them in plain words. 2 set alpha before you look at any results. 3 run test then decide from the p-value.
m4-type1: error matrix the four outcomes of a test reality h₀ true (no effect) h₀ false (real effect) your decision reject h₀ keep h₀ type i (α) false positive · launch a dud correct power = 1 − β correct confidence = 1 − α type ii (β) false negative · miss a win cost asymmetry in business error what happened cost mitigation type i launched a change that doesn't work wasted budget, bad ux lower α, replicate type ii missed a real improvement lost opportunity more traffic, larger n sample sizing in python # sample size to detect a target effect (approximate) from statsmodels.stats.power import zt_ind_solve_power n = zt_ind_solve_power ( effect_size= 0.2 , alpha= 0.05 , power= 0.8 , ratio= 1 ) trade-off lower α reduces false positives but increases false negatives. balance by cost. when to use it use it when setting alpha and sample size, and weighing the cost of a false alarm (type i) against a missed effect (type ii). avoid or switch when you ignore power: a small sample can easily miss a real effect. business example choosing a stricter alpha for a costly product change. type i and ii errors errors: false positive vs missed win ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice chase tiny alpha, ignore misses lower alpha raises type ii balance alpha by cost trade-off between errors launch a dud type i false positive lower alpha, replicate guards against type i underpowered test missed real improvement larger n for power 0.8 more traffic cuts type ii result: wasted budget or lost gains result: errors matched to business cost mistake each error has a different cost. best practice plan sample size for the effect you need. trade-off lower alpha cuts false positives, raises misses. three fixes to apply 1 type i false positive: launch a dud. 2 type ii false negative: miss a win. 3 size n zt_ind_solve_power gives n.
m4-pvalue: definition probability of seeing data at least as extreme as observed, if h₀ is true . when to use it use it when summarizing how surprising your data would be if the null hypothesis were true. avoid or switch when you read it as the probability that the null is true, or ignore effect size and confidence intervals. business example reporting the p-value together with the size of the lift. see it — p-value in the tail where the p-value lives observed stat p-value h₀ distribution not what you think ❌ not "probability h₀ is true" ❌ not a measure of effect size ✅ probability of this data given h₀ always pair report p-value + effect size + confidence interval together. live: p-value vs impact worked variant lifts 3.00% → 3.02%. huge n → tiny p → "significant." but 0.02 pp is a rounding error in business terms. statistically ≠ practically. p-value p-value: significant is not important ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice p small, so ship it 3.00% to 3.02% on huge n judge 0.02 pp in business terms a rounding error p as p(h0 is true) not what it measures p is p(data | h0) probability of this data given h0 p-value reported alone no effect size report p + effect size + ci all three together result: tiny gains treated as wins result: balanced, honest conclusions mistake statistically significant is not practically important. best practice pair significance with practical impact. always pair p-value, effect size and confidence interval. three fixes to apply 1 read p right data given h0, not h0 given data. 2 add effect show the size of the change. 3 add ci show the range of plausible values.
m4-alpha: definition cutoff for rejecting h₀. commonly 0.05. when to use it use it when before the test, to set the false-alarm risk: 0.05 is a common default, stricter for costly mistakes. avoid or switch when you change alpha after seeing the result. business example using 0.01 when a wrong launch decision is expensive. see it — α as a threshold common α levels α = 0.01 strict / regulated α = 0.05 default α = 0.10 exploratory rule pick α before looking at results. choosing it after = p-hacking. keep it consistent across experiments for governance. significance level alpha: choosing it after the result ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice move alpha to make p pass that is p-hacking pick alpha before looking fixed threshold different alpha per experiment no governance keep alpha consistent across experiments 0.05 for everything ignores the stakes match alpha to stakes 0.01 strict, 0.10 exploratory result: cherry-picked significance result: trustworthy, governed testing mistake choosing alpha afterward invalidates the test. best practice set it first, keep it steady. rule pick alpha before looking at results. three fixes to apply 1 pre-set write alpha in the test plan. 2 be consistent same alpha across experiments. 3 match risk stricter where errors cost more.
m4-corr-caus: definitions correlation: variables move together. causation: one causes the other. when to use it use it when interpreting any relationship between two variables, and deciding whether you need an experiment. avoid or switch when you use causal wording for an observational correlation. business example ice cream sales and sunburn rise together; the season drives both. see it — the ice cream trap confounded by summer ice cream sales drowning cases hot weather ☀️ correlation ↑↑ but the real driver is hot weather how to test causation randomize the treatment (a/b test). control for confounders (seasonality, region). replicate the effect across samples and time. syntax — correlation vs experiment # correlation (observational) df[[ 'ice_cream' , 'drownings' ]]. corr () # causation (experimental) # randomize users to control / variant, then compare correlation vs causation correlation: the ice cream trap ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice ice cream drives drownings hot weather confounds randomize to control or variant a/b test act on a correlation alone no cause shown control for confounders seasonality, region ignore seasonality and region confounders unchecked replicate across samples and across time result: wrong cause, wrong action result: causal claims you can back mistake variables move together without causing each other. best practice correlation suggests, experiments prove. how to test randomize, control confounders, and replicate. three fixes to apply 1 randomize assign users to control or variant. 2 control adjust for confounders like season. 3 replicate repeat across time and samples.
m4-ab-conclusion: drafted for you filled-in conclusion using control 3.00% vs variant 3.30%. when to use it use it when after an a/b test, to give stakeholders the effect, uncertainty, decision and caveats in one place. avoid or switch when you report only a p-value or only the winner. business example a one-page recommendation on whether to ship variant b. see it a/b result 3.00% control 3.30% variant +0.30 pp (+10% rel.) p ≈ 0.23 → not significant error bars = 95% ci, they overlap the write-up business question does the new checkout experience increase conversion rate? metric & sample conversion rate = conversions ÷ visitors. control n=10,000. variant n=10,000. result control: 3.00% (300 / 10,000) variant: 3.30% (330 / 10,000) uplift: +0.30 pp (relative +10%) statistical test two-proportion z-test. with p ≈ 0.20 we fail to reject h₀ at α = 0.05. 95% ci for the uplift includes 0. conclusion statistical: uplift not significant at this n. practical: 0.30 pp would matter if real, but we can't separate from noise yet. recommendation: extend the test or increase traffic. don't launch on this evidence. python check from statsmodels.stats.proportion import proportions_ztest z, p = proportions_ztest ([ 300 , 330 ], [ 10000 , 10000 ]) print (f "z={z:.3f}, p={p:.4f}" ) # → z ≈ -1.21, p ≈ 0.225 → not significant a/b write-up a/b write-up: launching on noise ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice variant 3.30% beats 3.00%, ship p about 0.23 say uplift not significant fail to reject h0 at 0.05 report uplift without ci interval includes 0 report the 95% ci for uplift includes 0 skip metric and sample size reader cannot judge state metric, n, and test conversions / visitors, 10,000 each result: launching on noise result: decision-ready conclusion mistake not significant at this n: do not launch. best practice extend the test or add traffic. structure question, metric, result, test, conclusion. three fixes to apply 1 state metric definition and n for each arm. 2 split verdict statistical versus practical impact. 3 recommend extend the test; do not launch.
m4-test-selector: when to use it use it when before you run any test: match the test to the data type, the number of groups, paired or independent samples and the assumptions. avoid or switch when you choose a test because it is familiar and skip the checks. business example deciding between a t-test, chi-square, anova or a non-parametric test. decision tree which test to use what is your outcome? numeric (mean) categories chi-square or 2-prop z-test (a/b) 1 group vs benchmark 2 groups independent 3+ groups compare means one-sample t two-sample t anova same entity before/after → paired t skewed / ranks → non-parametric quick reference design test 1 numeric group vs benchmark one-sample t-test 2 independent numeric groups two-sample t-test numeric, before/after same entity paired t-test 2 categorical variables chi-square numeric, 3+ groups anova assumptions fail non-parametric test selection test choice: the wrong test for the design ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice t-test on two categories outcome is not numeric chi-square or 2-prop z for categorical outcomes many t-tests for 3+ groups inflates false positives anova for 3+ groups numeric means compared independent test on before/after same entity measured twice paired t for before/after same entity result: invalid p-values result: a valid test every time mistake the test must match the data and design. best practice start with the outcome type. decision outcome type, groups, then pick the test. three fixes to apply 1 name outcome numeric or categories? decide first. 2 count groups one, two, or three plus groups. 3 check assumptions if they fail, go non-parametric.
m4-ttest: purpose compare means under three scenarios. when to use it use it when comparing means of a numeric outcome between two groups, against a target value, or in paired before and after data, with roughly normal data or a large sample. avoid or switch when there are more than two groups (anova), the data is small and skewed (mann-whitney), or the outcome is a proportion (chi-square or a proportion test). business example do two stores differ in average basket size? see it — one-sample vs target sample mean vs target x̄ = 32 min sample mean μ = 30 min target vs three variants type use example one-sample 1 group vs benchmark delivery vs 30 min sla two-sample 2 independent groups profit north vs south paired before/after same entity handle time pre/post training syntax # one-sample from scipy.stats import ttest_1samp, ttest_ind, ttest_rel t, p = ttest_1samp (deliveries, popmean= 30 ) # two-sample independent t, p = ttest_ind (profit_north, profit_south) # paired t, p = ttest_rel (handle_after, handle_before) t-tests t-tests: the wrong variant ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice ttest_ind for before/after ignores the pairing ttest_rel for pre/post handle time per agent two-sample for one sla one group vs 30 min ttest_1samp vs the sla popmean = 30 compare means, skip context delivery 32 vs 30 ttest_ind for north vs south independent groups result: wrong variance, wrong p result: a valid comparison of means mistake pick the variant by how data was collected. best practice one, two or paired: match the design. three variants one-sample, two-sample, paired. three fixes to apply 1 one-sample one group vs a benchmark. 2 two-sample two independent groups. 3 paired before and after, same entity.
m4-chi: purpose test association between two categorical variables using a contingency table. when to use it use it when testing association between two categorical variables, or whether counts fit an expected pattern, using counts rather than percentages. avoid or switch when expected counts are small (use fisher's exact test), or the data is paired (use mcnemar). business example is plan type related to churn? contingency table convert not convert total mobile a=120 b=5880 a+b=6000 desktop c=180 d=3820 c+d=4000 total a+c=300 b+d=9700 n=10000 visual — observed vs expected conversion rate by device observed mobile 2.0% desktop 4.5% expected if independent mobile 3.0% desktop 3.0% device has an effect syntax from scipy.stats import chi2_contingency table = [[ 120 , 5880 ], [ 180 , 3820 ]] chi2, p, dof, expected = chi2_contingency (table) association ≠ causation device matters but the experiment is what proves cause. chi-square chi-square: association is not cause ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice compare raw counts mobile 120 vs desktop 180 compare rates: 2.0% vs 4.5% normalize by group size skip the expected table 3.0% each if independent chi2_contingency(table) observed vs expected say device causes conversion only association shown follow up with an experiment a/b on mobile checkout result: causal claim without proof result: valid association finding mistake device matters, but only an experiment proves cause. best practice test association, then experiment for cause. purpose test two categorical variables via a table. three fixes to apply 1 build table conversion by device in a contingency table. 2 compare observed vs expected rates. 3 experiment prove cause with an a/b test.
m4-anova: purpose compare means across 3+ groups without inflating false-positive risk. when to use it use it when comparing means across three or more groups with one test, followed by post-hoc comparisons if it is significant. avoid or switch when there are only two groups (t-test), or the data is clearly non-normal or has unequal variances (consider welch or kruskal-wallis). business example does average satisfaction differ across four regions? see it mean profit by category 120 electronics 80 fashion 45 grocery anova asks: do any groups differ? syntax from scipy.stats import f_oneway f, p = f_oneway (electronics_profit, fashion_profit, grocery_profit) # if significant → post-hoc pairwise comparisons from statsmodels.stats.multicomp import pairwise_tukeyhsd pairwise_tukeyhsd (df.profit, df.category). summary () follow-up anova says "at least one differs." tukey tells you which pairs. anova anova: many t-tests, more false alarms ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice pairwise t-tests on 3 groups inflates false positives f_oneway on all groups one test for the means stop at a significant f which group differs? tukey post-hoc if significant pairwise_tukeyhsd read f as all groups differ it says at least one read: at least one differs tukey says which pairs result: inflated false-positive risk result: controlled error, clear pairs mistake multiple tests raise the chance of a fluke. best practice anova first, then tukey for the pairs. follow-up anova: at least one differs; tukey: which pairs. three fixes to apply 1 one test f_oneway for 3+ groups. 2 post-hoc run tukey only if significant. 3 report name the differing pairs.
m4-nonparam: purpose rank-based tests when normality or variance assumptions fail. when to use it use it when the data is ordinal, skewed or has outliers, or the sample is small: mann-whitney for two groups, wilcoxon for paired data, kruskal-wallis for three or more. avoid or switch when parametric assumptions hold, because you would give up some power. business example comparing satisfaction ratings (1 to 5) between two versions of a page. see it — means vs medians skewed data → median test is safer outlier data heavily right-skewed alternatives parametric non-parametric two-sample t-test mann-whitney u paired t-test wilcoxon signed-rank one-way anova kruskal-wallis syntax from scipy.stats import mannwhitneyu, wilcoxon, kruskal u, p = mannwhitneyu (group_a, group_b) w, p = wilcoxon (after, before) h, p = kruskal (g1, g2, g3) non-parametric tests non-parametric: t-test on skewed data ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice t-test on heavy right skew outlier drives the mean mann-whitney u replaces two-sample t assume normality blindly assumptions failed wilcoxon signed-rank replaces paired t ranks and medians ignored skewed data needs them kruskal-wallis replaces one-way anova result: unreliable p-values result: rank-based, robust result mistake outliers dominate mean-based tests. best practice switch to ranks when assumptions fail. swap skewed or outliers: use the rank-based test. three fixes to apply 1 check shape is the data skewed or has outliers? 2 pair up match each parametric test to its twin. 3 use medians safer on skewed data.
m4-python: key checks python calculators ✓ ci helper mean_ci with a t value. ✓ t helper one_sample versus a target. ✓ a/b helper counts and n for each arm. reusable three calculators you can copy into any notebook. when to use it use it when you want calculations to be reproducible and shareable, using scipy.stats and pandas. avoid or switch when you copy code without checking the test's assumptions or reading the output. business example running a t-test and a confidence interval in one notebook. 1. confidence interval for a mean import numpy as np from scipy import stats def mean_ci (values, conf= 0.95 ): x = np. asarray (values, dtype=float) n = len (x) m, se = x. mean (), stats. sem (x) h = se * stats.t. ppf (( 1 +conf)/ 2 , n- 1 ) return m-h, m, m+h 2. one-sample t-test from scipy import stats def one_sample (values, target): t, p = stats. ttest_1samp (values, popmean=target) return t, p 3. two-proportion z-test (a/b) from statsmodels.stats.proportion import proportions_ztest def ab_test (a, na, b, nb): stat, p = proportions_ztest ([a, b], [na, nb]) return stat, p # control 300/10000 vs variant 330/10000 z, p = ab_test ( 300 , 10000 , 330 , 10000 ) python calculators python tests: recoding from scratch ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice retype stats formulas each time typos in the ci math reuse mean_ci(values, conf) returns low, mean, high pass wrong arguments to ab_test rates instead of counts ab_test(300, 10000, 330, 10000) counts then n for each arm report z and p, no context no n or ci wrap one_sample(values, target) returns t and p result: inconsistent, error-prone result: repeatable, consistent analysis mistake ad-hoc code differs from notebook to notebook. best practice copy tested helpers into every notebook. reusable three calculators: ci, one- sample t, a/b z-test. three fixes to apply 1 ci helper mean_ci with a t value. 2 t helper one_sample versus a target. 3 a/b helper counts and n for each arm.
m4-template: key checks statistics communication template ✓ ask first one sentence business question first. ✓ show test name the test, p-value and ci. ✓ conclude statistical, practical, and action. use in every report five lines make any analysis decision-ready. when to use it use it when presenting statistical results to a non-technical audience in a consistent order: question, method, result, uncertainty, decision. avoid or switch when you list technical output without saying what to do. business example summarizing an a/b test for a product manager. # structure 1. question (business q in one sentence) 2. metric(s) (definition + units) 3. summary (mean/median/sd/iqr + n) 4. test (which test + p-value / ci) 5. conclusion (stat + practical impact + action) # worked example question : is north region aov above the 300 target? metric : ordervalue in usd summary : mean=320, median=305, sd=90, n=48 test : one-sample t vs μ=300 → t=1.54, p=0.13 conclusion: not statistically above target; keep monitoring. communication template report: analysis without a decision ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice dump numbers with no question reader sees no point open with one-sentence question is north aov above 300? skip the test line p-value and ci missing summary plus test mean 320, median 305, sd 90, n 48 end without a conclusion no stat, impact, action close: stat, practical, action keep monitoring result: report nobody can act on result: decision-ready analysis mistake findings unclear to the audience. best practice five lines make any report decision-ready. structure question, metric, summary, test, conclusion. three fixes to apply 1 ask first one sentence business question first. 2 show test name the test, p-value and ci. 3 conclude statistical, practical, and action.
m4-recap: everything in one row 1 descriptive 2 probability 3 inference 4 tests 5 practice the five lines descriptive summarizes center, spread, shape. probability models uncertainty and event likelihood. inference quantifies uncertainty with cis and tests. tests compare groups with formal evidence. correct interpretation prevents wrong decisions. carry-forward rules center without spread is misleading. p-value without effect size and ci is incomplete. correlation without experiment is not causation. choose the test that matches the design.
