m5-overview: purpose a chart is a decision tool, not a decoration. this module teaches you to pick the right chart, design it cleanly, and frame it as a story that drives action. what you'll be able to do choose the correct chart type for the question (comparison, trend, relationship, distribution, part-to-whole) apply design principles: color, labels, axes, and the removal of chart junk turn an analysis into a 3-part story with a headline and a call to action assemble a dashboard that a non-analyst can read in under 30 seconds module flow 4 tracks 1 charts 2 design 3 story 4 dashboards guiding principle if the chart doesn't change a decision, it doesn't belong on the page.
m5-roadmap: four tracks chart types design storytelling dashboards sequence matters chart types — match the visual to the question. design — make it clean, readable, and honest. storytelling — frame the finding as a narrative. dashboards — assemble a self-serve view for the team. practice re-draw three charts from your last report using these rules. the improvement is usually immediate.
m5-audience: rule the same data needs a different chart for an executive, an analyst, and a customer. same data, three audiences audience they want best chart executive the headline, the trend, the ask big kpi + single line + one annotation analyst peer full detail, distributions, edge cases small multiples, scatter, boxplot customer their own numbers, in context benchmark bar + their line highlighted visual — attention span ladder time each audience will give you exec 5–10 sec manager 1–2 min analyst 10+ min common mistake showing a dense analyst chart to an executive — they'll disengage before they see the point. know your audience audience: one chart does not fit all ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice dense analyst chart for an exec they disengage before the point big kpi, one line, one note executive: headline, trend, ask same report for every reader customers get ci and n = 20000 customer: benchmark bar their own line highlighted spend 10 minutes of detail execs give about 5 to 10 sec analyst: small multiples, scatter full detail and edge cases result: the point is never seen result: each reader gets the point mistake wrong detail for the reader loses the room. best practice same numbers, framing changes by audience. rule of thumb same data needs a different chart per audience. three fixes to apply 1 ask who reads executive, analyst or customer, before charting. 2 match the time exec 5-10 sec, manager 1-2 min, analyst 10+. 3 rewrite three ways one finding, three versions, best chart for each.
m5-chart-selector: rule match the chart to the question , not to the data you happen to have. decision table question chart compare categories bar (vertical or horizontal) trend over time line relationship between two numerics scatter distribution of one numeric histogram / boxplot density across two dimensions heatmap parts of a whole (few slices) pie / donut (max 5) how components add to a total waterfall visual question → chart compare trend relation distrib. parts bar line scatter hist. pie tie-breaker if two charts are valid, pick the one the audience can read fastest. chart selector chart choice: match the question ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice pick chart by data on hand not by the question asked start from the question compare, trend, relation, parts pie for 8 categories parts of a whole, max 5 distribution: histogram or a boxplot of one numeric bar for a trend over time line shows the trajectory trend: line, bridge: waterfall two numerics: scatter result: reader misses the answer result: chart fits the question mistake the chart answers a question nobody asked. best practice if two charts fit, pick the faster to read. tie-breaker if two charts are valid, pick the fastest to read. three fixes to apply 1 name the question compare, trend, relation, distribution, parts. 2 check data shape 1 category + 1 number is a bar; 2 numbers a scatter. 3 cap the pie five slices at most, else switch to a bar chart.
m5-bar: use for comparing a numeric value across categories. rules sort by value , not alphabetically — the eye finds the story instantly. start the axis at zero. bar length encodes magnitude; truncating lies. use horizontal bars when category names are long. one color for one series. only highlight a bar if it's the point of the chart. good vs bad sorted vs unsorted unsorted a b c d sorted desc c a b d syntax — python import seaborn as sns sns. barplot (data=df. sort_values ( 'sales' , ascending= false ), x= 'sales' , y= 'region' ) never don't truncate the y-axis on a bar chart. the bar's length is the message. bar charts bar charts: length is the message ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice alphabetical regions eye cannot find the story sort_values by sales, desc west 420, east 310, north 190 y-axis starts at 25, not 0 bar length no longer = magnitude zero baseline always bar length encodes magnitude rainbow bar colors one series, six colors one color, one highlighted bar only if it is the point result: sizes look misleading result: ranking read at a glance mistake truncated bars lie about the gap. best practice sorted, zero-based and one highlight. rule of thumb sort by value, start at zero. long names: go horizontal. three fixes to apply 1 sort descending order by value, not by alphabet. 2 zero baseline never truncate the axis on a bar chart. 3 long labels use horizontal bars when names are long.
m5-line: use for trends of one or more series over a continuous axis (usually time). rules time on the x-axis , always left-to-right. limit to 3–5 series . more than that and the eye can't track them. don't connect missing data with a straight line — show a gap. annotate the inflection point ("campaign launched here"). visual two series with annotation campaign launch variant control syntax — python import matplotlib.pyplot as plt plt. plot (df[ 'date' ], df[ 'variant' ], label= 'variant' ) plt. plot (df[ 'date' ], df[ 'control' ], label= 'control' , linestyle= '--' ) plt. axvline (x=launch_date, color= 'green' , linestyle= ':' ) best for weekly/monthly kpis, a/b test trajectories, cohort retention curves. line charts line charts: show the trend, not the tangle ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice 10 series on one chart eye cannot track beyond 3 to 5 limit to 3-5 series variant vs control, dashed straight line over missing weeks hides a data gap show a gap for missing data do not connect across it no note at the launch week reader guesses why it moved plt.axvline(x=launch_date) label: campaign launch result: no clear story result: trend and cause visible mistake spaghetti lines hide what changed. best practice time runs left to right, annotate the inflection. rule of thumb time on x, 3-5 series, annotate the turning point. three fixes to apply 1 cap the series three to five lines, so the eye can follow. 2 show gaps missing data is a break, not a straight line. 3 annotate mark the event, e.g. campaign launch.
m5-scatter: use for showing the relationship between two numeric variables. rules each dot = one entity (customer, store, day). add a trend line only if the correlation is real. use size or color to encode a third dimension (e.g. revenue). log scale when the values span orders of magnitude. visual revenue vs visits, one dot per store visits (x) → revenue (y) syntax — python import seaborn as sns sns. scatterplot (data=df, x= 'visits' , y= 'revenue' , size= 'orders' , alpha= 0.7 ) correlation ≠ causation a tight scatter still doesn't prove one variable causes the other. look for confounders. scatter plots scatter: two numbers, one dot per entity ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice trend line on a weak cloud implies a relationship not there trend line if correlation real each dot = one store linear axes over orders of size small values crushed together log scale for wide ranges spans orders of magnitude read a tight fit as cause visits cause revenue? maybe not look for confounders size dots by orders (alpha 0.7) result: false story from the dots result: honest relationship view mistake correlation is read as causation. best practice third variable via size or color. remember correlation is not causation. check for confounders. three fixes to apply 1 fit only if real add a trend line when the pattern is clear. 2 use log scale when values span orders of magnitude. 3 encode a third dot size or color for orders or revenue.
m5-histogram: use for showing the distribution of a single numeric variable. rules bin width matters. too wide hides shape; too narrow creates noise. show the mean/median lines if the point is central tendency. compare two distributions by overlaying or using side-by-side. never use a histogram for categories — that's a bar chart. visual order value distribution (right-skewed) median mean business use right-skewed order values → report the median, not the mean, to your stakeholders. histograms histograms: mean vs median in skew ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice report mean on skewed orders one 310 order among 22 to 44 report the median right-skew: median for stakeholders bins too wide or too narrow hides shape or adds noise tune bin width show shape without noise histogram for categories that is a bar chart job bars for categories histogram for one numeric result: typical order overstated result: typical value reported mistake the mean is pulled up by a few big orders. best practice mark mean and median on the chart. rule of thumb right-skewed values: report the median, not the mean. three fixes to apply 1 use the median skewed order values need a robust center. 2 test bin width try a few widths before you publish. 3 mark both lines draw mean and median to show the skew.
m5-heatmap: use for density or intensity across two categorical dimensions (e.g. day × hour). rules sequential palette for magnitude, diverging for above/below zero. label the cells if the audience needs exact numbers. sort rows and columns by value, not alphabetically. visual traffic by hour × weekday mon tue wed thu fri sat sun 0–6 6–12 12–18 18–24 darker = more traffic. wednesday 12–18 is the peak. best for staffing plans, campaign send times, server load analysis. heatmaps heatmaps: intensity across two dimensions ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice rainbow palette for magnitude order of colors is unclear sequential palette for magnitude darker = more traffic alphabetical rows and columns mon, sun, tue, wed scrambled diverging for above/below zero sort rows and columns by value no cell labels when exact reader cannot get 1840 sessions label cells when numbers matter wed 12-18 peak: 1840 result: hot spots are hard to find result: peaks found at a glance mistake peaks hide in a noisy grid. best practice pivot day by time block then colour it. rule of thumb sequential for magnitude, diverging around a midpoint. three fixes to apply 1 pick the palette sequential or diverging, matched to the data. 2 sort the axes by value, not by alphabet. 3 label cells print values when the reader needs exact numbers.
m5-pie: use sparingly pie charts are hard to read. use a bar chart unless you have a strong reason. when a pie is ok you have 2–5 slices , no more. one slice is clearly the point ("62% of revenue comes from one channel"). the audience is non-technical and expects the metaphor. when it's not more than 5 categories — the slices become unreadable. you need to compare close values — the eye can't compare angles. there's a time dimension — use a line chart instead. visual pie vs bar — same data 62% pie — hard to compare 62% 34% 4% bar — instant comparison rule of thumb if you're about to make a pie, ask: "would a bar be clearer?" usually yes. pie and donut charts pies: use sparingly ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice 8 slices in one pie slices become unreadable 2-5 slices, one is the point 62% from one channel close values by angle 62% vs 34% is hard to judge bar for close values direct 62, referral 34, other 4 pie across time periods a time dimension needs a line line chart for time pie only for one snapshot result: shares cannot be compared result: instant comparison mistake the eye cannot compare angles. best practice shares sum to 100%; ask: would a bar be clearer? rule of thumb about to make a pie? ask: would a bar be clearer? three fixes to apply 1 limit slices two to five slices, no more. 2 swap to bars when values are close or many. 3 use a line anything over time belongs on a line.
m5-waterfall: use for showing how individual positive and negative contributions add up to a total. classic example start with last month's revenue, add new customers, subtract churned customers, add expansion revenue → this month's revenue. visual revenue bridge: $100k → $118k 100 start +15 new −8 churn +11 expand 118 end why it works shows both gains and losses on the same axis. answers "what changed and by how much?" in one glance. executives love it for month-over-month and budget-vs-actual reviews. also called bridge chart, cascade chart. waterfall charts waterfall: what changed and by how much ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice two bars: 100 and 118 hides what drove the gain bridge: 100 to 118 start, new +15, churn -8, expand +11 steps that do not reconcile +15, -8, +11 must give 118 check the running total 100, 115, 107, 118 gains and losses same color churn -8 hidden among adds signed steps on one axis gains and losses together result: the why is invisible result: change explained in a glance mistake start and end alone do not explain change. best practice good for month-over-month and budget vs actual. rule of thumb start + signed steps = end. the bridge must reconcile. three fixes to apply 1 list signed steps positive and negative contributions in order. 2 reconcile running total must land on the end value. 3 show both sides gains and losses on one shared axis.
m5-design-overview: definition chart design is the discipline of removing everything that doesn't help the viewer get the point. the four design levers lever question color is it encoding meaning, or just decoration? labels does the title state the takeaway? axes is the scale honest and readable? junk can i delete anything else? visual — before vs after cluttered vs clean before after rule if you can remove it and the chart still makes the point, remove it. design principles design: remove what does not help ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice 6 colors, no meaning color used as decoration 1 highlight color color encodes meaning title: monthly revenue names the variable only revenue grew 12% after q2 title states the takeaway truncated axis, 3d, shadows distort and distract zero baseline, no 3d delete what adds nothing result: the point is buried result: point lands fast mistake clutter hides the message. best practice score color, labels, axes and junk before and after. rule of thumb if you can remove it and the point stays, remove it. three fixes to apply 1 audit color is it meaning or decoration? 2 audit title does it state the takeaway? 3 audit axis and junk honest scale; delete the rest.
m5-color: rule color should encode meaning, not decorate. if two colors are on the chart, the viewer must know why. three palette types type use for example sequential magnitude (low → high) light blue → dark blue diverging above/below a midpoint red ← white → blue categorical unordered groups distinct hues, similar lightness visual — palette types sequential · diverging · categorical sequential diverging categorical anti-patterns rainbow palettes for ordered data. red/green as the only distinction (colorblind). brand colors used for every category. color color: meaning, not decoration ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice rainbow for ordered data no natural low to high sequential: light to dark blue magnitude, low to high red/green as the only cue colorblind readers cannot split it diverging: red, white, blue above or below a midpoint brand color for every category no meaning behind each color document the color map #3b82f6 main, #f59e0b highlight result: colors confuse the reader result: color carries meaning mistake two colors, no reason the viewer can see. best practice grey for context, one colour for the point. rule of thumb if two colors are shown, the viewer must know why. three fixes to apply 1 match palette type sequential, diverging or categorical by data. 2 avoid red/green do not make it the only distinction. 3 keep a color key same meaning across all charts.
m5-labels: key checks labels & titles ✓ write the finding mobile converts 2x worse than desktop. ✓ add units every axis gets its unit. ✓ label directly skip the legend when you can. rule the title should state the takeaway , not the variable name. bad vs good titles bad good "monthly revenue" "revenue grew 12% after the q2 campaign" "conversion rate by device" "mobile converts 2× worse than desktop" "customer count" "we lost 340 customers in march — the largest drop of the year" label checklist axis labels with units (e.g. "$ usd", "minutes"). legend only when needed — direct labeling is cleaner. annotate the point — a single arrow + 3 words beats a paragraph. source line at the bottom if the data comes from elsewhere. test if a stranger reads only the title, do they know what happened? labels and titles titles: state the takeaway ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice title: monthly revenue names the variable revenue grew 12% after q2 title says what happened axis with no units $ usd or minutes missing axis labels with units $ usd, minutes legend for every series reader hunts back and forth direct labels plus one note arrow and 3 words, source line result: reader must work it out result: message read from the title mistake a stranger reading the title learns nothing. best practice annotate the point; add a source line. test read only the title: do you know what happened? three fixes to apply 1 write the finding mobile converts 2x worse than desktop. 2 add units every axis gets its unit. 3 label directly skip the legend when you can.
m5-axes: rule the axis is a scale — treat it with the same honesty as a measurement. key rules bars must start at zero. bar length = magnitude. truncating lies. lines may not start at zero if the change is small — but label the axis clearly so the viewer knows. log scale when values span orders of magnitude (e.g. 1 to 1,000,000). consistent time intervals. don't mix daily and monthly on the same x-axis. visual — truncation trap same data, honest vs misleading honest (zero baseline) values: 30–45 truncated (misleading) looks like 3× growth — actually 1.5× tip if a chart only works because the axis is truncated, the chart is not honest. axes axes: a scale must be honest ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice bars start at 25 values 30 to 45 look like 3x growth zero baseline for bars heights 30 to 45 stay honest linear axis from 1 to 1,000,000 small values vanish log scale for huge ranges spans orders of magnitude daily and monthly on one x-axis mixed time intervals consistent time intervals pick one grain per axis result: 1.5x growth looks like 3x result: honest 1.5x growth mistake axis choice changes the story. best practice lines may truncate if the axis is labelled. tip if it needs a truncated axis to work, it is not honest. three fixes to apply 1 start bars at zero bar length is magnitude. 2 use log when wide values from 1 to 1m need a log scale. 3 keep time even one interval along the axis.
m5-junk: key checks chart junk ✓ audit each element does it carry data? yes or no. ✓ put back only what the chart needs to communicate. ✓ direct-label replace legends with labels on the marks. definition chart junk is anything on the chart that doesn't help the viewer understand the data. coined by edward tufte. common junk 3d bars and pies — distort values, add nothing. gradients and shadows — decoration, not information. redundant gridlines — every value is already on the data mark. heavy borders and backgrounds — compete with the data. clip art and mascots — distract, never inform. overstuffed legends — direct-label instead. test — subtract until it breaks remove one element at a time. when the chart stops communicating, put that element back. everything else was junk. famous principle "maximize the data-ink ratio" — tufte. the ink should be data, not decoration. chart junk chart junk: maximize the data-ink ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice 3d bars and pies distort values, add nothing flat 2d bars keep marks that carry data 8 gridlines and shadows decoration, not information drop gridlines, add data labels values sit on the marks overstuffed legend, clip art distract from the data direct-label, no clip art legend only if needed result: ink spent on decoration result: clean, readable chart mistake everything competes with the data. best practice ink is data, not decoration. test subtract one element at a time until the chart breaks. three fixes to apply 1 audit each element does it carry data? yes or no. 2 put back only what the chart needs to communicate. 3 direct-label replace legends with labels on the marks.
m5-accessibility: key checks accessibility ✓ pick safe palettes okabe-ito, viridis, rdbu. ✓ add a second cue shape, pattern or direct labels. ✓ check contrast 4.5:1 text; alt text on every chart. rule if a chart only works for people with perfect color vision and 20/20 eyesight, it's not finished. checklist colorblind-safe palettes. ~8% of men can't distinguish red and green. contrast ≥ 4.5:1 between text and background. don't rely on color alone — use shape, pattern, or direct labels. alt text for every chart on a webpage. font size ≥ 12px for chart text; ≥ 14px for axis labels. sortable tables alongside the chart for screen readers. colorblind-safe palettes name use okabe-ito 8-color categorical — safe for all common types viridis sequential — perceptually uniform rdbu diverging — safe for red/green colorblind test convert your chart to grayscale. if it still reads, it's accessible. accessibility accessibility: readable by everyone ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice green on red, hue only contrast 1.4, fails 4.5:1 okabe-ito or viridis colorblind-safe palettes color as the only signal colorblind readers lose it add shape, pattern, labels do not rely on color alone no alt text, tiny fonts screen readers get nothing alt text, 12px+ text, table contrast at least 4.5:1 result: some readers are excluded result: chart works for all viewers mistake about 8% of men cannot tell red from green. best practice navy on white: 12.6 passes with ease. test convert the chart to grayscale. if it still reads, it is safe. three fixes to apply 1 pick safe palettes okabe-ito, viridis, rdbu. 2 add a second cue shape, pattern or direct labels. 3 check contrast 4.5:1 text; alt text on every chart.
m5-story-overview: idea a chart shows data. a story shows what to do about it. analysts who tell stories get their recommendations acted on. the 3-part arc part purpose example setup what we were trying to learn "we wanted to know if the new checkout lifts conversion." tension what surprised us or what's at stake "conversion rose 0.3pp — but the test isn't significant yet." resolution what to do next "extend the test one more week before deciding." story arc 1 setup 2 tension 3 resolution rule never end a presentation on a chart. end on a decision. storytelling story: end on a decision ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice show the chart and stop data without a so what setup: what we wanted to learn does new checkout lift conversion skip the tension conversion +0.3 pts, not significant tension: what surprised us only +0.3 pts, not yet significant end on a chart no recommendation made resolution: what next extend the test one more week result: recommendation not acted on result: clear decision for the room mistake a chart shows data; a story shows action. best practice fill one row per part before building slides. rule of thumb never end on a chart. end on a decision. three fixes to apply 1 write setup the question we set out to answer. 2 state tension the surprise or the stake. 3 give resolution the next action to take.
m5-narrative: key checks narrative arc ✓ cut to three keep charts that support the ask. ✓ set up the gap what you expected vs what you saw. ✓ close with action so i recommend z. definition the narrative arc is the emotional shape of your finding. it carries the audience from "so what?" to "now what?" 4-beat structure context — "we expected x." conflict — "but we saw y." evidence — "here's the chart that shows why." action — "so i recommend z." worked example — a/b test applied context: "we expected the new checkout to lift conversion by 0.5pp." conflict: "the variant delivered +0.3pp, but our test isn't statistically significant yet." evidence: "here's the ci — it straddles zero." action: "extend the test one more week before launching." anti-pattern "here are 14 charts" is not a story. pick the 3 charts that support the recommendation and drop the rest. narrative arc narrative arc: four beats ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice here are 14 charts a pile of charts, no story pick the 3 supporting charts drop the rest skip the expectation context missing: expected +0.5 pts context then conflict expected +0.5, got +0.3 pts end on the ci chart no action stated evidence then action ci (-0.2, 0.8) so run 1 more week result: audience asks so what result: so what leads to now what mistake evidence with no path to action. best practice one line per beat, with real numbers. rule of thumb context, conflict, evidence, action: one line each. three fixes to apply 1 cut to three keep charts that support the ask. 2 set up the gap what you expected vs what you saw. 3 close with action so i recommend z.
m5-headline: key checks headline first ✓ rewrite last report first sentence is the ask. ✓ order by audience exec: headline first; analyst: question first. ✓ delete the rest cut what does not support the ask. rule lead with the takeaway. method and detail come after. executive vs analyst ordering for an executive for an analyst peer headline question so what data source recommended action method supporting chart result method (if asked) caveats and next steps headline first headline first: lead with the answer ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice open with the question executive waits for the answer headline first takeaway in the first sentence method before result source and method up front so what, then action recommendation second recommendation buried last after caveats and charts method if asked chart supports, not leads result: execs stop reading early result: decision in the first lines mistake detail first loses the busy reader. best practice analysts keep method and caveats. rule of thumb lead with the takeaway. method comes after. three fixes to apply 1 rewrite last report first sentence is the ask. 2 order by audience exec: headline first; analyst: question first. 3 delete the rest cut what does not support the ask.
m5-5sec: key checks 5-second rule ✓ write the takeaway replace the variable-name title. ✓ delete the rest fewer elements, bigger key number. ✓ log the test tester, reply, point understood. definition if a stranger can't get the point of your chart in five seconds, it's not finished. how to run the test show the chart to a colleague for exactly 5 seconds. hide it. ask: "what was the point?" if they can't answer, the chart failed — not the colleague. what usually fixes it a takeaway title instead of a variable name. one highlighted element (color, annotation, or callout). fewer elements — delete anything that isn't the point. bigger font on the key number. try it run this test on the last dashboard you shared. most people find 2–3 charts that fail. 5-second rule 5-second rule: can a stranger get it ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice variable name as title funnel: lots of boxes takeaway title say what happened everything highlighted no single focus one highlighted element color, note or callout never test on a stranger blame the colleague show 5 sec, hide, ask what was the point? result: the chart fails the test result: point understood quickly mistake most dashboards have 2-3 failing charts. best practice if they cannot answer, the chart failed. test show for exactly 5 seconds, then ask for the point. three fixes to apply 1 write the takeaway replace the variable-name title. 2 delete the rest fewer elements, bigger key number. 3 log the test tester, reply, point understood.
m5-cta: key checks call to action ✓ name the action say what you want the room to do. ✓ set scope and date who, how many, by when. ✓ add a measure how we will know it worked. rule every chart should answer "so what?" and "now what?" — even if the answer is "keep monitoring." strong vs weak ctas weak strong "conversion is up." "roll out the new checkout to 100% of traffic." "churn is a problem." "launch a win-back campaign for the 340 churned users." "more research needed." "run a second experiment with 20k more users." template # fill in the blanks because we observed __[finding]__, and because it matters for __[kpi]__, i recommend we __[specific action]__ by __[date]__, and we'll know it worked if __[measure]__. common mistake ending on "any questions?" without ever stating what you want the room to do. call to action call to action: name the next step ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice conversion is up. finding with no action roll out checkout to 100% action, scope and date: mar 31 churn is a problem. no scope, no owner win-back for 340 churned users by apr 15 more research needed. nothing asked of the room run a second experiment with 20k more users result: room leaves without a decision result: clear ask and a measure mistake weak calls to action stall decisions. best practice state how you will know it worked. template because we saw x, i recommend y by date, success = z. three fixes to apply 1 name the action say what you want the room to do. 2 set scope and date who, how many, by when. 3 add a measure how we will know it worked.
m5-dash-overview: definition a dashboard is a self-serve view of the metrics a team needs to make decisions, refreshed on a schedule. three types type purpose refresh operational real-time monitor — is anything broken? live / hourly analytical explore a question — why did this happen? daily / weekly strategic track long-term goals — are we on track? monthly / quarterly dashboard purposes operational analytical strategic rule one dashboard, one question. mixing operational and strategic views creates noise. dashboards dashboards: one dashboard, one question ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice live monitor mixed with goals operational plus strategic operational: is anything broken hourly no named question data dump, not a decision analytical: where we lose people daily one refresh for all views hourly vs monthly needs differ strategic: are we on track monthly result: noise, no decision result: each view answers one question mistake mixed purposes create noise. best practice one audience and one question each. rule of thumb one dashboard, one question. do not mix types. three fixes to apply 1 pick the type operational, analytical or strategic. 2 write the question put it at the top of the page. 3 set the refresh live or hourly, daily, monthly.
m5-layout: rule the eye starts top-left. put the most important number there. z-pattern layout reading order of a dashboard 1 — kpi headline 2 — supporting metric 3 — trend chart (the story) 4 — breakdown table / filters below hierarchy rules most important first. top-left of the screen. related metrics grouped. don't split a kpi from its drivers. consistent sizes. equal-weight tiles for equal-weight metrics. whitespace. cramped dashboards are unreadable. test cover the bottom half. does the top half tell the whole story? layout and hierarchy layout: put the headline top-left ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice kpi buried in the lower right eye starts top-left revenue kpi at position 1 primary decision metric kpi split from its drivers revenue far from conversion conversion kpi at position 2 group related metrics cramped tiles, uneven sizes no whitespace trend line 3, table 4 equal tiles, whitespace result: reader hunts for the point result: story reads top to bottom mistake top half must tell the story. best practice z-pattern reading order. test cover the bottom half. does the top tell the story? three fixes to apply 1 most important first top-left of the screen. 2 group drivers keep kpi next to its drivers. 3 match sizes equal weight, equal tile size.
m5-kpi: anatomy a kpi card is the atomic unit of a dashboard: big number, delta, and sparkline trend. anatomy kpi card monthly revenue $1.24m ▲ +12.4% vs last month rules big number. 2–3× the size of any other text. delta vs comparison. "vs last month", "vs target", "vs same month last year". direction with color — but not color alone (use ▲/▼ symbols too). sparkline to show shape of the trend, not exact values. anti-pattern a kpi card without a comparison tells you nothing — is $1.24m good? kpi cards kpi cards: number, delta, trend ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice $1.24m with no comparison is it good or bad? +12.4% vs last month delta vs a comparison big number same size as text no focal point number 2-3x larger big number is the focus green or red only for direction colorblind readers lose it triangle up/down plus color not color alone result: card tells you nothing result: status clear in a glance mistake a number without a comparison is empty. best practice sparkline shows shape, not exact values. anatomy big number + delta + sparkline = kpi card. three fixes to apply 1 add a baseline vs last month, target or last year. 2 size the number 2-3 times larger than other text. 3 use symbols too triangle plus color for direction.
m5-filters: key checks filters & drilldowns ✓ limit to three keep the ones the team uses. ✓ set defaults choose the view they most need. ✓ add drilldown click a bar to see its rows. rule filters exist so the viewer can answer their own question — not so you can avoid picking a default view. global vs local filter type scope example global applies to whole dashboard date range, region local applies to one tile top-n on a single chart drilldown patterns click a bar → see its rows — instant detail without a new report. hierarchy — year → quarter → month → day. cross-filter — clicking one chart filters the others. anti-pattern filter sprawl — 12 dropdowns on one dashboard. pick the 3 filters the team actually uses. filters and drilldowns filters: a few that people use ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice 12 dropdowns on one page filter sprawl pick the 3 filters in use date range, region, top-n no default view chosen viewer builds from scratch sensible defaults last 30 days, all regions every filter global top-n on one tile affects all global vs local scope top-n 10 on one tile result: viewer lost in controls result: self-serve answers mistake filters used to avoid choosing a default. best practice drill from bar to rows; hierarchy year to day. rule of thumb filters let viewers answer their own question. three fixes to apply 1 limit to three keep the ones the team uses. 2 set defaults choose the view they most need. 3 add drilldown click a bar to see its rows.
m5-mobile: reality most executives will open your dashboard on a phone, in a meeting, on 4g. design for that first. rules vertical stack — mobile reads top-to-bottom. one number per screen — the biggest kpi takes the fold. tap-friendly targets — filters need ≥ 44px height. charts over tables — tables don't fit on phones. load time under 3 sec. compress images and cache aggressively. desktop vs mobile same data, two layouts desktop (grid) mobile (stack) test open your dashboard on your own phone. if you have to pinch and zoom, redesign it. mobile and responsive mobile: design for the smallest screen ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice wide table of 12 columns needs pinch and zoom vertical stack, charts over tables one number per screen small filter buttons under 44px, hard to tap tap targets 44px or taller filters easy to hit heavy tile over 3 seconds trend chart loads slowly load in under 3 sec compress and cache result: execs give up on a phone result: readable in a meeting mistake most open it on a phone, on 4g. best practice test each tile on a real phone. test open it on your phone. if you pinch and zoom, redesign. three fixes to apply 1 stack vertically biggest kpi takes the fold. 2 size the taps at least 44px high. 3 check load time under 3 seconds per tile.
m5-checklist: use before every share 10 checks. takes 2 minutes. saves a meeting. the 10 checks does the title state the takeaway , not the variable? is the chart type the right one for the question? does the axis start at zero (bars) or is truncation honest and labeled? is there one highlighted element showing what matters? are axis labels in units the audience recognizes? can a colorblind viewer still read it in grayscale? have you removed every non-essential element ? does the chart have a 5-second takeaway ? is there a clear call to action ? is the source and date shown? checklist flow chart type design story accessibility most common miss chart #1 — the title. a great chart with a lazy title still fails. pre-publish checklist pre-publish: 10 checks before you share ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice lazy title on a great chart check 1 is the most missed title states the takeaway not the variable share without a source line no source or date source and date shown check 10 of 10 skip the grayscale test colorblind viewer cannot read grayscale and 5-second test plus a clear call to action result: avoidable rework meeting result: ships at 9 of 10 or higher mistake a great chart with a lazy title fails. best practice takes 2 minutes and saves a meeting. rule of thumb score 1 per check passed. ship at 9 or higher. three fixes to apply 1 run all 10 type, axis, color, labels. 2 score it one point per pass. 3 fix the title first it is the most common miss.
m5-recap: module flow 1 charts 2 design 3 story 4 dashboards the five lines match the chart to the question — comparison, trend, relationship, distribution, part-to-whole. design is subtraction — remove anything that isn't the point. title = takeaway. lead with the finding, not the variable. every chart ends with a call to action — "so what / now what". dashboards serve a decision , not a data dump. carry-forward rules if a chart doesn't change a decision, cut it. bar charts start at zero. always. run the 5-second test on every chart before you share it. design for the smallest screen first. next you now have the full analytics toolkit: types, data, stats, and visuals. time to build a portfolio project end-to-end.

m6-dataset: key checks dataset used ✓ list the grain one row per what, for each table. ✓ pick one level sum at one grain only. ✓ check keys match the key on both sides. schema e-commerce tables reused from module 5 for continuity. tables & columns table columns grain customers customer_id, name, city, state, created_at 1 row per customer orders order_id, customer_id, order_date, status, total_amount 1 row per order order_items order_id, product_id, quantity, unit_price 1 row per item per order products product_id, product_name, category, price 1 row per product payments payment_id, order_id, payment_date, method, amount 1 row per payment key insight orders has one row per order, but order_items has many rows per order. joining them multiplies rows and can overcount revenue. dataset used dataset: know each table's grain ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice join orders to order_items one order, many item rows read the grain column first orders: 1 row per order sum(total_amount) after join order total repeated per item sum items or orders, not both pick the right grain assume 1 row per customer sam lee has no orders know the join keys customer_id, order_id, product_id result: revenue is overcounted result: totals at the right grain mistake orders is 1 row per order, items many per order. best practice know grain before you join. rule of thumb know the grain of every table before joining. three fixes to apply 1 list the grain one row per what, for each table. 2 pick one level sum at one grain only. 3 check keys match the key on both sides.
m6-granularity: rule always confirm the grain (level of detail) of each table before joining. grain examples table grain one row per orders order-level order order_items item-level item within an order customers customer-level customer visual — row multiplication orders (1 row) × order_items (3 rows) = 3 rows orders 1 row per order × order_items many rows per order = 3× rows summing order.total_amount after the join overcounts revenue. fix grain issues pre-aggregate order_items to order level before joining. use distinct on order_id when appropriate. use window functions to compute per-order metrics without collapsing rows. test pick a known order_id and verify row duplication after the join. granularity grain: rows multiply on join ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice join orders to order_items 1 row x 3 rows = 3 rows pre-aggregate items to order one row per order first sum(o.total_amount) post-join order 101 counted twice distinct on order_id or window per-order metrics assume the join is safe never checked a known order_id test one known order_id verify row duplication result: revenue overcounted (3x) result: revenue matches the source mistake order total repeats on every item row. best practice confirm grain before joining. rule of thumb always confirm the grain of each table before joining. three fixes to apply 1 aggregate first roll items up to order level. 2 use distinct on order_id where it fits. 3 spot-check pick an order, count rows after the join.
m6-joins-matter: key checks why joins matter in analytics ✓ map the tables list tables the question needs. ✓ choose the join inner or left, on purpose. ✓ explain it join type and reason, in plain words. reality real analytics questions almost always span multiple tables. why correct joins matter joins connect customers, orders, items, products, and payments correctly. correct joins prevent kpi errors like double counting or missing records. the type of join changes meaning: inner vs left alters totals and coverage. analysts must explain join logic clearly to non-technical stakeholders. example — "revenue by category" -- requires 3 tables joined correctly select p.category, sum(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) as revenue from orders o join order_items oi on o.order_id = oi.order_id join products p on oi.product_id = p.product_id where o.status = 'completed' group by p.category; communication when sharing a query, state which join type you used and why. it builds trust. why joins matter joins: the type changes the meaning ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice pick any join type inner vs left changes totals choose join to match question coverage vs valid relations leave out a bridge table category needs 3 tables orders to items to products revenue by category share sql with no explanation stakeholders cannot trust it state join type and why builds trust result: kpi errors, missing records result: trusted, explainable kpis mistake wrong join, wrong double count or gap. best practice say which join and why. rule of thumb real questions span tables; join type changes totals. three fixes to apply 1 map the tables list tables the question needs. 2 choose the join inner or left, on purpose. 3 explain it join type and reason, in plain words.
m6-inner-join: definition returns rows where matching keys exist in both tables. when to use you only want records with valid relationships on both sides. metrics that require full valid relationships (e.g., paid orders). most common join used in reporting queries. visual inner join = intersection a b only matching rows non-matching rows dropped live example -- orders with a customer record select o.order_id, c.name, o.total_amount from orders o inner join customers c on o.customer_id = c.customer_id; watch out inner join drops non-matching rows — this can hide data quality issues if you're not careful. inner join inner join: silently drops non-matches ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice inner join customers to orders sam lee (no orders) vanishes inner only for valid pairs paid orders with a customer use it for coverage counts all customers expected left join for full coverage keep sam lee visible never compare row counts hidden data quality issue compare counts pre and post 5 order rows come back result: missing rows go unnoticed result: intentional row coverage mistake non-matching rows are dropped. best practice use when both sides must exist. rule of thumb inner = intersection. non-matches are dropped. three fixes to apply 1 ask what to keep matches only, or all left rows? 2 count before after compare rows to spot loss. 3 switch to left when coverage matters.
m6-left-join: definition returns all rows from the left table and matches from the right when present. when to use finding missing relationships — e.g., orders with no payment record. data quality checks and funnel analysis. defensive default when you don't want to lose left-side records. visual left join = all of a + matches from b a b all of a nulls where b has no match live example — orders with no payment -- find orders missing a payment record select o.order_id, o.total_amount, p.payment_id from orders o left join payments p on o.order_id = p.order_id where p.payment_id is null; pattern the where right_key is null filter is the classic "anti-join" for finding missing records. left join left join: keep all, find the gaps ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice inner join payments to orders unpaid orders disappear left join orders to payments keeps every order skip the null check no way to find the missing where p.payment_id is null classic anti-join lose left rows in analysis funnel drops a step default when keeping the base data checks and funnels result: missing payments stay hidden result: missing records found mistake gaps are only visible when kept. best practice nulls show where the right side has no match. pattern left join + where right_key is null = anti-join. three fixes to apply 1 start from base put the full list on the left. 2 filter null keys is null finds the gaps. 3 use for funnels counts per step stay intact.
m6-right-join: definition returns all rows from the right table and matches from the left when present. when to use less common; many queries can be rewritten as left join by flipping tables. useful if the right table is considered the full base list. audits where payments might exist without corresponding orders. visual right join = all of b + matches from a a b all of b nulls where a has no match live example -- payments with or without a matching order select p.payment_id, p.amount, o.order_id from orders o right join payments p on o.order_id = p.order_id; best practice most analysts standardize on left join for readability. flip the tables instead of using right join. right join right join: flip the tables instead ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice mix left and right in one query reader tracks two directions standardize on left join one direction everywhere right join orders to payments base table is hard to spot flip tables instead payments left join orders reach for it by default rarely needed right for audits only payments without an order result: harder code review result: same result, clearer sql mistake mixed directions confuse readers. best practice same rows as the swapped left join. best practice write left join only; swap the tables. three fixes to apply 1 keep one direction always left for readability. 2 swap the tables put the full list first. 3 audit with care use right only when needed.
m6-full-outer-join: definition returns all rows from both tables, matching where keys align. when to use reconciliation between two sources (orders vs payments). comparing and auditing data pipelines. finding records that exist in one table but not the other. visual full outer join = all rows from both a b all rows nulls on both sides possible live example — reconciliation -- compare orders and payments side by side select o.order_id, o.total_amount, p.payment_id, p.amount from orders o full outer join payments p on o.order_id = p.order_id; compatibility not supported natively in older mysql versions. use a union of left and right joins as a workaround. full outer join full outer join: reconcile both sides ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice left join orders to payments misses payment 905, no order full outer join on order_id both unmatched sides appear assume sources always agree order 104 has no payment check null on each side 104 unpaid, 905 orphan run full join in old mysql not natively supported union of left and right workaround for old mysql result: one-sided mismatches missed result: both gaps found mistake only one side is checked. best practice use for reconciling two sources. rule of thumb reconcile with full outer; nulls mark mismatches. three fixes to apply 1 join both ways keep rows from each table. 2 read the nulls left null vs right null. 3 check compatibility use union if unsupported.
m6-cross-join: definition produces every possible combination of rows between two sets (cartesian product). when to use building grids like date × category for reporting. creating a date scaffold then left joining metrics onto it. small lookup tables where every combination is needed. visual cross join = every combination dates mon tue wed categories books games music result (9 rows) mon · books mon · games mon · music tue · books tue · games tue · music wed · ... × = live example — date scaffold -- build a grid of every date × every category with date_scaffold as ( select generate_series ( '2024-01-01' ::date, '2024-12-31' ::date, '1 day' ) as d ) select d.d, c.category from date_scaffold d cross join ( select distinct category from products) c; caution can explode in size quickly — 1m × 1m = 1 trillion rows. use only on small tables. cross join cross join: grids, not big tables ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice cross join two big tables 1m x 1m = 1 trillion rows cross join small lookups 3 days x 3 categories = 9 group by only, no scaffold days with no sales vanish date scaffold, then left join zeros show on the grid join by accident, no on surprise cartesian product use on purpose every combination needed result: query explodes, gaps remain result: complete grid, zeros included mistake combinations multiply fast. best practice build date x category grids safely. caution rows = a x b. use only on small tables. three fixes to apply 1 keep sets small dates and categories only. 2 build a scaffold cross join, then left join facts. 3 estimate rows multiply the table sizes first.
m6-multiple-conditions: key checks multiple join conditions ✓ add a second key amount, date or version. ✓ do not over-filter each condition may drop valid rows. ✓ validate compare row counts to expected. definition sometimes one key is not enough to match rows correctly. when you need multiple conditions joining on order_id and amount to avoid incorrect matches. joining on dates and versions when tables have history. avoiding incorrect many-to-many joins when a single key has duplicates. live example -- match order_items to payments on order_id and amount select oi.order_id, oi.quantity * oi.unit_price as line_total, p.amount from order_items oi join payments p on oi.order_id = p.order_id and (oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) = p.amount; test too many restrictive conditions can accidentally drop valid matches. always validate with sample records and counts. multiple join conditions join keys: one key is not always enough ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice join on order_id only duplicate keys give wrong matches on order_id and amount narrow the match too many strict conditions valid matches get dropped add a date window payment within 3 days skip validation no sample check or counts validate with samples compare counts before and after result: wrong or missing matches result: correct, tested matches mistake many-to-many joins inflate rows. best practice order 105 paid after 8 days: no match. test more conditions need counts and a sample check. three fixes to apply 1 add a second key amount, date or version. 2 do not over-filter each condition may drop valid rows. 3 validate compare row counts to expected.
m6-self-join: key checks self join ✓ use less-than compare keys with less-than to drop mirrored pairs. ✓ try lag first window functions are often cleaner. ✓ alias clearly name each role of the table. definition a table joins to itself to compare or relate its own rows. when to use hierarchical data like employees with managers. comparing a customer's first order to later orders. "next purchase" or "previous status" within the same table. live example — list every earlier order for the customer -- this returns all earlier orders, not only the immediately previous one select o1.order_id as current_order, o1.order_date as current_date, o2.order_id as previous_order, o2.order_date as previous_date from orders o1 left join orders o2 on o1.customer_id = o2.customer_id and o2.order_date < o1.order_date; modern alternative window functions (lag) are often cleaner. but self-joins are still important to understand. self join self join: pair rows once ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice self-join customers, no filter ana-sam and sam-ana both appear a.customer_id before b.customer_id each pair once join on earlier date alone all earlier orders, not just prior consider lag for previous order cleaner than a self-join skip aliases same table, two roles, confusing alias o1 and o2 current_order, previous_order result: mirrored pairs, extra rows result: clean pairs and history mistake each pair shows twice. best practice self-joins: employees and managers, next purchase. rule of thumb self-join with a.id before b.id to avoid mirrors. three fixes to apply 1 use less-than compare keys with less-than to drop mirrored pairs. 2 try lag first window functions are often cleaner. 3 alias clearly name each role of the table.
m6-double-counting: critical joining orders to order_items multiplies rows when orders have multiple items. summing order.total_amount after the join can double or triple revenue. example of the trap one order × three items = inflated total orders order_id = 100 total_amount = $300 order_items 100, itema, $100 100, itemb, $100 100, itemc, $100 naive join 100 · $300 (itema) 100 · $300 (itemb) 100 · $300 (itemc) sum = $900 correct revenue: $300. naive sum: $900. 3× overcount. fixes pre-aggregate order_items to order level before joining. use distinct on order_id when appropriate. sum at the correct grain — sum order_items only, or sum orders only, not both. test with a known order_id and verify row duplication. rule always know the grain of both tables before you join. join double counting double counting: 3 items, 3x revenue ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice join orders to order_items $300 order repeats on 3 rows pre-aggregate items first one row per order sum(o.total_amount) after join $900 instead of $300 sum at one grain items only or orders only no spot check order 101 twice: 720, not 600 test a known order_id verify row duplication result: revenue 3x overcounted result: correct revenue of $300 mistake sum of both tables at once is wrong. best practice grain of both tables known first. rule of thumb know the grain of both tables before you join. three fixes to apply 1 pre-aggregate roll items up to order level. 2 sum one side never sum both sides of a join. 3 spot-check compare to a known total.
m6-subquery-why: key checks why subqueries matter ✓ filter on derived having count(*) at least 3 inside the in subquery. ✓ nest the average compute it live, do not hard-code the 120. ✓ practice a common interview topic: master it. definition a subquery is a query nested inside another query. what they enable filter based on derived metrics — e.g., customers with ≥ 3 orders. compute benchmarks or intermediate results inside a query. simplify logic that would be complex with only joins. used in both select and where clauses for flexible conditions. example — customers with 3+ orders select customer_id, name from customers where customer_id in ( select customer_id from orders group by customer_id having count(*) >= 3 ); interview tip many analytics interview questions rely on subqueries. master them. why subqueries subqueries: filter on derived metrics ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice join and group just to filter convoluted logic in with group by having customers with 3 or more orders hard-code the average 120 breaks when data changes compute avg in a subquery orders above average skip subqueries entirely interview questions need them use in select and where flexible conditions result: brittle, hard-to-read sql result: dynamic, readable filters mistake static values go stale as the data changes. best practice derived metrics update with the data. rule of thumb a subquery computes a value, the outer query uses it. three fixes to apply 1 filter on derived having count(*) at least 3 inside the in subquery. 2 nest the average compute it live, do not hard-code the 120. 3 practice a common interview topic: master it.
m6-scalar-subquery: key checks scalar subquery ✓ return one cell one row, one column. ✓ compute, do not type benchmark from live data. ✓ match filters same status in both places. definition a subquery that returns exactly one value (one row, one column). when to use in select to compute a constant benchmark value. in where for comparisons against a single computed number. overall averages, totals, or thresholds used across the result set. live example — compare each order to overall average -- flag orders above the overall average select order_id, total_amount, (select avg(total_amount) from orders where status = 'completed' ) as avg_order, total_amount - (select avg(total_amount) from orders where status = 'completed' ) as diff_from_avg from orders where status = 'completed' ; rule the subquery must return exactly one value, or the query errors. use limit 1 if needed. scalar subquery scalar subquery: exactly one value ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice subquery returns many rows query errors out select avg(total_amount) one row, one column hard-code the 120 average stale when data changes use it in where or select compare to a benchmark repeat the avg subquery inline same filter written twice limit 1 if needed same status filter both places result: errors or stale benchmarks result: one benchmark, reused mistake scalar needs one row and one column. best practice flag orders above the overall average. rule a scalar subquery returns one value, or the query errors. three fixes to apply 1 return one cell one row, one column. 2 compute, do not type benchmark from live data. 3 match filters same status in both places.
m6-correlated-subquery: key checks correlated subquery ✓ prefer exists for has-record checks. ✓ add an index on the correlated key. ✓ consider a join often the faster form. definition a subquery that references columns from the outer query's row. characteristics logically executed once per outer row (optimizer may optimize this). commonly used with exists to check if related records exist. useful for conditions like "customers who have at least one completed order." can be slower if not indexed or if written inefficiently. live example — customers with recent orders -- customers who ordered in the last 30 days select c.customer_id, c.name from customers c where ( select count(*) from orders o where o.customer_id = c.customer_id and o.order_date >= current_date - interval '30 days' ) > 0; performance tip correlated subqueries often rewrite as joins or exists for better performance. correlated subquery correlated: re-runs for each row ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice count(*) over zero for existence counts every match use exists for has-order stops at the first match no index on customer_id inner query rescans orders index the join column customer_id in orders use on every large table per-row logic gets slow rewrite as a join when big often faster result: slow query on large tables result: same answer, faster mistake inner query re-runs per outer row. best practice use correlation for per-row benchmarks. performance tip rewrite as join or exists for speed. three fixes to apply 1 prefer exists for has-record checks. 2 add an index on the correlated key. 3 consider a join often the faster form.
m6-exists: key checks exists ✓ test existence ask if a row exists, do not count rows. ✓ correlate tie the inner query to the outer row. ✓ write select 1 cleaner than listing columns nobody reads. definition exists returns true if its subquery returns at least one row. when to use testing existence of related records efficiently. more robust than in for relationship checks in many scenarios. stops evaluating as soon as it finds a match — often faster. segmentation, activation, and retention filters. live example — customers with at least one completed order select c.customer_id, c.name from customers c where exists ( select 1 from orders o where o.customer_id = c.customer_id and o.status = 'completed' ); pattern select 1 inside exists — the optimizer doesn't care what you select, only whether rows exist. exists exists: stop at the first match ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice in with a big subquery builds the full list first where exists (select 1 ...) true at the first match count(*) over zero as a test counts every row link on c.customer_id correlated to the outer row select columns inside exists the optimizer ignores them select 1 inside only row existence matters result: slower, noisier relation checks result: faster yes/no per customer mistake counting is overkill for yes or no. best practice great for activation and retention filters. pattern select 1 inside exists; the optimizer needs rows only. three fixes to apply 1 test existence ask if a row exists, do not count rows. 2 correlate tie the inner query to the outer row. 3 write select 1 cleaner than listing columns nobody reads.
m6-in-vs-exists: key checks in vs exists ✓ avoid not in when nulls are possible. ✓ use exists for has-orders, has-payments. ✓ keep in small short fixed value lists. rule use in for small static lists. use exists for relational checks against another table. comparison dimension in exists best for small, static value lists related records in another table null handling can behave unexpectedly with nulls safe — checks existence only performance builds full list first short-circuits on first match index use depends often leverages indexes on join key live examples -- in (good for small static list) select * from orders where status in ( 'completed' , 'shipped' , 'processing' ); -- exists (better for relational check) select * from customers c where exists ( select 1 from orders o where o.customer_id = c.customer_id and o.status = 'completed' ); analyst default prefer exists for "has orders" / "has payments" style conditions. in vs exists not in with null returns zero rows ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice not in (1,2,3,null) returns 0 rows not exists (...) returns 1 (sam lee), safe in on a big subquery builds the full list first exists for relation checks short-circuits at first match exists for a small static list overkill for 3 statuses in for a short static list completed, shipped, processing result: sam lee missing, wrong list result: right rows, null-safe mistake a null in the list breaks not in. best practice prefer exists for has orders/payments. rule of thumb in for small static lists, exists for related tables. three fixes to apply 1 avoid not in when nulls are possible. 2 use exists for has-orders, has-payments. 3 keep in small short fixed value lists.
m6-cte-basics: key checks ctes (common table expressions) ✓ break into steps one idea per cte. ✓ name by content completed_orders, monthly. ✓ define once reference many times. definition ctes use the with keyword to define named subqueries. why ctes improve readability by breaking complex logic into steps. can be reused within the same main query for clarity. like temporary views that exist only for the lifetime of the query. standard best practice for structuring analytical sql. live example with completed_orders as ( select * from orders where status = 'completed' ) select customer_id, sum (total_amount) as lifetime_value from completed_orders group by customer_id; style name ctes after what they contain, not after the query step: completed_orders beats cte1 . cte basics ctes: name the steps ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice nested subqueries 3 levels deep reader decodes inside-out with completed_orders as (...) step 1 named and readable name it cte1 says nothing about contents name by what it contains completed_orders beats cte1 repeat the same subquery copy and paste filters reuse within the main query define once result: sql hard to read and fix result: readable, reusable steps mistake logic stays tangled. best practice a cte lives for one query only. style name ctes after what they contain. three fixes to apply 1 break into steps one idea per cte. 2 name by content completed_orders, monthly. 3 define once reference many times.
m6-cte-chain: best practice structure complex queries as a chain of named ctes, each doing one thing. the 4-step pattern cte 1 — base filters (status, date range) to reduce data volume early. cte 2 — join dimensions like customers or products to enrich rows. cte 3 — aggregate to the grain you need (daily, monthly, customer-level). final select — format columns, sorting, and final calculations. visual cte chain 1 base 2 join dims 3 aggregate 4 final select live example with base_orders as ( select * from orders where status = 'completed' and order_date >= current_date - interval '90 days' ), enriched as ( select o.*, c.state, c.name as customer_name from base_orders o join customers c on o.customer_id = c.customer_id ), by_state as ( select state, count (*) as orders, sum (total_amount) as revenue from enriched group by state ) select * from by_state order by revenue desc ; debugging when something breaks, run each cte separately to isolate the issue. cte chain cte chain: one job per step ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice one giant select filters, joins and totals tangled base cte filters first status and date range filter late, after joins joins run on all rows join dimensions in cte 2 customers, state debug the whole query at once cannot find the broken step aggregate then final select by_state, order by revenue result: slow, fragile queries result: clear steps, easy debugging mistake hard to isolate what went wrong. best practice check row counts after each cte. 4-step pattern base, join, aggregate, final select. three fixes to apply 1 filter early cut volume in the first cte. 2 one job each filter, enrich, aggregate. 3 run each cte isolate the broken step.
m6-temp-tables: key checks temporary tables ✓ store once reuse heavy results. ✓ start with ctes simpler for most work. ✓ add indexes on the temp table. definition temporary tables physically store intermediate results for a session. when to use you reuse the same heavy intermediate result many times. the database would otherwise recompute expensive work. you need to add indexes to the intermediate result. live example create temp table recent_orders as select * from orders where order_date >= current_date - interval '90 days' ; -- now use it multiple times without recomputation select count (*) from recent_orders; select sum (total_amount) from recent_orders; practical in many analyst workflows, ctes are sufficient. use temp tables when performance demands it. temporary tables temp tables: store heavy results once ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice recompute a heavy result query repeated many times create temp table recent_orders reuse without recomputing temp table for a tiny step a cte is enough use ctes for light steps temp when performance demands no index on the temp table later queries stay slow index the intermediate result faster repeat queries result: wasted compute or clutter result: fast reuse within a session mistake wrong tool for the job. best practice stored for the session only. rule of thumb cte by default; temp table when the cost demands. three fixes to apply 1 store once reuse heavy results. 2 start with ctes simpler for most work. 3 add indexes on the temp table.
m6-recursive-cte: key checks recursive cte ✓ start at the root anchor the top level. ✓ step down join children, depth + 1. ✓ cap the depth guard against cycles. definition a recursive cte allows a cte to reference itself to build hierarchical results. when to use traversing trees such as category hierarchies or org charts. pathfinding or graph-like data problems. less common in ecommerce but valuable to know. live example — category hierarchy with recursive category_tree as ( -- anchor: top-level categories select category_id, category_name, parent_id, 1 as depth from categories where parent_id is null union all -- recursive: children of the previous level select c.category_id, c.category_name, c.parent_id, ct.depth + 1 from categories c join category_tree ct on c.parent_id = ct.category_id ) select * from category_tree order by depth, category_id; watch out add a depth limit or a termination condition — infinite loops are possible. recursive cte recursive cte: always end the loop ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice recursive part with no stop infinite loop possible add a depth limit depth + 1, stop at a cap forget the anchor row parent_id is null missing anchor at the top where parent_id is null use for flat data not a hierarchy union all the next level join child to category_tree result: runaway query result: full tree in depth order mistake cycles never end. best practice org charts and category hierarchies. watch out anchor + recursion + termination condition. three fixes to apply 1 start at the root anchor the top level. 2 step down join children, depth + 1. 3 cap the depth guard against cycles.
m6-window-intro: definition window functions compute values across related rows without collapsing them. how they differ from group by group by collapses rows into one per group. window functions keep the original rows and add a computed column. perfect for ranking, running totals, moving averages, and cohort logic. syntax revolves around over() with optional partition by and order by . visual group by vs window function group by a a a sum window a · 10 a · 20 a · 30 a · 10 · 60 a · 20 · 60 a · 30 · 60 analyst essential window functions are the single most valuable skill for intermediate sql. window functions window functions: keep the rows ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice group by to add an average collapses rows avg(total_amount) over () average beside every order join back to the total extra subquery step partition by and order by per-group logic skip window functions single most valuable skill ranking, running totals moving averages, cohorts result: detail lost, sql longer result: detail and total together mistake one row per group only. best practice window keeps rows and adds a column. rule of thumb group by collapses rows; a window keeps them. three fixes to apply 1 use over() compute without collapsing. 2 add partition by per customer or category. 3 add order by for running calculations.
m6-over-partition: key checks over() & partition by ✓ partition group rows by customer so totals restart. ✓ order set the row order for running calculations. ✓ frame choose which rows count in the window. definition over() specifies that a function is a window function. the three parts partition by divides rows into groups (like categories or customers) while keeping rows separate. order by inside over defines the ordering for running calculations. window frame controls which rows are included (e.g. rows between 6 preceding and current row). live example sum (total_amount) over ( partition by customer_id order by order_date rows between unbounded preceding and current row ) as cumulative_spend read it as "for each customer, in date order, sum everything from the start up to the current row." over and partition by over(): read the three parts ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice over (order by) for customer sum runs across all customers partition by customer_id restarts per customer no partition by one big group order by order_date defines the running order ignore the frame rows between left implicit rows unbounded preceding start to current row result: totals mix customers result: per-customer cumulative spend mistake cumulative spans every customer. best practice each row keeps detail and a total. read it as for each customer, in date order, sum up to this row. three fixes to apply 1 partition group rows by customer so totals restart. 2 order set the row order for running calculations. 3 frame choose which rows count in the window.
m6-row-number: key checks row_number ✓ add a tiebreaker order_id after the date. ✓ partition one count per group. ✓ filter in a cte select where rn = 1. definition row_number assigns a unique sequential number within a partition. common uses find the "first" or "latest" row per group (e.g., per customer). deduplicating records. building snapshots. live example — first order per customer with ranked as ( select order_id, customer_id, order_date, total_amount, row_number () over ( partition by customer_id order by order_date asc ) as rn from orders ) select * from ranked where rn = 1 ; deterministic only with unique order by if two rows have the same order_date, row_number picks arbitrarily. add a tiebreaker (e.g., order_id). row_number row_number: needs a unique order ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice order by order_date alone tied dates pick arbitrarily add a tiebreaker order_id deterministic result no partition by one number for everyone partition by customer_id restart per customer filter rn = 1 in the same select window not allowed in where wrap in cte, then rn = 1 first order per customer result: non-repeatable first rows result: one stable row per customer mistake ties give arbitrary results. best practice also used for deduplicating. rule of thumb order by must be unique or add a tiebreaker. three fixes to apply 1 add a tiebreaker order_id after the date. 2 partition one count per group. 3 filter in a cte select where rn = 1.
m6-rank-dense-rank: definitions rank assigns ranks with gaps after ties (1, 1, 3, 4, ...) dense_rank assigns ranks without gaps after ties (1, 1, 2, 3, ...) visual comparison same data, three ranking functions value row_number rank dense_rank 100 1 1 1 100 2 1 1 90 3 3 2 85 4 4 3 85 5 4 3 70 6 6 4 live example — top 3 products per category with ranked as ( select p.category, p.product_name, sum (oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) as revenue, dense_rank () over ( partition by p.category order by sum (oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) desc ) as rnk from order_items oi join products p on oi.product_id = p.product_id group by p.category, p.product_name ) select * from ranked where rnk <= 3 ; choose want gaps? rank. want 1-2-3 regardless of ties? dense_rank. rank vs dense_rank ranking: pick the right tie rule ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice row_number for ties leo and mia split arbitrarily rank when gaps wanted 1, 2, 2, 4 rank expecting 1-2-3 sam shows 4, not 3 dense_rank for 1-2-3 1, 2, 2, 3 top 3 with rank gaps change who is in partition by category top 3 per category result: unfair or surprising ranks result: ties handled on purpose mistake ties 300 and 300 are mishandled. best practice choose the rule before you query. choose want gaps? rank. want 1-2-3 regardless of ties? dense_rank. three fixes to apply 1 expect ties decide what ties mean. 2 pick by need gaps or no gaps, decide before querying. 3 partition rank within each group.
m6-lag-lead: key checks lag and lead ✓ order the window month order is required. ✓ guard the divide nullif on the divisor. ✓ handle first row null is expected. definition lag accesses a value from a previous row within a window. lead accesses a value from a following row within a window. live example — month-over-month change with monthly as ( select date_trunc( 'month' , order_date) as month, sum (total_amount) as revenue from orders where status = 'completed' group by 1 ) select month, revenue, lag (revenue) over ( order by month) as prev_month_revenue, revenue - lag (revenue) over ( order by month) as mom_change from monthly; pattern add nullif to guard against divide-by-zero for the % change. lag and lead lag: the first month has no prior ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice divide by lag(revenue) directly zero gives an error guard with nullif safe divide-by-zero ignore the null first month 2026-01 has no previous expect null in month 1 show as blank lag without order by month rows in random order over (order by month) lag looks one row back result: errors or wrong % change result: -50.0% then +30.0% correct mistake previous row is undefined at the start. best practice lead looks forward the same way. pattern lag(x) over (order by month) with nullif for % change. three fixes to apply 1 order the window month order is required. 2 guard the divide nullif on the divisor. 3 handle first row null is expected.
m6-running-total: definition a running total shows how a metric accumulates over time. common uses cumulative revenue, orders, or signups (ytd or all-time). tracking pace against a goal. feeding cumulative line charts for dashboards. visual daily sales + running total daily cumulative live example select order_date, sum (total_amount) as daily_revenue, sum ( sum (total_amount)) over ( order by order_date) as running_total from orders where status = 'completed' group by order_date order by order_date; read the nested sum as "sum the daily sums, in order of date, row by row." running total running total: sum the daily sums ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice sum() over with no group by totals per order, not per day sum(sum(total_amount)) over nested: sum of daily sums no order by inside over same total on every row order by order_date 120, 200, 400, 450, 600 mix cancelled with completed wrong accumulation where status = completed count valid orders only result: total does not accumulate result: clean cumulative line mistake order is required to accumulate. best practice feeds cumulative charts and pace vs goal. read nested sum as sum the daily sums, in date order, row by row. three fixes to apply 1 group first daily revenue by date. 2 order the window date order accumulates. 3 filter status completed orders only, so totals are valid.
