m6-moving-average: definition a moving average smooths noisy data over a rolling window. common windows 7 days — weekly pattern removal 14 days — balance of smoothness and reactivity 30 days — monthly trend, very smooth visual raw daily + 7-day moving average 7-day ma live example select order_date, sum (total_amount) as daily_revenue, avg ( sum (total_amount)) over ( order by order_date rows between 6 preceding and current row ) as revenue_7d_ma from orders where status = 'completed' group by order_date order by order_date; rule use a moving average whenever the daily metric fluctuates and you want to show the underlying trend. moving average moving average: smooth the noise ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice plot only raw daily values noise hides the trend add a 7-day moving average removes weekly pattern wrong window size 30-day too smooth to react rows between 6 preceding and current row trust the first rows fewer than 3 values used treat early rows with care or drop them result: trend hidden or lagging result: trend visible beside daily data mistake early rows use a short window. best practice 14 days balances smooth and reactive. rule use a moving average when the daily metric fluctuates. three fixes to apply 1 pick a window 7, 14 or 30 days. 2 set the frame 6 preceding plus current. 3 flag the start early rows are short.
m6-partition-per-group: key checks partition by for per-group windows ✓ name the segment customer, category, state. ✓ partition on it window restarts per group. ✓ order inside date or value order. definition partition by lets you compute windows per group, such as per customer or per state. when to use customer-level cumulative spend. category-level running totals. state-level rankings. any business question that's best answered per-segment. live example — running total per customer select customer_id, order_id, order_date, total_amount, sum (total_amount) over ( partition by customer_id order by order_date rows between unbounded preceding and current row ) as lifetime_spend_so_far from orders where status = 'completed' order by customer_id, order_date; power pattern this is one of the most powerful patterns in analytics sql. master it. per-group windows partition by: one window per group ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice running total across all customers mixes spend between people partition by customer_id lifetime_spend_so_far rank products globally not within each category partition by category rank restarts per group loop or separate query per group slow and duplicated one query, all segments customer, category, state result: segments blur together result: per-segment answers in one query mistake no restart per group. best practice a power pattern in analytics sql. rule of thumb per-segment question? use partition by the segment. three fixes to apply 1 name the segment customer, category, state. 2 partition on it window restarts per group. 3 order inside date or value order.
m6-cohort-analysis: definition a cohort groups customers based on a shared start event (e.g., first purchase month). what it answers "are the customers we acquire sticking around?" cohort definitions you must decide the event that defines cohort membership (usually first completed order). time granularity (monthly or weekly). what counts as returning activity (completed orders in later periods). the retention window (e.g., 12 months of offsets). live example with first_purchase as ( select customer_id, min (date_trunc( 'month' , order_date)) as cohort_month from orders where status = 'completed' group by customer_id ), activity as ( select fp.cohort_month, date_trunc( 'month' , o.order_date) as activity_month, o.customer_id from orders o join first_purchase fp on o.customer_id = fp.customer_id where o.status = 'completed' ) select cohort_month, activity_month, (extract(year from activity_month) - extract(year from cohort_month))* 12 + (extract(month from activity_month) - extract(month from cohort_month)) as month_offset, count ( distinct customer_id) as active_customers from activity group by 1 , 2 , 3 order by 1 , 3 ; cohort table visualization retention heatmap (power bi-style) cohort m0 m1 m2 m3 m4 jan 2024 100% 62% 48% 41% 37% feb 2024 100% 55% 44% 38% 32% mar 2024 100% 58% 46% 40% 35% darker = higher retention. each row is one acquisition cohort. key technique cohort analysis is a hallmark of ecommerce, saas, and subscription businesses. cohort analysis cohorts: define the rules first ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice cohort by any order not the first completed order min(date_trunc) first purchase cohort month per customer count(*) not count(distinct) same customer counted twice count(distinct customer_id) active customers by offset skip retention window months never compared set a window, e.g. 12 months month offset m0, m1, m2 result: retention numbers drift result: m0 100%, m1 62%, m2 48% mistake rules left undefined. best practice each row is one acquisition cohort. decide up front event, grain, return and retention window. three fixes to apply 1 define the event first completed order. 2 count distinct count customers, not repeat orders. 3 compute offsets months since cohort.
m6-time-series: key checks time series in analytics ✓ build the spine a row per date. ✓ left join facts fill missing days with 0. ✓ reuse the base daily, weekly, monthly. definition time series focuses on how metrics change over time. key metrics daily revenue orders per day active customers cancellation rate what sql adds window functions compute growth, trends, and moving averages. outputs feed directly into dashboards and reports. a structured daily or monthly table becomes the backbone of bi visuals. pattern build one base query per time grain (daily, weekly, monthly) and reuse it across many reports. time series in analytics time series: do not lose empty days ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice plain group by on dates 2026-01-22 has no row use a calendar spine every date has a row rolling window over gaps skips the missing day left join metrics onto it show zeros, not gaps rewrite the query per report daily, weekly, monthly one base query per grain reuse across reports result: charts and windows skip days result: complete, reusable series mistake missing days vanish from the output. best practice structured daily table backs bi visuals. pattern one base query per time grain, reused everywhere. three fixes to apply 1 build the spine a row per date. 2 left join facts fill missing days with 0. 3 reuse the base daily, weekly, monthly.
m6-daily-metrics: key checks daily metrics pack (base query) ✓ write it once share the base query. ✓ filter status completed only. ✓ roll up date_trunc to week or month. purpose one base query that powers line charts and basic time-series analysis. the query select order_date, count (*) as orders, sum (total_amount) as revenue, avg (total_amount) as aov from orders where status = 'completed' group by order_date order by order_date; what you get column meaning order_date day orders order count revenue sum of order values aov average order value reuse this is the foundation for daily, weekly (via date_trunc), and monthly rollups. daily metrics base daily base query: one row per day ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice rewrite kpi logic in every query definitions drift one base query orders, revenue, aov per day include cancelled orders status filter missing where status = completed only valid orders average of daily averages aov rolled up wrongly roll up with date_trunc weekly and monthly result: conflicting kpi numbers result: one source for every kpi mistake every report defines revenue differently. best practice foundation for rolling calculations. reuse daily base feeds weekly and monthly rollups. three fixes to apply 1 write it once share the base query. 2 filter status completed only. 3 roll up date_trunc to week or month.
m6-active-customers: purpose analogous to dau (daily active users) for ecommerce. the query select order_date, count ( distinct customer_id) as active_customers from orders where status = 'completed' group by order_date order by order_date; visual daily active customers one dot per day — unique customers with at least one order next step roll up to weekly or monthly for smoother trends. active customers per day active customers: count distinct, don't add ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice count(*) as active customers counts orders, not people count(distinct customer_id) unique customers per date add up daily active counts same people counted again never sum across days 38, 41, 36 stay separate plot only the daily dots noisy day-to-day roll up to week or month smoother trend result: activity overstated result: true daily active customers mistake orders are not unique customers. best practice ecommerce version of daily active users. rule of thumb distinct counts per day are not additive across days. three fixes to apply 1 count distinct unique customers only. 2 do not sum days re-count at the new grain. 3 roll up weekly or monthly.
m6-rolling-30: key checks rolling 30-day active customers ✓ build daily active one row per day and customer. ✓ query the range distinct over 30 days. ✓ consider approx hyperloglog if exact counts are not needed. challenge a 30-day active customer metric counts unique customers over rolling windows. why it's hard distinct counts don't work naturally with window functions. you need to avoid counting the same customer twice across days. naive approaches are slow or wrong. approaches precompute activity at daily grain and use range-based queries. use specialized functions in some warehouses (e.g., bigquery, snowflake). approximate methods like hyperloglog when exact counts aren't required. live example — daily grain pre-aggregation with daily_active as ( select order_date, customer_id from orders where status = 'completed' group by order_date, customer_id ) -- then use this in range queries or approximate counting select * from daily_active; next topic look up "window functions with distinct" — this is a great research topic once basics are solid. rolling 30-day active rolling 30-day: distinct is not additive ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice sum 30 daily active counts 115 where true is 52 pre-aggregate to daily grain group by order_date, customer_id distinct inside a window not supported naturally range query over that table distinct customers per window naive self-join per day slow or wrong warehouse functions or hyperloglog when approximate is fine result: same customer counted repeatedly result: true 30-day distinct count mistake daily returns inflate the sum. best practice 52 distinct, not 115. rule of thumb rolling distinct needs a daily customer table, not sums. three fixes to apply 1 build daily active one row per day and customer. 2 query the range distinct over 30 days. 3 consider approx hyperloglog if exact counts are not needed.
m6-reporting-pattern: key checks reporting query pattern (analyst template) ✓ filter first valid records and range. ✓ enrich then window dimensions, then rankings. ✓ aggregate and format final grain, bi-ready. template a 5-step pattern for building any analytics reporting query. the 5 steps build a filtered base cte for valid records and time range. join dimensions like customers and products to enrich data. use window functions for rankings, running totals, comparisons. aggregate to the final reporting grain (daily, monthly, category, customer). format output columns and sorting for consumption by bi tools. live example with base_orders as ( select order_id, customer_id, order_date, total_amount from orders where status = 'completed' and order_date >= current_date - interval '90 days' ), enriched as ( select o.*, c.state from base_orders o join customers c on o.customer_id = c.customer_id ), with_running as ( select state, order_date, total_amount, sum (total_amount) over ( partition by state order by order_date) as running_state_revenue from enriched ), by_state as ( select state, sum (total_amount) as total_revenue from with_running group by state ) select state, round (total_revenue, 2 ) as revenue from by_state order by revenue desc ; reuse this template scales to any reporting query — swap the ctes for your needs. reporting query pattern report query: five steps, every time ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice one query, no structure filters, joins, windows mixed base cte, then join dimensions valid records, 90 days filter after the joins joins process all rows windows, then aggregate running total by state gaps in the date range no calendar spine format and sort for bi round(total_revenue, 2) result: report breaks and cannot re-run result: a report you can re-run daily mistake hard to reuse or debug. best practice swap the ctes for any new question. template base, join, window, aggregate, format. three fixes to apply 1 filter first valid records and range. 2 enrich then window dimensions, then rankings. 3 aggregate and format final grain, bi-ready.
m7-overview: purpose this module upgrades you from spreadsheet analysis to programmatic analytics. you'll set up python, learn core syntax, and use pandas to load, clean, transform, and export analysis-ready datasets. what you'll learn set up python + jupyter workflow for analytics write clean python: variables, types, conditions, loops, functions use numpy for fast numeric arrays and vectorized operations use pandas for dataframes: filtering, joins, grouping, reshape produce analysis-ready datasets for power bi and reporting module flow six sections 1 env 2 python 3 pandas 4 ops 5 numpy 6 export guiding principle clarity beats cleverness. write python that a teammate can read six months later.
m7-objectives: by the end of this module you will be able to build a complete python analytics workflow from raw csv to clean bi-ready outputs. five objectives, one workflow 1 setup 2 syntax 3 pandas 4 numpy 5 export five objectives # objective detail 1 install & configure python anaconda / vs code / jupyter workflow 2 core python syntax data structures for analytics use cases 3 pandas load & transform load, inspect, clean, transform data 4 numpy numeric computing efficient arrays, basic statistics 5 export & reproducibility csv/excel outputs, clean notebooks prerequisite module 6 (intermediate sql) — you now bring sql thinking into python.
m7-tools: stack the standard python analytics stack. free, open source, industry-standard. the stack: each layer builds on the one below python 3 numpy pandas matplotlib jupyter vs code + git the tools tool purpose python 3.x core language pip / conda package management jupyter notebook exploratory analysis + docs pandas core data manipulation numpy fast numeric arrays matplotlib basic plots for qa vs code scripts + debugging git version control setup path install anaconda → create environment → install packages → open jupyter → test imports.
m7-why-python: reality excel breaks at scale. python doesn't. five reasons automates repetitive reporting and data cleaning. connects to files, databases, apis, and cloud tools. handles messy real-world data better than spreadsheets. scales from quick analysis to production pipelines. pairs well with bi tools (power bi) for end-to-end workflows. excel vs python excel manual, breaks at scale python automated, scalable, reproducible why python excel by hand: redoing work every month ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice copy 12 monthly files by hand open and paste each one pd.concat of a glob one line loads every file data > remove duplicates by click no record of what was removed df.drop_duplicates() same rule applied every run redo the pivottable monthly manual steps, easy to slip df.groupby(region) in a notebook run the notebook next month result: slow, error-prone reports result: repeatable, scalable output mistake manual work breaks as data volume grows. best practice script once, rerun unchanged next month. rule of thumb if you will do it again, script it instead of clicking. three fixes to apply 1 automate loads glob the files and concat them in code. 2 script the cleaning put cleaning steps in code, not menus. 3 rerun it run the notebook for each new month.
m7-workflow: the 5-step loop every python analytics project follows the same rhythm. the steps define the question + required metrics. collect data (csv/sql/api) and validate schema. clean : types, missing values, duplicates, outliers. transform : joins, aggregations, feature columns. export outputs and document assumptions in notebook. workflow flow 1 define 2 collect 3 clean 4 transform 5 export loop real projects iterate. cleaning reveals a question, transformation suggests a new metric. analytics workflow jumping to charts: skipping the loop ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice start coding with no question no metric list defined define question and metrics first which regions are growing? load data and trust the schema no row count or dtypes check collect, then validate schema row count plus dtypes check export without notes assumptions live in your head document assumptions in notebook export clean_orders.csv with notes result: wrong metrics, no audit trail result: traceable, trusted outputs mistake skipping steps hides errors until the dashboard. best practice define, collect, clean, transform, export. the 5-step loop define, collect, clean, transform, export. then iterate. three fixes to apply 1 define first write the question and the metric list. 2 validate input check row counts and dtypes on load. 3 log assumptions note every choice in the notebook.
m7-env-setup: simplest path anaconda gives you python + all the analytics tools in one installer. five steps from install to a working notebook 1 anaconda 2 create env 3 install 4 jupyter 5 test setup steps install anaconda (simplest for analytics stack). create an environment (keeps projects isolated). install : pandas, numpy, matplotlib, jupyter. open jupyter from the environment. test imports to confirm setup works. test imports import pandas as pd import numpy as np import matplotlib print (pd.__version__, np.__version__) tip one environment per project prevents dependency conflicts. environment setup no test: assuming setup worked ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice install packages, never import errors surface mid-analysis test imports right after install print(pd.__version__, np.__version__) one shared environment for all dependencies conflict one environment per project prevents dependency conflicts ignore the prompt env name wrong env may be active check the env name in prompt (analytics) shows it is active result: it worked yesterday bugs result: a notebook that just runs mistake setup problems show up late and are hard to trace. best practice if both versions print, setup is good. test imports import pandas, numpy, matplotlib, print versions. three fixes to apply 1 test imports print pandas and numpy versions once. 2 isolate create one env for each project. 3 check the prompt confirm the active env name first.
m7-conda-venv: recommended for analysts conda manages both python packages and system-level dependencies. environments are disposable: environment.yml rebuilds one conda create activate install export environment.yml → same versions every time commands # create conda create -n analytics python=3.11 # activate conda activate analytics # install the stack conda install pandas numpy matplotlib jupyter # freeze versions for reproducibility conda env export > environment.yml recovery if you break an environment, recreate it from environment.yml . exact same versions, every time. conda environments unfrozen environments: can't rebuild ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice conda install, never export versions live only on your pc conda env export > environment.yml pins exact package versions fix a broken env in place hours lost to guesswork recreate from environment.yml conda env create -f environment.yml share code, not versions teammate gets different pandas share environment.yml with code same versions every time result: it only runs on my machine result: identical setup for everyone mistake no record means no reliable rebuild. best practice environments are disposable and rebuildable. freeze versions conda env export > environment.yml after install. three fixes to apply 1 export write environment.yml once packages work. 2 rebuild recreate instead of repairing a broken env. 3 share commit the yml next to your code.
m7-pip-venv: lightweight alternative venv ships with python — no anaconda needed. two ways to isolate a project conda manages python + system libraries venv + pip ships with python, lightweight vs new to python: conda. comfortable: venv. commands # create python -m venv .venv # activate (windows) .venv\scripts\activate # activate (mac/linux) source .venv/bin/activate # install pip install pandas numpy matplotlib jupyter # save dependencies pip freeze > requirements.txt choose conda if you're new. pip/venv if you're already comfortable with python. pip and venv unpinned pip: different versions later ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice pip install into global python projects collide python -m venv .venv per project isolated and lightweight skip pip freeze no list of what you used pip freeze > requirements.txt pinned versions recorded pick a tool by habit conda vs venv not considered conda if new, venv if comfortable choose deliberately result: broken installs, mixed versions result: reinstallable in one command mistake global installs leak between projects. best practice pip install -r requirements.txt rebuilds. choose new to python: conda. comfortable: venv + pip. three fixes to apply 1 isolate create .venv inside each project. 2 pin freeze to a requirements.txt file. 3 rebuild pip install -r on a fresh machine.
m7-jupyter: definition jupyter is an interactive notebook for exploring data and documenting analysis side by side. a notebook mixes notes, code and results # orders qa markdown in [1]: df.shape out[1]: (5000, 7) code ⏵ key concepts cells — code vs markdown (explain + run). run order matters — restart the kernel if state becomes messy. headings + notes make analysis readable. one idea per cell for clarity. export notebook to html/pdf when sharing. essential shortcuts shift+enter run cell, move to next ctrl+enter run cell, stay esc + a insert cell above esc + b insert cell below esc + m change to markdown esc + y change to code esc + 0,0 restart kernel discipline restart & run all before sharing a notebook. hidden state is the #1 source of "it worked yesterday." jupyter notebooks hidden state: it worked yesterday ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice run cells out of order variables from deleted cells linger restart kernel, run all first esc + 0,0 then run top to bottom share without a rerun reader gets different results restart and run all before sharing proves it works from scratch giant cells with many ideas hard to read and debug one idea per cell with markdown headings and notes explain steps result: results nobody can reproduce result: a clean, shareable notebook mistake hidden state is the #1 cause of broken notebooks. best practice readable top to bottom and reproducible. discipline restart and run all before sharing a notebook. three fixes to apply 1 restart kernel clear messy state with esc + 0,0. 2 one idea keep each cell to a single purpose. 3 export save to html or pdf when sharing.
m7-folder-structure: best practice a predictable folder layout makes every project easier to hand off. a predictable layout for every project data/raw never overwrite data/clean cleaning outputs notebooks exploration scripts reusable pipelines outputs final datasets project/ (+ readme.md, requirements.txt) standard layout project/ ├── data/ │ ├── raw/ # never overwrite │ └── clean/ # outputs of cleaning ├── notebooks/ # exploration ├── scripts/ # reusable pipelines ├── outputs/ # final datasets + charts ├── readme.md # steps + assumptions └── requirements.txt rules never overwrite raw data. always write to clean/ or outputs/ . name outputs with dates — clean_orders_2025-12-06.csv . readme documents what each folder holds and how to run the pipeline. why it matters three months from now, you'll thank yourself. project folders overwriting raw data: no way back ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice save cleaned file over the raw csv original data is gone data/raw is never overwritten write to data/clean or outputs everything in one folder raw, clean and code mixed standard layout every project data, notebooks, scripts, outputs name output final_v2_new.csv no date, no clue which is latest date outputs, add a readme clean_orders_2025-12-06.csv result: lost source, confused handoff result: easy handoff, safe source mistake nobody can retrace what you changed. best practice three months later, you will thank yourself. golden rule raw is read-only. write only to clean or outputs. three fixes to apply 1 protect raw never overwrite files in data/raw. 2 use the layout same folders in every project. 3 document readme lists steps and assumptions.
m7-variables: definition variables store values: numbers, text, dates, collections. names should explain themselves x = read_csv(...) unclear, d = "2024-01-01" orders_df = ... date_start = "2024-01-01" vs rules descriptive names: total_revenue , orders_df . avoid overwriting built-ins like list , dict , sum . use upper_case for constants — date_start , file_path . clarity beats cleverness. good vs bad # bad d = '2024-01-01' x = pd. read_csv ( 'f.csv' ) # good date_start = '2024-01-01' orders_df = pd. read_csv ( 'orders.csv' ) # constants at the top of the file data_dir = 'data/raw' output_dir = 'outputs' analytics tip if you have to explain the variable name out loud, rename it. variables and naming cryptic names: x, d, and sum ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice x = pd.read_csv('f.csv') says nothing about the data orders_df = pd.read_csv(f) name says what the object is d = '2024-01-01' what date is d? date_start = '2024-01-01' upper_case for constants sum = df['rev'].sum() overwrites the built-in sum total_revenue = df['rev'].sum() built-in sum stays safe result: code nobody can read later result: code that reads like a sentence mistake if you must explain it, the name is wrong. best practice clarity beats cleverness. constants go at the top. naming test if you explain a name aloud, rename it. three fixes to apply 1 describe use total_revenue and orders_df. 2 protect built-ins never reuse list, dict or sum. 3 constants up top data_dir and output_dir at file start.
m7-data-types: definition python has a small set of primitive types. knowing them prevents broken metrics. six types you will meet constantly int 42 float 3.14 str "paid" bool true none none datetime 2024-01-15 amounts stored as str are the top cause of wrong metrics the primitives type example use for int 42 counts, ids, years float 3.14 revenue, rates, ratios str "completed" status, names, categories bool true / false flags, filters none none missing value datetime 2024-01-15 dates, times inspecting and converting type ( 42 ) # <class 'int'> int ( '42' ) # 42 float ( '3.14' ) # 3.14 str ( 42 ) # '42' # dates are not strings — parse them from datetime import datetime datetime. strptime ( '2024-01-15' , '%y-%m-%d' ) top cause of wrong metrics amounts stored as strings. parse to numbers before doing math. core data types amounts as strings: wrong metrics ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice do math on amount stored as str '100' is text, not a number float('3.14') before any math parse amounts to numbers leave dates as strings no filtering or grouping by date datetime.strptime(s, fmt) dates are not strings: parse them use int for missing values none is the missing marker check type() when results look odd know int, float, str, bool, none result: wrong sums and broken sorts result: correct metrics and date logic mistake strings that look like numbers are the top cause. best practice parse first, calculate second. top cause of bad metrics amounts stored as strings. parse to numbers first. three fixes to apply 1 parse amounts convert str to float before math. 2 parse dates use strptime or to_datetime. 3 inspect use type() when a result looks wrong.
m7-strings: definition strings are immutable text. cleaning them is 80% of data prep. clean text step by step 1 " completed " 2 .strip() 3 .lower() 4 "completed" cheat sheet # f-strings for output rev = 1234567.89 print (f 'revenue = ${rev:,.2f}' ) # revenue = $1,234,567.89 # clean whitespace ' completed ' . strip () # 'completed' # normalize case 'completed' . lower () # 'completed' 'completed' . upper () # 'completed' # replace patterns '$1,234' . replace ( '$' , '' ). replace ( ',' , '' ) # '1234' # split / join 'a,b,c' . split ( ',' ) # ['a','b','c'] ',' . join ([ 'a' , 'b' , 'c' ]) # 'a,b,c' use case normalize category and status labels so groupby doesn't fragment them. string operations dirty labels: one status, many groups ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice ' completed ' left untrimmed spaces create a new category ' completed '.strip() trim whitespace first 'completed' vs 'completed' groupby splits them in two 'completed'.lower() one casing for every label '$1,234' used as is symbols block numeric math .replace('$','').replace(',','') strip symbols, then convert result: fragmented groupby results result: one clean category per label mistake cleaning text is 80% of data prep. best practice strip, lower, replace, then group. clean order strip, then lower, then replace, then analyze. three fixes to apply 1 trim use .strip() on every text column. 2 case use .lower() so labels match. 3 symbols remove $ and commas before converting.
m7-collections: definitions three collection types with different properties. list, tuple, set [ ] list ordered · mutable duplicates allowed ( ) tuple ordered · fixed duplicates allowed { } set unordered · mutable unique values only comparison type ordered? mutable? unique? use for list yes yes no collections you modify tuple yes no no fixed groupings set no yes yes dedup, membership examples # list — ordered, mutable statuses = [ 'completed' , 'pending' , 'completed' ] statuses. append ( 'shipped' ) # tuple — fixed grouping point = ( 3 , 5 ) # x, y # set — unique values, fast membership unique_statuses = set (statuses) # {'completed', 'pending', 'shipped'} # analytics: find unique categories in a column unique_cats = set (df[ 'category' ]) len (unique_cats) analytics use sets are perfect for validating unique categories or ids. membership checks are o(1). lists, tuples, sets wrong collection for the job ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice list to find unique categories duplicates stay in the list set(df['category']) for uniques unique values only list for fast membership checks slow scan of every item set for membership: o(1) lookup fast validation of ids list for a fixed pair (x, y) can be changed by accident tuple point = (3, 5) ordered and fixed result: slow code, accidental edits result: clean, fast, safe code mistake each type has a job. mixing them up costs you. best practice list to modify, tuple to fix, set to dedupe. pick by property modify: list. fixed: tuple. unique or lookup: set. three fixes to apply 1 use set find unique categories or ids. 2 use list collections you append to or change. 3 use tuple fixed groupings that must not change.
m7-dicts: definition a dict maps keys → values. perfect for replacements and mappings. a dictionary as a lookup table completed completed complete complete "completed" dict: many dirty keys → one canonical value basics # direct access (keyerror if missing) d = { 'ca' : 'california' , 'ny' : 'new york' } d[ 'ca' ] # 'california' # safe access with default d. get ( 'tx' , 'unknown' ) # 'unknown' analytics pattern — status normalization status_map = { 'completed' : 'completed' , 'complete ' : 'completed' , 'completed' : 'completed' , 'pending' : 'pending' , 'pending' : 'pending' , } df[ 'status_clean' ] = df[ 'status' ]. map (status_map) # any unmapped value becomes nan — investigate it best practice keep mappings in a separate config section or file. document the rules for stakeholders. dictionaries many dirty labels, no lookup table ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice chain many if/elif on status long and hard to maintain status_map in a config section many variants to one canonical value d['tx'] with no default keyerror when key is missing d.get('tx', 'unknown') safe access with a default ignore nan after map unmapped values slip by investigate nan after .map() unmapped values need review result: crashes and silent nan labels result: one canonical label each mistake hard-coded fixes pile up and break. best practice keep mappings separate from the logic. dict as lookup df['status'].map(status_map) then check nan. three fixes to apply 1 map use a dict for label normalization. 2 default use .get() to avoid keyerror. 3 check nan review anything left unmapped.
m7-conditionals: definition conditions express business rules: what bucket does this row belong to? business rules become thresholds new regular vip 300 1000 spend → if spend ≥ 1000 scalar example spend = 1200 if spend >= 1000 : tier = 'vip' elif spend >= 300 : tier = 'regular' else : tier = 'new' # tier = 'vip' vectorized in pandas (preferred for large data) import numpy as np df[ 'tier' ] = np. where ( df[ 'spend' ] >= 1000 , 'vip' , np. where (df[ 'spend' ] >= 300 , 'regular' , 'new' ) ) document thresholds vip ≥ 1000 is a business decision. write it down where the code lives. business rules undocumented thresholds and row loops ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice if/elif run row by row slow on large data np.where nested vectorized fast across every row magic number 1000 in code nobody knows why vip is 1000 document vip >= 1000 a business decision, written down check lowest tier first spend >= 300 catches vips too highest threshold first 1000 vip, then 300 regular, else new result: slow, wrong, unexplained tiers result: fast, correct, explained tiers mistake order and docs matter for business rules. best practice write the rule where the code lives. test is the threshold written down beside the code? three fixes to apply 1 vectorize use np.where for large dataframes. 2 document comment each business threshold. 3 order test the top tier first.
m7-boolean-gotchas: critical these bugs cost hours if you don't know them. pandas filters need & and parentheses df[a == 1 and b > 2] valueerror: truth value is ambiguous df[(a == 1) & (b > 2)] element-wise, parenthesised and / or compare whole series; & / | compare row by row the rules use not why & / | and / or pandas filters require element-wise (cond1) & (cond2) cond1 & cond2 parentheses for operator precedence x is none x == none identity check, not equality numeric compare string compare '100' < '20' is true live example # wrong — raises valueerror df[df[ 'status' ] == 'completed' and df[ 'revenue' ] > 100 ] # right df[(df[ 'status' ] == 'completed' ) & (df[ 'revenue' ] > 100 )] tip build complex filters step by step. test each condition alone before combining. boolean gotchas and / or in pandas filters ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice df[a == 1 and b > 2] valueerror: truth value ambiguous df[(a == 1) & (b > 2)] element-wise and parenthesised cond1 & cond2 without parentheses operator precedence breaks it (cond1) & (cond2) parentheses fix precedence x == none to test for missing equality, not identity x is none identity check is correct result: errors and wrong filters result: correct row-by-row filters mistake these bugs cost hours. learn them once. best practice build filters one condition at a time. use & and | for pandas, never and / or. three fixes to apply 1 use & and | pandas filters need element-wise logic. 2 parentheses wrap every condition in brackets. 3 compare types numeric, not string: '100' < '20' is true.
m7-loops: rule use loops for small tasks. avoid them for row-level dataframe work. row loops vs vectorized code (1m rows, illustrative) iterrows() minutes vectorized milliseconds use loops for files and apis, not for dataframe rows good uses reading multiple files (e.g., monthly csvs). calling an api for each entity. running an experiment multiple times (simulation). batch processing with clear, small units of work. bad uses iterating over every row of a million-row dataframe. anything pandas can vectorize. examples # good — read multiple files import glob, pandas as pd frames = [] for path in glob.glob ( 'data/raw/orders_*.csv' ): frames. append (pd. read_csv (path)) df = pd. concat (frames, ignore_index= true ) # good — enumerate for index + item for i, name in enumerate ([ 'a' , 'b' , 'c' ]): print (i, name) # bad — row iteration on big data for idx, row in df. iterrows (): df. loc [idx, 'total' ] = row[ 'qty' ] * row[ 'price' ] # good — vectorized equivalent df[ 'total' ] = df[ 'qty' ] * df[ 'price' ] speed vectorized pandas is often 100× faster than row loops. loops iterrows() on a million rows ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice for row in df.iterrows() minutes on 1m rows vectorized column math milliseconds on 1m rows loop to build a new column pandas can vectorize it loop over files with glob read orders_*.csv, then concat copy-paste per monthly file repeats code for each file loop for api calls, simulations small, clear units of work result: minutes instead of milliseconds result: fast, readable pipelines mistake row loops waste time. vectorize instead. best practice loops for files and apis, not dataframe rows. rule of thumb loop over files and apis. vectorize dataframe rows. three fixes to apply 1 vectorize use column math, not row loops. 2 loop files use glob for monthly csv files. 3 batch keep each loop unit small.
m7-functions: definition a function packages logic into a named, reusable unit. small functions form a pipeline 1 load() 2 clean() 3 build_kpis() 4 export() one job each · docstring · return a dataframe, not a print the 5 principles small — one job, one function. clear inputs/outputs — return a dataframe or metric, not prints. docstrings — explain what it does and why. pure — no hidden state; same inputs → same outputs. pipeline-friendly — load → clean → transform → export. example def clean_amounts (df, col= 'amount' ): """strip $ and commas, convert to numeric.""" s = (df[col]. astype ( str ) . str . replace ( r'[\$,]' , '' , regex= true )) df[col + '_clean' ] = pd. to_numeric (s, errors= 'coerce' ) return df orders = clean_amounts (orders, 'total_amount' ) reuse once clean_amounts works, use it in every project. that's the payoff. function design one big script with prints ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice one long block of code many jobs in a single place small functions, one job each load, clean, build_kpis, export print() the result nothing to pass downstream return a dataframe clear inputs and outputs no docstring why does it exist? docstring on every function explain what it does and why result: untestable, hard to reuse result: a readable, reusable pipeline mistake hidden state means different results later. best practice same inputs give the same outputs. 5 principles small, clear i/o, docstring, pure, pipeline-friendly. three fixes to apply 1 small one job per function, one clear return. 2 return data return a dataframe, do not print it. 3 document add a docstring to each function.
m7-error-handling: definition try/except catches errors so your pipeline doesn't die mid-run. try / except keeps a pipeline alive try read_csv(path) success log rows read except filenotfounderror log + return none catch specific errors. never a bare except. rules wrap i/o (files, apis) in try/except. log errors with context (filename, row counts). continue only when safe — otherwise re-raise the error. always validate outputs even if the code "ran successfully." live example import pandas as pd import logging def safe_read_csv (path): try : df = pd. read_csv (path) logging. info (f 'read {path}: {len(df)} rows' ) return df except filenotfounderror: logging. error (f 'missing file: {path}' ) return none except pd.errors.emptydataerror: logging. warning (f 'empty file: {path}' ) return none never use a bare except: . you'll swallow bugs you needed to see. try/except bare except hides the real error ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice except: pass swallows every error except filenotfounderror catch specific errors only no logging of failures which file failed? unknown logging.error with filename context: file and row counts trust it because it ran no output validation validate outputs after the run re-raise when unsafe to continue result: silent failures, wrong data result: failures you can see and fix mistake a pipeline that runs is not one that is right. best practice wrap i/o, log, and re-raise if needed. rule catch specific errors. never a bare except. three fixes to apply 1 be specific name the exception you expect. 2 log context record file name and row counts. 3 validate check outputs even if code ran.
m7-pandas-intro: definition pandas gives you two objects: dataframe (a table) and series (one column). the two objects dataframe — 2d table (rows + columns). series — 1d array with an index. vectorized — operations run across all rows at once. supports join / groupby / pivot — like sql in python. visual dataframe vs series dataframe id name rev 1 alice 1200 2 bob 800 series (one column) rev 1200 800 foundation pandas is the foundation for the rest of python analytics. dataframe and series treating a table like a single column ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice confuse dataframe and series df['rev'] is 1d, df[['rev']] is 2d dataframe = table, series = column rows plus columns vs one column loop over rows for math ignores vectorized operations operate on whole columns runs across all rows at once export to excel for joins pandas already does join/groupby use join, groupby, pivot sql thinking in python result: type errors and slow code result: concise, sql-like workflows mistake know which object you are holding. best practice pandas is the base for what follows. remember dataframe is 2d table. series is one 1d column. three fixes to apply 1 know the object check if you hold a table or a column. 2 vectorize act on whole columns at once. 3 think sql join, group and pivot in pandas.
m7-read-csv: definition pd.read_csv loads a file into a dataframe. always inspect it right after. from file to dataframe, then inspect orders.csv read_csv() dataframe .head() .shape .dtypes .info() basic read import pandas as pd df = pd. read_csv ( 'data/raw/orders.csv' ) inspect immediately df. head () # first 5 rows df.shape # (rows, cols) df.columns # column names df.dtypes # column types df. info () # types + missing counts common options pd. read_csv (path, sep= ';' , # different separator encoding= 'utf-8' , # file encoding parse_dates=[ 'order_date' ], # parse date cols na_values=[ '' , 'n/a' ], # extra missing markers dtype={ 'customer_id' : str } # force type ) validate compare row count vs source expectations. a silent truncation is a silent bug. reading csv loading a file and never looking ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice pd.read_csv, then straight to math types and blanks unchecked head, shape, dtypes, info() inspect immediately after load let ids load as numbers leading zeros are lost dtype={'customer_id': str} force ids to stay text ignore separator and encoding garbled columns or errors sep, encoding, na_values options parse_dates=['order_date'] result: broken columns found late result: a trustworthy dataframe mistake always inspect right after loading. best practice load deliberately, then inspect. habit read_csv, then head(), shape, dtypes, info(). three fixes to apply 1 inspect run head and info() right after load. 2 force types use dtype for id columns. 3 set options set sep, encoding and na_values.
m7-quick-checks: rule run these five checks on every new dataset before any analysis. five checks before any analysis info() types + nulls isna() missing counts duplicated() repeat rows describe() outliers value_counts() label variants the 5 checks # 1. types and missing values df. info () # 2. missing counts per column df. isna (). sum () # 3. duplicate rows df. duplicated (). sum () # 4. numeric stats df. describe () # 5. categorical sanity df[ 'status' ]. value_counts () what each tells you check catches info() wrong types, missing counts isna().sum() columns with too many missing values duplicated().sum() ingestion bugs, duplicate rows describe() outliers, wrong scales, impossible values value_counts() label variants, typos, casing issues habit run these every time. it takes 30 seconds and prevents hours of debugging. quick data checks analysing data you never checked ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice start metrics on a new file duplicates and blanks hidden df.info() and df.isna().sum() types and missing counts skip describe() outliers and wrong scales missed df.duplicated().sum() ingestion bugs and repeat rows skip value_counts() casing variants go unseen describe() and value_counts() outliers and label variants result: wrong numbers, found late result: problems caught before analysis mistake bad data gives bad insight. best practice five checks on every new dataset. five checks info, isna, duplicated, describe, value_counts. three fixes to apply 1 types and nulls run info() and isna(). sum(). 2 duplicates run duplicated().sum() first. 3 labels run value_counts() on categories.
m7-select-filter: definition select columns and filter rows using boolean conditions. a filter is a true/false mask over rows id region rev 1 east 120 2 west 80 3 east 240 4 north 60 true false true false mask df[df.region == 'east'] rows where mask is true select columns df[ 'revenue' ] # one column → series df[[ 'id' , 'revenue' ]] # two columns → dataframe filter rows # single condition df[df[ 'status' ] == 'completed' ] # multi-condition — wrap each in parentheses df[(df[ 'status' ] == 'completed' ) & (df[ 'revenue' ] > 100 )] # category groups with isin df[df[ 'state' ]. isin ([ 'ca' , 'ny' , 'tx' ])] # time windows df[df[ 'order_date' ] >= '2024-01-01' ] # not null df[df[ 'customer_id' ]. notna ()] most common bug missing parentheses in multi-condition filters. python evaluates & before == without them. selecting and filtering missing parentheses in a filter ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice df[a == 'x' and b > 100] raises a valueerror (cond1) & (cond2) each condition in parentheses df[a == 'x' & b > 100] precedence gives wrong result df[df['state'].isin([...])] one test for a category group chain == for many states long and error-prone df[df['customer_id'].notna()] keep non-null rows only result: errors or wrong rows result: exactly the rows you meant mistake the most common bug: missing parentheses. best practice a filter is a true/false mask over rows. tip test each condition alone, then combine. three fixes to apply 1 parentheses wrap every condition before using &. 2 use isin test several values in one call. 3 test steps run each mask alone first.
m7-sort-topn: definition sort by one or more columns, then take the first n rows. sort descending, keep the head .head(3) .sort_values( 'revenue', ascending=false) basic sort df. sort_values ( 'revenue' , ascending= false ). head ( 10 ) multi-column sort df. sort_values ( [ 'category' , 'revenue' ], ascending=[ true , false ] ) top n per group # top 3 products per category (df. sort_values ([ 'category' , 'revenue' ], ascending=[ true , false ]) . groupby ( 'category' ) . head ( 3 )) deterministic ties sort by an extra column (like product_id ) so ties always resolve the same way. sorting and top-n top n that changes every run ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice sort_values().head(), ties open tied rows may swap order add product_id as extra sort key ties always resolve the same way top 3 overall, not per group wrong answer for each category sort, then groupby().head(3) top 3 products per category default ascending sort smallest values come first ascending=false for revenue largest first, then head(10) result: unstable, misleading rankings result: repeatable, correct top-n mistake ties resolve at random without a tiebreak. best practice sort first, then take the head. top n sort_values(desc), then head(n). three fixes to apply 1 break ties add an id column to the sort. 2 per group use groupby().head(n) after sorting. 3 descending set ascending=false for top-n.
m7-new-columns: rule vectorize. never loop row-by-row to create a column. a new column is arithmetic on other columns qty unit_price revenue 3 20 60 2 45 90 5 12 60 df["qty"] * df["unit_price"] one line, every row at once arithmetic df[ 'revenue' ] = df[ 'qty' ] * df[ 'unit_price' ] conditional (np.where) import numpy as np df[ 'flag' ] = np. where (df[ 'revenue' ] > 1000 , 'high' , 'low' ) multiple conditions (np.select) conds = [ df[ 'revenue' ] > 1000 , df[ 'revenue' ] > 300 , ] labels = [ 'high' , 'mid' ] df[ 'tier' ] = np. select (conds, labels, default= 'low' ) datetime features df[ 'order_date' ] = pd. to_datetime (df[ 'order_date' ]) df[ 'month' ] = df[ 'order_date' ].dt. to_period ( 'm' ). astype ( str ) df[ 'weekday' ] = df[ 'order_date' ].dt.day_name() df[ 'quarter' ] = df[ 'order_date' ].dt.quarter performance vectorized pandas on a million rows takes milliseconds. row loops take minutes. new columns looping row by row to make a column ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice for loop to set revenue slow, one row at a time df['qty'] * df['unit_price'] one line, every row at once if/else per row for flag rewrites logic by hand np.where or np.select flags and tiers, vectorized dates left as text month and weekday not available to_datetime then .dt features month, weekday, quarter result: slow code, no date features result: fast, readable feature columns mistake never loop row by row to create a column. best practice vectorize. a new column is arithmetic on others. rule vectorize. never loop row by row. three fixes to apply 1 arithmetic multiply columns, do not loop. 2 conditions use np.where or np.select. 3 date features use .dt after to_datetime.
m7-missing-strategy: rule every missing value has a meaning. decide the meaning before you fill or drop. decide the meaning before you fill a missing value unknown? fill 'unknown' / 0 not applicable? leave null + flag data error? correct or drop three questions unknown? → fill with 'unknown' or 0 not applicable? → leave null or flag it data error? → drop or correct with source options matrix approach use when risk fill with constant meaning is clear ('unknown', 0) hides the missing pattern fill with mean/median numeric, roughly symmetric distorts distribution forward fill (ffill) time series, last value valid propagates stale values drop rows missing rate is tiny may introduce bias keep with flag missingness itself is signal more columns to manage never blindly fill id fields. customer_id = 0 creates a fake customer that skews group counts. missing values strategy filling before asking what it means ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice fillna(0) on every column hides the missing pattern ask: unknown, n/a, or error? decide the meaning first fill with mean on skewed data distorts the distribution median only if roughly symmetric constant when meaning is clear ffill on unordered data propagates stale values keep a flag when it is signal drop only tiny missing rates result: hidden gaps, biased numbers result: documented, defensible choices mistake never blindly fill or drop. best practice every missing value has a meaning. three questions unknown: fill. not applicable: flag. error: fix or drop. three fixes to apply 1 ask why decide the meaning before you fill. 2 match method pick fill, drop or flag by cause. 3 flag it keep a column marking the gap.
m7-missing-examples: definition common patterns for handling missing data, with the checks that go with them. measure missing counts before and after 17 0 12 12 city amount red = before green = after fill amount: flag first, then fill fill patterns # categorical: fill with 'unknown' df[ 'city' ] = df[ 'city' ]. fillna ( 'unknown' ) # numeric: only fill 0 if business approves df[ 'amount' ] = df[ 'amount' ]. fillna ( 0 ) # time series: forward-fill only when justified df[ 'price' ] = df[ 'price' ]. ffill () always measure before/after before = df. isna (). sum () df[ 'city' ] = df[ 'city' ]. fillna ( 'unknown' ) after = df. isna (). sum () print (pd. dataframe ({ 'before' : before , 'after' : after })) flag missingness # keep a flag for modeling or diagnostics df[ 'amount_was_missing' ] = df[ 'amount' ]. isna (). astype ( int ) df[ 'amount' ] = df[ 'amount' ]. fillna ( 0 ) documentation every fill/drop decision belongs in the notebook or code comments. missing value fixes filling without measuring ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice fillna(0) on amount unapproved zero is a business claim fillna('unknown') for city clear label for categories no before/after counts cannot prove what changed isna().sum() before and after compare the two counts ffill with no justification old values copied forward amount_was_missing flag flag first, then fill result: invented numbers, no proof result: measured, transparent fills mistake silent fills change your totals. best practice fill 0 only if the business approves. check compare isna().sum() before and after every fill. three fixes to apply 1 measure print counts before and after. 2 fill with care use 0 only with approval. 3 flag add a was_missing column first.
m7-duplicates: definition duplicates inflate counts and distort metrics. find and fix them before analysis. duplicates on the business key: keep the latest order_id updated_at 1001 jan 3 1002 jan 4 1002 jan 6 1003 jan 5 order_id updated_at 1001 jan 3 1002 jan 6 1003 jan 5 before: 4 rows after: 3 rows (keep="last") detect # any full-row duplicates df. duplicated (). sum () # duplicates on a subset (business key) df. duplicated (subset=[ 'order_id' ]). sum () fix # sort first so we keep the latest record df = (df. sort_values ( 'updated_at' ) . drop_duplicates (subset=[ 'order_id' ], keep= 'last' )) validate # compare metrics before/after df. groupby ( 'month' )[ 'revenue' ]. sum () # if numbers change a lot, investigate upstream root cause large duplicate counts usually mean an ingestion bug. flag it — don't just silently drop. duplicates duplicates inflate counts and revenue ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice ignore duplicates same order counted twice duplicated(subset=['order_id']) detect on the business key drop_duplicates() on all columns misses repeats of order_id sort_values('updated_at') first then drop_duplicates, keep='last' keep whichever row comes first may keep an outdated record compare revenue before/after big change: check upstream result: inflated counts and revenue result: one latest row per order mistake duplicates distort every metric. best practice fix the root cause upstream too. rule sort, dedupe on the key, then compare before/after. three fixes to apply 1 detect count duplicates on the business key. 2 keep latest sort by updated_at, keep last. 3 validate compare grouped totals before and after.
m7-numeric-conversion: definition pd.to_numeric converts strings to numbers, coercing bad values to nan. strip symbols, then to_numeric(errors="coerce") "$1,200" " 85.5 " "n/a" .str.replace(r"[\$,]", "") .str.strip() pd.to_numeric(…) 1200.0 85.5 nan ← count the nan the pattern # clean the string first, then convert s = (df[ 'amount' ]. astype ( str ) . str . replace ( r'[\$,]' , '' , regex= true ) . str . strip ()) df[ 'amount_num' ] = pd. to_numeric (s, errors= 'coerce' ) # how many values failed to convert? df[ 'amount_num' ]. isna (). sum () # sanity check the range df[ 'amount_num' ]. describe () why errors='coerce' errors='raise' — stops at first bad value (annoying). errors='coerce' — sets bad values to nan, lets you count and inspect them. count the nan if many values became nan, you have a data quality problem upstream. investigate before proceeding. numeric conversion converting without counting failures ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice float() on '$1,200' raises an error on symbols str.replace then str.strip clean the string first errors='raise' on a messy column stops at the first bad value pd.to_numeric(s, errors='coerce') bad values become nan coerce, then ignore the nan failures vanish quietly isna().sum() and describe() count nan, sanity check range result: crashes or silent lost values result: clean numbers, known failures mistake nan you do not count is data you lost. best practice clean, convert, count the nan. pattern clean string, to_numeric, count nan, check range. three fixes to apply 1 strip symbols remove $ and commas first. 2 coerce use errors='coerce' to find bad values. 3 count nan many nan means investigate.
m7-datetime-conversion: definition dates must be parsed into datetime objects to unlock filtering, grouping, and resampling. parse once, then derive features "03/01/2026" to_datetime() .dt.year .dt.month .dt.day_name() is_weekend unparseable dates become nat: count them parse df[ 'order_date' ] = pd. to_datetime ( df[ 'order_date' ], errors= 'coerce' ) # count failed parses (became nat) df[ 'order_date' ]. isna (). sum () derived date features df[ 'year' ] = df[ 'order_date' ].dt.year df[ 'month' ] = df[ 'order_date' ].dt. to_period ( 'm' ). astype ( str ) df[ 'week' ] = df[ 'order_date' ].dt.isocalendar().week df[ 'weekday' ] = df[ 'order_date' ].dt.day_name() df[ 'is_weekend' ] = df[ 'order_date' ].dt.weekday >= 5 timezone for time zones, parse with utc=true then convert with .dt.tz_convert() . be consistent across the pipeline. datetime conversion dates left as text ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice sort dates stored as strings 03/01 may sort before 12/31 to_datetime(errors='coerce') parse once to_datetime with no check bad dates quietly turn to nat isna().sum() on the date column count nat after parsing mixed formats, one guess day and month can be swapped derive .dt.year, month, weekday features from parsed dates result: wrong ordering and lost dates result: reliable time-based analysis mistake unparsed dates break filters and groups. best practice parse once, then derive features. pattern parse once, count nat, then derive date features. three fixes to apply 1 parse use to_datetime early in the pipeline. 2 count nat count failed parses right away. 3 derive add year, month and weekday columns.
m7-string-normalization: why category fragmentation breaks groupby metrics. 'completed' and 'completed ' become two categories. four spellings, one category completed completed completed complete strip · lower · map completed groupby now returns 1 row, not 4 the pattern # 1. trim whitespace df[ 'status' ] = df[ 'status' ]. str . strip () # 2. normalize casing df[ 'status' ] = df[ 'status' ]. str . lower () # 3. map known variants to canonical labels status_map = { 'complete' : 'completed' , 'completed' : 'completed' , 'pending' : 'pending' , 'canceled' : 'cancelled' , 'cancelled' : 'cancelled' , } df[ 'status_clean' ] = df[ 'status' ]. map (status_map) # 4. check what didn't map df[df[ 'status_clean' ]. isna ()][ 'status' ]. unique () before / after # before — 4 different 'completed' variants completed, completed , completed, complete # after — 1 canonical value completed result groupby now produces one row per real category, not four. string normalization four spellings, four categories ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice group by raw status completed and completed differ str.strip() then str.lower() trim and fix the case first trailing space ignored 'completed ' is its own group status_map with .map() variants to canonical labels complete vs completed left variants never merged check what did not map unmapped values need review result: fragmented groupby results result: one row per true category mistake category fragmentation breaks metrics. best practice groupby returns 1 row, not 4. pattern strip, lower, map, then check unmapped. three fixes to apply 1 trim and case use strip then lower on labels. 2 map map variants to one label. 3 check inspect values that did not map.
m7-groupby: definition groupby splits, applies a function, and combines — exactly like sql group by. split, apply, combine 40 60 books 200 150 electr. 90 110 games split by category sum() books 100 electronics 350 games 200 combine · like sql group by basic pattern df. groupby ( 'category' )[ 'revenue' ]. sum () multiple aggregations (df. groupby ( 'category' ) . agg ( orders = ( 'order_id' , 'nunique' ), revenue = ( 'revenue' , 'sum' ), aov = ( 'revenue' , 'mean' ) ) . reset_index ()) common aggregations function meaning sum total mean average count row count nunique unique count min / max extremes metric grain always state whether your metric is order-level, item-level, or customer-level. grain errors inflate numbers. groupby aggregations aggregating without stating the grain ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice mean revenue labelled total wrong function for the metric agg(revenue=('revenue','sum')) named, explicit aggregations count orders using rows repeated orders inflate counts nunique on order_id counts each order once unnamed aggregate columns output is hard to read reset_index() on the result flat table ready to use result: metrics nobody can interpret result: clear, comparable metrics mistake state the grain and the function used. best practice split, apply, combine, like sql group by. metric grain always state what one row of the result means. three fixes to apply 1 name outputs use named agg columns for clarity. 2 nunique use it for unique orders. 3 reset index return a flat table.
m7-kpi-table: goal build a clean monthly kpi table that powers power bi cards and trend lines. order rows to a monthly kpi table to a power bi card id month rev 1 jan 80 2 jan 60 3 feb 90 month orders rev jan 2 140 feb 1 90 revenue $230 groupby + agg → one row per month the code # 1. create the month key df[ 'month' ] = (df[ 'order_date' ] .dt. to_period ( 'm' ) . astype ( str )) # 2. aggregate to the month grain kpi = (df. groupby ( 'month' ) . agg ( orders = ( 'order_id' , 'nunique' ), revenue = ( 'revenue' , 'sum' ), aov = ( 'revenue' , 'mean' ) ) . reset_index ()) # 3. round for readability kpi[ 'aov' ] = kpi[ 'aov' ]. round ( 2 ) kpi[ 'revenue' ] = kpi[ 'revenue' ]. round ( 2 ) output shape month orders revenue aov 2024-01 1,240 98,400.00 79.35 2024-02 1,180 94,200.00 79.83 2024-03 1,320 108,750.00 82.39 reuse export to csv and connect directly to power bi cards and trends. monthly kpi table summarizing without a month key ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice group by raw order_date one row per day, not month dt.to_period('m').astype(str) create the month key count rows as orders order lines inflate orders agg orders=('order_id','nunique') revenue, orders, aov per month hand-type totals into bi numbers drift from the data one row per month, export it feeds power bi cards and trends result: noisy trend, unreliable cards result: clean one-row-per-month table mistake wrong grain makes wrong kpis. best practice groupby plus agg gives one row per month. grain check does the table have one row per month? three fixes to apply 1 month key build a month column first. 2 aggregate use groupby and agg for kpis. 3 reset index return a flat table for bi.
m7-pivot: definition pivot reshapes long data into matrix form. category × month performance views. long format to a category × month matrix cat mon rev bk jan 12 bk feb 11 el jan 45 el feb 49 jan feb books 12 11 elec. 45 49 pivot_table(index, columns, values) live example pivot = df. pivot_table ( index = 'category' , columns = 'month' , values = 'revenue' , aggfunc = 'sum' , fill_value = 0 ) pivot output shape category 2024-01 2024-02 2024-03 books 12,340 11,200 13,450 electronics 45,600 48,900 52,100 games 28,100 26,300 30,200 use cases category × month performance heatmap. cohort retention tables (see module 6). regional × product sales views. fill_value=0 prevents nan in the matrix and keeps dashboards clean. pivot tables long data when you need a matrix ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice read long rows to compare hard to spot category trends pivot_table(index, columns) category by month matrix blank cells from missing combos nan in the matrix fill_value=0 no blank cells pivot with no aggfunc default is mean, not sum aggfunc='sum' for revenue state the aggregation result: slow, misleading comparisons result: readable category by month view mistake long format hides the category by month pattern. best practice feeds heatmaps and cohort views. shape index = rows, columns = cols, values + aggfunc. three fixes to apply 1 reshape use pivot_table for matrices. 2 state aggfunc set sum, not the default. 3 fill blanks set fill_value=0 for empty cells.
m7-merge: definition pd.merge joins dataframes like sql joins. four join types, same as sql inner matches only left all left rows right all right rows outer everything four join types # inner df. merge (other, on= 'customer_id' , how= 'inner' ) # left (most common for analytics) df. merge (other, on= 'customer_id' , how= 'left' ) # right df. merge (other, on= 'customer_id' , how= 'right' ) # outer df. merge (other, on= 'customer_id' , how= 'outer' ) joining on different column names df. merge (other, left_on= 'cust_id' , right_on= 'customer_id' , how= 'left' ) handling column name clashes df. merge (other, on= 'id' , suffixes=( '_orders' , '_customers' )) watch out join keys must match types (str vs int silently fails). many-to-many merges inflate rows — validate row counts. always check for unexpected missing join coverage. merging dataframes merging without checking row counts ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice how='inner' by default unmatched orders silently dropped how='left' for analytics keep every left-side row join on a non-unique key rows multiply check key uniqueness first row counts stay as expected same column name in both clashing columns confuse results suffixes=('_orders','_customers') left_on and right_on if names differ result: lost or duplicated rows result: enriched data, no row surprises mistake a bad merge changes your totals. best practice compare row counts before and after. watch after a left join, row count must not change. three fixes to apply 1 choose how left join is the usual analytics choice. 2 check keys confirm the key is unique. 3 suffixes rename clashing columns.
m7-merge-example: goal enrich orders with customer attributes and build a regional kpi table. after a left join, row counts must not change order cust a1 c1 a2 c2 a3 c9 + cust state c1 ca c2 ny order state a1 ca a2 ny a3 nan before: 3 rows after: 3 rows · 1 unmatched the merge df = orders_df. merge ( customers_df, on= 'customer_id' , how= 'left' ) validate join coverage # count unmatched orders missing = df[ 'state' ]. isna (). sum () print (f 'unmatched orders: {missing}' ) # compare row counts print ( 'before:' , len (orders_df)) print ( 'after: ' , len (df)) # if counts differ, investigate — inner merge may have dropped rows group by state state_kpi = (df. groupby ( 'state' , as_index= false ) . agg ( orders = ( 'order_id' , 'nunique' ), revenue = ( 'revenue' , 'sum' ) ) . sort_values ( 'revenue' , ascending= false )) document add a comment stating the join rule and grain: "one row per order, joined to one row per customer." merge validation trusting a join with no coverage check ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice merge, then groupby at once unmatched orders hidden left join orders to customers keep all orders skip before/after row counts dropped rows go unseen print len before and after 3 rows before, 3 rows after ignore nan in state a3 has no customer match count state.isna().sum() report unmatched orders result: regional kpis that undercount result: validated join, honest kpis mistake unmatched rows vanish from the kpi table. best practice if counts differ, investigate. check after a left join, row counts must not change. three fixes to apply 1 left join keep every order row in the result. 2 compare print row counts before and after. 3 count gaps report unmatched orders.
m7-concat: definition pd.concat stacks dataframes vertically (rows) or horizontally (columns). stack monthly files and keep a source column orders_jan.csv orders_feb.csv orders_mar.csv pd.concat rows add up: 120 + 118 + 131 stacking monthly files import glob, pandas as pd files = glob.glob ( 'data/raw/orders_*.csv' ) frames = [] for path in files: df = pd. read_csv (path) df[ 'source_file' ] = path # traceability frames. append (df) combined = pd. concat (frames, ignore_index= true ) rules ignore_index=true — clean integer index for the stacked result. validate column alignment — schema drift breaks concat silently. add a source_file column for debugging (which file did this row come from?). check total row counts — sum of parts should equal the whole. schema drift if one file has an extra or renamed column, concat creates nan. inspect columns of each file first. concatenation stacking files with schema drift ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice concat with no source column cannot trace a bad row df['source_file'] = path traceability for each row keep old index values duplicate index labels ignore_index=true clean integer index assume columns line up schema drift breaks silently validate column alignment compare columns across files result: untraceable, misaligned rows result: rows add up: 120+118+131 mistake concat fails silently on mismatched columns. best practice check row sums after stacking. check combined rows must equal the sum of the files. three fixes to apply 1 trace add a source_file column. 2 reset index use ignore_index=true on the result. 3 validate compare columns and row totals.
m7-numpy: definition numpy arrays enable efficient math without python loops. pandas uses numpy internally. one nan poisons mean(); nanmean() ignores it 1 2 nan 4 np.mean → nan np.nanmean → 2.33 vectorized: arr * 2 acts on every element, no loop pandas is built on numpy arrays why numpy vectorized operations — no explicit loops. handles nan-aware math ( np.nanmean , etc.). used for scaling, normalization, and simulations. foundation for pandas and most ml libraries. common operations import numpy as np arr = np. array ([ 1 , 2 , np.nan, 4 ]) arr * 2 # vectorized multiply np. nanmean (arr) # mean ignoring nan np. nansum (arr) # sum ignoring nan np. sqrt (arr) # element-wise sqrt np. where (arr > 2 , 'hi' , 'lo' ) # conditional basic statistics np. mean (arr), np. median (arr), np. std (arr) use case quick statistical baselines and transformations before feeding into pandas or a model. mistake vs best practice: numpy one nan poisons np.mean() ✗ common mistake ✗ np.mean on data with nan returns nan for the whole array ✗ python loop over elements slow versus arrays ✗ arr * 2 written as a loop no need to loop result: nan results, slow code ✓ best practice ✓ np.nanmean(arr) ignores nan: 2.33 in the example ✓ vectorized arr * 2 acts on every element ✓ np.nansum and nan-aware math scaling and simulations result: correct, fast numeric math mistake: one nan spoils the whole average. nan-safe use np.nan* functions when data has gaps. best practice: pandas is built on numpy arrays. three fixes to apply 1 nan-aware use nanmean and nansum. 2 vectorize apply math to whole arrays. 3 know the base pandas runs on numpy.
m7-matplotlib: purpose plot to validate data trends and detect anomalies during exploration. three qa plots: trend, shape, comparison plt.plot plt.hist plt.bar three go-to plots import matplotlib.pyplot as plt # line — time series plt. plot (kpi[ 'month' ], kpi[ 'revenue' ]) plt. title ( 'monthly revenue' ) plt. xticks (rotation= 45 ) plt. show () # histogram — distribution plt. hist (df[ 'revenue' ], bins= 30 ) plt. show () # bar — category comparison kpi2 = df. groupby ( 'category' )[ 'revenue' ]. sum () plt. bar (kpi2.index, kpi2.values) plt. show () rules keep it simple — this is for qa, not for reports. export figures when needed: plt.savefig('outputs/chart.png') . use power bi for final visuals — matplotlib is for exploration. goal validate your data before shipping it to a dashboard. matplotlib qa plots pretty charts when you need qa ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice spend hours styling a qa plot this is not the report plt.plot for monthly revenue trend over time skip plotting before export spikes and gaps unseen plt.hist(df['revenue'], bins=30) shape and outliers wrong chart for the question pie where a trend is needed plt.bar for category totals compare categories result: wasted time, missed anomalies result: fast anomaly detection mistake plots here are for checking data. best practice keep it simple. use power bi for reports. three qa plots line for trend, histogram for shape, bar to compare. three fixes to apply 1 trend line plot for time series. 2 shape histogram for the distribution. 3 compare bar chart for categories.
m7-case-messy: scenario a real orders csv with currency symbols, commas, blanks, and mixed date formats. messy csv in, bi-ready csv out $1,200 03/01 n/a 2026-1-3 $1,200 03/01 amount dates drop dedup export clean .csv each step is one line of pandas, in order problems & fixes problem fix amount has $ and , strip symbols → to_numeric(errors='coerce') blanks in amounts decide: fill 0 or flag as missing mixed date formats to_datetime(errors='coerce') + manual checks duplicate order_ids drop_duplicates on sorted data full pipeline import pandas as pd raw = pd. read_csv ( 'data/raw/orders.csv' ) # 1. clean amounts raw[ 'amount' ] = (raw[ 'amount' ]. astype ( str ) . str . replace ( r'[\$,]' , '' , regex= true ) . str . strip ()) raw[ 'amount' ] = pd. to_numeric (raw[ 'amount' ], errors= 'coerce' ) # 2. clean dates raw[ 'order_date' ] = pd. to_datetime (raw[ 'order_date' ], errors= 'coerce' ) # 3. drop rows missing critical fields raw = raw. dropna (subset=[ 'order_id' , 'order_date' ]) # 4. dedup raw = (raw. sort_values ( 'order_date' ) . drop_duplicates (subset=[ 'order_id' ], keep= 'last' )) # 5. export raw. to_csv ( 'outputs/clean_orders.csv' , index= false ) deliverable clean_orders.csv + kpi pack tables, ready for power bi. messy csv case fixing one symptom at a time ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice leave $ and commas in amount math fails or returns text strip symbols, to_numeric coerce blanks become nan you can count parse mixed dates with no check bad dates become nat unseen to_datetime coerce, then check review the failed parses export before removing duplicates repeat order_ids inflate totals sort, then drop_duplicates export a clean dataset result: a messy file passed to bi result: a bi-ready clean csv mistake skipping a step passes the problem on. best practice each step is one line in order. pipeline order amounts, dates, blanks, dedupe, export. three fixes to apply 1 amounts strip symbols, then to_numeric. 2 dates parse with coerce and check. 3 dedupe sort, then drop duplicates.
m7-case-leaderboard: scenario which 10 products drive the most revenue, and how concentrated is that revenue? top products and how concentrated revenue is bars: revenue line: cumulative % top 3 ≈ 68% the code # 1. compute line-level revenue df[ 'revenue' ] = df[ 'quantity' ] * df[ 'unit_price' ] # 2. aggregate to product grain prod = (df. groupby ([ 'product_id' , 'product_name' ]) . agg ( units = ( 'quantity' , 'sum' ), revenue = ( 'revenue' , 'sum' ) ) . reset_index ()) # 3. top 10 by revenue top10 = (prod. sort_values ( 'revenue' , ascending= false ) . head ( 10 ) . copy ()) # 4. revenue share % total = prod[ 'revenue' ]. sum () top10[ 'revenue_share_pct' ] = (top10[ 'revenue' ] / total * 100 ). round ( 2 ) output shape rank product units revenue share % 1 wireless headphones 1,240 $124,000 12.4% 2 smart watch 980 $98,000 9.8% 3 coffee maker 1,150 $86,250 8.6% reuse export to power bi for leaderboard visuals and concentration analysis. product leaderboard ranking products without the share ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice rank revenue with no total no sense of concentration revenue = quantity * unit_price line-level revenue first group by product name only names can repeat across ids groupby product_id, product_name aggregate to product grain revenue summed before line math quantity x price skipped sort desc, head(10), add share % cumulative % shows concentration result: a list with no context result: leaderboard with concentration mistake a top 10 alone hides how concentrated sales are. best practice top 3 share tells the story. formula share % = product revenue / total revenue. three fixes to apply 1 line revenue create revenue per line first. 2 product grain group by product_id and name. 3 add share add share % and cumulative %.
m7-export: rule clean exports are the handoff to bi. make them friendly. validate, then hand off to power bi 1 assert checks 2 to_csv 3 power bi index=false · snake_case · iso dates · versioned file name the pattern df. to_csv ( 'outputs/clean.csv' , index= false ) best practices snake_case columns — total_revenue , not total revenue . dates as datetime or iso strings — power bi parses them correctly. index=false — no unnamed column in the output. validate counts and totals before export. version the outputs — clean_orders_2025-12-06.csv . validation before export assert df[ 'order_id' ]. is_unique , 'duplicates found!' assert df[ 'revenue' ]. min () >= 0 , 'negative revenue!' print (f 'rows: {len(df):,} | total revenue: ${df.revenue.sum():,.2f}' ) never export without validating row counts and totals. wrong exports ship silently. export for power bi exporting with an unnamed index column ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice to_csv without index=false unnamed index column appears df.to_csv(path, index=false) no extra column columns like total revenue spaces and mixed case in bi snake_case, iso dates total_revenue, 2025-12-06 export without assert checks duplicates and negatives slip in assert is_unique, min() >= 0 validate counts and totals first result: messy bi model, broken refresh result: a clean bi-ready export mistake exports are a handoff. make them friendly. best practice validate, then hand off, with versioned file names. rule validate, then to_csv with index=false. three fixes to apply 1 index always set index=false on export. 2 naming snake_case columns and iso dates. 3 assert check uniqueness and totals first.
m7-reproducibility: rule notebooks are for exploration. scripts are for repeatability. prototype in a notebook, ship as a script 1 notebook 2 functions 3 script 4 git run it any time, get the same output the pattern prototype in notebook for learning and exploration. convert stable work into scripts for repeatability. keep config variables at the top for easy changes. use functions for pipeline steps. track changes with git to preserve history. script structure # scripts/build_kpis.py import pandas as pd # --- config --- data_dir = 'data/raw' output_dir = 'outputs' def load (): ... def clean (df): ... def build_kpis (df): ... def export (df): ... if __name__ == '__main__' : df = load () df = clean (df) kpi = build_kpis (df) export (kpi) result run the script any time and get the same output. that's reproducibility. reproducibility notebook only: can't rerun ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice keep the pipeline in a notebook run order decides the result convert stable work to a script python scripts/build_kpis.py edit paths inside cells config buried in the code config at top, functions for steps load, clean, build_kpis, export no version history cannot see what changed track changes with git history preserved result: a result nobody can reproduce result: same output on every run mistake notebooks are for exploration. best practice prototype in a notebook, ship as a script. rule notebooks explore. scripts repeat. three fixes to apply 1 script it move stable code to a script. 2 config put paths and dates at the top. 3 use git track every change over time.
