m7-checklist: use before every export 10 checks. takes 2 minutes. saves a broken dashboard. ten checks; #4 is the one most often missed ✓ snake_case ✓ iso dates ✓ unique key ! numeric amounts ✓ no blanks ✓ clean labels ✓ row counts ✓ totals match ✓ source file ✓ versioned amounts stored as strings the 10 checks are column names snake_case ? are dates datetime or iso strings ? is the primary key unique (no dupes)? are amounts numeric , not strings? have missing values been resolved or documented? are categories normalized (no 'completed' vs 'completed ')? do row counts match expectations? do totals match the source system? is there a source file / date for traceability? is the export versioned (e.g., clean_2025-12-06.csv )? most common miss check #4 — amounts stored as strings. always convert before export. pre-export checklist exporting with string amounts ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice amounts left as strings the most often missed check amounts numeric, not strings check dtypes before export row counts not compared dropped rows go unnoticed row counts match expectations primary key unique, no dupes totals not tied to source dashboard numbers disagree totals match the source system source file and date recorded result: a broken dashboard result: two minutes saves a dashboard mistake skipping the checklist costs a broken dashboard. best practice ten checks before every export. ten checks snake_case, iso dates, unique key, numeric amounts, totals. three fixes to apply 1 dtypes confirm amounts are numeric. 2 counts compare row counts to expectations. 3 totals match totals to the source.

m8-overview: data cleaning is a repeatable loop data cleaning is a repeatable loop 01 profile types, nulls, duplicates 02 define rules valid values and exceptions 03 transform correct approved defects 04 validate counts, totals, constraints 05 monitor new loads reveal drift 06 repeat update versioned rules expand diagram purpose data cleaning enables reliable and trustworthy analytical results. it is the discipline that makes every other analytics skill usable. core truths real-world business datasets are rarely clean or structured. cleaning must always precede analysis and predictive modeling. poor data quality consistently leads to incorrect business decisions. guiding principle cleaning is not a step you complete — it is a discipline you apply iteratively throughout the analytics lifecycle.
m8-why-matters: impact cleaning is the difference between an insight that changes a decision and one that misleads the room. four reasons cleaning matters reason why accuracy ensures accuracy in sales, finance, and revenue insights trust improves stakeholder trust in dashboards and reports truth prevents misleading trends caused by incorrect raw data efficiency reduces costly rework during later analytical stages cost of bad data 1 bad data wrong numbers 2 wrong decisions misallocated budget 3 lost trust stakeholders disengage why cleaning matters dirty data: wrong numbers, wrong decisions ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice report counts from raw exports customer count 1204 vs 1131 clean clean before you count dedupe, then recount customers trust the first average avg spend 142.6 vs 98.4 clean recheck averages after cleaning compare dirty vs clean results treat blanks as zero missing age shown as 0 keep blanks as true nulls missing is not the same as 0 result: misleading trends, lost trust result: insights that hold up mistake dashboards show wrong figures to the room. best practice stakeholders trust the numbers they see. rule of thumb bad data gives wrong numbers, then wrong decisions. three fixes to apply 1 accuracy clean first so sales and revenue figures are right. 2 trust show dirty vs clean totals to build confidence. 3 less rework fixing early avoids costly rework in later stages.

m9-correlation: definition correlation measures the strength and direction of a linear association between two numeric variables. correlation strength and direction (not causation) r ≈ +0.9 r ≈ 0 r ≈ −0.9 four rules correlation measures association strength. it does not imply causation . high correlation may be spurious. eda avoids causal assumptions. classic trap ice cream sales and drowning deaths are correlated — because both rise in summer. correlation correlation is not causation ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice read r as a cause ice cream and drownings say the variables are associated r measures linear association ignore the hidden driver both rise in summer look for a third variable temperature drives both trust any high r high correlation may be spurious check for spurious links avoid causal assumptions result: false causal conclusions result: honest association claims mistake temperature is the hidden driver, not ice cream. best practice strength and direction, never cause. remember correlation measures linear association only. three fixes to apply 1 measure r gives strength and direction. 2 seek look for hidden third variables. 3 avoid make no causal claim from r.
m9-simpson: definition a trend that appears in aggregated data reverses when you break it into subgroups. four points aggregated data may mislead. trends can reverse within subgroups. eda investigates data at multiple levels. avoids incorrect conclusions. aggregated looks flat, subgroups reverse aggregated flat / no trend by subgroup opposite directions simpson's paradox the trend reverses in subgroups ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice trust the aggregate b looks better overall break results into subgroups a wins in each group skip subgroup views a wins in every group check at multiple levels aggregate and group views ignore case mix a treated more hard cases compare the group mix hard cases explain the gap result: wrong winner chosen result: the true effect is seen mistake the aggregate points the wrong way. best practice trends can reverse within subgroups. rule always check the aggregate against its subgroups. three fixes to apply 1 split break the data by key segments. 2 compare check subgroup trend vs overall trend. 3 explain find the mix that drives the reversal.
m9-grouped: definition compare a metric across categories — region, cohort, product, channel. compare groups on centre and spread east west north whiskers = spread west: big spread, only 12 orders four points eda compares metrics across segments. examples include region, cohort, or product. group-level patterns reveal drivers. supports segmentation strategy. df. groupby ( 'region' )[ 'revenue' ]. agg ([ 'mean' , 'median' , 'count' ]) habit always look at spread within each group, not just the mean. grouped analysis don't trust a group mean alone ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice rank groups by mean only west has the highest mean report mean, median, count groupby().agg(['mean','median','count']) ignore group size west has only 12 orders show the count per group flag small groups like west skip spread within groups whiskers show spread plot spread per group box plot by region result: a thin group looks best result: fair group comparisons mistake 12 orders can mislead a whole ranking. best practice always look at spread within each group. habit look at spread within each group, not just the mean. three fixes to apply 1 aggregate use groupby with mean, median, count. 2 count show n beside each group. 3 spread box plot every group to see spread.
m9-crosstab: definition a cross-tab counts how many observations fall into each combination of two categorical variables. cross-tab: joint counts become rates per row converted not rate mobile 180 5820 3.0% desktop 150 2850 5.0% four points cross-tabs summarize joint distributions. they reveal dependency patterns. common in behavioral analysis. eda uses them before modeling. pd. crosstab (df[ 'device' ], df[ 'converted' ], normalize= 'index' ) cross-tabulation counts become rates per row ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice compare raw counts mobile 180 vs desktop 150 normalise by row pd.crosstab(..., normalize='index') ignore group totals mobile has 6000 rows read the rate mobile 3.0% vs desktop 5.0% skip joint distributions dependency patterns missed cross-tab before modeling reveal dependency patterns result: volume mistaken for performance result: true rates compared mistake bigger groups look like better groups. best practice joint counts become rates per row. formula rate = converted / row total, for every row. three fixes to apply 1 count build the joint count table. 2 normalise convert counts to rates per row. 3 compare read rates, not raw counts.

m9-multivariate: reality most real phenomena involve multiple variables interacting. several variables at once: position, size and colour x = tenure · y = spend · size = tickets · colour = segment four points most phenomena involve multiple variables. univariate views are incomplete. eda explores interactions. multivariate analysis adds realism. multivariate thinking most phenomena need several variables ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice look at one column at a time univariate views are incomplete explore variables jointly tenure, spend, tickets, segment ignore combinations combinations matter look for combinations each row is a point in 4-d use one chart channel position only encode with size and colour x, y, size and colour result: joint patterns are missed result: realistic, richer insight mistake single columns miss what variables do together. best practice look for combinations that matter. remember each row is a point in many dimensions. three fixes to apply 1 combine plot several variables together. 2 encode use size and colour for extra variables. 3 interpret look for combinations, not columns.
m9-curse: definition as the number of variables grows, data becomes sparse and distances become meaningless. more dimensions, same data: space becomes empty 1d: 10 points, dense 2d: sparser 3d: mostly empty four points more variables increase complexity. distances become less meaningful. noise dominates signal. eda helps reduce dimensions. rule more features rarely means better models. feature selection beats feature dumping. curse of dimensionality more features, emptier space ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice add every feature available feature dumping select features deliberately selection beats dumping trust distances in high dimensions distances lose meaning reduce dimensions eda helps cut the count assume more means better noise dominates the signal keep features that add signal fewer, relevant variables result: sparse data, weak models result: denser data, stronger models mistake each added dimension needs 10x more data. best practice dense in 1d, mostly empty in 3d. rule more features rarely means better models. three fixes to apply 1 select pick features on purpose, not by habit. 2 reduce cut dimensions where redundant. 3 check watch data density as features grow.
m9-multicollinearity: definition highly correlated predictors confuse models and inflate coefficient variance. two predictors pointing the same way carry the same information price price_with_tax vif ≫ 10 drop one of the two four consequences highly correlated predictors cause instability. models become hard to interpret. eda identifies redundant features. simplification improves robustness. eda tool use a correlation matrix or vif to spot redundancy early. multicollinearity two predictors, one signal ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice keep price and price_with_tax same information twice drop one of the pair keep price or price_with_tax ignore redundancy vif is far above 10 check vif flag vif well above 10 read unstable coefficients models hard to interpret simplify the feature set improves robustness result: unstable, inflated coefficients result: stable, readable model mistake correlated predictors confuse the model. best practice redundant features are found early. eda tool use a correlation matrix or vif to spot redundancy. three fixes to apply 1 scan run a correlation matrix first. 2 measure compute vif for each predictor. 3 drop remove one of each redundant pair.
m9-correlation-matrix: definition a grid showing pairwise correlation between all numeric variables. four points matrices summarize numeric relationships. they reveal clusters of related features. eda uses them as diagnostic tools. heatmaps improve interpretation. correlation heatmap rev units profit disc rev units profit disc correlation matrix read the heatmap, don't just draw it ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice read it as causation revenue and units: 0.82 use a heatmap colour makes the grid readable skip the heatmap raw numbers are hard to scan find related clusters revenue and units move together ignore feature clusters related features go unnoticed spot opposing pairs discount pulls the other way result: clusters and redundancy missed result: relationships seen at a glance mistake a grid of numbers hides structure. best practice matrices are diagnostic tools, not proof. remember pairwise grid of every numeric variable. three fixes to apply 1 plot show the matrix as a heatmap. 2 cluster look for groups of related features. 3 follow up investigate strong pairs further.
m9-dim-reduction: idea fewer, smarter features often beat many noisy ones. fewer, smarter features 12 correlated features 3 components keep most variance four points reducing variables improves clarity. combines related dimensions. simplifies visualization. eda introduces reduction techniques conceptually. dimension reduction fewer, smarter features ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice keep all 12 correlated features many noisy features combine related features 12 features into 3 components plot only raw columns hard to visualise keep most of the variance 3 components keep most variance treat every feature as unique related dimensions stay split visualise in fewer dimensions simplifies the picture result: noisy, hard-to-read data result: clearer, simpler data mistake complexity grows with every column. best practice fewer, smarter features often beat many. idea fewer, smarter features beat many noisy ones. three fixes to apply 1 combine merge correlated features into components. 2 keep variance retain components that carry most variance. 3 visualise plot in two or three dimensions.
m9-pca: definition principal component analysis transforms correlated variables into a smaller set of uncorrelated components. pca finds the directions of greatest variance pc1 (52%) pc2 (24%) components are mathematical, not business concepts four points pca transforms variables into components. each component captures variance. reduces dimensionality. used for insight, not interpretation. caution components don't have business meaning — they're mathematical constructs. pca pca: components are math, not meaning ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice give components business names pc1 is not 'customer value' treat components as math directions of greatest variance use pca to explain results for insight, not interpretation use pca to reduce and view insight, not interpretation ignore variance explained pc1 52%, pc2 24% check variance explained first two hold 76% result: false business stories result: valid reduction, honest claims mistake components are mathematical constructs. best practice a 2-d picture is a fair summary here. caution components have no business meaning on their own. three fixes to apply 1 transform turn correlated variables into components. 2 check read variance explained per component. 3 caution never label components as business concepts.
m9-temporal: idea time adds complexity. trends, seasonality, and cycles appear. four points time adds complexity. trends, seasonality, and cycles appear. eda analyzes temporal patterns. time awareness is critical. trend + seasonality underlying trend up, weekly wiggles on top temporal eda time adds trend and seasonality ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice treat rows as unordered time order ignored plot values over time trend up, wiggles on top average across all dates december spike averaged away look for yearly spikes december spikes every year ignore seasonality weekly and yearly cycles missed separate trend from season level climbs underneath result: cycles mistaken for change result: trend and cycle told apart mistake a seasonal spike reads as a real shift. best practice time awareness is critical. check plot against time before any average. three fixes to apply 1 plot draw the series over time. 2 season look for repeating cycles by day, week, year. 3 trend separate the long-term level.
m9-stationarity: definition stationary data has stable statistical properties over time (mean, variance, autocorrelation). stationary vs non-stationary series stationary: stable mean and spread non-stationary: drifting mean four points stationary data has stable properties. non-stationary data changes over time. eda identifies instability. important for forecasting. why it matters most forecasting models assume stationarity. if it's violated, they misbehave. stationarity drifting mean breaks forecasts ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice forecast on drifting data series b drifts upward check for stable mean and spread series a is stationary skip the stability check mean and spread not compared spot instability in eda plot and compare windows ignore changing variance models misbehave difference drifting series forecasting models need it result: forecasts that misbehave result: stable inputs for forecasting mistake most models assume stationarity. best practice stable mean, variance, autocorrelation. why it matters if stationarity is violated, models misbehave. three fixes to apply 1 plot look at the series over time. 2 test compare mean and spread across periods. 3 difference transform drifting series first.
m9-cohorts: definition group users by their start time (signup month, first purchase week) and track their behavior over time. cohort retention triangle jan 100% 45% 30% 22% 18% feb 100% 45% 30% 22% mar 100% 45% 30% apr 100% 45% month 0 month 1 month 2 read across: how long does each cohort stay? four points cohorts group users by start time. tracks behavior over time. reveals retention patterns. eda commonly uses cohorts. question it answers "are newer users sticking around better than older users did?" cohort analysis cohorts: do newer users stick? ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice pool all users together average retention hides trends group users by start month jan, feb, mar, apr cohorts ignore signup time old and new users mixed track behavior over time month 0, 1, 2 across read one cohort only misses the comparison compare cohorts at month 2 newer 33% vs 30% result: retention trends hidden result: clear retention patterns mistake newer cohorts' gains are blended away. best practice read across: how long does each cohort stay? question it answers are newer users sticking better than older ones? three fixes to apply 1 group assign users to start-month cohorts. 2 track follow each cohort over months. 3 compare compare cohorts at the same age.

m9-outliers: rule investigate first, decide later. never remove silently. investigate first, decide later error, vip or real event? typical values outlier four points outliers may represent rare events. they can dominate metrics. eda treats outliers cautiously. context determines action. reminder some outliers are the story. removing them hides what you should be looking at. outliers investigate first, decide later ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice delete outliers silently some outliers are the story investigate each outlier error, vip or real event? keep them without a check they dominate the metrics let context decide keep, fix or flag it assume 48000 is an error could be a real b2b order report with and without show the effect on metrics result: story hidden or metrics skewed result: an informed, documented choice mistake removal hides what you should look at. best practice rare events can be the finding. rule investigate first, decide later. never remove silently. three fixes to apply 1 investigate trace each outlier to its source. 2 decide use context to keep or fix. 3 document record what you did and why.
m9-noise: definition noise is random variation that obscures the underlying pattern. signal is the pattern itself. smoothing reveals the signal under the noise daily noisy values 7-day average four points noise obscures patterns. eda separates meaningful trends from randomness. smoothing techniques help. overfitting is avoided. technique moving averages and rolling windows turn noisy daily data into readable trend lines. noise vs signal smooth the noise, keep the signal ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice read every daily jump as a trend noise obscures patterns smooth with a 7-day average rolling window on daily data chase random wiggles overfitting follows separate trend from randomness eda reveals meaningful trends plot raw daily values only steady rise stays hidden plot raw and smoothed see the steady rise result: random variation taken as real result: a readable trend line mistake daily numbers jump around, then fade. best practice the rolling average shows a steady rise. technique use moving averages and rolling windows. three fixes to apply 1 smooth apply a rolling average to daily data. 2 compare overlay raw and smoothed lines. 3 resist do not fit random wiggles.
m9-documentation: rule if it isn't documented, it didn't happen. your future self will thank you. one notebook cell per finding 1 question 2 finding 3 chart 4 decision 5 open q four points eda must be documented. insights guide future analysis. reproducibility matters. professional analysts document eda. format notebook markdown cells work great — figures, findings, and open questions in one place. eda documentation if it isn't documented, it didn't happen ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice explore with no written record findings live in your head one notebook cell per finding question, finding, chart leave charts without findings no decision, no open question record decisions and open qs guides future analysis skip reproducibility others cannot repeat it keep notebooks reproducible markdown cells with figures result: undefendable, unrepeatable eda result: defensible, repeatable eda mistake insights are lost to your future self. best practice finding, evidence, decision, open question. format question, finding, chart, decision, open question. three fixes to apply 1 write log each finding as you go. 2 decide note decisions and the reason for each. 3 repeat make the notebook re-runnable.
m9-iterative: reality eda is not a linear checklist. it loops. eda loops: every answer raises the next question explore find question explore again loop back four points eda is not linear. new insights trigger deeper analysis. analysts revisit earlier steps. iteration strengthens understanding. expect this you will go back to univariate after doing multivariate. that's not wasted time — that's eda. iterative eda eda loops, it doesn't line up ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice treat eda as a linear list one pass, then done expect to loop explore, find, question, repeat never revisit earlier steps back to univariate? wasted time return to earlier steps univariate after multivariate stop at the first answer skip the next question let answers raise questions each answer triggers the next result: shallow understanding result: deeper understanding mistake follow-up questions never get asked. best practice iteration strengthens understanding. expect this going back is not wasted time. that is eda. three fixes to apply 1 loop cycle explore, find, question. 2 revisit go back to earlier steps. 3 follow chase each new question to the next step.
m9-vs-automation: balance automated eda tools speed up exploration. they cannot replace judgment. automation accelerates, judgment decides automation profile, flags, speed you context, doubt, decisions vs four points automated eda accelerates exploration. human judgment remains essential. automation supports, not replaces thinking. eda is an intellectual process. eda vs automation automation flags, you decide ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice accept the auto-profile report flags without context use automation for speed profile, flags, speed skip your own checks tools cannot see context add your own context judgment and doubt let the tool think for you eda is an intellectual process you make the decisions automation supports thinking result: flags without meaning result: fast and thoughtful eda mistake speed replaces human judgment. best practice automation lists flags; judgment reads them. balance automation accelerates; judgment decides. three fixes to apply 1 profile let tools scan the data quickly. 2 interpret you judge what flags mean. 3 decide own the final call; tools only assist.
m9-business: rule patterns without context are useless. insights must be actionable. only insights that change an action are finished 1 pattern 2 insight 3 action 4 impact four points eda connects data to business questions. insights must be actionable. patterns without context are useless. eda aligns analytics with strategy. ask "if we acted on this insight, what would change?" if the answer is nothing, the insight isn't ready. eda in business only actionable insights are finished ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice report patterns with no context useless to the business link patterns to business asks pattern, insight, action stop at the chart pattern without action name the action and impact insight, action, impact skip the so what no decision attached ask what would change if nothing, it is not ready result: insights nobody acts on result: insights that change actions mistake patterns without context are useless. best practice eda aligns analytics with strategy. ask if we acted on this, what would change? three fixes to apply 1 context tie each pattern to a business question. 2 action state what to do about it. 3 impact say what should change once you act.
m9-pitfalls: beware eda without discipline becomes storytelling without evidence. four ways eda goes wrong overread noise no domain context confirmation bias no discipline four pitfalls overinterpreting noise. ignoring domain knowledge. confirmation bias. eda requires discipline. antidote ask "what would have to be true for this pattern to be wrong?" and go look for it. eda pitfalls eda without discipline is a story ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice overread noise 20 comparisons at 5% treat small effects with caution expect one false hit in 20 skip domain knowledge no context for the pattern bring in domain context ask people who know the data look only for what you expect confirmation bias try to prove yourself wrong what would make this false? result: false findings reported result: findings that hold up mistake one false positive is expected by chance. best practice go look for the evidence against it. antidote what would have to be true for this to be wrong? three fixes to apply 1 count track how many comparisons you ran. 2 context use domain knowledge to check each pattern. 3 disprove hunt for counter- evidence.
m9-ethics: reality eda can expose sensitive patterns. responsible analysis is mandatory. protect people in small groups 128 41 212 77 n = 3 small cells can identify individuals: suppress or merge groups below your minimum size (e.g. n < 10) four points eda can expose sensitive patterns. privacy must be respected. bias must be acknowledged. responsible analysis is mandatory. example even aggregated eda can expose rare categories that identify individuals. small cells deserve protection. eda ethics protect people in small groups ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice publish every small cell a cell of n = 3 suppress or merge small groups minimum size, e.g. n under 10 ignore sensitive patterns eda can expose them respect privacy handle sensitive patterns with care skip bias acknowledgment aggregates can still identify acknowledge bias state limits openly result: individuals can be identified result: people protected mistake rare categories can reveal individuals. best practice responsible analysis is mandatory. rule set a minimum group size and enforce it. three fixes to apply 1 check look for tiny cells in every table. 2 merge combine or suppress them before sharing. 3 disclose state bias and limits openly.
m9-story: idea eda uncovers stories hidden in data. not all stories are obvious. from data to story 1 data 2 pattern 3 insight 4 story four points eda uncovers stories hidden in data. not all stories are obvious. analysts synthesize insights. storytelling begins here. next your storytelling in module 5 is only as strong as the eda behind it. eda as story from data to a story ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice hand over raw charts stakeholders must decode them turn findings into sentences one a stakeholder can act on report only obvious findings not all stories are obvious dig for hidden stories look past the obvious list facts with no synthesis no insight, no story synthesise: pattern to insight data, pattern, insight, story result: findings nobody acts on result: clear stories that land mistake patterns stay buried in the notebook. best practice storytelling starts in eda. next module 5 storytelling is only as strong as your eda. three fixes to apply 1 find surface patterns in the data. 2 distil turn them into insights that carry meaning. 3 tell write a sentence people can act on.
m9-transition-modeling: bridge eda informs model choice. features are selected deliberately. assumptions are validated. model choice is a consequence of eda 1 eda 2 features 3 assumptions 4 model four points eda informs model choice. features are selected deliberately. assumptions are validated. models become explainable. rule model choice should be a consequence of eda, not a default. transition to modeling model choice follows eda ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice pick a default model chosen before looking choose the model from findings eda informs model choice throw in every feature selected by habit select features deliberately based on what eda showed skip assumption checks unvalidated assumptions validate assumptions models become explainable result: unexplainable models result: explainable, justified models mistake choices have no evidence behind them. best practice every choice traces to a finding. rule model choice is a result of eda, not a default. three fixes to apply 1 list write down eda findings before modeling. 2 map link each to a modeling choice. 3 validate check assumptions before fitting.

m10-communication: definition data visualization communicates insight. charts translate numbers into meaning, and visuals influence decisions. from data to decision: the chart is the bridge 1 data 2 chart 3 insight 4 decision four principles data visualization communicates insight. charts translate numbers into meaning. visuals influence decisions. design is responsibility. guiding principle if the chart doesn't change how someone thinks or acts, it isn't finished. visualization as communication charts: a bridge from data to decision ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice chart with no stated insight viewer must guess the point name the insight on every chart up 18% since launch weekly signups line, no headline are we growing? stays unanswered tie chart to a question churn by plan: who is leaving? report ends at the chart no decision named state the decision it supports fix basic onboarding result: pretty chart, no action result: insight leads to decision mistake chart shows data, nobody acts on it. best practice each chart carries an insight and a decision. test if it changes no thinking or action, it is not finished. three fixes to apply 1 add insight write the finding as the chart headline. 2 ask the question pick the chart from the question it answers. 3 name the action end with the decision the chart supports.
m10-not-decoration: principle charts are analytical tools first. aesthetics support clarity, not replace it. function first, then polish decoration pretty, message unclear function plain, message obvious vs four points charts are analytical tools. aesthetics support clarity. decoration without purpose misleads. form follows function. test if you removed the decoration and the message is unchanged, the decoration was never needed. not decoration decoration: pretty but message unclear ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice gradient background adds no data plain background message is obvious 3d bars adds no data, distorts reading flat bars lengths read directly clip-art icon in the corner adds no data one accent colour on the key bar highlights the point result: pretty, message unclear result: plain, message obvious mistake decoration without purpose misleads the reader. best practice aesthetics support clarity, never replace it. test remove it: if the message is unchanged, it was not needed. three fixes to apply 1 remove 3d flat bars read more accurately. 2 drop clip art if it adds no data, delete it. 3 keep one accent colour only the key bar and add value labels.
m10-cognitive-load: definition humans have limited attention. visual clutter overwhelms cognition; good design reduces mental effort. four points humans have limited attention. visual clutter overwhelms cognition. good design reduces mental effort. visualization manages attention. attention budget focused on data distracted by clutter cognitive load clutter: overloading limited attention ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice 24 competing visual elements about 18.0 seconds to answer cut to 9 elements about 4.0 seconds to answer every series highlighted nothing stands out focused view, one highlight 5 elements, about 2.5 seconds decorative extras on the chart eyes wander off the data keep only what supports the point attention stays on data result: slow, error-prone reading result: faster, more accurate read mistake clutter overwhelms limited attention. best practice good design reduces mental effort. rule of thumb fewer competing elements means a faster read. three fixes to apply 1 cut clutter remove every element that adds no answer. 2 one highlight draw the eye to the single key point. 3 spend attention treat focus as a budget for the data.
