m10-evolution-tools: rule tools evolve rapidly. principles remain constant. software changes, theory doesn't. tools change, principles stay excel tableau power bi python web perception · clarity · honesty (constant) four points tools evolve rapidly. principles remain constant. software changes, theory doesn't. master fundamentals. timeline excel → tableau → power bi → python viz → web viz. every tool inherits the same principles. evolution of tools chasing tools instead of principles ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice learn each tool's buttons only tools evolve rapidly zero baseline in any tool excel, tableau, power bi tool defaults decide the design defaults may break rules hierarchy and consistency apply in every tool principles dropped on migration excel to power bi reproducible charts in python same perception rules on web result: skills expire with each tool result: skills carry across tools mistake software changes; theory does not. best practice every tool inherits the same principles. rule master fundamentals; tools will change. three fixes to apply 1 learn rules perception, honesty. 2 override fix defaults that break rules. 3 port skills take principles to new tools.
m10-bi: context bi emphasizes consistency and speed. standard metrics dominate. interactivity supports exploration. bi: one trusted definition per metric 1 sources 2 metric layer 3 dashboard 4 decision standard metrics keep every team on the same number four points bi emphasizes consistency and speed. standard metrics dominate. interactivity supports exploration. design discipline required. visualization in bi teams reporting different numbers ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice each team defines its own revenue different totals revenue: net sales after returns owner: finance churn calculated per dashboard no single definition churn: cancelled / start customers owner: customer success metrics without owners nobody to ask metric layer feeds dashboards one trusted definition result: numbers disputed in meetings result: every team on the same number mistake no shared metric definition. best practice standard metrics keep teams aligned. rule one definition per metric, with a named owner. three fixes to apply 1 define write each metric once. 2 assign owner name who maintains it. 3 one layer dashboards read from it.
m10-data-science: context models produce complex outputs. visuals explain predictions. interpretability matters. explaining a model: which features drive the prediction tenure 38% support tickets 27% plan 18% region 9% device 8% illustrative four points models produce complex outputs. visuals explain predictions. interpretability matters. visualization bridges model and user. visualization in data science a model nobody can explain ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice share predictions only black box feature-importance bar chart tenure 38%, tickets 27% raw model output tables stakeholders cannot discuss sorted bars of drivers plan 18%, region 9%, device 8% skip interpretability no reason for the prediction label values as illustrative interpretability matters result: stakeholders distrust the model result: black box becomes discussable mistake complex output with no explanation. best practice visuals bridge model and user. rule explain predictions with visuals, not only scores. three fixes to apply 1 show drivers chart feature importance. 2 sort biggest driver first. 3 label mark illustrative values.
m10-maturity: progression visualization skill deepens with practice and feedback. maturity ladder charts clarity narrative impact four levels level focus beginner focuses on charts intermediate focuses on clarity advanced focuses on narrative expert focuses on impact maturity levels stopping at a valid chart ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice ask only: is the chart valid? beginner focus clarity: readable in 5 seconds? intermediate skip the 5-second readability test clarity untested narrative: what is the story? advanced never ask what will change impact unmeasured impact: what will change? expert result: correct charts, little effect result: charts that change decisions mistake chart choice alone is not the goal. best practice use the last column as a pre-publish check. ladder charts, clarity, narrative, then impact. three fixes to apply 1 clarity test the 5-second read. 2 narrative find the story. 3 impact name what changes.
m10-review: practice peer review catches issues. fresh eyes spot bias. iteration improves quality. review loop draft feedback revise share ask: what is confusing? four points peer review catches issues. fresh eyes spot bias. iteration improves quality. review is essential. process show the draft. ask "what's confusing?" listen. revise. repeat. review process publishing without fresh eyes ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice share the first draft no one checks it ask: what is confusing? legend became direct labels defend your design feedback is ignored fix what is found axis reset to zero baseline review once and stop no iteration repeat until clear round 4: published result: confusing charts go out result: each round gives a change mistake own bias goes unnoticed. best practice fresh eyes spot bias. process show draft, ask, listen, revise, repeat. three fixes to apply 1 ask what is confusing? 2 listen do not defend. 3 iterate repeat until clear.
m10-trust: reality clear visuals build credibility. inconsistent visuals erode trust. consistency earns credibility clear + consistent trust and adoption rise messy + inconsistent every number gets questioned four points clear visuals build credibility. inconsistent visuals erode trust. design reflects professionalism. trust drives adoption. visualization and trust small inconsistencies erode trust ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice different y-axis, same metric erodes trust consistent colours and scales builds trust unlabelled estimates erodes trust label estimates clearly say what is estimated no source or date every number gets questioned source and date on every chart builds trust result: every number is questioned result: trust and adoption rise mistake messy visuals cost adoption. best practice credibility is earned by small, steady choices. rule clear and consistent earns credibility. three fixes to apply 1 same axis same metric, same scale. 2 label estimates mark them as estimates. 3 cite source and date always.
m10-long-term: principle design systems scale. ad-hoc visuals do not. strategic design saves time. ad hoc visuals vs a reusable system each report restyled one template, reused four points design systems scale. ad-hoc visuals do not. strategic design saves time. consistency compounds value. investment a reusable style guide pays back 10× over a year of reporting. long-term thinking restyling every report from scratch ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice ad hoc: 0 setup hours 6 hours per report design system: 40 setup hours 2 hours per report restyle each report 288 total hours at 48 reports one template, reused 136 total hours at 48 reports skip a template savings never compound invest in a style guide consistency compounds result: 288 hours a year (example) result: 136 hours a year (example) mistake ad hoc visuals do not scale. best practice figures are an example, not a benchmark. rule setup costs hours once; every later report is faster. three fixes to apply 1 set up once invest in a template. 2 reuse apply it to each report. 3 compound savings grow each year.
m10-skill: reality visualization combines art and science. practice improves intuition. practice raises intuition chart 1 chart 100 feedback speeds this up four points visualization combines art and science. practice improves intuition. feedback accelerates growth. skill develops over time. visualization as skill making charts without feedback ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice make a few charts, no review feedback received: low 5 to 6 charts a week steady practice same focus every week no deliberate growth rotate focus each week choice, colour, annotation practice only when free intuition builds slowly seek feedback, 3 per week accelerates growth result: slow improvement result: intuition grows over time mistake charts without feedback stall. best practice deliberate practice with feedback. rule practice improves intuition; feedback speeds it up. three fixes to apply 1 practise make charts weekly. 2 rotate focus one skill at a time. 3 get feedback ask others to review.
m10-validation: rule charts must be validated. numbers should match visuals. errors undermine credibility. chart numbers must equal table numbers chart: west bar = 4100 = table 410 west is 10× off 4100 ≠ 410 four points charts must be validated. numbers should match visuals. errors undermine credibility. verification is mandatory. common bug y-axis scale off by 10×. always cross-check the chart against the summary table. visual validation chart says 4100, table says 410 ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice publish without cross-check west bar 4100 vs table 410 compare chart to summary table east 540 matches trust the chart total chart total 4995 check against an independent total table total 1305 ignore axis and unit scale west bar is 10x too large fix axis or unit bug west back to 410 result: errors undermine credibility result: chart equals table mistake numbers and visuals do not match. best practice verification is mandatory. check chart numbers must equal table numbers. three fixes to apply 1 cross-check compare chart to table. 2 total check use an independent total. 3 fix units find the 10x bug.
m10-recap: module flow 1 perception 2 design 3 story 4 ethics the five lines visualization is communication. design shapes understanding. ethics and clarity matter. great visuals enable decisions. principles outlast tools.
m11-overview: purpose design dashboards that drive decisions rather than merely display data. this module covers the full lifecycle: requirements, design, dax, performance, security, deployment, and adoption. what you'll build executive dashboard — 7 kpis, mobile-first, 10-second insight operational dashboard — drill-through, rls, what-if self-service solution — certified dataset + thin reports documentation package — kpi dictionary + quick-start + video module flow six sections 1 design 2 dax 3 interact 4 perf & rls 5 deploy guiding principle a dashboard is a decision tool. if it doesn't change what someone does, it failed.
m11-objectives: by the end of this module you will be able to design, build, deploy, and maintain production-grade bi dashboards. five objectives, one chain: question to maintained dashboard 1 design 2 kpis 4 standards 5 deploy five objectives # objective detail 1 design for decisions dashboards that drive action, not just display 2 translate questions to kpis balanced scorecards, leading + lagging 3 self-service analytics reduce dependency on it 4 enterprise standards security, performance, governance 5 deploy & maintain production dashboards with confidence prerequisite modules 1–7 — you now bring analytics, sql, and python into bi.
m11-why-fail: gartner 2024 70% of dashboards are ignored after 3 months. primary causes unclear purpose — nobody knows what decision it supports. too many metrics — death by kpi (>7–9 on one page). slow load times — users abandon anything over 5 seconds. no mobile support — executives check on phones. poor information architecture — users hunt for insights. no stakeholder involvement during planning. failure drivers unclear purpose too many kpis slow load no mobile no stakeholder involvement design against every one of these. why dashboards fail dashboards: why most are ignored ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice no decision in mind nobody knows what it supports write the charter first purpose, audience, decision 30 kpis on one page death by kpi, over 7 to 9 cut to 5 to 9 kpis each one tied to an action slow load, desktop only over 5 seconds, no phone view test speed and mobile under 5 s, phone layout built result: ignored within 3 months result: used and trusted daily mistake dashboards fail when they serve no one. best practice design against every failure driver. failure check purpose, kpis, speed, mobile, stakeholders: all covered? three fixes to apply 1 state purpose name the decision it supports before building. 2 limit kpis keep 5 to 9 metrics per page, no more. 3 involve users bring stakeholders in during planning.
m11-requirements: rule no wireframing until the dashboard charter is signed by the sponsor. the 5-step requirements framework (charter before wireframe) 1 workshops 2 moscow 3 map to kpis 4 charter 5 sign-off the 5-step framework 1-hour discovery workshops with each user group separately. moscow prioritization — must / should / could / won't have. document business questions first → map to metrics → map to visuals. one-page dashboard charter signed by sponsor. record latency requirements — real-time (<5s), daily, weekly. charter contents section what it captures purpose what decision does this support? audience who uses it, how often? kpis 5–9 metrics with definitions latency refresh cadence + acceptable load time scope in / out of scope owner named accountable person sponsor signature approval before building why a charter it prevents scope creep and gives you a formal "no" when requests come in later. requirements gathering requirements: charter before wireframe ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice wireframe on day one before any sign-off sign a one-page charter sponsor approves first mix all users in one meeting loudest voice sets scope 1-hour workshop per group then moscow: must/should/could skip latency and scope no refresh or load target record latency and scope real-time under 5s, daily, weekly result: scope creep, rework result: a formal no to extras mistake no charter means no way to say no. best practice charter first, wireframe second. rule of thumb no wireframing until the charter is signed. three fixes to apply 1 run workshops meet each user group separately for 1 hour. 2 prioritise use moscow, map needs to kpis then visuals. 3 get sign-off sponsor signs purpose, kpis, latency, scope.
m11-personas: rule different users need different views. never mix all on one dashboard. one persona = one page ceo 7 kpis · mobile ops manager drill-down · variance analyst explore · what-if summary page · hierarchy page · exploration page the three core personas persona needs design choice ceo 7 high-level kpis, mobile-first, 10-second insight single summary page, no filters operations manager drill-down to region/store, compare vs target hierarchy + variance visuals analyst export, parameters, what-if, ad-hoc filters full exploration page + bookmarks use case format # write every use case like this "as a <persona>, i want <goal> so that <reason>." # example "as an operations manager, i want to compare store revenue vs target so that i can prioritize coaching visits." architecture implication one persona = one page or tab. clear separation keeps each view focused. user personas personas: one user, one page ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice ceo, ops, analyst on one page everyone sees everything one persona, one page summary, hierarchy, exploration filters on the ceo view execs wanted a 10-second read ceo: 7 kpis, mobile, no filters ops: drill-down; analyst: what-if vague wishes as use cases show me sales data write as a persona i want goal so that reason result: cluttered page, no one served result: focused views per role mistake mixed audiences make a view nobody uses. best practice separate pages keep each view focused. use case format as a persona, i want a goal so that a reason. three fixes to apply 1 split pages one persona equals one page or tab. 2 match needs ceo summary, ops variance, analyst exploration. 3 write stories persona, goal, reason for every use case.
m11-info-arch: definition information architecture is the logical grouping and layout of everything on the dashboard. techniques card-sorting exercise — users group metrics into logical clusters. 5-second rule — users must understand the story in 5 seconds. low-fidelity tools — balsamiq, figma, or even powerpoint. mobile first — prototype on the smallest screen, then scale up. standard layout top-to-bottom dashboard flow 1 — summary banner 2 — 4–6 kpi cards 3 — supporting charts 4 — table / detail rule of thumb most important at the top-left, least important at the bottom-right. info architecture layout: top-left first, 5-second story ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice key number at bottom-right reader hunts for the story most important at top-left summary, 4 to 6 kpi cards, charts design desktop first phone view squeezed in later prototype mobile first then scale up to desktop start building in the tool no sketch or card sort card-sort and wireframe balsamiq, figma or powerpoint result: users hunt for insight result: story clear in 5 seconds mistake layout hides the most important metric. best practice sketch first, then build the layout. 5-second rule users grasp the story in 5 seconds or redesign. three fixes to apply 1 flow down banner, kpi cards, charts, then detail table. 2 card sort let users group metrics into logical clusters. 3 sketch low-fi wireframe before you open the bi tool.
m11-kpi-smart: definition every kpi must be specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, time-bound. a kpi that fails any letter is a wish, not a kpi s specific m measurable a achievable r relevant t time-bound "improve satisfaction" ✗ "csat ≥ 4.0 by q4" ✓ smart breakdown letter meaning bad → good s specific "satisfaction" → "csat score post-resolution" m measurable "improve" → "% above 4.0" a achievable not 100% in a week r relevant tied to a business objective t time-bound "by q4" not "eventually" good vs bad good monthly recurring revenue (mrr) growth % vs target. bad "improve customer satisfaction" — not measurable. kpi dictionary fields name — canonical kpi label definition — formula in words calculation — exact dax or sql data source — table + column owner — named accountable person refresh — cadence miller's law executive dashboards max out at 5–9 kpis. beyond that, decision-making degrades. kpi definition kpis: smart or just a wish ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice improve customer satisfaction not measurable csat score post-resolution specific and measurable satisfaction with no source which score, which survey? csat at or above 4.0 measurable threshold eventually, or 100% in a week no deadline, not achievable by q4, tied to an objective time-bound and relevant result: a wish, not a kpi result: clear, trackable kpi mistake a kpi failing any letter cannot be tracked. best practice write it in a kpi dictionary entry. miller's law executive dashboards max out at 5 to 9 kpis. three fixes to apply 1 be specific name the exact score and its data source. 2 make measurable use a number or percent against a target. 3 set a deadline time-bound, named owner, refresh cadence.
m11-leading-lagging: definitions lagging: tells you what happened. leading: predicts what will happen. comparison lagging (outcome) leading (driver) revenue website conversion rate profit avg deal size churn rate support resolution time net promoter score first-response time market share pipeline velocity visual best dashboards show both lagging nps = 42 (outcome) what happened leading avg resolution = 18h what to fix pattern each executive kpi should have 2–3 leading drivers shown next to it. that turns the dashboard from reporting to managing. leading vs lagging indicators: show what happened and why ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice only revenue and churn lagging: tells you after the fact pair with 2 to 3 leading drivers revenue with qualified pipeline nps alone, no driver nothing to fix next nps next to resolution time lagging beside the driver pick drivers at random not tied to the goal map goal to lead and lag retention: churn and weekly users result: reporting, not managing result: dashboard that drives action mistake outcomes alone show what you can no longer fix. best practice show both side by side: outcome and driver. pattern each executive kpi gets 2 to 3 leading drivers beside it. three fixes to apply 1 pair them put a driver next to every outcome kpi. 2 know the types lagging: what happened. leading: what will. 3 act early fix the driver before the outcome slips.
m11-balanced-scorecard: definition the balanced scorecard forces leadership to see trade-offs across four dimensions. the four perspectives perspective sample kpis financial revenue, ebitda, cash flow customer nps, retention rate, market share internal processes cycle time, defect rate, on-time delivery learning & growth employee engagement, training hours, innovation index visual four perspectives quadrant financial revenue · ebitda · cash customer nps · retention · share internal processes cycle · defect · delivery learning & growth engagement · training why it works prevents over-indexing on financials. surfaces leading indicators of future performance. balanced scorecard scorecard: more than financials ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice only revenue and ebitda financial view only financial: revenue, ebitda, cash target vs actual per kpi no customer or process kpis nps and cycle time missing customer: nps, retention, share leading signal of revenue ignore learning and growth engagement not tracked process and learning kpis cycle time, training hours result: short-term, one-sided view result: trade-offs visible to leaders mistake over-indexing on financials hides drivers. best practice four perspectives surface future performance. four perspectives financial, customer, process, learning and growth. three fixes to apply 1 balance views cover all four perspectives on one page. 2 set targets show target, actual and status for each kpi. 3 see trade-offs let leaders weigh competing dimensions.
m11-okr-kpi: definitions objectives are qualitative and inspirational. key results are quantitative and measurable. kpis are the operational metrics that track progress. the chain okr → kr → kpi 1 objective 2 key result 3 dashboard kpi worked example chain objective: "become market leader." key result: "reach 40% market share by q4." dashboard kpi: "market share % vs competitors." traceability matrix objective key result dashboard kpi owner grow revenue +20% yoy revenue vs ly vp sales improve retention churn < 3% monthly churn % vp cs operational excellence cycle time < 48h avg cycle time vp ops quarterly review re-audit the matrix with leadership every quarter. prevents kpi drift from strategy. okr to kpi okr to kpi: keep strategy traceable ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice kpis with no objective metrics nobody asked for chain okr, kr, kpi objective to dashboard metric objective with no key result become market leader, untracked key result is quantified 40% market share by q4 set the matrix once kpis drift from strategy re-audit every quarter with leadership, named owners result: kpi drift from strategy result: every kpi traces to a goal mistake dashboards track things nobody needs. best practice traceability matrix keeps focus. the chain objective, then key result, then dashboard kpi. three fixes to apply 1 link each kpi tie it to a key result and an objective. 2 quantify krs objectives inspire, key results are measurable. 3 review quarterly re-audit the matrix with leadership.
m11-kpi-cards: rule one kpi card = actual, target, previous, variance, and trend. all in a single glance. anatomy of a good kpi card recommended kpi card monthly recurring revenue $1.24m ▲ +12.4% vs target previous: $1.10m · target: $1.20m rules use bullet charts or sparklines — not gauges (stephen few). show actual, target, previous, % variance in one card. conditional formatting — red / amber / green thresholds agreed with owner. micro-trend sparkline for last 12 months. tooltip with definition and calculation logic. anti-pattern a kpi card showing only one number and no comparison tells you nothing. is $1.24m good? bad? trend? kpi card design kpi cards: a number needs context ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice show $1.24m alone good? bad? trending? actual, target, previous, variance $1.24m, +12.4% vs target use a gauge takes space, hard to compare bullet chart or sparkline 12-month micro-trend colors without agreed thresholds red/amber/green by guess thresholds agreed with owner plus tooltip with definition result: a number that tells nothing result: status clear at a glance mistake one number and no comparison is not a kpi. best practice everything in a single glance. one card rule actual, target, previous, variance and trend. three fixes to apply 1 add comparison show target and prior period beside the value. 2 skip gauges bullet charts and sparklines read better. 3 agree colors set rag thresholds with the kpi owner.
m11-visual-perception: definition how humans see and process visuals. ignoring this = ineffective dashboards. encode the most important number with position and length position length colour area 3d / pie angle reading order: top-left → bottom-right · max 5–6 colours pre-attentive attributes color — hue, intensity, brightness size — length, area, volume position — 2d location is the most accurate encoding shape — subtle but useful for series gestalt principles principle applied proximity group related items; separate unrelated similarity same color/shape = same meaning continuity aligned items read as a series closure shapes with implied boundaries group reading order left-to-right, top-to-bottom — for western audiences. limit palette to 5–6 colors maximum. align all objects to an invisible grid. no 3d and no pie charts — the eye can't compare angles or volumes accurately. stephen few the best visuals use minimal ink to convey maximum information. visual perception perception: encode with position, length ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice 3d charts and pie angles eye cannot compare angles bars: position and length most accurate encodings 10 colors across the page palette beyond 5 to 6 limit palette to 5 to 6 colors same color means same thing objects placed ad hoc no grid, no grouping align to a grid, group related top-left to bottom-right flow result: misread values, noise result: instant, accurate reading mistake weak encodings force readers to guess. best practice use pre-attentive cues on key numbers. encoding order position, length, then colour, area; avoid 3d and pie. three fixes to apply 1 use position 2d position is the most accurate encoding. 2 cap colors five to six colors maximum per dashboard. 3 apply gestalt proximity, similarity, continuity, closure.
m11-accessibility: standard wcag aa — the baseline for professional dashboards. requirements 4.5:1 contrast ratio minimum between text and background. color-blind safe palettes — colorbrewer or power bi defaults. never rely on color alone — add patterns, icons, or labels. provide a dark mode version if the corporate standard requires it. test with online accessibility tools — microsoft accessibility insights. colorblind-safe palettes palette use colorbrewer categorical and sequential okabe-ito 8-color categorical, safe for all types viridis sequential, perceptually uniform grayscale test blue green amber red → grayscale → test convert your dashboard to grayscale. if it still reads, it's accessible. color and accessibility accessibility: never color alone ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice red/green status only fails for color-blind users add icon or label to color pattern, icon or text status light grey text on white below 4.5 to 1 contrast contrast of 4.5:1 or better wcag aa baseline skip testing assume the palette works convert to grayscale to test plus accessibility insights result: some users cannot read it result: readable by everyone mistake color alone excludes part of your audience. best practice use colorbrewer, okabe-ito or viridis palettes. grayscale test if it still reads in grayscale, it is accessible. three fixes to apply 1 add cues icons, patterns or labels beside every color. 2 check contrast text needs 4.5:1 against its background. 3 pick safe palettes colorbrewer, okabe-ito, viridis.
m11-datasource-refresh: rule choose the connection mode based on latency and volume — not on ease. pick the connection mode by latency and volume directquery live · source load import fast · scheduled composite mix of both live conn. existing model incremental refresh for datasets over 10 gb · gateway cluster · failure alerts connection modes mode best for latency directquery real-time < 10k rows live import performance with larger data scheduled refresh composite mix both mixed live connection existing ssas / aas model live refresh strategies incremental refresh for datasets > 10 gb. dataflows / shared datasets to avoid duplication. gateway ha cluster in enterprise environments. monitor refresh history — set up email alerts for failures. never use directquery "just because." it shifts compute to the source and often hurts performance. connections and refresh connections: pick by latency, not ease ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice directquery just because pushes compute to the source import for speed, dq for live real-time under 10k rows full reload of a huge dataset over 10 gb every time incremental refresh over 10 gb refresh only what changed no refresh alerts failures found by users monitor refresh history email alerts on failure result: slow reports, stale data result: fast, reliable refresh mistake choosing for ease hurts performance. best practice match mode to latency and volume. rule choose the mode by latency and volume, not ease. three fixes to apply 1 match mode import, directquery, composite or live. 2 refresh smart incremental refresh and a gateway ha cluster. 3 share dataflows avoid duplicated data with shared datasets.
m11-data-modeling: rule a clean data model is the foundation of every performant dashboard. seven rules start with: star schema, one date table, single direction fact date product customer region one-to-many, single direction: dimension → fact the seven rules always use star schema — fact + dimension tables. create a dedicated date table and mark it as the date table. hide unnecessary columns and tables from report view. single-direction relationships — use bidirectional only when required. use dax studio to analyze model performance. turn off auto date/time if not using it. remove unused columns early in power query. why single-direction bidirectional relationships slow queries and can produce ambiguous filter results. data modeling data model: star, single direction ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice flat table or snowflake hard for dax to filter star schema: fact plus dimensions one marked date table bidirectional everywhere slow, ambiguous filters single-direction relationships bidirectional only when required leave unused columns in auto date/time left on hide and remove extra columns trim early in power query result: slow, ambiguous queries result: fast, predictable model mistake a messy model hurts every visual. best practice audit with dax studio before you ship. rule a clean data model is the foundation of performance. three fixes to apply 1 build a star fact table in the middle, dimensions around it. 2 one direction dimension to fact, single filter flow. 3 trim the model hide or remove what reports never use.
m11-star-schema: definition fact tables in the center, dimension tables around them. structure star schema fact sales dim date dim customer dim product dim store rules one dedicated date table marked as date table. single-direction relationships — fact → dimension. hide all surrogate keys and technical columns. validate with dax studio + best practice analyzer. why stars stars make every query faster and every measure more predictable. star schema star schema: facts at the center ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice everything in one wide table repeated text on every row factsales plus dim tables grain: one row per order line visible surrogate keys clutter in the field list hide keys and technical columns only business fields visible relationships both ways fact to dimension and back single direction, dim to fact one dedicated marked date table result: bigger model, unclear filters result: faster, predictable measures mistake wide tables make queries slower. best practice validate with best practice analyzer. why stars faster queries and more predictable measures. three fixes to apply 1 split tables facts in the center, dimensions around. 2 hide keys surrogate and technical columns stay hidden. 3 validate run dax studio and the best practice analyzer.
m11-date-table: rule every time intelligence measure depends on a proper date table. a complete date table is what time intelligence stands on date year qtr working 2026-01-01 2026 q1 0 2026-01-02 2026 q1 1 2026-01-03 2026 q1 0 mark as date table hide fact dates auto date/time off no gaps · every day present · one row per day required columns date — the primary key year , month , quarter , week workingday — flag for business days fiscalyear , fiscalquarter if used creating it in dax datetable = calendarauto () -- or specify a range datetable = calendar ( date ( 2020 , 1 , 1 ), date ( 2030 , 12 , 31 )) -- add useful columns year = year (datetable[date]) month = format (datetable[date], "mmm yyyy" ) quarter = "q" & quarter (datetable[date]) workingday = if ( weekday (datetable[date], 2 ) <= 5 , 1 , 0 ) configuration mark as date table in table tools. hide original date columns from fact tables. turn off auto date/time in options. common mistake using a fact table's date column directly in visuals. it works — until it silently breaks time intelligence. date table date table: every day, one row ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice rely on auto date/time hidden tables per date column calendar(date(2020,1,1), ...) complete range, no gaps date table with gaps missing days break ytd add year, qtr, workingday fiscalyear if you use it never mark it as date table time functions misfire mark as date table hide fact dates, auto off result: wrong ytd and yoy results result: reliable time intelligence mistake time intelligence needs a proper calendar. best practice one date table, one row per day. rule every time-intelligence measure needs a proper date table. three fixes to apply 1 build it use calendar or calendarauto in dax. 2 add columns year, month, quarter, workingday flag. 3 mark it set as date table and turn auto date/time off.
m11-measures-columns: rule measures calculate at query time. calculated columns consume memory. choose wisely. default to a measure; column only for row-level logic measure (query time) sum(sales[amount]) one number per filter context no memory cost calculated column (refresh) sales[profit] / sales[revenue] one value per row, stored uses model memory comparison type when computed use for measure query time aggregations, kpis calculated column refresh time row-level logic examples -- measure (always preferred for aggregation) total sales = sum (sales[amount]) -- calculated column (rare, only for row-level) profit margin % = sales[profit] / sales[revenue] -- only if used row-by-row in a table visual rules never use calculated columns for aggregations. never use a calculated column when a measure will do. calculated columns consume memory — they're stored in the model. common mistake column "total sales" using sum — this is wrong. it creates one number per row, not one total. measures vs columns measures first, columns rarely ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice column total sales for sums stored on every row total sales = sum(sales[amount]) computed at query time column when a measure works uses model memory measure for kpis and sums no memory cost aggregation in a column ignores filter context column only for row-level logic profit / revenue per row result: bloated model, wrong totals result: lean model, right totals mistake columns are stored in the model. best practice default to a measure, column as exception. rule measures at query time; columns cost memory. three fixes to apply 1 use measures aggregations and kpis belong in measures. 2 column sparingly only for row-by-row logic in a table. 3 check memory calculated columns are stored at refresh.
m11-dax-time: definition dax time intelligence functions compute period-over-period comparisons. time intelligence: wrap in calculate to shift the filter context sales sales ly yoy % calculate( [total sales], sameperiodlastyear(date)) ytd · rolling · parallel period essential functions function purpose totalytd year-to-date total sameperiodlastyear compare to same period prior year datesinperiod rolling window dateadd shift a date range parallelperiod full period in parallel common pattern -- same period last year sales ly = calculate ( [total sales], sameperiodlastyear (datetable[date]) ) -- yoy % change yoy % = divide ( [total sales] - [sales ly], [sales ly] ) always wrap in calculate time intelligence functions return a table; they must be used inside calculate to affect the filter context. dax time intelligence time intelligence: wrap in calculate ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice sameperiodlastyear alone returns a table, not a value calculate([sales], sply(...)) shifts the filter context divide with the slash error when last year is blank divide(sales - ly, ly) safe yoy % change time function on fact dates not on a marked date table use datetable[date] totalytd, dateadd, datesinperiod result: errors or no shift result: correct ytd and yoy mistake the filter context is never changed. best practice wrap, then compare with divide. always wrap time functions in calculate. three fixes to apply 1 use calculate it lets the function affect filter context. 2 safe divide divide handles blank or zero denominators. 3 pick function ytd, rolling, parallel, or shifted range.
m11-dax-vars: rule every complex measure uses var / return. var / return: named steps, reused results 1 var current 2 var previous 3 return divide readable · computed once · debug by returning a var why var readability — breaks a formula into named steps. performance — computed once, reused. debugging — you can return a var to inspect it. pattern yoy growth % = var current = [total sales] var previous = calculate ( [total sales], sameperiodlastyear (datetable[date]) ) return divide (current - previous, previous) debug tip replace the return with just previous temporarily to see what that var computes. dax variables var / return: named steps ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice repeat calculate in a formula same logic written twice var previous = calculate(...) computed once, reused one nested 6-line expression hard to read and debug var current, var previous return divide(current, previous) guess which part fails no way to inspect steps return previous to debug inspect any var result: slow, unreadable measures result: readable, faster measures mistake repeated logic is recomputed each time. best practice name each step, debug by returning one. rule every complex measure uses var / return. three fixes to apply 1 name steps break a formula into named variables. 2 compute once a var is reused, not recalculated. 3 debug easily return a single var to see its value.
m11-dynamic-measures: definition users pick which kpi to display from a slicer, without you building 10 separate visuals. one slicer picks which measure the visual shows slicer ● revenue ○ orders ○ aov switch(true(), selectedvalue(...)) one visual disconnected table · no relationship · dynamic title the pattern create a disconnected table with measure names. use switch(true(), selectedvalue(...)) to pick a measure. add a slicer bound to the disconnected table. combine with dynamic titles using selectedvalue. code -- disconnected table (no relationships) measureselector = datatable ( "measure" , string, { { "revenue" }, { "orders" }, { "aov" } } ) -- dynamic measure selected measure = switch ( true (), selectedvalue (measureselector[measure]) = "revenue" , [total sales], selectedvalue (measureselector[measure]) = "orders" , [total orders], selectedvalue (measureselector[measure]) = "aov" , [aov] ) -- dynamic title dynamic title = selectedvalue (measureselector[measure], "select a metric" ) adoption 90%+ of executive dashboards use this pattern. users love the flexibility. dynamic measures one slicer, many measures ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice build 10 separate visuals one per kpi switch(true(), selectedvalue(...)) pick revenue, orders or aov slicer joined to the model relationship filters wrongly disconnected measureselector table no relationships, slicer bound static visual title title ignores the selection dynamic title with selectedvalue title follows the choice result: clutter, hard maintenance result: one visual, user choice mistake duplicated visuals multiply the upkeep. best practice one visual replaces many. pattern disconnected table, switch, selectedvalue. three fixes to apply 1 use a table create a disconnected table of measure names. 2 switch measure return the measure the slicer picked. 3 match title title shows the selected measure.
m11-parameters: rule give users control without giving them chaos. four parameter patterns what-if slider → measure dynamic title text follows slicer top n n from a slicer field param swap fields give control without chaos what-if parameters forecast sales = [total sales] * ( 1 + selectedvalue (growthrate[growthrate], 0 )) dynamic titles title = "revenue for " & selectedvalue (region[name], "all regions" ) top n with others top n sales = calculate ( [total sales], topn ( selectedvalue (topn[n], 10 ), allselected (product[name]), [total sales], desc ) ) others = [total sales] - [top n sales] field parameters let users swap measures or dimensions on the fly. combine with bookmarks for guided analysis. parameters parameters: control without chaos ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice hardcode growth rate 5% change means editing dax growthrate what-if slider forecast = sales * (1 + rate) static title revenue wrong when region changes title with selectedvalue revenue for region, or all fixed top 10 users cannot change n topn[n] slicer, default 10 topn plus others result: rigid, constantly rebuilt result: user control, no rebuilds mistake hardcoded values need an analyst each time. best practice parameters give control safely. rule give users control without giving them chaos. three fixes to apply 1 what-if a slider feeds a number into a measure. 2 dynamic title text follows the slicer selection. 3 top n n comes from a slicer, remainder as others.
m11-topn: definition show the top n items and roll everything else into "others" — automatically adjusts to filters. top n plus others: no long tail product a 96 product b 82 product c 66 product d 51 others 68 n = 4 (slicer) allselected the pattern -- top n by product, respecting current filters top n sales = calculate ( [total sales], topn ( selectedvalue (topn[n], 10 ), allselected (product[name]), [total sales], desc ) ) -- everything else others = [total sales] - [top n sales] why it matters prevents the "long tail" that makes bar charts unreadable. adjusts dynamically when the user filters region, category, etc. uses allselected so it respects slicers but not the visual's own filter. rankx vs topn topn is often simpler and faster for this pattern. rankx is more flexible for computed rank columns. top n plus others top n + others: no long tail ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice chart every product long tail, unreadable bars topn with selectedvalue(n, 10) n chosen from a slicer fixed filter on top 10 ignores slicers allselected(product[name]) respects slicers dynamically drop the rest silently totals no longer add up others = total - top n sales everything else rolled up result: unreadable, wrong totals result: clean chart, totals tie mistake the tail hides the main story. best practice top n plus others always ties to total. formula others = total sales minus top n sales. three fixes to apply 1 limit bars show top n, roll up the rest. 2 use allselected respect slicers but not the visual filter. 3 tie out top n plus others equals the total.
m11-drilldown: definitions drill-down navigates a hierarchy within the same visual. drill-through jumps to a dedicated detail page with context filters passed along. down a hierarchy, or through to the detail drill-down year ▸ qtr ▸ month same visual drill-through right-click ▸ detail page context passed exception negative variance → the rows behind it + comparison feature drill-down drill-through scope same visual new page use for year → quarter → month exception investigation context passed automatic configurable fields return native needs "back" button best practice use drill-through for exception analysis: click a negative variance → detail page with those rows. combine both for maximum flexibility. add a "back" button on every drill-through page. teach users the difference via tooltip instructions. mobile caveat drill-through can be awkward on phones. hide it if it doesn't work well. drill-down vs through drill-down or drill-through ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice confuse the two users click and get lost drill-down: year, qtr, month same visual, automatic context drill-down for exceptions stays in the same visual drill-through for exceptions negative variance to detail rows no back button drill-through page is a dead end back button on every page tooltip explains the difference result: lost users, no root cause result: fast path to root cause mistake different jobs, one tool used for both. best practice combine both, teach the difference. rule down a hierarchy, or through to the detail page. three fixes to apply 1 drill down move along a hierarchy inside one visual. 2 drill through jump to a detail page with context passed. 3 add back place a back button on each detail page.
m11-bookmarks: definition bookmarks capture the state of a report page — useful for clean navigation and show/hide panels. bookmarks switch saved page states bookmark 1: filters visible filters bookmark 2: filters hidden ⇄ button action → bookmark · name every visual in the selection pane first best uses replace slicers with bookmarks for cleaner design (show/hide panels). buttons with icons for reset all, back, info. guided tour using a bookmark navigator pane (overview → performance → actions). sync slicers across pages but break sync where needed. example — show/hide filters # bookmark 1: filters visible save state with filter panel open # bookmark 2: filters hidden save state with filter panel closed # button "show filters" action → bookmark → "filters visible" # button "hide filters" action → bookmark → "filters hidden" pro tip use the selection pane to give every visual a meaningful name before creating bookmarks. bookmarks and buttons bookmarks: clean navigation ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice permanent slicer panel screen full of filters show/hide filter panel bookmark buttons: show filters, hide filters unnamed visuals selection pane is a mess name every visual first selection pane before bookmarks no reset or back button users get stuck in a state icon buttons: reset, back, info bookmark navigator guided tour result: cluttered, confusing report result: clean, guided report mistake clutter hides the visuals that matter. best practice bookmark states, not more slicers. pro tip name every visual in the selection pane first. three fixes to apply 1 save states bookmarks capture a page state. 2 name visuals use meaningful names in selection pane. 3 add buttons reset, back and info with icons.
m11-whatif: definition a slider that feeds a value into measures, enabling live scenario analysis. a slider feeds a number into a measure growth rate 0–50% forecast = [sales] × (1 + rate) live scenario analysis: growth, discount, cost reduction setup modeling → new parameter → numeric range . set min / max / increment (e.g., 0% to 50% growth). power bi auto-creates a slicer and a calculated table. reference the parameter in a measure. the measure forecast sales = [total sales] * ( 1 + selectedvalue (growthrate[growthrate], 0 )) use cases growth rate scenarios in forecasting. discount sensitivity in pricing. cost reduction targets in budgets. also works in tableau the same concept applies with tableau's parameters — different ui, same math. what-if analysis what-if: a slider drives the measure ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice edit growth in the formula static forecast, one scenario new parameter: numeric range 0% to 50% growth, set step separate report per scenario copies drift apart forecast = sales * (1 + rate) live scenario analysis no default value blank slicer breaks the measure selectedvalue(growthrate, 0) default of 0 when none result: one fixed scenario only result: live scenario analysis mistake scenarios need a rebuild each time. best practice growth, discount, cost: one slider each. the measure forecast = total sales * (1 + selectedvalue(rate, 0)). three fixes to apply 1 add slider modeling, new parameter, numeric range. 2 reference it use the parameter in a measure. 3 set default give selectedvalue a fallback value.
m11-field-params: definition field parameters let users swap what a visual is showing — dimension or measure — without rebuilding the report. field parameters swap dimensions and measures axis region | category | state | store measure: revenue | orders | aov one dynamic visual analyst pages only; the executive page keeps its defaults setup modeling → new parameter → fields . select the dimensions and measures users can pick from. drag the parameter to the axis / legend / values field. example # user can choose: axis: region | category | state | store measure: revenue | orders | aov | profit when to use exploration-heavy pages. analyst personas who need flexibility. replacing multiple hardcoded visuals with a single dynamic one. caution don't put field parameters on the executive page. execs want defaults, not choices. field parameters field parameters: swap, don't rebuild ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice hardcode a visual per field region, category, state, store one visual, swap axis region | category | state | store field parameter on exec page execs want defaults, not choices keep exec page on defaults parameters on analyst pages only rebuild reports to change axis every request is a project swap measure too revenue | orders | aov | profit result: report sprawl, confused execs result: flexible exploration page mistake duplicated visuals and unwanted options. best practice flexibility for analysts, defaults for execs. caution not on the executive page. execs want defaults. three fixes to apply 1 new parameter modeling, new parameter, fields. 2 drag to axis place it on axis, legend or values. 3 right audience use it for exploration and analysts.
m11-mobile: reality 60% of executives use phones or tablets. mobile is not optional. rules mobile view is mandatory — design it deliberately. stack kpi cards vertically — one per row. enlarge fonts ≥ 18 pt — readability on small screens. use card visuals instead of tables on mobile. hide drill-through on mobile if it's not practical. test on an actual phone via the power bi mobile app. desktop vs mobile same data, two layouts desktop (grid) mobile (stack) test open your dashboard on your own phone. if you pinch and zoom, redesign it. mobile layout mobile: design the phone view ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice desktop grid squeezed on a phone 7 kpi cards in a row stack kpi cards, one per row cards instead of tables wide tables and tiny fonts pinch and zoom to read fonts at 18 pt or larger hide drill-through if awkward never open it on a phone assumed it just works test in power bi mobile app real phone, real use result: execs cannot read it result: readable on any device mistake 60% of executives use phones or tablets. best practice design mobile deliberately. test if you pinch and zoom, redesign it. three fixes to apply 1 stack cards one kpi per row on the phone layout. 2 enlarge text use 18 pt or bigger on small screens. 3 test on phone open it in the mobile app yourself.
m11-performance: target under 5-second load time on mobile. performance analyzer shows which visual is slow header 3.2s card 1 0.4s card 2 0.4s chart 1 0.9s chart 2 1.5s table 3.9s performance analyzer: fix the slowest visual first (target: under 5 s on mobile) the checklist reduce visuals per page to ≤ 12. remove unused columns / rows early in power query. use aggregations for tables > 5m rows. avoid bi-directional relationships and many-to-many unless necessary. set refresh parallelism appropriately. disable "auto date/time" if not needed. check file size — bigger isn't better. run performance analyzer on every page. performance analyzer view → performance analyzer. records how long each visual takes to render. performance checklist performance: under 5 seconds ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice 20 visuals on one page header alone takes 3.2s 12 visuals or fewer per page split into pages never run performance analyzer guess which visual is slow performance analyzer each page fix the slowest visual first keep every column unused data, auto date on remove unused columns early aggregations for over 5m rows result: users leave before it loads result: under 5 s on mobile mistake slow pages are abandoned. best practice measure first, then fix the slowest. target under 5 seconds load time on mobile. three fixes to apply 1 cut visuals keep each page to 12 or fewer visuals. 2 run analyzer view, performance analyzer on every page. 3 trim model remove unused columns, disable auto date/time.
m11-perf-killers: warning these are the most common performance killers. fix them before you ship. common killers and their fixes >12 visuals split pages bi-directional single direction unused columns remove early many-to-many bridge table high cardinality bin or drop also: var auto date/time off killers and fixes killer impact fix too many visuals (>12) slow rendering split into pages or bookmarks bi-directional relationships slow queries use single-direction unused columns in model memory waste remove in power query many-to-many joins ambiguous, slow reshape data or use bridge tables high-cardinality columns huge memory bin, group, or remove complex dax without vars recompute cost use var / return auto date/time enabled hidden date tables turn off in options target < 5 seconds load on mobile. if you're not there, run performance analyzer to find the bottleneck. performance killers performance killers and fixes ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice bidirectional, many-to-many slow queries, ambiguous results single-direction or bridge table reshape data first complex dax without vars recompute cost each time var / return in measures compute once high-cardinality columns huge memory use bin, group or remove columns turn auto date/time off result: slow, bloated report result: under 5 s on mobile mistake ship these and users wait. best practice fix the killers before you ship. target under 5 seconds on mobile; else run performance analyzer. three fixes to apply 1 split pages more than 12 visuals? use pages or bookmarks. 2 drop unused remove unused columns in power query. 3 turn off auto disable auto date/time in options.
m11-rls: definition rls restricts data by user — each person sees only their rows. row-level security: the filter sits on the dimension users ann@co.com raj@co.com li@co.com role: region managers [state] = userprincipalname() fact rows own region only test with view as roles · assign azure ad groups in the service step-by-step open power bi desktop → modeling → manage roles . create a role (e.g., "region managers"). write a dax filter on a dimension table. test with view as roles . publish. assign users or azure ad groups in the service. dax patterns -- static: users in this role see only ca [state] = "ca" -- dynamic: user sees their own state [state] = userprincipalname () -- hierarchy: user sees their subtree pathcontains (employee[path], userprincipalname ()) best practices combine with azure ad groups for scalability. document every role and test case. mandatory for multi-tenant dashboards . common mistake rls filter on the fact table when it should be on the dimension. filters propagate fact → dim only in the correct direction. row-level security rls: filter on the dimension ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice same report copied per region many copies to maintain [state] = userprincipalname() one role, each sees own rows hardcode [state] = ca for all static role per person filter on a dimension table azure ad groups assign users publish without testing nobody tried view as roles test with view as roles then publish and document result: data leaks, heavy upkeep result: each user sees own rows mistake everyone could see every row. best practice dynamic filter, tested, documented. pattern filter a dimension with userprincipalname(). three fixes to apply 1 create role modeling, manage roles, write a dax filter. 2 use groups assign azure ad groups in the service. 3 test first view as roles in desktop before publish.
m11-connection-strategies: rule pick the mode based on latency requirements and data volume — not on convenience. trade-offs by connection mode import speed freshness size directquery speed freshness size composite speed freshness size score 1–5 · illustrative. choose by latency and volume, not convenience comparison mode best for trade-off import fast performance, < 50 gb snapshot data, refresh latency directquery real-time, always hits source slower, source load composite mix import + directquery + dataflows complex to maintain live connection existing ssas / aas model limited modeling incremental refresh mandatory for datasets > 5 million rows. configure in power query with rangestart / rangeend parameters. refresh only changed data — massive time savings. use parameters switch connections between dev / test / prod with parameters instead of hardcoding. connection strategies connection strategy: latency and volume ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice directquery for convenience hits the source every click import under 50 gb fast, snapshot data full refresh over 5m rows hours of reload incremental refresh rangestart / rangeend parameters hardcode dev/prod servers edit connection per release parameters for dev/test/prod switch without editing result: slow reports, fragile releases result: fast refresh, easy releases mistake convenience picks the wrong mode. best practice choose by need, not by convenience. rule pick the mode by latency and volume, not convenience. three fixes to apply 1 match mode import, directquery, composite or live. 2 refresh deltas mandatory over 5 million rows. 3 use parameters swap sources per environment.
m11-deployment-pipelines: definition power bi deployment pipelines move content from dev → test → prod with rules and approvals. the three stages dev → test → prod 1 dev 2 test 3 prod benefits one-click deployment with rules (change connection strings, parameters). separate dataset and report for team development. mandatory for enterprise governance — audit trail of what shipped when. free alternative if you don't have premium: use .pbit template files + parameters. save a template without data, share it, and each environment supplies its own parameters. rule never edit prod directly. always promote from dev → test → prod. deployment pipelines pipelines: dev, test, prod ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice edit prod directly change goes live untested promote dev, test, prod one-click deployment hardcode connection strings breaks in each stage deployment rules and parameters connection strings change per stage no audit trail unknown what shipped when stage checklist and approvals audit trail of releases result: broken reports in production result: governed, repeatable releases mistake live edits skip every check. best practice promote, never edit in prod. rule never edit prod directly. always promote. three fixes to apply 1 three stages dev, test and prod workspaces. 2 use rules auto-switch connection strings by stage. 3 no premium share .pbit templates plus parameters.
m11-version-control: rule if it isn't versioned, it isn't production. three levels of version control; never email .pbix files basic individuals onedrive / sharepoint advanced teams git + tabular editor enterprise regulated azure devops pipelines levels of version control level tool when basic onedrive / sharepoint individual work advanced git + tabular editor team development enterprise azure devops pipelines regulated industries best practices store .pbix in onedrive / sharepoint with version history enabled. advanced: use git with .pbit templates + tabular editor external tools. deploy via workspace — separate dataset and report for team development. use deployment pipelines (dev → test → prod) in premium. tag releases with version numbers and a change log. never email .pbix files around. use sharepoint or git — one source of truth. version control versioning: one source of truth ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice email .pbix files around final_v3_final.pbix onedrive or sharepoint version history enabled overwrite with no history cannot roll back git with .pbit, tabular editor team development untagged releases no change log tag releases, keep change log pipelines for dev, test, prod result: conflicting copies, no rollback result: traceable, recoverable releases mistake nobody knows which file is current. best practice one source of truth, versioned. rule if it isn't versioned, it isn't production. three fixes to apply 1 basic individuals use onedrive or sharepoint. 2 advanced teams use git and tabular editor. 3 enterprise regulated: azure devops pipelines.
m11-documentation: rule if users need to ask you how to use the dashboard, documentation failed. the documentation package and where it lives quick-start pdf teams 5-min video stream kpi dictionary sharepoint feedback form in report monthly office hours keep the questions coming back to you, not around you the documentation package one-page quick-start guide — key questions answered. 5-minute video walkthrough — recorded once, watched forever. data dictionary + kpi catalog — in sharepoint or confluence. monthly "dashboard office hours" — walk-in support. feedback form — microsoft forms embedded in the dashboard. where to put documentation artifact location quick-start pdf pinned in teams channel video stream or youtube (unlisted) kpi dictionary sharepoint / confluence feedback form embedded in report underrated the feedback form is what keeps the dashboard alive. users tell you what's missing; you fix it. documentation documentation: so users never ask ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice ship with no guide users email you questions one-page quick-start, 5-min video pinned in teams, on stream kpi definitions in your head no data dictionary kpi dictionary in sharepoint data dictionary and catalog no feedback channel problems stay hidden embedded forms feedback monthly dashboard office hours result: constant support requests result: self-serve, steady improvement mistake if users must ask, documentation failed. best practice write once, support many. rule if users need to ask how, documentation failed. three fixes to apply 1 quick-start one page answering the key questions. 2 video record a 5-minute walkthrough once. 3 feedback form embed it so questions come back to you.
m11-change-mgmt: reality the best dashboard in the world fails if nobody uses it. adoption is a loop, not a launch date pilot (5 users) › train › roll out › track usage › improve weekly active ≥ 60% · session > 90 s · mobile > 30% the adoption playbook never release without training. run a pilot with 5 power users. get feedback before the wider rollout. collect feedback via a forms embedded in the dashboard. track usage in the power bi admin portal (views, unique users). celebrate wins publicly when targets are hit. adoption metrics to track metric target weekly active users ≥ 60% of target audience avg time per session > 90 sec mobile sessions > 30% of total feedback submission rate 1 per 20 users per month rule if you're not tracking usage, you don't know if the dashboard is working. change management adoption: a loop, not a launch date ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice release without training hope people find it train before release pilot with 5 power users big-bang rollout no pilot feedback collect feedback in the report embedded forms, then roll out never check usage do not know if it works track admin portal usage weekly active 60% or more result: dashboard nobody opens result: measured, growing adoption mistake the best dashboard fails unused. best practice pilot, train, track, improve. rule if you're not tracking usage, you don't know it works. three fixes to apply 1 pilot first five users, then the wider rollout. 2 train never release without training. 3 track views, unique users, session over 90 s.
m11-exec-dashboard: purpose give a ceo the entire business in one screen, in 10 seconds. layout executive dashboard layout top banner — 7 kpis with sparklines trend chart variance chart waterfall action items table owners · due dates · status design specs top banner — 7 kpis with sparklines. middle — 4 key charts: trend, variance, waterfall, mix. bottom — action items table with owners + due dates. mobile layout — stacked, one kpi per row. total load time — target < 4 seconds. the 10-second test can a ceo glance at this on a phone for 10 seconds and know whether to act? if not, redesign. executive dashboard executive view: the 10-second test ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice dozens of charts and filters ceo cannot find the answer 7 kpis with sparklines on top trend, variance, waterfall, mix desktop-only layout ceo checks on a phone stacked mobile, one kpi per row load time under 4 seconds numbers with no action no owners or due dates action items table at bottom owners, due dates, status result: no decision in 10 seconds result: know whether to act, fast mistake too much to scan, nothing to act on. best practice entire business, one screen. 10-second test glance on a phone: know whether to act, or redesign. three fixes to apply 1 top banner seven kpis with sparklines. 2 four charts trend, variance, waterfall, mix. 3 action table owners and due dates at the bottom.
m11-ops-dashboard: purpose enable an ops manager to investigate exceptions and model scenarios. design specs real-time elements — live kpis at the top. drill-through pages — region → store → product hierarchy. what-if forecasting panel — sliders for scenario analysis. export to powerpoint button — one-click share. rls applied by region — each manager sees only their data. visual operational layout live status banner region hierarchy what-if panel exception table + drill-through pattern ops dashboards are wider than they are deep. show more, but organize by process step. operational dashboard ops view: investigate exceptions ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice summary only, no drill cannot find which store region, store, product drill exception table: store 14 at -18% everyone sees all regions no rls by region rls applied by region managers see only their data static numbers no scenario or export what-if sliders, powerpoint export live kpis at the top result: exceptions stay unexplained result: fast root cause, easy sharing mistake a summary cannot explain a miss. best practice investigate, model, then share. pattern ops pages are wider than deep; organize by process step. three fixes to apply 1 live banner real-time kpis at the top. 2 drill-through region to store to product hierarchy. 3 what-if panel sliders for scenario analysis.
m11-self-service: goal reduce it requests by giving analysts a certified dataset + template reports. the blueprint shared certified dataset — one source of truth, owned by the data team. thin reports + template .pbix — analysts build on top, not from scratch. row-level security + dynamic filtering built in. usage tracking — see who's using what. feedback loop — embedded form + monthly review. impact before vs after before 100 it tickets/month after ≤ 20 it tickets/month result certified dataset + template reports reduce it requests by 80%+. self-service self-service: certified dataset ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice every analyst builds own model numbers disagree shared certified dataset one source of truth all requests go to it about 100 tickets a month thin reports on a template analysts build on top no usage tracking do not know who uses what rls, usage tracking, feedback monthly review loop result: conflicting numbers, it backlog result: it requests cut by 80%+ mistake many sources, many versions of truth. best practice certify once, reuse everywhere. blueprint certified dataset plus thin template reports. three fixes to apply 1 certify data data team owns one shared dataset. 2 thin reports connect to the dataset, never copy it. 3 track and loop usage tracking and a feedback form.

m12-overview: purpose build, diagnose, and improve linear and logistic regression models. interpret them correctly for business decisions. this module bridges classical statistics and modern machine learning. what you'll be able to do understand core ml concepts and terminology build, diagnose, and improve linear + logistic regression models evaluate regression and classification performance correctly interpret coefficients, odds ratios, and business implications complete a full end-to-end predictive modeling project module flow six sections 1 concepts 2 linear 3 regularize 4 logistic 5 metrics guiding principle a simple model you can explain beats a complex model you can't defend.
m12-objectives: by the end of this module you will be able to take a business question, build a model, evaluate it honestly, and translate the output into an action. five objectives: from question to deployed model 1 concepts 2 build 3 evaluate 4 interpret 5 project five objectives # objective detail 1 core ml concepts terminology, workflow, bias-variance 2 build regression models linear and logistic from scratch 3 evaluate performance regression and classification metrics 4 interpret coefficients betas, odds ratios, business language 5 end-to-end project from question to deployed model prerequisite module 4 (statistics) — you need distributions, p-values, and confidence intervals.
m12-why-matters: roi predictive modeling is one of the highest-leverage skills in analytics. the numbers 5–6% profitability outperformance for companies using predictive analytics (mckinsey). 84% of executives say ai/ml is critical to strategy. customer churn prediction saves enterprises $200m+ annually. price optimization models increase margins 2–8%. visual — where the value comes from business impact of predictive modeling churn $200m+ saved pricing 2–8% margin lift profitability 5–6% vs peers you will leave able to deliver real roi with regression — no deep learning required.
m12-ml-types: definition machine learning splits into three main paradigms. this module focuses on one. the three paradigms type data examples supervised labeled regression, classification unsupervised no labels clustering, dimensionality reduction reinforcement reward signals game playing, robotics emerging semi-supervised — small labeled + large unlabeled. self-supervised — labels derived from the data itself (e.g., llms). where this module focuses supervised this module unsupervised later reinforcement not covered scope this module = supervised learning only: regression + classification.
m12-workflow: definition the same crisp-dm cycle from module 1, updated for predictive modeling. the six steps business understanding — define the roi question. data understanding & acquisition . data preparation — 70–80% of the time. modeling . evaluation — against a business metric. deployment & monitoring . crisp-dm for ml business data prep model eval deploy reality data prep dominates. the modeling step is often the shortest — and the one most beginners over-focus on. ml workflow workflow: don't over-focus on modeling ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice jump straight to modeling skip the business question start with the roi question business understanding comes first rush data preparation it takes 70-80% of the time budget time for data prep plan for 70-80% of the effort judge by a generic score evaluation not tied to the roi evaluate on a business metric then deploy and monitor result: polished model, no value result: model that solves the need mistake beginners fixate on the modeling step. best practice modeling is often the shortest step. rule of thumb data prep dominates the cycle; modeling is often the shortest. three fixes to apply 1 ask roi first define the business question before touching any data. 2 plan for prep reserve most of the schedule for cleaning and sourcing. 3 close the loop judge on a business metric and monitor after deploy.
m12-train-val-test: rule split data three ways. never let the test set inform model choices. the three sets set size purpose training 70% model learns patterns validation 15% tune hyperparameters test 15% final unbiased performance data split training (70%) val (15%) test (15%) syntax — scikit-learn from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split x_train, x_temp, y_train, y_temp = train_test_split ( x, y, test_size= 0.30 , random_state= 42 , stratify=y ) x_val, x_test, y_val, y_test = train_test_split ( x_temp, y_temp, test_size= 0.50 , random_state= 42 , stratify=y_temp ) data leakage touching the test set during tuning leaks information and inflates performance estimates. train/val/test data split: never tune on the test set ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice tune on the test set peek at it to pick hyperparameters tune on validation only 15% validation set for tuning train and score on same data no unseen data for evaluation hold out a 15% test set one final unbiased score split without stratify=y class mix differs across sets use stratify=y, random_state=42 same class mix, reproducible split result: inflated performance result: honest performance estimate mistake touching the test set leaks information. best practice train 70, validate 15, test 15. rule never let the test set inform any model choice. three fixes to apply 1 split three ways train 70%, validate 15%, test 15%. 2 tune on validation pick hyperparameters here and leave test untouched. 3 score test once report the final number from the test set only.
m12-overfitting: definitions overfitting: model memorizes training data, fails on new data. underfitting: model too simple, poor on both training and test. visual underfit · sweet spot · overfit underfitting too simple sweet spot just right overfitting memorizes noise symptoms symptom diagnosis low train error, high test error overfitting (high variance) high train error, high test error underfitting (high bias) low train error, low test error sweet spot fixes overfit → regularize, simplify, more data. underfit → add features, complexify, less regularization. over/underfitting fitting: memorizing vs too simple ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice judge by training error only low train error looks great compare train and test error gap shows high variance ignore the test error gap low train, high test error read the symptom table high both means high bias apply the wrong remedy add features to an overfit model match fix to diagnosis overfit: regularize, simplify result: fails on new data result: sweet spot: both errors low mistake overfit memorizes; underfit is too simple. best practice low train and low test error is the goal. rule of thumb overfit: regularize or simplify. underfit: add features. three fixes to apply 1 check both errors compare train error with test error every time. 2 diagnose first name it: variance or bias before changing the model. 3 apply the right fix overfit needs more data; underfit needs complexity.
m12-bias-variance: formula total error = bias² + variance + irreducible error. the trade-off simple models → high bias, low variance. complex models → low bias, high variance. regularization moves you left on the complexity axis. goal: minimize total error (sweet spot). bias-variance curve sweet spot bias² variance total error ← simpler | complexity | more complex → rule of thumb if you can't beat a simple model, the added complexity isn't earning its keep. bias-variance bias-variance: complexity isn't free ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice always pick the complex model low bias but high variance balance bias and variance aim for the sweet spot use a model that is too simple high bias, low variance regularize to cut variance moves you left on complexity ignore irreducible error expect zero error compare to a simple model complexity must earn its keep result: high total error result: minimized total error mistake total error = bias squared + variance + irreducible. best practice minimize total error, not one term. rule of thumb can't beat a simple model? extra complexity isn't earning. three fixes to apply 1 find the sweet spot tune complexity to minimize total error. 2 use regularization trade a little bias for lower variance. 3 benchmark simple keep the simple model unless the complex one wins.
m12-split-practices: rule the split is a research protocol. follow it or your metrics lie. the split is a protocol: tune on validation, touch test once train 70% val 15% test 15% fit the model tune touch once stratify classification splits · time series: split by date, never shuffle the rules 60/20/20 or 70/15/15 — both common in industry. stratified split for classification — preserves class %. never tune on the test set — that's data leakage. small data? use cross-validation instead. set random_state = 42 for reproducibility. stratified split example from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split x_train, x_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split ( x, y, test_size= 0.20 , random_state= 42 , stratify=y # keeps class balance ) time series never randomly shuffle. use timeseriessplit so training data always precedes test data. split practices splits: the split is a protocol ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice random split for classification class percentages drift stratify=y on classification keeps class percentages randomly shuffle time series future rows train the model use timeseriessplit training always precedes test single split on small data unstable estimate use cross-validation if small more reliable than one split result: metrics that lie result: trustworthy metrics mistake break the protocol and the metrics lie. best practice set random_state = 42 for reproducibility. rule the split is a protocol. follow it or metrics lie. three fixes to apply 1 stratify classes pass stratify=y to keep class balance in each set. 2 respect time order use timeseriessplit so past trains and future tests. 3 cross-validate small data? use k-fold instead of one split.
