m12-cross-validation: definition split data into k folds. train on k-1, validate on 1. repeat k times. rules k=5 or k=10 most common. each sample used in validation exactly once. more reliable performance estimate than a single split. stratified k-fold for imbalanced classes. time-series → timeseriessplit (no random shuffle). 5-fold cross-validation fold 1 val train fold 2 train val train fold 3 train val train fold 4 train val train fold 5 train val syntax from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score, stratifiedkfold cv = stratifiedkfold (n_splits= 5 , shuffle= true , random_state= 42 ) scores = cross_val_score (model, x, y, cv=cv, scoring= 'roc_auc' ) print (scores. mean (), scores. std ()) why it works every row is validated exactly once, giving a more stable estimate than a single split. cross-validation cross-validation: one split is fragile ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice trust a single split score depends on the luck of the draw use k=5 or k=10 folds every row validated exactly once plain k-fold on imbalanced data class mix varies per fold stratifiedkfold for imbalance preserves class proportions shuffle time-series folds leaks future into training timeseriessplit for time data no random shuffle result: unstable estimate result: stable performance estimate mistake one split can flatter or punish the model. best practice report mean and std of the fold scores. rule of thumb train on k-1 folds, test on 1, repeat k times. three fixes to apply 1 average the folds report scores.mean() and scores.std() together. 2 stratify folds stratifiedkfold keeps the class mix steady. 3 keep time order use timeseriessplit when rows are time-ordered.
m12-baseline: rule if your model can't beat a trivial baseline, it isn't ready. what baseline to use task baseline classification predict majority class regression predict mean or median example worked 95% non-churn → baseline accuracy = 95%. a model with 94% accuracy is worse than the baseline, even if it looks high. report lift over baseline, not just accuracy. lift over baseline baseline 95% model 97% +2 pp lift baseline models baselines: high accuracy can still lose ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice report accuracy alone 94% sounds high build a trivial baseline first majority class or mean/median skip a baseline no yardstick to beat compare against the baseline model must beat it ignore class imbalance 95% are non-churn report lift over baseline not just accuracy result: 94% model loses to baseline result: honest, defensible value mistake the majority-class baseline already scores 95%. best practice lift over baseline shows real gain. rule if a model can't beat a trivial baseline, it isn't ready. three fixes to apply 1 set the baseline classify: majority class. regress: mean or median. 2 compare first score the baseline on the same test data. 3 report lift show gain over baseline, not raw accuracy.
m12-simple-linear: equation y = β₀ + β₁x + ε components β₀ = intercept (value of y when x = 0). β₁ = slope (effect of x on y). ε = error term (unexplained variation). goal minimize sum of squared errors (sse) . ordinary least squares (ols) finds the best line. visual ols best-fit line residual syntax from sklearn.linear_model import linearregression model = linearregression () model. fit (x_train, y_train) print (model.intercept_, model.coef_) assumption linear relationship between x and y. check with a scatter plot first. simple regression linear fit: check linearity first ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice fit without plotting assume the relationship is linear scatter plot before fitting confirm a linear pattern misread the intercept value of y when x = 0 read beta0 as the intercept beta1 is the slope ignore the error term treat the line as exact remember epsilon exists ols minimizes the sse result: wrong line, wrong story result: justified best-fit line mistake a straight line on curved data misleads. best practice y = b0 + b1x + error, fit by ols. check assumption: linear relationship between x and y. three fixes to apply 1 plot first draw a scatter plot before fitting any line. 2 name the terms intercept, slope, and error each have a meaning. 3 use ols minimize the sum of squared errors for the best line.
m12-intercept-slope: plain english "for each 1-unit increase in x, y increases by β₁ units, holding all else constant." worked example applied β₁ = 0.35 → $1k more ad spend → $350 more revenue. rules only valid within the observed range of x. never extrapolate far outside the data. always report the confidence interval. valid range vs extrapolation valid range extrapolation ⚠ business framing always translate β₁ into a business statement. "0.35" means nothing to a stakeholder; "$350 per $1k ad spend" does. reading beta1 beta1: translate and stay in range ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice report raw beta1 = 0.35 means nothing to stakeholders state it in business terms $1k ad spend: $350 more revenue extrapolate far outside x beyond the observed range stay within the observed range valid range only give no confidence interval point estimate only always report the ci show the uncertainty result: misleading claims result: clear, defensible statement mistake 0.35 alone tells a stakeholder nothing. best practice each 1-unit rise in x moves y by beta1. rule of thumb each 1-unit rise in x moves y by beta1, all else equal. three fixes to apply 1 translate turn 0.35 into $350 per $1k of ad spend. 2 respect the range never extrapolate far beyond the data. 3 add the ci report the confidence interval with beta1.
m12-multiple-linear: equation y = β₀ + β₁x₁ + β₂x₂ + … + βₚxₚ + ε multiple regression gives "all else equal" effects predictors ad spend price · region y = b0 + b1x1 + b2x2 + ... each beta: effect of that x holding others fixed watch for correlated predictors (multicollinearity) why it matters controls for confounding variables. enables "all else equal" statements. more realistic business modeling. risk multicollinearity — predictors correlated with each other cause unstable coefficients. syntax from sklearn.linear_model import linearregression model = linearregression () model. fit (x_train, y_train) import pandas as pd coefs = pd. dataframe ({ 'feature' : x_train.columns, 'coef' : model.coef_ }) interpretation each coefficient is the effect of that variable holding all others constant . this is the superpower of multiple regression. multiple regression multiple regression: hold others constant ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice model one predictor only confounders left uncontrolled add controls for confounders more realistic business model ignore correlated predictors multicollinearity risk check predictor correlation watch for unstable coefficients read a coefficient in isolation forget the other variables say all else equal effect holding others constant result: unstable, confounded effects result: clean all-else-equal effects mistake unstable coefficients mislead decisions. best practice each coefficient holds all other variables constant. rule y = b0 + b1x1 + ... + bpxp each beta: others held fixed. three fixes to apply 1 control confounders include variables that move both x and y. 2 check correlation look for correlated inputs before trusting betas. 3 interpret all else state each effect with the rest held constant.
m12-dummy-vars: rule categorical variables must be encoded as 0/1 dummies before regression. dummy variables: drop one category as the baseline region_east 1 region_west 0 region_south 0 region_north 0 dropped: baseline k categories → k-1 dummies keep all k and they sum to 1: collinear with the intercept the dummy variable trap if region has values east, west, south, north, and you create dummies for all of them, they sum to 1 — perfectly collinear with the intercept. always drop one as the baseline. correct encoding # region: east, west, south, north # drop north as the baseline import pandas as pd df = pd. get_dummies (df, columns=[ 'region' ], drop_first= true ) # creates: region_west, region_south, region_east # region_north is the reference (baseline) interpretation β_west = additional effect vs the baseline (north), holding other variables constant. yes / no # binary categories → 1/0 directly df[ 'is_vip' ] = (df[ 'tier' ] == 'vip' ). astype ( int ) common mistake using drop_first=false and creating perfect multicollinearity. sklearn will still fit, but coefficients become meaningless. dummy variables dummy trap: drop one category ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice dummies for all four regions east, west, south, north drop one as the baseline north is the reference use drop_first=false perfect multicollinearity pd.get_dummies(drop_first=true) creates west, south, east feed raw text categories must be 0/1 dummies encode binary as 1/0 (tier == 'vip').astype(int) result: meaningless coefficients result: clear effect vs baseline mistake dummies sum to 1: collinear with the intercept. best practice beta_west = effect vs the baseline, north. rule always drop one dummy as the baseline category. three fixes to apply 1 drop one leave out one category as the reference level. 2 use drop_first get_dummies(drop_first=true) avoids the trap. 3 read vs baseline each beta compares to the dropped category.
m12-assumptions-1: definition five assumptions must hold for ols to give trustworthy estimates and standard errors. five assumptions: check in order, linearity first linearity x and y linear independence rows not related equal variance constant spread normal errors for p-values no collinearity predictors differ if linearity fails, nothing downstream is valid the five assumptions assumption what it means linearity relationship between x and y is linear independence observations are independent homoscedasticity constant error variance normality of residuals for valid inference (p-values, cis) no perfect multicollinearity predictors aren't perfectly correlated check order check each assumption in order before trusting p-values. if linearity fails, nothing downstream is valid. ols assumptions assumptions: check before p-values ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice read p-values straight away assumptions never checked check all five assumptions linearity, independence, variance skip the linearity check everything downstream breaks check in order linearity fails: stop there ignore non-constant variance homoscedasticity assumed test residual normality needed for valid p-values, cis result: untrustworthy estimates result: trustworthy inference mistake invalid assumptions give invalid standard errors. best practice no perfect multicollinearity is the fifth check. rule of thumb if linearity fails, nothing downstream is valid. three fixes to apply 1 check in order start with linearity, then work down the list. 2 test variance look for constant error variance (homoscedasticity). 3 then infer trust p-values and cis only after the checks pass.
m12-assumptions-2: definition four diagnostic plots reveal which assumption is violated. four diagnostic plots, four assumptions residuals vs fitted linearity and spread q-q plot normality scale-location equal variance leverage influential points fix violations before reporting p-values the four plots plot checks residuals vs fitted linearity & homoscedasticity q-q plot normality of residuals scale-location heteroscedasticity residuals vs leverage influential points syntax — statsmodels import statsmodels.api as sm import matplotlib.pyplot as plt x_with_const = sm. add_constant (x) model = sm. ols (y, x_with_const). fit () print (model. summary ()) # four diagnostic plots fig = plt. figure (figsize=( 10 , 8 )) sm.graphics. plot_regress_exog (model, 'x1' , fig=fig) rule fix assumption violations before reporting p-values. otherwise your inference is wrong. diagnostic plots diagnostics: plot before you report ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice print the summary only model.summary() and move on residuals vs fitted checks linearity, homoscedasticity never plot residuals violations stay hidden q-q plot checks residual normality report p-values with violations inference is wrong scale-location and leverage heteroscedasticity, influential points result: wrong inference reported result: violations found and fixed mistake violations hide behind a clean summary. best practice four plots reveal which assumption broke. rule fix assumption violations before reporting p-values. three fixes to apply 1 plot residuals residuals vs fitted shows shape and spread. 2 check normality use the q-q plot on the residuals. 3 spot influence residuals vs leverage flags influential points.
m12-multicollinearity: definition multicollinearity = predictors highly correlated with each other. vif flags predictors that duplicate each other vif under 5 vif 5 to 10 vif over 10 remove a variable · combine with pca · or use ridge vif thresholds vif interpretation < 5 fine 5 – 10 watch > 10 serious — fix it symptoms high r² but no significant predictors. unstable coefficients — small data changes swing them wildly. signs flip unexpectedly. solutions remove one variable from the correlated group. pca to combine into orthogonal components. ridge regression to stabilize coefficients. syntax from statsmodels.stats.outliers_influence import variance_inflation_factor import pandas as pd vif = pd. dataframe () vif[ 'feature' ] = x.columns vif[ 'vif' ] = [ variance_inflation_factor (x.values, i) for i in range (x.shape[ 1 ])] print (vif) never ignore multicollinearity makes coefficients unstable. never interpret them without checking vif. multicollinearity vif: don't interpret unstable betas ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice interpret betas without vif never check the correlation compute vif per feature variance_inflation_factor ignore vif above 10 serious, needs a fix act when vif > 10 5-10: watch; under 5: fine trust flipped signs small data changes swing betas remove, combine, or shrink drop one, pca, or ridge result: unstable, misleading betas result: stable, interpretable betas mistake high r2 but no significant predictors is a warning. best practice check vif before reading any coefficient. test vif under 5 fine; 5-10 watch; above 10 fix it. three fixes to apply 1 run vif compute it for every feature before interpreting. 2 drop or combine remove one variable or use pca components. 3 use ridge ridge stabilizes correlated coefficients.
m12-feature-selection: definition choosing the right subset of predictors for the model. four ways to choose predictors forward start empty, add best backward start full, drop worst stepwise add and drop lasso (l1) penalty selects then apply business judgement: will the variable exist at prediction time? the methods method how it works forward selection start empty, add best one at a time backward elimination start full, remove worst one at a time stepwise combination of forward + backward l1 (lasso) automatic selection via penalty business over p-values cheap variables are more valuable than marginally better r². interpretability beats 0.01 extra points of r². data availability at prediction time matters — you can't use a variable you won't have. practical lasso gives you an automatic, reproducible answer. use it as a starting point, then apply business judgment. feature selection features: business over p-values ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice chase marginal r2 gains complexity for 0.01 of r2 prefer interpretability beats 0.01 extra points of r2 use unavailable variables not known at prediction time check availability at prediction only use what you will have trust automatic selection blindly no business judgment start with lasso (l1) then apply business judgment result: costly, unusable model result: practical, usable model mistake you can't use a variable you won't have. best practice cheap variables beat a slightly better r2. rule of thumb lasso is a starting point; business judgment finishes it. three fixes to apply 1 value simplicity choose the explainable model over a tiny r2 gain. 2 check availability confirm each feature exists at prediction time. 3 start with lasso reproducible selection, then add business review.
m12-r2-adjusted: definitions r² = variance explained by the model. always increases with more variables. adjusted r² = r² penalized for the number of predictors. adding variables always lifts r2; adjusted r2 can punish them 2 vars r2 0.70 5 vars r2 0.74 15 vars r2 0.77 2 vars adj 0.69 5 vars adj 0.72 15 vars adj 0.68 r2 only rises adjusted r2 can fall (illustrative) comparison metric use for r² reporting only adjusted r² comparing models with different predictor counts rough guidance r² > 0.8 — strong. r² > 0.6 — acceptable in social science / business. r² < 0.3 — model explains little; investigate. never chase r² alone. check residuals — a high r² with violated assumptions is a false comfort. r2 vs adjusted r2 r-squared: don't chase r2 alone ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice compare models by plain r2 always rises with more variables use adjusted r2 to compare penalized for predictor count chase a high r2 ignore the residuals use r2 for reporting only not for model comparison overlook low r2 below 0.3 model explains little check residuals too assumptions must hold result: false comfort, bloated model result: fair model comparison mistake high r2 with violated assumptions misleads. best practice above 0.6 acceptable in business; above 0.8 strong. rule adjusted r2 compares models with different predictor counts. three fixes to apply 1 compare adjusted use adjusted r2 when the predictor counts differ. 2 read the scale below 0.3 means investigate the model. 3 check residuals never trust r2 without a residual check.
m12-rmse-mae-mape: definitions three ways to measure regression error. each tells a different story. three ways to measure regression error rmse punishes big errors mae robust to outliers mape percent error pick the one that matches how the business feels the error comparison metric what it measures best for rmse √mean(squared error) — punishes big errors when large errors hurt most mae mean(|error|) — robust to outliers when outliers shouldn't dominate mape mean(|error|/actual) — % error revenue / price prediction business interpretation mape example mape 8% → forecasts are off by 8% on average. directly meaningful to a stakeholder. syntax from sklearn.metrics import mean_squared_error, mean_absolute_error import numpy as np rmse = np. sqrt ( mean_squared_error (y_test, y_pred)) mae = mean_absolute_error (y_test, y_pred) mape = np. mean (np. abs ((y_test - y_pred) / y_test)) * 100 choose one pick the metric that matches how the business experiences the error — then stick with it. rmse mae mape error metrics: match the business ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice pick a metric at random each tells a different story rmse when big errors hurt punishes large errors use rmse when outliers mislead squared errors dominate mae when outliers shouldn't rule robust to outliers report raw error for revenue stakeholders want a percent mape for revenue or price mape 8%: off by 8% on average result: error told the wrong way result: error stakeholders understand mistake the metric hides how the business feels error. best practice pick one metric and stick with it. rule match the metric to how the business experiences the error. three fixes to apply 1 choose by cost use rmse if big errors hurt the most. 2 guard outliers use mae so outliers don't dominate. 3 speak in percent use mape for revenue and price forecasts.
m12-regularization-why: definition regularization adds a penalty to the loss function to prevent overfitting. a penalty on coefficients prevents overfitting ridge l2 shrink all lasso l1 zero some elastic net both loss = error + alpha x penalty adds a little bias to cut variance: total error falls the three families type penalty effect ridge (l2) α × σ βⱼ² shrinks coefficients toward zero lasso (l1) α × σ |βⱼ| sets some coefficients exactly to zero elastic net mix of l1 + l2 combines both behaviors when to regularize many features relative to observations. correlated predictors — ridge stabilizes them. suspect overfitting — training error much lower than validation. trade-off regularization adds bias to reduce variance. done right, it lowers total error. why regularize regularization: penalize complexity ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice fit many features, few rows overfit risk is high ridge (l2): alpha x sum beta^2 shrinks coefficients toward zero leave correlated predictors alone coefficients stay unstable lasso (l1): alpha x sum |beta| sets some exactly to zero ignore train vs validation gap training error much lower elastic net: mix l1 and l2 combines both behaviors result: overfit, unstable model result: lower total error mistake no penalty means the model memorizes noise. best practice adds bias to cut variance. done right, error falls. rule of thumb regularize with many or correlated features, overfit. three fixes to apply 1 use ridge stabilizes correlated predictors. 2 use lasso zeroes out weak features automatically. 3 use elastic net blend both penalties when unsure.
m12-ridge: penalty α × σ βⱼ² behavior shrinks large coefficients toward zero. no feature selection — all coefficients stay nonzero (just smaller). best when you have many correlated features. α (lambda) chosen via cross-validation. visual — coefficient shrinkage ridge shrinks but keeps all coefficients β₁ β₂ β₃ β₄ β₅ ridge: all shrunk, none zero syntax from sklearn.linear_model import ridgecv model = ridgecv (alphas=[ 0.01 , 0.1 , 1 , 10 , 100 ], cv= 5 ) model. fit (x_train, y_train) print (model.alpha_) use ridge when you believe all features contribute, but their coefficients are unstable due to correlation. ridge (l2) ridge: shrink, don't expect selection ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice expect ridge to drop features all coefficients stay nonzero use ridge for correlated features stabilizes unstable coefficients pick alpha by guesswork not chosen via cv use ridgecv with cv=5 alphas 0.01 to 100 use ridge for sparse truth few features really matter read model.alpha_ the cv-chosen strength result: wrong tool, wrong expectation result: stable shrunken coefficients mistake ridge shrinks but keeps every coefficient. best practice penalty: alpha x sum of squared betas. use ridge when all features help but coefficients are unstable. three fixes to apply 1 match the case pick ridge for many correlated features. 2 tune by cv ridgecv picks alpha across your grid. 3 keep all features expect smaller, not zero, coefficients.
m12-lasso: penalty α × σ |βⱼ| behavior drives irrelevant coefficients exactly to zero. built-in feature selection. great for sparse models — only a few predictors matter. path diagram shows coefficients shrinking to zero as α increases. visual — coefficient path lasso path: coefficients hit zero increasing α → fewer nonzero coefficients syntax from sklearn.linear_model import lassocv model = lassocv (cv= 5 , random_state= 42 ) model. fit (x_train, y_train) import pandas as pd selected = pd. series (model.coef_, index=x.columns) print (selected[selected != 0 ]) use lasso when you suspect only a few features matter and you want automatic selection. lasso (l1) lasso: zeroes out weak features ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice use lasso when all features matter real signals get zeroed use lasso for sparse models only a few predictors matter ignore which coefficients vanish never print the nonzero ones use lassocv(cv=5) alpha picked by cv tune alpha manually not cross-validated list selected[selected != 0] see what survived result: signal dropped by accident result: compact, selected model mistake lasso sets some beta to exactly zero. best practice built-in feature selection. nonzero betas survive. use lasso when only a few features likely matter. three fixes to apply 1 fit sparse cases choose lasso when few features carry signal. 2 cross-validate lassocv picks alpha for you. 3 review survivors print nonzero coefficients and sanity check them.
m12-elastic-net: definition combines l1 + l2 penalties. you control the balance with l1_ratio . l1_ratio slides between ridge and lasso pure ridge balanced pure lasso l1_ratio = 0 0.5 1 elasticnetcv finds the penalty and the mix together how l1_ratio works l1_ratio behavior 1 pure lasso 0 pure ridge 0.5 balanced why elastic net scikit-learn's default for many datasets. handles correlated groups better than pure lasso. most used in industry in 2025 for tabular data. syntax from sklearn.linear_model import elasticnetcv model = elasticnetcv ( l1_ratio=[ 0.1 , 0.3 , 0.5 , 0.7 , 0.9 ], cv= 5 , random_state= 42 ) model. fit (x_train, y_train) print (model.l1_ratio_, model.alpha_) practical start with elasticnetcv. it finds both the right penalty and the right mix. elastic net elastic net: pick the mix by cv ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice pure lasso on correlated groups handles them poorly use elasticnetcv finds the penalty and the mix fix l1_ratio by hand mix chosen without testing try l1_ratio 0.1 to 0.9 1 is lasso, 0 is ridge tune alpha and ratio separately miss the best pair start here for tabular data handles correlated groups result: unstable feature selection result: tuned penalty and balance mistake pure l1 or l2 may fit the data badly. best practice read model.l1_ratio_ and model.alpha_. rule of thumb l1_ratio 1 = lasso, 0 = ridge, 0.5 = balanced. three fixes to apply 1 start with encv elasticnetcv tunes alpha and the mix together. 2 grid the ratio offer several l1_ratio values to try. 3 read both report l1_ratio_ and alpha_ after fitting.
m12-choosing-alpha: rule never choose α manually. let cross-validation pick it. the 5-step process use cross-validation grid search. plot coefficient paths vs log(α). pick α where cv error is lowest. never choose manually. use ridgecv, lassocv, elasticnetcv. cv error vs α best α log(α) → cv error syntax from sklearn.linear_model import ridgecv, lassocv, elasticnetcv import numpy as np alphas = np. logspace (- 3 , 3 , 50 ) ridge = ridgecv (alphas=alphas, cv= 5 ). fit (x_train, y_train) lasso = lassocv (cv= 5 ). fit (x_train, y_train) common mistake picking α by eye from the path plot. cv is the only defensible way. choosing alpha alpha: let cross-validation pick ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice pick alpha by eye from the coefficient path plot grid search with cv np.logspace(-3, 3, 50) choose alpha manually no validation behind it pick alpha with lowest cv error read the cv error vs alpha plot tune alpha on the test set leaks information use ridgecv, lassocv, elasticnetcv built-in alpha search result: indefensible alpha result: defensible regularization mistake cv is the only defensible way. best practice plot coefficient paths vs log(alpha). rule never choose alpha manually. let cross-validation pick it. three fixes to apply 1 grid search try alphas on a log scale with cv. 2 min cv error choose the alpha with the lowest cv error. 3 use the cv classes ridgecv, lassocv, and elasticnetcv do it.
m12-logistic-intuition: purpose predict the probability of a binary outcome. how it works input: any real number. output: probability between 0 and 1. sigmoid function: 1 / (1 + e^(-z)). decision boundary at p = 0.5 (adjustable). math: linear regression on log-odds. sigmoid function p = 0.5 z = β₀ + β₁x₁ + … probability syntax from sklearn.linear_model import logisticregression model = logisticregression (max_iter= 1000 ) model. fit (x_train, y_train) proba = model. predict_proba (x_test)[:, 1 ] business use churn, fraud, conversion, loan default — any yes/no prediction. logistic regression logistic: probability, not a line ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice use linear regression for yes/no output can leave 0 to 1 sigmoid: 1 / (1 + e^(-z)) output between 0 and 1 always use a 0.5 cutoff boundary is adjustable tune the decision boundary default p = 0.5, adjustable use predict() only throws away the probabilities predict_proba(x_test)[:, 1] get the class probability result: impossible predictions result: valid probabilities mistake linear output isn't a probability. best practice churn, fraud, conversion, default. formula linear regression on log-odds gives probability via sigmoid. three fixes to apply 1 use the sigmoid squash any real number into 0 to 1. 2 tune the cutoff move the threshold to fit business cost. 3 keep probabilities use predict_proba for ranking and risk.
m12-logit-probs: equation log(p / (1 − p)) = β₀ + β₁x₁ + … key concepts odds = p / (1 − p). β₁ = change in log-odds per unit x. exp(β₁) = odds ratio (multiplicative effect). example worked if p = 0.75, odds = 0.75 / 0.25 = 3 ("3 to 1"). if β₁ = 0.5, exp(0.5) ≈ 1.65 → each unit x multiplies odds by 1.65. odds vs probability probability 0 to 1 (bounded) odds 0 to ∞ (unbounded) why log-odds log-odds range from −∞ to ∞, so linear regression assumptions can apply. log-odds log-odds: odds are not probabilities ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice read beta1 as a probability change it is a change in log-odds odds = p / (1 - p) p = 0.75: odds 3 to 1 confuse odds with probability p = 0.75 is not odds of 0.75 beta1 is log-odds per unit x linear on the logit skip exp(beta1) multiplicative effect missed exp(0.5) is about 1.65 each unit multiplies odds by 1.65 result: effects misreported result: correct multiplicative effect mistake beta1 lives on the log-odds scale. best practice log-odds range from minus to plus infinity. formula log(p / (1 - p)) = b0 + b1x1 exp(b1) = odds ratio. three fixes to apply 1 compute odds divide p by (1 - p) before comparing. 2 read log-odds beta is per unit x on the logit scale. 3 exponentiate exp(beta) gives the odds multiplier.
m12-odds-ratios: rule exp(β) is the multiplicative effect on odds, not probability. reading odds ratios: exp(beta) or = 1.0 no effect or = 1.35 35% higher odds or = 0.72 28% lower odds or = 2.5 2.5x the odds odds ratio is not a probability change reference values exp(β) interpretation = 1.0 no effect = 1.35 35% higher odds = 0.72 28% lower odds = 2.5 2.5× higher odds = 4.2 4.2× higher odds business example applied "smokers have 4.2× higher odds of heart disease." — always paired with a confidence interval. syntax import numpy as np import pandas as pd odds_ratios = np. exp (model.coef_[ 0 ]) df_or = pd. dataframe ({ 'feature' : x.columns, 'coef' : model.coef_[ 0 ], 'odds_ratio' : odds_ratios }) common mistake saying "35% higher probability" when the odds ratio is 1.35. odds ≠ probability. odds ratios odds ratio: odds, not probability ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice say 35% higher probability when the odds ratio is 1.35 say 35% higher odds exp(beta) = 1.35 read raw beta as the effect not exponentiated use np.exp(model.coef_[0]) convert before reporting quote the ratio with no ci uncertainty hidden pair the ratio with a ci smokers: 4.2x higher odds result: effect overstated or misread result: accurate, defensible claim mistake odds do not equal probability. best practice 1.0 means no effect; 0.72 is 28% lower odds. rule exp(beta) is the multiplicative effect on odds, not probability. three fixes to apply 1 say odds write higher odds, never higher probability. 2 exponentiate report exp(coef), not raw coefficients. 3 add a ci always give the interval with the ratio.
m12-multiclass-logistic: definition when the outcome has more than two classes (e.g., bronze/silver/gold). two ways to handle more than two classes one-vs-rest one binary model per class bronze? silver? gold? softmax (default) one model, all probabilities p(b)+p(s)+p(g) = 1 explain with marginal effects or shap two approaches method how one-vs-rest (ovr) one model per class softmax (multinomial) direct probabilities for all classes scikit-learn default scikit-learn uses softmax (multinomial) by default for multi-class. syntax from sklearn.linear_model import logisticregression # softmax (multinomial) — default model = logisticregression (multi_class= 'multinomial' , max_iter= 1000 ) # or one-vs-rest model_ovr = logisticregression (multi_class= 'ovr' ) interpretation harder than binary — use marginal effects or shap for stakeholder explanations. multi-class logistic multi-class: choose and explain ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice apply binary logic to 3+ classes bronze, silver, gold softmax (multinomial) direct probabilities for all classes ignore the default method softmax is the sklearn default one-vs-rest (ovr) one model per class explain with binary odds ratios harder to interpret use marginal effects or shap explain to stakeholders result: confusing stakeholder story result: clear multi-class model mistake multi-class is harder to interpret. best practice set multi_class explicitly when it matters. rule of thumb more than two classes: softmax or ovr, then explain. three fixes to apply 1 pick a method choose softmax or ovr on purpose. 2 know the default scikit-learn defaults to softmax. 3 explain simply use marginal effects or shap for stakeholders.
m12-confusion-matrix: definition four counts (tp, tn, fp, fn) that reveal what a classifier actually did. the matrix confusion matrix pred + pred − true + true − tp fn fp tn accuracy = (tp + tn) / total useless when imbalanced 99% negative class → always predicting negative gives 99% accuracy but zero business value. syntax from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix, classification_report cm = confusion_matrix (y_test, y_pred) print (cm) print ( classification_report (y_test, y_pred)) first step always check class distribution before choosing a metric. confusion matrix accuracy: useless when imbalanced ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice report accuracy only (tp + tn) / total check class distribution first before choosing a metric skip the class distribution imbalance goes unseen print confusion_matrix see what the model did ignore the four counts tp, tn, fp, fn run classification_report per-class precision and recall result: 99% accuracy, zero value result: true picture of the model mistake always predicting negative scores 99%. best practice four counts reveal what a classifier did. check look at class balance before choosing any metric. three fixes to apply 1 check balance count the classes before picking a metric. 2 read the matrix use tp, tn, fp, fn to see the errors. 3 use the report classification_report shows each class.
m12-precision-recall: definitions precision = tp / (tp + fp) — "of predicted positive, how many real?" recall = tp / (tp + fn) — "of actual positive, how many caught?" which mistake costs more: a false alarm or a miss? precision of predicted positives, how many are real? tp/(tp+fp) recall of actual positives, how many caught? tp/(tp+fn) fraud, churn, disease: favour recall · spam filter: favour precision trade-off focus optimize cost of being wrong high precision fewer false alarms miss real cases high recall catch most cases more false alarms business context fraud / churn → maximize recall (missing a case is expensive). spam filter → maximize precision (misclassifying real email is bad). medical screening → prioritize recall (missing disease is fatal). syntax from sklearn.metrics import precision_score, recall_score p = precision_score (y_test, y_pred) r = recall_score (y_test, y_pred) choose by cost which error is more expensive — a false positive or a false negative? that tells you which to optimize. precision vs recall precision vs recall: pick by error cost ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice maximize both blindly they trade off fraud, churn: maximize recall missing a case is expensive optimize precision for fraud misses real cases spam filter: maximize precision misfiling real email is bad ignore which error costs more false positive or negative medical screening: favor recall missing disease is fatal result: wrong errors minimized result: metric matches the cost mistake missing a fraud case is expensive. best practice precision = tp / (tp + fp). recall = tp / (tp + fn). rule of thumb ask which error costs more, fp or fn. optimize for it. three fixes to apply 1 price the errors weigh false positives and false negatives. 2 favor recall when missing a case is the bigger cost. 3 favor precision when false alarms are the bigger cost.
m12-f1: formula f1 = 2 × (precision × recall) / (precision + recall) f1 punishes imbalance between precision and recall p=.9 r=.9 f1 0.90 p=.9 r=.1 f1 0.18 p=.5 r=.5 f1 0.50 f1 = 2pr / (p+r): if one is near 0, f1 collapses why f1 harmonic mean of precision and recall. single metric when you care about both. default for imbalanced classification. punishes extreme imbalance — if one is 0, f1 is 0. averaging for multi-class average meaning macro unweighted mean across classes micro aggregates tp/fp/fn globally weighted weighted by class support syntax from sklearn.metrics import f1_score f1 = f1_score (y_test, y_pred) f1_macro = f1_score (y_test, y_pred, average= 'macro' ) practical use f1 when you can't decide whether precision or recall matters more. f1-score f1: when both errors matter ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice average precision and recall hides a weak side f1 = 2pr / (p + r) harmonic mean punishes imbalance use accuracy on imbalanced data misleading score default for imbalanced classes one score for both ignore multi-class averaging macro, micro, weighted differ pick macro, micro, or weighted know what each aggregates result: weak side hidden result: balanced single metric mistake if one is 0, f1 is 0. a plain mean hides it. best practice use f1 when you can't pick precision or recall. formula f1 = 2 x (precision x recall) / (precision + recall) three fixes to apply 1 use the harmonic f1 drops to 0 if either side is 0. 2 prefer over accuracy f1 is the imbalanced-class default. 3 choose averaging macro is unweighted; weighted uses support.
m12-roc-auc: definition roc plots true positive rate vs false positive rate across all thresholds. auc summarizes it. auc interpretation auc quality 1.0 perfect 0.9 – 1.0 excellent 0.8 – 0.9 good 0.7 – 0.8 acceptable 0.5 random guessing roc curve auc = 0.85 random (0.5) false positive rate → true positive rate syntax from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score, roc_curve auc = roc_auc_score (y_test, y_proba) fpr, tpr, _ = roc_curve (y_test, y_proba) why auc robust to class imbalance, threshold-independent, and easy to compare across models. roc and auc auc: judge across all thresholds ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice judge at one threshold only misses the full trade-off plot tpr vs fpr roc_curve across thresholds read auc 0.5 as decent that is random guessing summarize with roc_auc_score use y_proba, not labels compare models by eye no single summary number read the auc scale 0.8-0.9 good, 0.9-1.0 excellent result: weak model looks fine result: threshold-free comparison mistake auc 0.5 equals random guessing. best practice auc is robust to imbalance and easy to compare. test 0.5 random; 0.7-0.8 acceptable; 0.8-0.9 good. three fixes to apply 1 score with proba pass predicted probabilities to roc_auc_score. 2 use the scale read auc against the quality bands. 3 compare models rank models by auc on the same test data.
m12-pr-curve: definition plots precision vs recall across all thresholds. better than roc when the positive class is rare. when to use pr instead of roc rare positives — fraud (0.1%), churn (2%), disease (0.5%). you care more about the positive class. class imbalance is severe. visual pr curve — area under curve = average precision ap = 0.72 recall → precision syntax from sklearn.metrics import precision_recall_curve, average_precision_score precision, recall, _ = precision_recall_curve (y_test, y_proba) ap = average_precision_score (y_test, y_proba) use cases churn, fraud, medical diagnosis — anywhere the positive class is what matters. pr curve pr curve: when positives are rare ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice use roc for rare positives fraud 0.1%, disease 0.5% use the pr curve precision_recall_curve ignore the positive class it's the one that matters summarize with average precision average_precision_score overlook severe imbalance roc can look rosy use for churn, fraud, diagnosis positive class is the focus result: rare-class weakness hidden result: honest rare-event view mistake severe imbalance needs a sharper lens. best practice area under the curve is average precision. rule of thumb rare positives: choose pr over roc. three fixes to apply 1 switch to pr use it when positives are rare. 2 report ap average precision summarizes the curve. 3 focus positives judge the class the business cares about.
m12-choosing-metric: rule the metric must match the business cost of each error type. match the metric to the cost of each error revenue rmse or mape churn auc or f1 fraud recall at 90% precision a/b test business kpi lift balanced classes only: accuracy decision table task best metric revenue prediction rmse / mape churn prediction auc or f1 fraud detection recall at 90% precision a/b testing business kpi lift balanced classification accuracy (only then) never optimize accuracy on imbalanced data. you'll build a model that always predicts the majority class and think it's great. tie-breaker ask: which error is more expensive? that's the metric to optimize. choosing a metric metric: match the cost of each error ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice optimize accuracy when skewed majority class always wins revenue: rmse or mape error in business units use one metric for every task ignores business cost churn: auc or f1 fraud: recall at 90% precision skip the a/b business kpi model score is not value balanced classes only: accuracy a/b testing: business kpi lift result: always predicts majority class result: metric tied to business cost mistake you build a model that looks great but isn't. best practice which error costs more? optimize that one. rule metric must match business cost of each error type. three fixes to apply 1 map task to metric use the decision table for each problem. 2 avoid accuracy skip it on imbalanced data entirely. 3 ask the cost which error costs more? optimize that one.
m12-interpretation: rule a model you can't explain to a stakeholder isn't ready for production. tools for explaining a model to a stakeholder coefficient plot direction and size confidence intervals uncertainty partial dependence one variable at a time shap (module 13) per-row contributions "cut price $10 and sales rise 8%" is a coefficient turned into a decision interpretation tools tool shows coefficient plots direction and size of each effect confidence intervals uncertainty around coefficients partial dependence plots how predictions change as one variable varies shap values per-row feature contributions (advanced) business translation applied "if we reduce price by $10, sales increase 8%." that's a coefficient translated into a decision. always include uncertainty point estimates alone are misleading. report confidence intervals or ranges. next module module 13 covers shap and advanced interpretation in depth. interpretation interpretation: explain with uncertainty ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice ship a model nobody can explain not ready for production coefficient plots direction and size of each effect report point estimates alone misleading without uncertainty confidence intervals, pdps uncertainty and shape of effect hand over raw coefficients no decision attached translate to a decision cut price $10: sales up 8% result: stakeholders don't trust it result: explainable, decision-ready mistake point estimates alone are misleading. best practice shap values are covered in module 13. rule a model you can't explain isn't ready for production. three fixes to apply 1 plot effects show direction and size with coefficient plots. 2 show uncertainty report confidence intervals or ranges. 3 translate turn each coefficient into a business decision.
m12-pitfalls: warning these five mistakes kill more predictive modeling projects than any technical failure. five pitfalls that sink projects data leakage test-set tuning wrong business goal over-engineering no monitoring write the assumptions, deployment plan and monitoring metric before building the five pitfalls pitfall why it hurts data leakage using future info inflates performance test set tuning metrics become optimistic lies ignoring business context model optimizes the wrong thing over-engineering complex model when linear works no monitoring model decays without anyone noticing prevention write down the model's assumptions, deployment plan, and monitoring metric before you build it. common pitfalls pitfalls: five project killers ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice use future info as features data leakage inflates results remove leakage up front only past info as features tune on the test set metrics become optimistic lies keep the test set untouched honest metrics over-engineer, never monitor complex model; no monitoring fit the business, then monitor linear first; track decay result: project fails after launch result: reliable model in production mistake these kill more projects than technical failure. best practice write assumptions, plan and metric before building. prevention write down assumptions, plan and monitoring metric first. three fixes to apply 1 block leakage exclude any future information. 2 protect the test never tune on the test set. 3 monitor track a metric so decay doesn't go unnoticed.
m12-final-checklist: use before shipping six checks. skip one and the model isn't ready. the checklist business problem clearly defined. data cleaned, no leakage. assumptions checked. cross-validated performance. interpretable to stakeholders. deployed and monitored. model readiness flow business data assumptions cv interpret deploy most common miss step 6 — deployment without monitoring. a model that isn't monitored is a model that will silently break. final checklist ship check: don't deploy blind ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice skip a checklist step then the model isn't ready define the business problem data cleaned, no leakage deploy without monitoring step 6 is the most common miss check assumptions cross-validate performance ship with leakage, no checks cleaning and diagnostics skipped make it interpretable deploy and monitor it result: model silently breaks result: ready to ship mistake an unmonitored model will silently break. best practice six checks. skip one and it isn't ready. check all six steps passed before shipping a model. three fixes to apply 1 define and clean state the problem; remove leakage. 2 validate check assumptions and cross-validate. 3 monitor deploy with monitoring so breaks are seen.
m12-recap: module flow 1 concepts 2 linear 3 regularize 4 logistic 5 metrics the five lines core concepts — bias-variance, splits, cross-validation, baseline. linear regression — coefficients, assumptions, diagnostics, vif. regularization — ridge, lasso, elastic net, choose α via cv. logistic regression — sigmoid, log-odds, odds ratios. metrics — match the metric to the business cost of each error. carry-forward rules never touch the test set during tuning. always beat a baseline before claiming success. report confidence intervals, not just point estimates. check assumptions before trusting p-values. deploy with monitoring — models decay. next up module 13 covers advanced model interpretation (shap), tree-based methods, and model deployment patterns.
m12-adv-interactions: key checks interaction and polynomial terms ✓ plot by group look for different slopes before modelling. ✓ add the term use x * z so main effects stay in the model. ✓ validate compare held-out error with and without the term. definition an interaction lets the effect of one predictor depend on another. a polynomial term lets the effect bend instead of staying a straight line. the model formula y = b0 + b1·x + b2·z + b3·(x × z) if b3 is not zero, the effect of x changes with the level of z. # statsmodels formula api: x*z adds x, z and x:z import statsmodels.formula.api as smf m = smf.ols('revenue ~ ad_spend * region_east + i(ad_spend**2)', data=df).fit() print(m.summary()) # center predictors first to keep coefficients readable df['ad_c'] = df['ad_spend'] - df['ad_spend'].mean() use it when watch out for the effect of ad spend differs by region always keep the main effects with the interaction residuals show a curve against a predictor high degrees overfit; validate on held-out data interpret with care with an interaction, b1 alone is the effect of x when z is zero, not the overall effect. say that in your report. interactions interactions: let effects depend on context ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice one slope for every group ignores that effects differ add x * z when effects differ test whether b3 is not zero add the product, drop main effects coefficients become unreadable keep the main effects interpret b1 at z = 0 high-degree polynomials fit noise, fail on new data center predictors, validate check on held-out data result: misleading average effect result: effect explained by context mistake one number hides a real difference. best practice say how the effect changes with z. rule of thumb interactions need a reason. keep them only if they validate. three fixes to apply 1 plot by group look for different slopes before modelling. 2 add the term use x * z so main effects stay in the model. 3 validate compare held-out error with and without the term.
m12-adv-quantile: key checks quantile regression ✓ pick quantiles median, plus the tail that matters to the business. ✓ fit each one run quantreg once per quantile. ✓ check crossing predicted quantiles should not cross. definition quantile regression models a chosen percentile of the outcome, such as the median or the 90th percentile, instead of the average. why use it median regression (q = 0.5) is far less affected by outliers than ordinary least squares. upper quantiles answer questions like "how long do the slowest 10% of orders take?" effects can differ across the distribution: the slope at q = 0.9 may not equal the slope at q = 0.5. # statsmodels quantile regression import statsmodels.formula.api as smf for q in [0.1, 0.5, 0.9]: m = smf.quantreg('delivery_days ~ distance + weight', df).fit(q=q) print(q, m.params['distance']) check fit each quantile separately and make sure the predicted quantiles do not cross. crossing lines signal a poor fit. quantile regression quantiles: model more than the average ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice model only the mean slow cases stay hidden fit the median for robustness q = 0.5 resists outliers let outliers steer the fit ols is pulled by extremes fit upper quantiles for slas q = 0.9 targets the slow tail assume one slope everywhere tail effects can differ compare slopes across quantiles see where effects change result: plan misses the tail result: plan covers the tail too mistake the mean says nothing about the slowest 10%. best practice fit each quantile separately. rule ask which part of the data the decision depends on. three fixes to apply 1 pick quantiles median, plus the tail that matters to the business. 2 fit each one run quantreg once per quantile. 3 check crossing predicted quantiles should not cross.
m12-adv-count: key checks poisson and negative binomial regression ✓ fit poisson use a glm with the poisson family. ✓ test dispersion compare pearson chi2 with residual df. ✓ add exposure offset by days or customers observed. definition count models for outcomes that are whole numbers of 0 or more, such as tickets per day or claims per customer. model assumes use when poisson variance equals the mean counts are well behaved negative binomial variance is larger than the mean overdispersed counts # poisson glm, then check overdispersion import statsmodels.api as sm import statsmodels.formula.api as smf m = smf.glm('tickets ~ users + promo', data=df, family=sm.families.poisson()).fit() ratio = m.pearson_chi2 / m.df_resid print(ratio) # well above 1 suggests overdispersion reading coefficients poisson coefficients are on the log scale: exp(b) is the multiplier on the expected count for a one-unit increase. exposure if observation windows differ (days, customers), include an exposure or offset so you model a rate, not a raw count. count models count data: choose the right family ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice ols on counts can predict negative counts start with poisson counts of 0 or more poisson without a check ignores overdispersion check variance against mean pearson chi2 / df well above 1 ignore different exposure longer windows look busier switch to negative binomial add an exposure or offset result: wrong errors and bad forecasts result: valid counts and rates mistake standard errors come out too small. best practice model a rate when exposure differs. rule of thumb variance far above the mean? use negative binomial. three fixes to apply 1 fit poisson use a glm with the poisson family. 2 test dispersion compare pearson chi2 with residual df. 3 add exposure offset by days or customers observed.
m12-adv-calibration: key checks probability calibration ✓ check plot a reliability curve on held-out data. ✓ fix use calibratedclassifiercv with cross-validation. ✓ re-check compare brier score before and after. definition a model is calibrated when a predicted 70% really happens about 70% of the time. good ranking (auc) does not guarantee good probabilities. how to check reliability curve: group predictions into bins and compare predicted vs observed rates. brier score: the mean squared gap between predicted probability and the 0/1 outcome. lower is better. # check, then fix calibration from sklearn.calibration import calibration_curve, calibratedclassifiercv from sklearn.metrics import brier_score_loss frac_pos, mean_pred = calibration_curve(y_test, p_test, n_bins=10) print(brier_score_loss(y_test, p_test)) cal = calibratedclassifiercv(model, method='isotonic', cv=5).fit(x_train, y_train) matters when you use probabilities directly, for example expected cost or a threshold tied to a business rule. calibrate on data the model has not trained on. calibration calibration: probabilities must be honest ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice judge only by auc ranking is not probability plot a reliability curve predicted vs observed rate use raw scores as probabilities a 0.8 may mean 0.6 report the brier score lower is better calibrate on training data the fix is overfit calibrate on held-out data platt or isotonic, with cv result: decisions on wrong risk numbers result: probabilities you can act on mistake expected cost is miscalculated. best practice a predicted 70% happens about 70% of the time. rule if you use the probability, check that it is calibrated. three fixes to apply 1 check plot a reliability curve on held-out data. 2 fix use calibratedclassifiercv with cross-validation. 3 re-check compare brier score before and after.
m12-adv-multiclass: key checks multinomial and ordinal logistic regression ✓ name the outcome decide: are the classes ordered or not? ✓ pick the model multinomial or ordinal logistic. ✓ validate check precision and recall per class. definition extensions of logistic regression for outcomes with more than two categories. model outcome example multinomial unordered categories plan chosen: basic, plus, pro ordinal ordered categories rating: low, medium, high # multinomial with scikit-learn (softmax over all classes) from sklearn.linear_model import logisticregression clf = logisticregression(max_iter=1000).fit(x_train, y_train) proba = clf.predict_proba(x_test) # one column per class assumption ordinal logistic assumes the effect of a predictor is the same across each step of the ordered scale (proportional odds). test it before trusting the result. multi-class logistic multi-class: match the model to the outcome ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice binary model on many classes collapses the categories multinomial for unordered classes one probability per class treat ordered ratings as unordered throws away the order ordinal for ordered scales low, medium, high assume proportional odds untested ordinal fit may be invalid test proportional odds same effect at each step result: lost information or wrong model result: probabilities that sum to one mistake the outcome type picks the model. best practice check a confusion matrix for every class. rule unordered: multinomial. ordered: ordinal. three fixes to apply 1 name the outcome decide: are the classes ordered or not? 2 pick the model multinomial or ordinal logistic. 3 validate check precision and recall per class.
m12-adv-robust-se: key checks robust standard errors ✓ plot residuals residual vs fitted shows unequal spread. ✓ refit use hc3, or cluster for repeat rows. ✓ compare check how p-values change versus classic ses. definition standard errors that stay valid when residual variance is not constant (heteroscedasticity). the coefficients do not change; the standard errors and p-values do. # same model, heteroscedasticity-robust standard errors import statsmodels.formula.api as smf ols = smf.ols('revenue ~ ad_spend + price', data=df).fit() rob = smf.ols('revenue ~ ad_spend + price', data=df).fit(cov_type='hc3') print(ols.bse, rob.bse) # clustered data (repeat customers): cov_type='cluster' use them when the residual-vs-fitted plot fans out. repeated rows from the same customer need clustered standard errors, not just hc3. not a cure-all robust standard errors fix inference, not a wrong model. if the shape is curved, fix the model first. robust standard errors robust errors: fix inference, not the model ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice trust classic ses on fan shape p-values come out too small check the residual plot first look for a fan shape ignore repeated customers rows are not independent refit with cov_type hc3 same coefficients, new ses use robust ses to hide a bad shape the model is still wrong cluster by customer id handles repeated rows result: overconfident conclusions result: honest confidence intervals mistake coefficients stay put; the p-values mislead. best practice report which standard errors you used. rule of thumb heteroscedastic residuals? report robust standard errors. three fixes to apply 1 plot residuals residual vs fitted shows unequal spread. 2 refit use hc3, or cluster for repeat rows. 3 compare check how p-values change versus classic ses.
m13-overview: purpose master tree-based models, clustering, hyperparameter tuning, and ensemble methods — the tools that dominate tabular data in industry and competitions. what you'll be able to do master tree-based models: decision trees → random forests → gradient boosting apply and interpret clustering techniques correctly perform professional hyperparameter tuning build and compare ensemble models deliver competition-grade projects and technical communication module flow six sections 1 trees 2 forests 3 boosting 4 clustering 5 tuning guiding principle for tabular data in 2025, tree ensembles beat almost everything — and they're the tools you'll use daily.
m13-objectives: by the end of this module you will be able to build, tune, and compare tree ensembles, cluster data intelligently, and deliver a competition-grade project. five objectives: trees, forests, boosting, clusters, tuning 1 trees 2 forests 3 boosting 4 clusters 5 tuning five objectives # objective detail 1 tree-based models decision trees → random forests → gradient boosting 2 clustering techniques k-means, hierarchical, dbscan, validation 3 hyperparameter tuning grid, random, optuna, hyperband 4 ensemble models bagging, boosting, stacking 5 project delivery competition-grade + communication prerequisite module 12 — regression, classification, cross-validation, metrics.
m13-why-trees: reality tree ensembles are the default for tabular data — and they aren't going away. why they dominate 73% of winning kaggle solutions (2023–2025) use tree ensembles. handle mixed data types — numeric + categorical together. handle missing values natively — no imputation needed. capture non-linear relationships and interactions. feature importance out-of-the-box. extremely robust — minimal preprocessing required. the industry standard the three winners xgboost all-round lightgbm fastest catboost categoricals rule of thumb if your data fits in a table, start with trees. reach for neural nets only when trees plateau. why trees trees first: default for tabular data ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice start with a neural net table data, 73% winners use trees start with a tree ensemble rf, xgboost, lightgbm first impute and scale everything trees need little preprocessing keep preprocessing minimal mixed types, native missing values skip feature importance miss free insight from the model read feature importance built in, out of the box result: slow, complex baseline result: fast, strong baseline mistake heavy tooling for a table that trees solve simply. best practice trees first, nets only when trees plateau. rule of thumb if your data fits in a table, start with trees. three fixes to apply 1 start simple fit a tree ensemble first and record the score. 2 skip fuss leave missing values and scales to the trees. 3 escalate late try neural nets only when trees stop improving.
m13-roadmap: six tracks follow in order — each builds on the previous. the sequence track topics decision trees cart, gini, pruning, importance random forests bagging, oob, hyperparameters gradient boosting xgboost, lightgbm, early stopping clustering k-means, hierarchical, dbscan tuning & ensembles optuna, stacking, comparison projects competition strategy + delivery learning path trees forests boost cluster tune ship
m13-tree-intuition: definition a decision tree recursively splits data to minimize impurity — like a flowchart of if-else questions. why they're useful recursively splits data to minimize impurity. naturally handles non-linear relationships and interactions. no need to scale features. interpretable — you can literally read the rules. visual sample classification tree income > 50k? yes no age > 30? predict: no predict: no predict: yes strength you can print a tree and hand it to a stakeholder. few models can do that. tree intuition decision trees: if-else rules you can read ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice scale features for a tree not needed, wasted effort skip scaling any feature scale works treat the tree as a black box never read the split rules print and read the tree hand the rules to a stakeholder expect it to split perfectly recursive splits just cut impurity think in impurity reduction each split minimizes impurity result: lost interpretability result: explainable model mistake extra steps, and the rules never reach stakeholders. best practice a flowchart anyone can follow and challenge. rule of thumb a tree is a flowchart of if-else questions. three fixes to apply 1 no scaling feed raw numeric and categorical features. 2 print the tree share the rules with non-technical reviewers. 3 check splits confirm each split makes business sense.
m13-cart: definition classification and regression trees — the underlying algorithm for scikit-learn's tree models. cart: greedy, one yes/no question at a time split pick best question measure gini / entropy repeat until pure or stop greedy: best split now, not a globally optimal tree impurity measures task metric classification gini impurity or entropy regression mean squared error (mse) how it builds at each node, test every feature & every possible split. choose the split that maximizes impurity reduction. greedy but globally optimal in practice. syntax from sklearn.tree import decisiontreeclassifier model = decisiontreeclassifier ( criterion= 'gini' , # or 'entropy' max_depth= 5 , min_samples_leaf= 10 , random_state= 42 ) model. fit (x_train, y_train) practical default criterion='gini' is fast and produces nearly identical trees to entropy. cart algorithm cart: pick the right impurity measure ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice gini for a regression tree regression needs mse, not gini match metric to the task gini or entropy; mse for regression agonize over entropy trees nearly identical to gini keep criterion gini fast, near-identical trees fit with no depth limit decisiontreeclassifier() defaults set max_depth=5 min_samples_leaf=10, random_state=42 result: wrong setup, overfit tree result: valid, constrained tree mistake time lost on a tiny choice while depth stays unchecked. best practice right metric, sensible limits, reproducible fit. practical default criterion gini is fast and nearly the same as entropy. three fixes to apply 1 match task classification: gini or entropy. regression: mse. 2 keep default use gini unless you have a specific reason. 3 cap growth set depth and leaf size before fitting.
m13-gini-entropy: formulas gini = σ p(1−p) entropy = −σ p log₂(p) gini impurity: 0.50 is a coin flip, 0 is pure 50/50 0.50 70/30 0.42 90/10 0.18 100/0 0.00 gini = 1 - sum(p²) · lower is purer comparison property gini entropy speed faster slightly slower tree depth shallower often slightly deeper final accuracy usually negligible difference scikit-learn default ✓ syntax # default model_gini = decisiontreeclassifier (criterion= 'gini' ) # alternative model_entropy = decisiontreeclassifier (criterion= 'entropy' ) choose stick with the default (gini) unless you have a specific reason to try entropy. gini vs entropy gini vs entropy: a debate that rarely matters ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice assume entropy is more accurate final accuracy: negligible difference keep the default gini faster, shallower trees switch criterion first before fixing depth or leaves tune depth and leaf size where accuracy really moves ignore the speed cost entropy is slightly slower try entropy only with reason criterion='entropy' as a test result: slower, no real gain result: fast, simple training mistake tuning effort spent where the payoff is negligible. best practice default first, alternatives only with a clear reason. formulas gini = sum p(1-p) entropy = -sum p log2(p) three fixes to apply 1 use default stay with gini for most tree models. 2 tune elsewhere spend effort on pruning parameters instead. 3 compare fairly if you test entropy, keep the split identical.
m13-tree-overfit: critical single trees overfit dramatically without constraints. the problem an unconstrained tree can create one leaf per training row — 100% training accuracy, 0% on new data. visual depth vs performance train error validation error sweet spot deeper tree → solutions pruning — cut back the tree after building. min_samples_leaf — require a minimum per leaf. max_depth — cap the depth. next step random forests solve this problem structurally — see the next section. tree overfitting tree overfitting: one leaf per row ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice fit an unconstrained tree grows to one leaf per row cap depth with max_depth stop growth early trust 100% training accuracy memorized, not learned require min_samples_leaf each leaf needs enough rows never compare train vs test depth vs performance unchecked prune after building cut back weak branches result: 100% train, 0% new data result: stable, generalizing tree mistake perfect on seen rows, useless on new ones. best practice train and test scores stay close together. rule of thumb train score far above test score means overfitting. three fixes to apply 1 cap depth set max_depth so the tree cannot memorize rows. 2 set leaf size use min_samples_leaf to avoid tiny leaves. 3 go forest random forests fix this structurally.
m13-pruning: rule never fit an unconstrained tree. set at least one pruning parameter. pruning trades training fit for generalisation depth 2 train 78% depth 5 train 88% depth 12 train 97% no limit train 100% limit max_depth · min_samples_leaf · ccp_alpha the parameters parameter what it does typical max_depth cap tree depth 3–10 min_samples_split min rows to split a node 20+ (default 2 is too low) min_samples_leaf min rows in a leaf 5–20 max_features features considered per split "sqrt" or 0.3–0.5 ccp_alpha cost-complexity pruning 0.0–0.05 syntax from sklearn.tree import decisiontreeclassifier model = decisiontreeclassifier ( max_depth= 5 , min_samples_split= 20 , min_samples_leaf= 10 , ccp_alpha= 0.005 , random_state= 42 ) priority max_depth is the most important. min_samples_leaf is a close second. pruning pruning: never fit an unconstrained tree ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice leave max_depth unset tree grows until pure set max_depth 3 to 10 most important parameter keep min_samples_split=2 default of 2 is too low use min_samples_split 20+ min_samples_leaf 5 to 20 set no pruning parameter not even one constraint add ccp_alpha 0.0 to 0.05 e.g. ccp_alpha=0.005 result: deep, overfit tree result: compact, generalizing tree mistake noise becomes rules and new data breaks them. best practice constrained splits keep only real patterns. rule set at least one pruning parameter. depth first. three fixes to apply 1 depth first max_depth is the most important parameter. 2 leaf second min_samples_leaf is a close second. 3 add cost pruning use ccp_alpha to trim weak branches.
m13-feature-importance: definition total reduction in impurity brought by each feature, normalized to sum to 1. rules not the same as statistical significance. great for quick insights — which features matter most? biased toward high-cardinality features — a caution. use permutation importance for a fairer picture. visual feature importance income 0.35 age 0.25 tenure 0.18 region 0.12 other 0.10 syntax import pandas as pd importance = pd. dataframe ({ 'feature' : x.columns, 'importance' : model.feature_importances_ }). sort_values ( 'importance' , ascending= false ) print (importance. head ( 15 )) fairness always plot top 15 with confidence intervals. single point estimates mislead. tree importance feature importance: not significance ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice read it as significance it is impurity reduction only use it for quick insight which features matter most trust high-cardinality scores biased toward many-valued features cross-check by permutation fairer than impurity importance report one point estimate no confidence interval shown plot top 15 with intervals show the uncertainty result: misleading driver story result: honest feature ranking mistake stakeholders chase features that are only artifacts. best practice importance with context and error bars. rule of thumb importance sums to 1; it is not statistical significance. three fixes to apply 1 not significance do not quote it as a p-value style result. 2 permute run permutation importance for a fairer picture. 3 show top 15 plot with intervals, not single numbers.
m13-tree-pros-cons: summary great for interpretation, bad for stability. that's why we ensemble them. trees: easy to explain, easy to overfit pros readable rules no scaling needed mixed data types cons high variance unstable to small data changes steps, not smooth trends advantages interpretable — can read the rules directly. fast to train and predict. no scaling needed — features on any scale work. handles mixed data types — numeric + categorical. non-linear relationships captured naturally. limitations high variance — small data change → big tree change. unstable — no reproducibility if data shifts. poor at linear relationships — needs many splits to approximate. easily overfits without pruning. next random forests combine many trees to fix variance — see the next section. tree trade-offs single trees: clear but unstable ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice ship one unpruned tree easily overfits use a tree to explain read the rules directly ignore instability small data change, big new tree ensemble to cut variance random forest averages trees use trees for linear signals needs many splits to approximate check for linear structure use a linear model if it fits result: fragile, unreproducible model result: stable and explainable mistake predictions shift whenever the data shifts. best practice trees for insight, ensembles for stability. rule of thumb great for interpretation, bad for stability. three fixes to apply 1 prune constrain every single tree you fit. 2 ensemble combine trees to fix high variance. 3 match shape pick linear models for linear relationships.
m13-rf-core: definition train many trees on bootstrapped samples with random feature subsets — then aggregate predictions. the algorithm bagging (bootstrap aggregating) — train many trees on bootstrapped samples. each tree sees ~63% of the data (with replacement). random subset of features at each split (default sqrt(n_features)). final prediction = average (regression) or majority vote (classification). why it works averaging many decorrelated trees dramatically reduces variance without increasing bias. random forest structure 1 data 2 vote 3 pred t1 t2 t3 syntax from sklearn.ensemble import randomforestclassifier model = randomforestclassifier (n_estimators= 500 , random_state= 42 ) random forest core random forest: bagging plus random features ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice train trees on identical data no bootstrap, trees correlate bootstrap each tree about 63% of rows, with replacement give every split all features no decorrelation between trees random features per split default sqrt(n_features) use a handful of trees averaging barely reduces variance use n_estimators=500 average or majority vote result: variance stays high result: lower variance, same bias mistake correlated trees make the same errors. best practice decorrelated trees cancel each other's errors. why it works averaging decorrelated trees cuts variance, not bias. three fixes to apply 1 bootstrap sample rows with replacement per tree. 2 sample features limit features at every split. 3 aggregate average for regression; vote for classification.
m13-oob: definition each tree never sees ~37% of the data — a natural validation set. oob: each tree is tested on rows it never saw trees many, different bootstrap random rows vote average / majority about 37% of rows are left out per tree: a free validation score why it's valuable free performance estimate without a separate validation set. oob score ≈ cross-validation score in practice. built into every tree — you get it for free. use oob_score=true in scikit-learn. syntax from sklearn.ensemble import randomforestclassifier model = randomforestclassifier ( n_estimators= 500 , oob_score= true , random_state= 42 ) model. fit (x_train, y_train) print (f "oob score: {model.oob_score_:.3f}" ) practical use oob as a quick check during hyperparameter search. use cv for the final report. out-of-bag error oob: a free validation set ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice burn data on a validation split though ~37% is unseen per tree use the unseen ~37% built-in validation, no holdout never set oob_score default is off, score unavailable set oob_score=true read model.oob_score_ after fit report oob as the final score it is a quick check only oob in search, cv to report quick check, then final cv result: wasted data, weak reporting result: fast, honest evaluation mistake less training data and an unfair final number. best practice oob approximates cv at no extra cost. rule of thumb oob for quick checks; cv for the final report. three fixes to apply 1 turn it on pass oob_score=true when you build the forest. 2 use in search compare settings quickly with oob. 3 confirm with cv report cross-validation at the end.
m13-rf-importance: three methods different ways to measure how much each feature matters. importance: prefer permutation or shap over default mdi mdi permutation shap mdi is biased toward high-cardinality features comparison method how reliability mean decrease impurity (mdi) default in sklearn biased toward high-cardinality features permutation importance shuffle each feature, measure degradation more reliable shap values game-theoretic attribution gold standard (next module) syntax — permutation importance from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance result = permutation_importance ( model, x_test, y_test, n_repeats= 10 , random_state= 42 ) print (result.importances_mean) always plot show the top 15 features with confidence intervals. single point estimates mislead. rf importance rf importance: default mdi misleads ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice trust default mdi blindly biased to high-cardinality features use permutation importance shuffle a feature, measure drop permute on training data only not on x_test, y_test run with n_repeats=10 evaluate on x_test, y_test show one number per feature no spread across repeats plot top 15 with intervals consider shap next module result: inflated, unstable ranking result: reliable ranking mistake noisy id-like columns look important. best practice importance that survives a repeat check. rule of thumb mdi is biased; permutation is more reliable. three fixes to apply 1 swap method prefer permutation over default mdi. 2 use test data measure on held-out data with 10 repeats. 3 show spread plot top 15 with confidence intervals.
m13-rf-hyperparams: rule five parameters do 90% of the work. tune them in this order. four random forest knobs worth tuning n_estimators trees: 200-500 max_depth limit growth max_features sqrt for classif. min_samples_leaf smooth: 3-10 more trees never overfit, they only cost time the parameters parameter range notes n_estimators 300–1000 more is better; diminishing returns > 500 max_features "sqrt" or 0.3–0.5 lower = more decorrelation max_depth none (unlimited) often left unlimited min_samples_leaf 5–50 higher = more regularized bootstrap true almost always true syntax from sklearn.ensemble import randomforestclassifier model = randomforestclassifier ( n_estimators= 500 , max_features= 'sqrt' , min_samples_leaf= 5 , bootstrap= true , random_state= 42 , n_jobs=- 1 ) tuning order n_estimators first (until cv plateaus), then max_features, then min_samples_leaf. rf hyperparameters rf tuning: five parameters, right order ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice tune everything at once five parameters do 90% of work tune n_estimators first 300 to 1000 until cv plateaus chase n_estimators past 500 diminishing returns then max_features sqrt or 0.3 to 0.5 set bootstrap to false almost always true then min_samples_leaf 5 to 50, higher is more regular result: slow search, tiny gains result: efficient, regularized forest mistake compute spent where little changes. best practice right order, right ranges, use n_jobs=-1. tuning order n_estimators, max_features, then min_samples_leaf. three fixes to apply 1 trees first raise n_estimators until the cv score plateaus. 2 decorrelate lower max_features for more decorrelation. 3 regularize raise min_samples_leaf to smooth the model.
