m13-rf-wins: definition rf is a fantastic baseline for tabular data — fast, robust, and interpretable. why random forest is the default first model robust few tuning needs handles mixed data types strong baseline out of the box free oob validation start here, then ask whether boosting is worth it when to reach for rf medium-sized tabular data (< 1m rows). mixed numeric + categorical features. need fast training and a good baseline. feature importance required for stakeholders. interpretability matters more than squeezing the last 1%. typical performance score range 0.82–0.92 auc on most business problems — often within a few points of the best possible model. rule start with rf. only move to boosting if you need the extra points. when rf wins random forest: the fast, strong baseline ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice jump straight to boosting before any baseline exists start with rf medium tabular data, under 1m rows squeeze the last 1% hurts interpretability expect 0.82 to 0.92 auc on most business problems skip feature importance stakeholders ask for it keep importance for stakeholders interpretability over last 1% result: complex model, no baseline result: quick, defensible baseline mistake cannot tell if the extra complexity paid off. best practice good score fast, with a story to tell. rule of thumb start with rf. move to boosting only for the extra points. three fixes to apply 1 baseline fit a random forest before anything fancier. 2 scope check confirm medium size and mixed feature types. 3 upgrade later boost only if rf plateaus.
m13-rf-limits: know the trade-offs rf is great, but it isn't free. where random forest struggles slow predict many trees big memory stores all trees weak at extrapolation cannot go beyond data hard to explain no single rule set trends outside the training range need linear or boosted models the limitations memory hungry — stores hundreds of trees. slower prediction than a single tree. poor extrapolation — always predicts within the training range. can overfit if not tuned. not the best for very high dimensional sparse data — linear models win there. when to pick something else situation better choice large data (> 1m rows) lightgbm sparse high-dim text linear / svm need extrapolation linear regression need monotonic predictions xgboost with constraints next gradient boosting solves some of these — see the next section. rf limitations random forest: know when to switch ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice rf on over 1m rows memory hungry, many stored trees large data: lightgbm over 1m rows rf for sparse text linear models win there sparse high-dim: linear or svm match model to data expect rf to extrapolate predicts only within training range need extrapolation: linear or xgboost with constraints result: slow, wrong-fit model result: model fits the situation mistake resources wasted and forecasts capped at range. best practice pick the tool for the data's shape. rule of thumb great, but not free: check size, sparsity, range. three fixes to apply 1 check size above 1m rows, move to lightgbm. 2 check sparsity high-dim text points to linear or svm. 3 check range need values outside training? use linear.
m13-rf-vs-tree: purpose show the same task solved by both models — and see why rf wins. forest vs single tree (illustrative) variance accuracy readability single tree forest side-by-side metric single tree random forest training accuracy 100% ~98% test accuracy ~72% ~85% stability low — changes with data high — averages out train time very fast fast (parallelizable) prediction time fastest fast interpretability full feature importance syntax from sklearn.tree import decisiontreeclassifier from sklearn.ensemble import randomforestclassifier from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score dt = decisiontreeclassifier (random_state= 42 ). fit (x_train, y_train) rf = randomforestclassifier (n_estimators= 500 , random_state= 42 ). fit (x_train, y_train) print ( "tree train:" , accuracy_score (y_train, dt. predict (x_train))) print ( "tree test: " , accuracy_score (y_test, dt. predict (x_test))) print ( "rf test: " , accuracy_score (y_test, rf. predict (x_test))) lesson a single tree overfits. rf's averaging is the fix. rf vs tree forest vs tree: train score lies ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice celebrate 100% train accuracy single tree test is ~72% compare on test accuracy rf reaches ~85% judge on training data gap hides overfitting read train vs test gap rf ~98% train, ~85% test pick tree for stability tree changes with the data choose rf for stability averaging stabilizes results result: ~72% on test data result: ~85% on test data mistake perfect fit on training, weak on unseen rows. best practice smaller gap, steadier predictions. test compare test accuracy, never training accuracy. three fixes to apply 1 split first hold out test data before fitting any model. 2 print both show train and test accuracy side by side. 3 trade off rf gives up some interpretability.
m13-gb-core: definition sequential trees where each new tree corrects the errors of the previous ones. boosting: each tree fixes the last tree's mistakes tree 1 fit target tree 2 fit errors tree 3 fit errors sum weighted total prediction = tree 1 + lr × tree 2 + lr × tree 3 ... how it works fit an initial (simple) model. compute residuals (errors) of the current model. fit a new tree to those residuals. add the new tree to the ensemble with a small weight. repeat for n_estimators rounds. why it works uses gradients (hence "gradient" boosting) to iteratively reduce the loss. much more powerful than bagging. implementations xgboost — industry standard, regularization built-in. lightgbm — 10–30× faster, leaf-wise growth. catboost — best for high-cardinality categorical features. rule for tabular data in 2025, boosting usually wins. reach for it when rf plateaus. boosting core gradient boosting: fix the last tree's errors ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice treat boosting like bagging it is sequential, not parallel fit residuals each round new tree corrects prior errors add full-weight trees each tree needs a small weight add trees with small weight repeat n_estimators rounds jump to boosting too early rf has not plateaued yet use xgboost or lightgbm catboost for high-cardinality result: overfit, hard to tune result: stronger tabular model mistake large steps chase noise after a few rounds. best practice gradients steadily cut the loss. rule of thumb reach for boosting when rf plateaus. three fixes to apply 1 compute residuals measure the current model's errors. 2 fit and add fit a tree to residuals; add it at small weight. 3 pick library xgboost, lightgbm, or catboost by need.
m13-boosting-vs-bagging: key difference bagging trains trees in parallel on different samples. boosting trains trees sequentially, each fixing the previous one's mistakes. bagging averages many; boosting corrects one by one bagging trees in parallel cuts variance hard to overfit boosting trees in sequence cuts bias can overfit: tune it comparison property bagging (rf) boosting (xgb/lgbm) training parallel sequential reduces variance bias (and variance) overfitting risk low higher — needs early stopping typical accuracy good often better training time fast slower hyperparameter sensitivity low high in practice boosting usually wins on tabular data. the cost is a more involved tuning process. boosting vs bagging boosting vs bagging: different fixes ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice expect boosting to be parallel trees train sequentially bagging cuts variance parallel, fast, low risk tune boosting like rf hyperparameter sensitivity is high boosting cuts bias too often better accuracy run boosting with no early stop higher overfitting risk add early stopping plan a more involved tuning result: overfit boosted model result: right tool, tuned properly mistake treated like a forest, it overfits. best practice more accuracy for more tuning effort. rule of thumb bagging reduces variance; boosting reduces bias. three fixes to apply 1 know the goal variance problem: bag. bias problem: boost. 2 expect cost boosting trains slower and is sensitive. 3 guard always set early stopping on boosting.
m13-xgboost: definition the workhorse of tabular ml — strong regularization, fast, and flexible. xgboost: the tabular-data workhorse regularised l1 + l2 built in missing values handled natively parallel fast training early stop built in pip install xgboost · xgbclassifier / xgbregressor why xgboost regularization (l1 & l2) built into the loss. handles missing values natively — no imputation needed. built-in cross-validation via the sklearn api. monotonic constraints — force features to have directional effects. industry standard 2025 for tabular data. syntax import xgboost as xgb model = xgb. xgbclassifier ( n_estimators= 1000 , learning_rate= 0.05 , max_depth= 6 , subsample= 0.8 , colsample_bytree= 0.8 , reg_alpha= 0.1 , reg_lambda= 1.0 , early_stopping_rounds= 50 ) model. fit (x_train, y_train, eval_set=[(x_val, y_val)], verbose= false ) when to use default choice for tabular data — up to ~1m rows, especially when you need regularization or monotonicity. xgboost xgboost: regularize and stop early ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice impute missing values by hand xgboost handles them natively leave missing values alone native handling no regularization terms l1 and l2 are built in set reg_alpha=0.1, reg_lambda=1.0 subsample=0.8, colsample_bytree=0.8 fixed 1000 rounds, no eval_set nothing detects overfitting pass eval_set and stopping early_stopping_rounds=50 result: overfit, extra work result: regularized, validated model mistake needless preprocessing and an uncontrolled model. best practice default choice for tabular data up to ~1m rows. when to use default for tabular data when you need regularization. three fixes to apply 1 skip imputing let xgboost route missing values itself. 2 regularize use l1, l2, and row and column sampling. 3 validate give an eval_set and stop after 50 rounds.
m13-lightgbm: definition microsoft's gradient boosting — faster and lower memory than xgboost. lightgbm: faster on big data, watch small data histogram bins features leaf-wise grows best leaf categoricals native support large data low memory leaf-wise growth can overfit small sets: cap num_leaves why lightgbm histogram-based splitting — 10–30× faster than xgboost. leaf-wise growth — often better accuracy. native categorical handling — no one-hot needed. lower memory usage. default choice for > 100k rows. syntax import lightgbm as lgb model = lgb. lgbmclassifier ( n_estimators= 1000 , learning_rate= 0.05 , num_leaves= 31 , max_depth=- 1 , categorical_feature= 'auto' , early_stopping_rounds= 50 ) model. fit (x_train, y_train, eval_set=[(x_val, y_val)]) note num_leaves (not max_depth) is the primary complexity control in lightgbm. lightgbm lightgbm: control complexity with num_leaves ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice one-hot encode categoricals lightgbm handles them natively categorical_feature auto no one-hot needed tune max_depth only num_leaves is the main control set num_leaves=31 max_depth=-1, tune leaves first use lightgbm on tiny data shines past 100k rows default for over 100k rows histogram splitting, 10-30x faster result: slow, mis-tuned model result: fast, lean, accurate mistake extra columns and the wrong complexity knob. best practice lower memory with leaf-wise growth. rule of thumb num_leaves, not max_depth, controls complexity. three fixes to apply 1 skip one-hot pass categoricals in as they are. 2 tune leaves start at num_leaves 31 and adjust. 3 add stopping use early_stopping_rounds 50 with eval_set.
m13-boosting-params: rule five parameters matter most. tune them in this order. four boosting dials: slow learning, shallow trees learning_rate 0.01-0.1 n_estimators many + early stop max_depth 3-8 subsample 0.7-0.9 lower learning rate needs more trees: that is normal the parameters parameter range effect learning_rate 0.01–0.1 lower = more trees needed but better generalization n_estimators 500–2000+ use early stopping to find the right number max_depth 3–10 deeper = more complex subsample 0.6–0.9 < 1.0 = stochastic gb — reduces overfitting colsample_bytree 0.6–0.9 feature sampling per tree syntax model = xgb. xgbclassifier ( learning_rate= 0.05 , n_estimators= 1000 , max_depth= 6 , subsample= 0.8 , colsample_bytree= 0.8 , early_stopping_rounds= 50 ) practical lower learning_rate + more trees usually beats higher learning_rate + fewer trees. boosting parameters boosting params: low rate, more trees ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice high learning_rate, few trees fast, but generalizes worse learning_rate 0.01 to 0.1 use 0.05 with more trees fix n_estimators by guessing use early stopping instead n_estimators 500 to 2000+ let early stopping choose leave subsample at 1.0 no stochastic regularization subsample 0.6 to 0.9 colsample_bytree 0.6 to 0.9 result: overfit, unstable score result: smoother, better generalization mistake quick fit that does not hold on new data. best practice small steps, many trees, sampled rows. rule of thumb low learning_rate plus more trees beats high plus fewer. three fixes to apply 1 lower the rate use 0.01 to 0.1 and add more trees. 2 let it stop set a big n_estimators; early-stop. 3 sample use subsample below 1.0 to reduce overfitting.
m13-early-stopping: definition stop training when validation error stops improving for n rounds. why it's essential prevents overfitting automatically. saves training time — no wasted rounds. finds the optimal n_estimators — often different from what you set. early stopping at best iteration best iteration stopping point (patience=50) syntax model = xgb. xgbclassifier ( n_estimators= 5000 , # maximum, not final early_stopping_rounds= 50 ) model. fit (x_train, y_train, eval_set=[(x_val, y_val)]) print (f "best iteration: {model.best_iteration}" ) rule always use early stopping with boosting. never guess n_estimators. early stopping early stopping: never guess n_estimators ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice guess n_estimators final number picked by feel set n_estimators=5000 a maximum, not the final number train all rounds wasted rounds after the best early_stopping_rounds=50 stop when validation stalls fit with no eval_set nothing to watch for overfitting pass eval_set=[(x_val, y_val)] read model.best_iteration result: overfit and wasted time result: optimal rounds, less time mistake validation error rises while training keeps going. best practice prevents overfitting automatically. rule always use early stopping with boosting. three fixes to apply 1 set a ceiling make n_estimators large; it is only a maximum. 2 watch validation give a separate eval_set to monitor. 3 report best print best_iteration after fitting.
m13-ensembles-of-ensembles: definition stack multiple models — rf + xgboost + lightgbm — with a simple meta-learner. the pattern train several diverse models on the same data. use their predictions as features for a meta-learner. the meta-learner is often simple: logistic or linear regression. visual stacked ensemble random forest xgboost lightgbm +more meta-learner (logistic) lift: +1–3% over best single model competition note stacking is standard in winning solutions. in production, evaluate whether the small lift justifies the operational complexity. stacking stacking: diverse models, simple meta-learner ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice stack near-identical models no diversity, no lift mix rf, xgboost, lightgbm diverse models, same data use a complex meta-learner adds its own overfitting meta-learner: logistic or linear predictions become features ship stacks by default ignores operational complexity weigh lift against complexity standard in winning solutions result: complexity without lift result: justified, measured lift mistake more moving parts for a tiny gain. best practice use stacking when the gain earns its cost. competition note stacking wins contests; in production, justify the lift. three fixes to apply 1 add diversity train different model families. 2 keep meta simple logistic or linear works well. 3 count the cost compare the lift with upkeep.
m13-clustering-overview: definition unsupervised learning — find natural groups in data without labels. clustering: unsupervised grouping of similar rows clustering has no target: you choose k and judge usefulness segments customers anomalies odd points compress prototypes use cases customer segmentation — group by behavior. anomaly detection — flag rows that don't fit any group. market discovery — identify untapped segments. image / document grouping — unsupervised organization. key realities no "right" answer — validation is subjective. always scale features first (except dbscan, which is distance-based). business interpretability is the real validation. rule if a stakeholder can't act on the clusters, they aren't useful — no matter the silhouette score. clustering basics clustering: no labels, no single answer ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice cluster unscaled features large units dominate distance scale features first except dbscan, distance-based trust the silhouette score alone technical score only validate by business meaning interpretability is real validation keep clusters nobody can use not actionable define the use case segmentation, anomalies, markets result: distorted, unusable groups result: groups people can act on mistake neat numbers that no stakeholder can act on. best practice scaled inputs and clusters with a purpose. rule of thumb if a stakeholder cannot act on it, it is not useful. three fixes to apply 1 scale standardize features before distance methods. 2 name them give every cluster a meaningful label. 3 tie to action start from the business decision.
m13-kmeans: algorithm iteratively assign points to the nearest centroid, then move centroids to the mean of their points. k-means in four steps 1 pick k centres 2 assign nearest centre 3 move centres to mean 4 repeat until stable scale features first · use n_init=10 · expects round, equal-size groups the steps choose k centroids randomly. assign points to the nearest centroid. move centroids to the mean of assigned points. repeat until convergence. properties very fast — o(n × k × iterations). assumes spherical clusters of similar size. sensitive to initialization — use k-means++. requires scaling — always standardize features first. syntax from sklearn.cluster import kmeans from sklearn.preprocessing import standardscaler x_scaled = standardscaler (). fit_transform (x) km = kmeans (n_clusters= 4 , random_state= 42 , n_init= 10 ) labels = km. fit_predict (x_scaled) set n_init=10 runs k-means with 10 different initializations and picks the best. always do this. k-means k-means: scale and restart ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice fit on raw features k-means requires scaling standardscaler first fit_transform(x) one random start sensitive to initialization n_init=10 with k-means++ picks the best of 10 starts assume round, equal clusters spherical, similar-size assumption check cluster shapes use dbscan if not spherical result: unstable, skewed clusters result: stable, comparable clusters mistake different runs give different answers. best practice fast, repeatable results across runs. rule always standardize and always set n_init=10. three fixes to apply 1 standardize scale before computing distances. 2 restart run 10 initializations and keep the best. 3 fix seed random_state=42 for repeatable runs.
m13-elbow: definition plot within-cluster sum of squares (wcss) vs k — look for the "elbow" where the curve flattens. visual elbow plot elbow (k=4) k → wcss syntax import matplotlib.pyplot as plt inertia = [] for k in range ( 1 , 11 ): km = kmeans (n_clusters=k, random_state= 42 , n_init= 10 ) km. fit (x_scaled) inertia. append (km.inertia_) plt. plot ( range ( 1 , 11 ), inertia, marker= 'o' ) plt. xlabel ( 'k' ); plt. ylabel ( 'wcss' ); plt. show () reality the elbow isn't always obvious. combine with the silhouette score. elbow method elbow method: do not pick k by eye alone ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice assume the elbow is obvious curves often flatten gradually plot wcss for k=1 to 10 look for where it flattens pick k from wcss alone one signal only add the silhouette score combine both signals forget n_init in the loop unstable inertia per k kmeans with n_init=10 in every loop pass result: arbitrary k, shaky clusters result: k backed by two signals mistake different analysts choose different k. best practice elbow plus silhouette raises confidence. rule of thumb the elbow is a hint, not a verdict. three fixes to apply 1 plot it plot km.inertia_ for each k from 1 to 10. 2 combine check silhouette beside the elbow. 3 stay stable use n_init=10 and a fixed seed.
m13-silhouette: definition measures how similar each point is to its own cluster vs other clusters. range: −1 to +1. silhouette: -1 to 1, higher means cleaner clusters -1 to 0 wrong cluster 0 to 0.25 weak 0.25 to 0.5 fair 0.5 to 1 strong average per cluster too: one weak cluster can hide in a good mean interpretation score meaning > 0.5 excellent structure 0.2 – 0.5 reasonable < 0.2 weak — reconsider k < 0 points misclassified syntax from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score for k in range ( 2 , 11 ): km = kmeans (n_clusters=k, random_state= 42 , n_init= 10 ) labels = km. fit_predict (x_scaled) score = silhouette_score (x_scaled, labels) print (f "k={k}, silhouette={score:.3f}" ) combine use elbow + silhouette together. if they agree, confidence is high. silhouette score silhouette: read the score bands ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice accept any positive score below 0.2 is weak above 0.5 is excellent 0.2 to 0.5 is reasonable ignore negative scores points sit in the wrong cluster below 0.2: reconsider k below 0 means misclassified use silhouette alone skip the elbow method loop k=2 to 10 compare elbow and silhouette result: weak k accepted as fine result: k chosen with evidence mistake poor structure is reported as success. best practice if both agree, confidence is high. reading the score range -1 to +1; above 0.5 excellent, below 0.2 weak. three fixes to apply 1 loop k score each k from 2 to 10 with silhouette_score. 2 use bands interpret the score by its range. 3 cross-check agree with the elbow before trusting k.
m13-hierarchical: definition build a tree of clusters — bottom-up (agglomerative) or top-down (divisive). key properties agglomerative — start with each point as its own cluster, merge closest pairs. produces a dendrogram — visualize the merge history. choose k by cutting the tree at a height. great for small data and visualization. o(n²) — slow on large data. visual dendrogram a b c d e f cut here → syntax from scipy.cluster.hierarchy import linkage, dendrogram, fcluster z = linkage (x_scaled, method= 'ward' ) labels = fcluster (z, t= 4 , criterion= 'maxclust' ) method choices ward (default), complete, average, single. ward minimizes within-cluster variance — good for most cases. hierarchical hierarchical: great small, slow big ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice run it on large data o(n squared), very slow use on small data where hierarchy is wanted ignore the dendrogram merge history goes unused read the dendrogram cut at a height to choose k guess the linkage single often chains clusters linkage method ward minimizes within-cluster variance result: slow run, murky clusters result: readable cluster hierarchy mistake waiting on big data and unclear groupings. best practice a clear merge history and defensible k. rule of thumb small data and want a hierarchy? use hierarchical with ward. three fixes to apply 1 check size keep n small; it is o(n squared). 2 cut the tree use fcluster with t=4 and maxclust. 3 default ward compare complete or average when needed.
m13-dbscan: definition density-based clustering — finds arbitrary shapes and labels noise points. dbscan: finds shaped clusters and flags outliers core points dense neighbourhood min_samples within eps noise points labelled -1 no cluster forced on them no k needed · tune eps with a k-distance plot core concepts core points — have ≥ min_samples neighbors within eps. border points — within eps of a core point but not core themselves. noise points — neither core nor border — labeled as outliers. parameters parameter meaning eps maximum distance between two neighbors min_samples minimum points to form a dense region strengths no need to specify k. finds arbitrary shapes — not just spherical. excellent for fraud/outlier detection. handles noise explicitly. syntax from sklearn.cluster import dbscan db = dbscan (eps= 0.5 , min_samples= 5 ) labels = db. fit_predict (x_scaled) # labels of -1 are noise n_clusters = len ( set (labels)) - ( 1 if - 1 in labels else 0 ) tuning tip use a k-distance plot (sorted k-nn distances) to choose eps. dbscan dbscan: eps and min_samples decide everything ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice guess eps sensitive to eps pick eps from a k-distance plot tuning tip from the topic run on unscaled data distances are meaningless scale first distance-based method ignore the -1 label noise points get lost treat -1 as noise subtract it from n_clusters result: one blob or all noise result: shaped clusters plus outliers mistake wrong eps merges or shatters the data. best practice no k needed, noise flagged explicitly. rule of thumb weird shapes or outliers? use dbscan. three fixes to apply 1 plot k-distance choose eps at the bend of the plot. 2 scale data standardize features before fitting. 3 count cleanly exclude label -1 when counting clusters.
m13-clustering-choice: decision guide match the algorithm to the data shape and business need. match the algorithm to the shape of your data k-means round, equal size, big data hierarchical small data, want a tree dbscan odd shapes, outliers gaussian mix overlap, soft membership decision table algorithm best for limitations k-means large data, spherical clusters assumes spherical, needs k hierarchical small data, need dendrogram o(n²) — slow on large data dbscan unknown k, noisy data, non-spherical sensitive to eps gaussian mixture soft clustering (probabilistic) assumes gaussian components quick heuristic big data + round clusters? k-means. small data + want hierarchy? hierarchical. outliers or weird shapes? dbscan. need probabilities? gaussian mixture. rule try k-means first. it's fast and often good enough. move to dbscan only if you suspect non-spherical structure. choosing clustering clustering choice: match algorithm to shape ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice k-means on odd shapes assumes spherical clusters big data, round: k-means fast and often good enough hierarchical on big data o(n squared), slow small data: hierarchical dendrogram view jump to dbscan first sensitive to eps outliers or shapes: dbscan gaussian mixture for probabilities result: poor fit, wasted runs result: algorithm fits the data mistake the algorithm assumptions do not match the data. best practice start simple, move on only if you suspect structure. rule of thumb try k-means first; dbscan if non-spherical structure. three fixes to apply 1 start fast run k-means as the first attempt. 2 check shape look for non-spherical structure. 3 need odds use gaussian mixture for soft clusters.
m13-cluster-validation: rule silhouette is a technical score. business interpretation is what actually validates clusters. a good cluster is stable, separated and actionable stability same on resamples? silhouette separation score profile are groups different? business can we act on it? metrics are necessary but the business test decides the four validations validation question business interpretability can you name each cluster meaningfully? stability do clusters persist across runs / samples? size balance are the clusters useful sizes? actionability can marketing target them differently? practical test try this write a 1-sentence persona for each cluster. if you can't, the clustering failed. common outcome high silhouette but clusters nobody can act on → re-cluster with different features. cluster validation cluster validation: silhouette is not enough ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice stop at a high silhouette technical score only name each cluster business interpretability never test stability clusters shift across runs re-run on samples do clusters persist? ignore size balance tiny or giant clusters check actionability can marketing target them? result: clusters nobody can act on result: validated, usable segments mistake high score, but marketing cannot use the groups. best practice four checks beat one score, each tied to the business. practical test write a 1-sentence persona per cluster, or re-cluster. three fixes to apply 1 write personas one sentence for each cluster. 2 test stability compare runs and samples. 3 re-cluster change features if no one can act.
m13-feature-engineering: definition transforming raw data into features that help trees find better splits. good features beat fancier algorithms ratios spend / visits dates age, recency lags last month encode target / one-hot fit encoders inside cross-validation to avoid leakage common transformations source features to create dates day_of_week, month, is_weekend, days_since_event numeric binning (sometimes helps) high-card categoricals target encoding interactions manual products or polynomial missing values indicator columns syntax # date features df[ 'order_date' ] = pd. to_datetime (df[ 'order_date' ]) df[ 'day_of_week' ] = df[ 'order_date' ].dt.dayofweek df[ 'month' ] = df[ 'order_date' ].dt.month df[ 'is_weekend' ] = df[ 'day_of_week' ] >= 5 # missing indicator df[ 'age_was_missing' ] = df[ 'age' ]. isna (). astype ( int ) # target encoding (careful with leakage!) target_mean = df. groupby ( 'category' )[ 'target' ]. mean () df[ 'category_te' ] = df[ 'category' ]. map (target_mean) leakage warning target encoding must be done inside cross-validation folds. doing it on the full dataset leaks the target. feature engineering tree features: engineer without leaking ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice feed raw dates to the tree splits cannot use the calendar create day_of_week, month is_weekend, days_since_event fill missing silently the missingness signal is lost add an age_was_missing flag isna().astype(int) target-encode on all rows leakage of the target target encode with care high-cardinality categoricals result: weaker splits, leaked score result: richer, leak-free features mistake inflated validation that fails in production. best practice better splits and an honest score. rule of thumb help trees find splits; never let the target leak in. three fixes to apply 1 expand dates pull weekday, month, and weekend flags. 2 flag missing add an indicator column per gap. 3 guard target compute encodings inside training folds.
m13-tuning-strategies: overview four approaches, ranked by efficiency. trials needed for a similar score (illustrative) grid random bayesian random search usually beats grid for the same budget comparison method how speed grid search exhaustive — try every combination slowest random search sample combinations randomly usually better than grid bayesian optimization learn from past trials fast, high quality successive halving / hyperband early-stop bad trials fastest why random > grid bergstra & bengio (2012) showed random search finds better hyperparameters in less time — because not all parameters matter equally. syntax — randomsearchcv from sklearn.model_selection import randomizedsearchcv param_dist = { 'n_estimators' : [ 100 , 300 , 500 , 1000 ], 'max_depth' : [ 3 , 5 , 7 , 10 ], 'min_samples_leaf' : [ 1 , 5 , 10 , 20 ] } search = randomizedsearchcv (model, param_dist, n_iter= 50 , cv= 5 , n_jobs=- 1 ) search. fit (x_train, y_train) practical always start with randomsearchcv — it's a much better use of time than grid search. tuning strategies tuning: stop brute-forcing the grid ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice exhaustive grid search slowest method randomizedsearchcv n_iter=50, cv=5 tune parameters equally not all parameters matter equally bayesian or hyperband learn from trials, drop bad ones tune by hand manual guessing tune via cv, not by hand bergstra and bengio, 2012 result: slow search, weak settings result: better settings, less time mistake hours of compute for a worse model. best practice random beats grid in less time. rule of thumb random search usually beats grid search. three fixes to apply 1 go random sample combinations with randomizedsearchcv. 2 learn use bayesian methods to guide trials. 3 cut early hyperband stops bad trials fast.
m13-optuna: definition modern hyperparameter optimization framework with pruning and pruning-based early stopping. optuna: a smarter search loop with early pruning suggest trial params train cv score prune stop weak trials learn better next try study.optimize(objective, n_trials=50) why optuna 5–20× faster than grid search. automatically prunes bad trials (saves compute). simpler api — define objective, call optimize. works with any model (sklearn, xgboost, lightgbm, pytorch). install pip install optuna syntax import optuna from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score def objective (trial): params = { 'n_estimators' : trial. suggest_int ( 'n_estimators' , 100 , 1000 ), 'max_depth' : trial. suggest_int ( 'max_depth' , 3 , 10 ), 'min_samples_leaf' : trial. suggest_int ( 'min_samples_leaf' , 1 , 50 ), 'learning_rate' : trial. suggest_float ( 'learning_rate' , 0.01 , 0.3 , log= true ) } model = xgb. xgbclassifier (**params) return cross_val_score (model, x_train, y_train, cv= 5 , scoring= 'roc_auc' ). mean () study = optuna. create_study (direction= 'maximize' ) study. optimize (objective, n_trials= 100 ) print (study.best_params) pro tip use log=true for learning_rate and other parameters that span orders of magnitude. optuna optuna: define an objective, let it prune ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice grid search every combination optuna is 5 to 20x faster write an objective(trial) call study.optimize fixed lists of values no continuous ranges suggest_int and suggest_float learning_rate 0.01 to 0.3, log=true let bad trials finish wastes compute prune poor trials works with sklearn, xgboost, lightgbm result: slow, narrow search result: faster, wider search mistake compute burned on trials that were never promising. best practice score by cross_val_score on training data. rule of thumb optuna: 5 to 20x faster than grid search. three fixes to apply 1 write objective return a cv score from each trial. 2 use ranges suggest ints and floats, log scale for rate. 3 prune let optuna stop weak trials early.
m13-model-comparison: rule never ship a model without comparing it to at least three alternatives. compare models on the same folds, with spread same split and folds baseline first mean ± std of cv scores cost time + memory a 0.5% gain inside the noise is a tie: pick the simpler one the framework compare at least 3 models — e.g., logistic, rf, xgboost. use the same train/validation/test split. report mean + std from cv. choose final model based on business metric + speed + interpretability. sample comparison table model auc (mean ± std) train time interpretability logistic 0.78 ± 0.02 fast high random forest 0.85 ± 0.01 medium medium xgboost 0.87 ± 0.01 slow low decision a 2-point auc lift isn't worth 10× slower inference. match the model to the deployment context. model comparison model comparison: never ship one model ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice compare against nothing fewer than three models compare 3 models logistic, rf, xgboost use different splits per model unfair comparison same split, cv mean and std e.g. 0.85 plus or minus 0.01 pick the top auc only ignores speed and interpretability weigh business metric and speed and interpretability result: unproven, hard-to-run model result: model fits the context mistake xgboost chosen for 0.87 without the trade-offs. best practice a 2-point auc lift may not justify 10x slower runs. rule compare at least three models on one split. three fixes to apply 1 build a table list auc mean and std, time, interpretability. 2 same split use identical train, validation, test sets. 3 match context choose for deployment, not leaderboard.
m13-ab-testing-ml: rule deploying a better model isn't enough — prove it improves the business metric. offline wins are not proof: test live offline test-set metric shadow run unseen a/b test real users decide ship or revert champion vs challenger, set success metric and sample size first the process deploy champion vs challenger side by side. measure actual business lift — not just auc. run for minimum detectable effect — statistical power. report on business kpi , not model metric. example churn model champion: 4.2% churn rate. challenger: 3.9% churn rate. business lift: 0.3 pp retention improvement → $x saved. reality a model with auc 0.85 that doesn't beat auc 0.80 on the business metric isn't worth deploying. a/b testing ml a/b test the model, not just the auc ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice deploy because auc is higher better offline, unproven online run champion vs challenger side by side report model metrics not the business kpi measure real business lift churn 4.2% to 3.9% stop the test early below minimum detectable effect run to the minimum effect statistical power first result: no proven business value result: proven 0.3 pp retention gain mistake a model with auc 0.85 may not beat auc 0.80. best practice report on the business kpi, not the model metric. rule of thumb prove it on the business metric before you ship. three fixes to apply 1 split traffic serve champion and challenger together. 2 measure kpi track churn, not auc. 3 wait for power run until the effect is detectable.
m13-fraud-case: scenario extreme class imbalance — 0.1% fraud rate. classic business problem. fraud case: rare events change every choice imbalanced 0.2% fraud pr-auc not accuracy cost-based threshold monitor drift accuracy of 99.8% can be a model that flags nothing the approach combine anomaly detection + supervised — dbscan to flag outliers, xgboost to score them. optimize for recall at fixed precision — e.g., 90% precision at maximum recall. cost-sensitive learning — weight the positive class appropriately. manual review pipeline — flag high-scoring cases for human review. result real example caught $2.3m in fraud in the first month — 3× the previous rule-based system. key lessons accuracy is useless on imbalanced data. precision-recall curve is more informative than roc here. cost-weighted metrics matter more than raw f1. feedback loop — analyst decisions become new training data. framework same approach works for spam, abuse detection, and manufacturing defects. fraud detection fraud at 0.1%: accuracy is useless ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice judge by accuracy predict no fraud: 99.9% correct recall at 90% precision use the precision-recall curve read the roc curve only misleading under imbalance weight the positive class cost-sensitive learning optimize raw f1 ignores the cost of misses dbscan flags, xgboost scores humans review high scores result: fraud passes undetected result: 3x the rule-based catch mistake high accuracy while the fraud goes through. best practice caught 2.3m dollars in the first month. rule of thumb imbalanced data: optimize recall at fixed precision. three fixes to apply 1 change metric use precision-recall, not accuracy. 2 weight classes penalize missed fraud more. 3 close the loop feed analyst decisions back as labels.
m13-competition-vs-prod: key contrast what wins a kaggle competition is not what ships to production. the best leaderboard model is rarely the best product competition one metric stack everything fixed data production cost + latency explainable, stable drifting data side-by-side competition production stack 50 models ship 1–3 models exploit test set quirks robust to data drift optimize leaderboard metric optimize business metric no monitoring continuous monitoring one-shot training retraining pipeline complexity allowed interpretability required reality check most kaggle solutions never deploy. the skills transfer, but the mindset is different. lesson learn from competitions, but design for production. simplicity and monitoring beat 1 extra point of auc. competition vs production kaggle wins vs production wins ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice stack 50 models leaderboard thinking ship 1 to 3 models simplicity wins exploit test set quirks breaks under data drift optimize the business metric robust to drift train once, no monitoring models decay monitor and retrain interpretability required result: fragile model that never ships result: maintainable, trusted model mistake great leaderboard rank, poor real-world value. best practice design for production, learn from competitions. lesson simplicity and monitoring beat 1 extra point of auc. three fixes to apply 1 keep it small prefer one to three models. 2 measure real track the business metric. 3 watch drift monitor and retrain on a schedule.

m13a-catboost-native: what "native" means catboost processes categorical features directly during training — no one-hot, no manual target encoding. it uses ordered target statistics. see it catboost encodes each row from earlier rows only rows in a random permutation: only earlier rows feed the encoding row 1 cat a y = 1 row 2 cat b y = 0 row 3 cat a y = 1 row 4 cat a y = 0 row 5 cat b y = 1 row 6 cat a y = ? encode row 6 (category a) from earlier a rows only: rows 1, 3 and 4 ts = (1 + 1 + 0 + prior 0.5) / (3 + 1) = 0.625 prior 0.5 is illustrative; rows 2 and 5 are category b and are ignored ordered statistics a row never sees its own label full-data averages each row sees its own label: leak how it works for a categorical feature with value v , catboost computes a target statistic using only examples that precede it in a random permutation, plus a prior: ts(v) = (σ yᵢ for preceding examples with value v + prior) / (count + 1) this prevents the target leakage that occurs when you compute target statistics on the full dataset. feature combinations catboost also automatically considers combinations of categorical features. for example, user_id × genre might reveal preferences that neither feature alone shows. why this beats manual encoding approach high-cardinality handling leakage risk effort one-hot explodes with cardinality none low naive target encoding works, but overfits high medium catboost ordered stats works at scale minimal none (built-in) syntax from catboost import catboostclassifier model = catboostclassifier ( iterations= 1000 , learning_rate= 0.05 , depth= 6 , cat_features=[ 'customer_id' , 'product_category' , 'region' ], one_hot_max_size= 10 , # only one-hot for small cardinality verbose= 100 ) model. fit (x_train, y_train, cat_features=cat_cols) when to use if your dataset has categorical features with over 20 unique values — especially ids — catboost is worth trying first. catboost categoricals categoricals: let the model encode them ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice one-hot a high-cardinality id thousands of sparse columns pass cat_features directly catboost encodes during training encode with the full-data mean target leaks into features rely on ordered statistics uses earlier rows plus a prior skip cat_features treats text as errors or numbers one-hot only small sets set one_hot_max_size result: slow, leaky or broken model result: scalable, low-leakage encoding mistake ids explode under one-hot encoding. best practice try catboost first when ids have many values. rule of thumb over 20 unique values? try native categorical handling. three fixes to apply 1 list cat columns pass them in cat_features, not as one-hot. 2 set one-hot limit use one_hot_max_size for small categories. 3 validate compare to a baseline on a time-based split.
m13a-target-encoding: a common leakage mistake naive target encoding is a copy of the target inside your features. it can inflate validation scores and then disappoint in production. see it encode inside the folds, and smooth the rare categories out-of-fold encoding (5 folds): the validation fold never encodes itself fold 1 learn from fold 2 learn from fold 3 encode me fold 4 learn from fold 5 learn from encoding for fold 3 is computed from folds 1, 2, 4 and 5 smoothing pulls rare categories toward the global mean (0.20) a: 200 rows 0.30 to 0.295 b: 5 rows 1.00 to 0.467 c: 50 rows 0.10 to 0.117 d: 1 row 1.00 to 0.273 global 0.20 raw mean encoded the correct approach — out-of-fold encoding from sklearn.model_selection import kfold import pandas as pd import numpy as np def target_encode_oof (train, test, col, target, n_splits= 5 , smoothing= 10 ): """out-of-fold target encoding with smoothing.""" global_mean = train[target]. mean () train_encoded = np. zeros ( len (train)) test_encoded = np. zeros ( len (test)) kf = kfold (n_splits=n_splits, shuffle= true , random_state= 42 ) for tr_idx, val_idx in kf. split (train): tr, val = train. iloc [tr_idx], train. iloc [val_idx] # compute encoding on training fold only agg = tr. groupby (col)[target]. agg ([ 'mean' , 'count' ]) # smoothing: blend with global mean agg[ 'encoded' ] = (agg[ 'mean' ] * agg[ 'count' ] + global_mean * smoothing) / (agg[ 'count' ] + smoothing) train_encoded[val_idx] = val[col]. map (agg[ 'encoded' ]). fillna (global_mean) # for test, use full training set agg_full = train. groupby (col)[target]. agg ([ 'mean' , 'count' ]) agg_full[ 'encoded' ] = (agg_full[ 'mean' ] * agg_full[ 'count' ] + global_mean * smoothing) / (agg_full[ 'count' ] + smoothing) test_encoded = test[col]. map (agg_full[ 'encoded' ]). fillna (global_mean) return train_encoded, test_encoded why oof works training rows get encodings computed from other folds only — no self-leakage. validation rows get encodings from the training fold — honest estimate. test rows get encodings from the full training set. smoothing formula encoded = (mean × count + global_mean × smoothing) / (count + smoothing) higher smoothing = more pull toward global mean for rare categories. this prevents overfitting on categories with few observations. rule target encoding must happen inside the cross-validation loop. if you encode before splitting, you've leaked the target. target encoding target encoding: encode inside the folds ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice encode before splitting the target leaks into features encode out-of-fold rows never see their own label use raw category means rare categories overfit smooth toward the global mean protects rare categories encode test with test labels not available in production test uses the training set only same as production result: strong cv, weak in production result: honest validation score mistake the feature is a copy of the answer. best practice encoding belongs inside the cv loop. formula (mean x count + global x s) / (count + s) three fixes to apply 1 split first make folds before any encoding. 2 smooth raise s for rare categories to pull toward global. 3 apply to test fit on full training data only.

bayesian-style option; add pruning to stop weak trials early the four strategies strategy how it works when to use grid search try every combination ≤ 3 params, small ranges random search sample randomly default for exploration bayesian (optuna tpe) model the objective, sample promising regions when trials are expensive hyperband / asha early-stop bad trials, allocate more to good ones many trials, large search spaces why random beats grid bergstra & bengio (2012) showed that when only a few hyperparameters matter, random search finds better configurations faster. grid search wastes trials varying unimportant parameters. optuna tpe + pruning — the modern default import optuna def objective (trial): params = { 'num_leaves' : trial. suggest_int ( 'num_leaves' , 15 , 255 , log= true ), 'learning_rate' : trial. suggest_float ( 'learning_rate' , 0.01 , 0.3 , log= true ), 'min_child_samples' : trial. suggest_int ( 'min_child_samples' , 5 , 100 ), 'subsample' : trial. suggest_float ( 'subsample' , 0.6 , 1.0 ), } model = lgb. lgbmclassifier (**params) score = cross_val_score (model, x, y, cv= 5 , scoring= 'roc_auc' ). mean () return score study = optuna. create_study (direction= 'maximize' ) study. optimize (objective, n_trials= 100 ) distributed tuning — ray tune for large search spaces, ray tune scales across multiple machines. use it when you have a cluster and need to run 1000+ trials. check maintenance before adopting any tuning library, check how actively it is maintained. optuna (single machine) and ray tune (distributed) are widely used choices. hpo strategies tuning: spend trials where they help ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice grid over many parameters most trials vary what is flat start with random search better coverage per trial tune on the test set test score becomes optimistic use optuna with pruning stops weak trials early run every trial to the end wastes time on clear losers score with cross-validation keep test data untouched result: slow search, inflated score result: better settings per trial mistake budget goes to unimportant settings. best practice scale to ray tune only when you need a cluster. rule of thumb few parameters matter. m13a-shap-production: why shap matters at scale when a model rejects a loan application, you need to explain why — not just what the prediction is. shap gives you per-prediction explanations. see it shap waterfall: why this prediction? one prediction explained: contributions add up from the base value base value 0.20 utilisation 92% +0.31 late payments 3 +0.14 income 42,000 -0.08 account age 9 yrs -0.05 prediction 0.52 pushes risk up pushes risk down treeexplainer at scale import shap # for lightgbm/xgboost/catboost — fast and exact explainer = shap. treeexplainer (model) # compute on a sample for speed (not all rows) sample = x_test. sample ( 5000 , random_state= 42 ) explanation = explainer(sample) # global: top features across all predictions shap. summary_plot (explanation) # local: why this prediction? shap. plots . waterfall (explanation[ 0 ]) # beeswarm: feature value + shap direction shap. summary_plot (explanation, plot_type= 'beeswarm' ) the version gotcha — critical for production silent bug in recent shap versions (0.45.0 and later), shap_values() for multi-output classifiers returns shape (n_samples, n_features, n_classes) — not a list. indexing shap_values[1] selects sample 1 , not the positive class. the modern explainer(x) call returns a consistent shap.explanation object that avoids this. check the version you have installed. precomputing shap for dashboards shap at inference time is often too slow. solution: precompute global shap values offline, store them, and serve them in your dashboard. # offline: precompute shap for all test data explanation = explainer(x_test) # store per-prediction feature contributions shap_df = pd. dataframe ( explanation.values, columns=[f 'shap_{c}' for c in x_test.columns], index=x_test.index ) # in dashboard: show top 3 features driving each prediction top_features = shap_df. iloc [customer_id]. abs (). nlargest ( 3 ) shap caveats correlated features — shap distributes attribution across correlated variables; the ranking can be misleading. kernelshap is slow — use treeexplainer for tree models. kernelexplainer for neural nets, with a sampling budget. not causal — shap shows model reliance, not real-world causation. test fidelity explanation methods (shap, lime, permutation importance) can disagree. compare them on your own model before you trust one in a report. shap in production shap in production: avoid silent bugs ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice index shap_values[1] blindly may pick a sample, not a class call explainer(x) directly returns a consistent explanation use kernelexplainer on trees very slow use treeexplainer on a sample fast for tree models read shap as causation it shows model reliance only precompute offline for dashboards store per-row contributions result: wrong or slow explanations result: fast, correct explanations mistake output shape changed across versions. best practice check correlated features before ranking them. rule shap explains the model, not the world. three fixes to apply 1 check the shape print the array shape before you index into it. 2 sample explain a few thousand rows, not all of them. 3 precompute store results so dashboards load instantly.
m13a-semi-supervised: the problem it solves labels are expensive. data is cheap. semi-supervised learning uses a small labeled set + a large unlabeled set to improve predictions. see it semi-supervised learning: labels grow round by round self-training loop: add only confident pseudo-labels labeled data 1,000 rows train model on all labels so far predict unlabeled 200,000 rows keep confident above a threshold try more labels, better features and stronger models first. always keep real labels for testing. when this matters fraud detection — you have confirmed fraud labels for a tiny share of transactions, and a very large unlabeled pool. medical diagnosis — expert-labeled records are rare; unlabeled patient data is abundant. customer segmentation — you know the segment of some customers, and want to infer the rest. common approaches method how it works self-training train on labeled data, predict on unlabeled, add high-confidence predictions to training set, repeat. label propagation spread labels through a similarity graph. pseudo-labeling same as self-training, popular in deep learning. practical rule start simple before reaching for semi-supervised techniques, first try: (1) more labeled data, (2) better features from unlabeled data, (3) stronger models on existing labels. semi-supervised is a last resort. where it fits it is most often considered where labels are scarce but unlabeled behavioural data is abundant, such as fraud, diagnostics and e-commerce. semi-supervised semi-supervised: last resort, not first ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice jump to pseudo-labels first cheaper fixes untested try more labels and features first often cheaper and safer trust low-confidence labels errors reinforce themselves add only high-confidence labels raise the threshold skip a clean labeled test set no honest evaluation hold out real labels for testing measure true gain result: confident, wrong labels result: gains you can verify mistake model errors feed back into training. best practice use it when labels are scarce but data is vast. rule of thumb exhaust simpler options first. then add unlabeled data. three fixes to apply 1 improve labels get more labeled data or better features. 2 set a threshold accept only high-confidence predictions. 3 test on labels evaluate on held-out true labels only.
