m14-story-arc: four beats every effective data story has the same shape. the four beats context — "here's the situation today." conflict — "but we have a problem / opportunity." resolution — "here's what the data says." call-to-action — "therefore, we must do x by y, owned by z." story arc 1 context 2 conflict 3 resolution 4 action worked example — churn applied context: "churn is stable at 6%. conflict: but it jumped to 8% last quarter." resolution: "apac high-value customers are leaving — 2.3× above average." action: "launch a loyalty program in apac by q2 — saves $18m." rule if any of the four beats is missing, the story falls flat. especially the action. story arc data story arc: four beats, all present ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice describe the data only no conflict or problem named context: the situation today churn stable at 6% skip the resolution no insight from the data conflict, then resolution jumped to 8%; apac leaving 2.3x end without an action falls flat, especially no cta call-to-action with owner loyalty program in apac by q2 result: story falls flat result: action-oriented story mistake facts shown, but no one knows what to do. best practice every beat present, ending in a dated, owned ask. rule if any beat is missing, the story falls flat. three fixes to apply 1 name conflict state the problem or opportunity. 2 show insight say what the data reveals. 3 end with action do x by y, owned by z.
m14-scqa: definition the most widely used executive-communication structure in consulting. the four parts part purpose situation the current, agreed-upon reality complication what changed or what problem emerged question the natural question the complication raises answer your recommendation worked example applied situation: churn is at 8%. complication: a new competitor launched 6 months ago. question: which customers are leaving and why? answer: high-value customers in apac → price sensitivity → launch loyalty program. scqa flow 1 situation 2 complication 3 question 4 answer origin barbara minto, mckinsey. still the standard after 40+ years. scqa scqa: situation to answer in four parts ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice start with a disputed claim situation must be agreed reality situation: agreed reality churn is at 8% skip the complication no change or problem stated complication: what changed new competitor 6 months ago jump past the question audience question left unasked question, then answer which customers leave and why? result: weak executive case result: clear consulting logic mistake the recommendation lands without any setup. best practice answer follows naturally from the question. origin barbara minto, mckinsey: the standard for 40+ years. three fixes to apply 1 agree first open with facts everyone accepts. 2 raise the question let the complication ask it for you. 3 answer give your recommendation last in the flow.
m14-pyramid: rule start every presentation with the answer on slide 1. the structure answer first — the recommendation goes on slide 1. supporting arguments — grouped in 3s. details — in the appendix only. pyramid structure answer / recommendation 3 supporting arguments details (appendix) why executives love it they never have to wait for the answer. it's on slide 1. everything else is proof. pyramid principle pyramid principle: answer on slide 1 ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice build up to the answer executives must wait for it answer first recommendation on slide 1 list arguments with no order not grouped in 3s group support in 3s 3 supporting arguments put details in the main deck belongs in the appendix only details to the appendix everything else is proof result: exec waits, loses the thread result: answer never in doubt mistake the point arrives too late to drive a decision. best practice executives never wait for the answer. rule start every presentation with the answer on slide 1. three fixes to apply 1 lead open with the recommendation. 2 group by 3 support it with three arguments. 3 park detail move the rest to the appendix.
m14-emotional: definition numbers alone don't move people. emotion + logic together drive action. facts inform; emotion moves people to act facts alone numbers on a slide audience nods nothing changes facts + feeling one human example then the data a clear ask four techniques technique example surprise "we are 42% worse than we thought." stakes "this costs us $4.7m per year." human stories "sarah from singapore cancelled because..." visual before/after show the change in a single image why it works emotion → memory. people remember stories, not slides. emotion → action. a number informs; a story compels. emotion → recall. your point survives the meeting. ethics never fabricate a story or exaggerate stakes. just highlight the real ones. trust is everything. emotion emotion plus logic drives action ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice present numbers alone numbers do not move people use surprise and stakes 42% worse; costs $4.7m a year exaggerate the stakes trust is everything tell a real human story sarah from singapore cancelled fabricate a human story ethics breach show visual before/after one image shows the change result: forgotten point, lost trust result: memorable, honest case mistake a number informs but does not compel. best practice your point survives the meeting. ethics highlight real stakes; never invent or inflate them. three fixes to apply 1 add stakes quantify the cost in dollars. 2 use a real story pick a true customer example. 3 show change use one before/after visual.
m14-famous-stories: pattern every famous data story has the same shape: clear conflict → data insight → massive action. famous data stories share one shape hook a surprising fact evidence one clear chart meaning what it implies action what to do next study how they open, show one idea, and end with a call to act the three classics company story impact netflix "house of cards" — viewing-data-driven content bet $100m+ investment, huge hit target pregnancy prediction from shopping patterns massive revenue lift — plus a pr lesson airbnb pricing algorithm launch enabled hosts, drove bookings what each teaches netflix: trust the data even when it contradicts conventional wisdom. target: insight without ethical care can backfire spectacularly. airbnb: the best data story is one that empowers the user. your turn every analyst has a story like this in their data. you just have to structure it.
m14-exec-summary: rule one slide. that's all the executive needs to decide. executive summary: answer first, then support answer the recommendation why 2-3 key findings impact numbers that matter ask decision needed a busy executive should be able to stop reading after this box what must be on the slide recommendation — the action you want. 3 key proofs — the evidence that supports it. financial impact — dollars, %, or lives saved. design constraints font ≥ 24 pt — readable from the back of the room. ≤ 30 words total. bold headline — the recommendation itself. example headline "we should launch a loyalty program in apac — saves $18m." why it works everything else in the deck is backup. the exec summary alone drives the decision. exec summary the 1-slide executive summary ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice spread the case over many slides exec needs one slide to decide recommendation, 3 proofs, impact dollars, percent, or lives saved write dense, small text not readable from the back font 24 pt or more 30 words total at most label instead of recommend headline is not the action bold headline is the ask launch loyalty in apac, saves $18m result: no decision made result: decision on one slide mistake the room reads, but does not decide. best practice everything else in the deck is backup. rule one slide is all the executive needs to decide. three fixes to apply 1 add 3 proofs support the ask with three key proofs. 2 quantify state the financial impact. 3 cut words stay under 30 words and 24 pt.
m14-slide-design: rule design is subtraction. every slide should have exactly one message. the principles 1 message per slide. 6×6 rule is dead — aim for 1 idea. white space is your friend. use color sparingly — one accent color. charts > tables > text. content hierarchy charts tables text common mistake filling slides with text because you're afraid of leaving something out. cut it. if it matters, it goes in the appendix. slide design slide design: subtract until one message ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice fill slides with text fear of leaving something out one message per slide aim for 1 idea chase the 6x6 rule that rule is dead use white space your friend, not wasted room use many colors not one accent color one accent color; charts first charts over tables over text result: crowded, unclear slides result: clean, focused slides mistake no one knows which point matters. best practice design is subtraction. cut it or appendix it. rule design is subtraction: one message per slide. three fixes to apply 1 cut text move extras to the appendix. 2 one accent use a single accent color. 3 chart first prefer charts to tables and text.
m14-chart-selector: rule match the chart to the question — not to what looks fancy. decision table question chart comparison bar / column trend line or area distribution histogram / boxplot composition stacked bar (only when needed) relationship scatter visual — question → chart chart selector bar line histogram stacked scatter comparison · trend · distribution · composition · relationship rule of thumb if you can't decide between two charts, pick the one your audience can read fastest. chart selection chart selection: match the question ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice pick the fanciest chart looks good, reads slowly comparison: bar or column trend: line or area stack everything stacked only when needed distribution: histogram or box relationship: scatter ignore the question asked chart does not match it composition: stacked bar only when needed result: slow, confusing chart result: fast, readable chart mistake the audience decodes instead of deciding. best practice question to chart, one clear match. rule of thumb between two charts, pick the one read fastest. three fixes to apply 1 name the question comparison, trend, spread, mix, or link. 2 pick the match use the chart in the decision table. 3 test speed choose what the audience reads fastest.
m14-action-titles: rule every chart title must be a sentence with insight — not a label. action titles state the finding, not the topic topic title "revenue by quarter" reader must find the point action title "revenue grew 28% yoy" the point is the headline bad vs good bad (label) good (action title) "churn by region" "apac churn 2.3× higher than average — driven by price" "revenue by month" "revenue grew 28% yoy — fastest since 2021" "customer satisfaction" "csat dropped after the march release — concentrated in mobile users" why it's the biggest upgrade executives read titles. if the title is a label, they have to interpret the chart. action titles force you to know your point. titles get quoted. a great title becomes the takeaway. test read only your titles from top to bottom. if they tell a coherent story, you're done. action titles action titles: the biggest upgrade ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice label the chart churn by region write the insight apac churn 2.3x higher, driven by price make execs interpret they read titles, not charts quantify the change revenue grew 28% yoy title before knowing the point no clear takeaway name the cause csat dropped after march release result: reader does the thinking result: titles tell the story mistake the insight stays hidden in the chart. best practice a great title becomes the takeaway. test read only your titles top to bottom. coherent story? three fixes to apply 1 use sentences every title states an insight. 2 force a point know the takeaway before charting. 3 run the test read titles alone in order.
m14-color-accessibility: rule color should carry meaning — and be readable by everyone. the rules maximum 5 colors total per deck or dashboard. colorblind-safe palette — okabe-ito, colorbrewer. never use red-green together as the only distinction. test with a color simulator — e.g., coblis. grayscale test blue amber purple green → grayscale → always add a second cue — icon, pattern, or direct label — so the chart works without color. color color: meaning for everyone ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice use a rainbow of colors more than 5 per deck limit to 5 colors per deck or dashboard red-green as only cue fails for colorblind viewers colorblind-safe palette okabe-ito or colorbrewer never test the palette no simulator check test with a simulator e.g. coblis; check grayscale result: unreadable for some viewers result: readable by everyone mistake meaning is lost without color vision. best practice a second cue backs up every color. always add an icon, pattern, or label so it works without color. three fixes to apply 1 cap colors keep to five at most. 2 pick safe use a tested palette. 3 add a cue icon, pattern, or direct label.
m14-exec-vs-peers: rule two audiences = two decks. don't try to serve both with one. same analysis, different audience, different order executives answer first impact and decision 5-10 minutes technical peers method and checks assumptions, limits then the result comparison dimension executives technical peers time 5–10 min 20–40 min focus big picture, $ impact methods, assumptions, code charts 3–4 simple many, detailed appendix full of backup full of proofs language business statistical the rule always have two versions ready. same analysis, different framing. trap showing a technical deck to an executive is the fastest way to lose the room. and vice versa. exec vs peers two audiences, two decks ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice one deck for everyone serves neither audience exec: 5 to 10 min, $ impact 3 to 4 simple charts technical deck for executives fastest way to lose the room peers: 20 to 40 min methods, assumptions, code business deck for peers lacks methods and proofs two versions ready same analysis, different framing result: lost room result: right deck for the room mistake wrong depth, wrong language. best practice business language or statistical language. rule two audiences means two decks. three fixes to apply 1 build two keep both versions ready. 2 tune language business for execs; statistical for peers. 3 match appendix backup for execs, proofs for peers.
m14-handling-qa: rule q&a is where reputations are built or broken. prepare for it harder than for the presentation itself. handling q&a: pause, answer, bridge back listen full question pause think first answer briefly, honestly bridge back to the point "i do not know, i will check and follow up" beats a guess the three rules anticipate the top 5 hard questions. prepare appendix slides for each. buy time with a bridge. "that's a great question — here's the sensitivity analysis." never say "i don't know." say: "i'll follow up by cob tomorrow." common hard questions question prepare "what if the assumptions are wrong?" sensitivity analysis slide "how confident are you in the numbers?" ci / range slide "why should we trust this model?" validation slide "what's the cost of being wrong?" cost / risk slide "how does this compare to the alternative?" model comparison slide never guess. never bluff. "i'll follow up" is respected. wrong answers destroy trust. handling q&a q&a: where reputations are made ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice prepare only the talk q&a needs more prep prepare top 5 hard questions an appendix slide for each guess or bluff wrong answers destroy trust buy time with a bridge great question, here is sensitivity answer cold, no bridge no time bought to think say: i will follow up by cob tomorrow result: trust destroyed result: respected, credible mistake one bluff undoes a strong presentation. best practice follow-up is respected; wrong answers are not. rule never guess. never bluff. follow up instead. three fixes to apply 1 prep 5 sensitivity, ci, validation, cost, comparison. 2 bridge acknowledge, then point to a slide. 3 follow up promise a dated reply.
m14-presenting-tips: rule you're not presenting slides. you're driving a decision. the tips open with the answer. don't build suspense. control the pace. pause after each key point. point at the chart. use a laser or cursor to guide attention. close with the cta. the final slide is the ask. watch the room. if eyes drift, you've lost them — reset. rehearse out loud. twice. minimum. structure 5-slide deck structure answer context evidence options cta reality if you only have 5 minutes, you need 5 slides. anything more is backup. presenting tips presenting: drive a decision ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice build suspense hold the answer back open with the answer close with the cta rush with no pauses pace uncontrolled pause after each key point point at the chart ignore the room eyes drifting unnoticed rehearse out loud twice minimum; reset if eyes drift result: lost audience, no decision result: decision-focused talk mistake slides were shown but nothing was decided. best practice the final slide is the ask. reality with 5 minutes, use 5 slides. the rest is backup. three fixes to apply 1 answer first no suspense; the answer opens. 2 control pace pause and guide with a cursor. 3 rehearse practice aloud, twice at minimum.
m14-reproducibility: definition reproducibility = someone else can rerun your analysis and get the same results. why it matters 70% of published research fails to reproduce (nature 2023). companies now require it for promotion. git + readme = your professional reputation. it saves you time — six months later, you can rebuild anything. visual reproducibility as a professional signal not reproducible trusted by nobody reproducible trusted, promoted, hired bottom line your analysis is only as valuable as the number of people who can rebuild it. reproducibility reproducible: anyone can rerun it ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice share results, not the method others cannot rerun it make reruns give same results definition of reproducible skip git and a readme reputation signal lost git plus readme your professional reputation trust memory six months later, rebuild fails document for future you rebuild anything in months result: work no one can verify result: trusted, promotable work mistake 70% of published research fails to reproduce. best practice companies now require it for promotion. bottom line value equals the number of people who can rebuild it. three fixes to apply 1 use git keep every project in a repo. 2 write readme explain how to rerun it. 3 save future time document while it is fresh.
m14-git-workflow: definition git is the version control standard. every professional project lives in a repo. git workflow: branch, commit, review, merge branch one task commit small, clear message pull request review merge to main never commit raw data with secrets or personal information the core workflow # clone the repo git clone https://github.com/you/project.git # create a branch for your feature git checkout -b feature/churn-model # stage and commit git add . git commit -m "feat: add churn model with xgboost" # push and open a pr git push origin feature/churn-model commit message conventions prefix use for feat: new feature or model fix: bug fix (e.g., handle missing values) docs: documentation only refactor: code restructure, no behavior change chore: tooling, dependencies never commit raw data, secrets, or .pbix files larger than 100 mb. use .gitignore . git workflow git: branch, commit, push, pr ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice commit raw data and secrets never commit these branch per feature git checkout -b feature/churn-model commit .pbix over 100 mb use .gitignore prefix commits feat, fix, docs, refactor, chore write vague commit messages no prefix convention push and open a pr git push origin feature/... result: leaked data, bloated repo result: clean, reviewable history mistake hard to review, hard to undo. best practice every professional project lives in a repo. never commit raw data, secrets, or large pbix files. use .gitignore. three fixes to apply 1 branch work on a feature branch. 2 prefix use feat: or fix: in messages. 3 ignore list data and secrets in gitignore.
m14-readme: rule the readme is the most important file in your repo. if it's bad, nothing else matters. a readme answers five questions fast what project purpose why the business problem how steps to run result key findings who contact, licence the readme is the first thing a recruiter reads the structure # project title ## business problem what decision does this analysis support? ## data sources where did the data come from? size? refresh? ## key findings (with visuals) 3 bullets + 1 chart per finding ## how to reproduce ```bash pip install -r requirements.txt python src/train.py ``` ## results & limitations what did we learn? what are the caveats? why it works recruiters read it in 30 seconds. collaborators can rebuild in 5 minutes. you remember what you did in 6 months. pro tip put the key chart near the top. a picture carries 80% of the readme's value. mistake vs best practice: readme readme: the most important file ✗ common mistake ✗ write a bad or empty readme nothing else matters then ✗ skip how to reproduce collaborators cannot rebuild ✗ hide the key chart picture carries 80% of value result: recruiters leave in 30 seconds ✓ best practice ✓ problem, data, findings 3 bullets plus 1 chart each ✓ how to reproduce pip install; python src/train.py ✓ results and limitations learned, plus caveats result: rebuild in 5 minutes mistake: no one can follow what you did. pro tip put the key chart near the top of the readme. best practice: recruiters read it in 30 seconds. three fixes to apply 1 state problem name the business decision it supports. 2 add repro steps give exact commands to rerun. 3 show a chart place the key visual near the top.
m14-notebook: rule a notebook is a story — with code as the supporting evidence. clean notebook: story first, code second title question asked setup imports, seed analysis small cells findings plain words restart and run all before you share it best practices table of contents — use the toc2 extension. hide code for executive notebooks — use nbextensions or a hide_code cell tag. markdown headers + explanatory text between code cells. widgets for interactivity — ipywidgets . export to html for sharing — never send a raw .ipynb to stakeholders. structure # 1. business problem (markdown) # 2. setup & imports (code) # 3. load data (code + markdown explanation) # 4. eda with charts (code + markdown findings) # 5. modeling (code + markdown decisions) # 6. results & limitations (markdown) test restart & run all. if the notebook breaks, it isn't reproducible. notebooks notebooks: a story with code evidence ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice send a raw ipynb to stakeholders export to html instead headers plus explanatory text between code cells code cells with no text needs headers and explanation table of contents; hide code toc2; hide_code tag for execs never rerun from scratch hidden state breaks it export to html to share widgets via ipywidgets result: broken, unreadable notebook result: readable, rerunnable story mistake not reproducible and not shareable. best practice problem first, limits last. test restart and run all. if it breaks, not reproducible. three fixes to apply 1 add text explain each step in markdown. 2 follow structure problem, setup, data, eda, model, results. 3 run all restart and run all before sharing.
m14-documentation: rule if you didn't document it, you'll re-derive it. waste of life. document the why, not only the what weak docs code with no notes no data dictionary "it works on my laptop" strong docs comments explain why data dictionary included requirements pinned the standards docstrings for every function — inputs, outputs, purpose. requirements.txt or environment.yml — pinned versions. sphinx or mkdocs for packages. data dictionary in /data folder. docstring example def clean_amounts (df, col= 'amount' ): """strip $ and commas, convert to numeric. args: df (pd.dataframe): input data col (str): column to clean returns: pd.dataframe: df with {col}_clean column added """ s = df[col]. astype ( str ). str . replace ( r'[$,]' , '' , regex= true ) df[col + '_clean' ] = pd. to_numeric (s, errors= 'coerce' ) return df data dictionary format column name | type | description | source | notes. documentation document it or re-derive it ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice skip docstrings purpose and i/o unknown docstring every function inputs, outputs, purpose no pinned requirements environment cannot be rebuilt pin versions requirements.txt or environment.yml no data dictionary columns unexplained data dictionary in /data name, type, description, source result: re-deriving your own work result: rebuildable project mistake undocumented work is wasted life. best practice sphinx or mkdocs for packages. rule if you did not document it, you will re-derive it. three fixes to apply 1 docstrings add args and returns to each function. 2 pin versions lock the environment. 3 dictionary column, type, source, notes.
m14-github-portfolio: rule your github is your live portfolio. make it easy to love. portfolio repo: show 3-5 polished projects pin best 3-5 repos readme each one reproduce env + data note results charts, findings quality over quantity: unfinished repos hurt more than they help the rules 3–5 high-impact projects maximum. one project per repo — not one giant repo. starred readme with animated gifs. clear folder structure: /data, /notebooks, /src, /results. repo structure project/ ├── readme.md # the star ├── requirements.txt ├── data/ │ └── data_dictionary.md ├── notebooks/ │ └── 01_eda.ipynb ├── src/ │ ├── train.py │ └── clean.py └── results/ └── churn_model_roc.png why it works recruiters scan in 30 seconds. structure tells them you're a professional before they read a word. github portfolio github: your live portfolio ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice show every project not just 3 to 5 3 to 5 high-impact projects maximum one giant repo for all one project per repo one project per repo starred readme with gifs flat, unstructured folders recruiters scan in 30 seconds clear folder structure /data /notebooks /src /results result: recruiter cannot find value result: professional at first glance mistake clutter hides your best work. best practice structure signals skill before a word is read. rule your github is your live portfolio. make it lovable. three fixes to apply 1 curate keep only 3 to 5 projects. 2 split repos one project in each repo. 3 organize use data, notebooks, src, results.
m14-project-criteria: rule not all projects are portfolio-worthy. choose the ones that tell a story. a hire-worthy project: question, data, insight, impact real question a business need real data not a toy set clear insight a finding impact a recommendation score each project against these four before you publish it four criteria criterion look for business impact $, %, lives saved technical depth at least one advanced technique clean code + storytelling readme, visualizations, conclusions bonus: deployed app streamlit, dash, power bi examples of strong portfolio projects churn prediction with $ saved. fraud detection with precision/recall. demand forecasting with mape. customer segmentation with personas. avoid titanic, iris, and other textbook datasets. pick a project with a real business question. project selection pick projects that tell a story ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice use titanic or iris textbook datasets show business impact $, percent, lives saved no business question no impact number one advanced technique real technical depth code with no storytelling missing readme and conclusions clean code plus storytelling bonus: streamlit, dash, power bi result: forgettable portfolio result: story-driven portfolio mistake not every project is portfolio-worthy. best practice churn, fraud, forecasting, segmentation. rule choose projects that tell a story, with a real question. three fixes to apply 1 ask real start from a real business question. 2 quantify report dollars saved or precision. 3 deploy add an app as a bonus.
m14-linkedin: rule linkedin is where recruiters find you. make every field count. linkedin headline: role + skills + quantified impact generic "data analyst" "passionate about data" specific role + tools a quantified result the four elements element what to do headline "data scientist | built churn model that saved $4.7m" featured section top 3 github repos + presentation deck about section 3-paragraph story (who, what, why) posting weekly — insights, not "i'm open to work" headline examples strong "data scientist | built churn model that saved $4.7m | python · sql · ml" "analytics leader | turned dashboards into 12% revenue lift | ex-fortune 500" weak "open to work" as your headline. every recruiter sees this on every candidate. stand out with impact. linkedin linkedin: make every field count ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice headline: open to work every candidate has it impact headline built churn model that saved $4.7m empty featured section no repos or deck feature top 3 repos plus deck featured section post only job-seeking notes not insights weekly insight posts 3-paragraph about: who, what, why result: blends into the pile result: stands out with impact mistake recruiters see the same headline everywhere. best practice quantified impact in every field. rule linkedin is where recruiters find you. three fixes to apply 1 quantify put a dollar result in the headline. 2 feature pin three repos and a deck. 3 post weekly share insights, not availability.
m14-checklist: use before you stand up 10 checks. takes 10 minutes. saves a career. before you present: five final checks answer first in 1 sentence action titles every slide accessible colour safe reproducible run all rehearsed timed rehearse out loud with a timer the 10 checks answer on slide 1 — recommendation, not context. 3 supporting proofs — grouped, tight. financial impact — quantified in $, %, or lives. action titles on every chart — sentences, not labels. ≤ 5 slides for a 5-minute presentation. appendix ready for the top 5 hard questions. colorblind-safe palette — tested in grayscale. rehearsed out loud twice. final slide = cta — the ask, owned and dated. backup plan — pdf copy in case tech fails. most common miss #1 — starting with context. executives don't want the journey; they want the destination.
m14-recap: module flow 1 story 2 slides 3 present 4 repro 5 brand the five lines story structure — context → conflict → resolution → cta. slide design — 1 message per slide, action titles, exec-first. presenting — answer first, rehearse twice, anticipate q&a. reproducibility — git + readme + notebooks anyone can rerun. brand — github portfolio + linkedin with quantified impact. carry-forward rules if you can't say it in a sentence, you haven't finished the analysis. answer first. context later. always. every chart title is a takeaway, not a label. reproducible work is trustworthy work. your portfolio is a live interview — make it count. final note you now have the technical skills and the communication skills. that combination is what gets promoted.
m15-overview: purpose one extreme value can drag the mean far from where most of your data sits. the median finds the true centre, so decisions reflect the typical case. what you'll be able to do spot when the mean is being pulled by an outlier find the median with the position formula, for odd and even counts choose mean or median on purpose, and say why remember the median does not delete the outlier. investigate it: it may be an error or an important real case. the median: optimizing the data the median: optimizing the data common mistake the skewed mean 12 13 14 15 80 370-46.9=323.1 --> mean = 26.8 outlier using mean with outliers misleads decisions. best practice the balanced median 12 13 14 15 80 median = 14 isolated outlier values sorted low to high; axis break before 80 median identifies the true typical patient. median position = (n + 1) / 2 goal: find the true center by completely neutralizing extreme outliers. three fixes 1 a → z sort data first always arrange values from lowest to highest before locating the center. 2 identify skew use median instead of mean whenever an extreme outlier is present. 3 ÷ 2 even numbers fix if two middle numbers exist, average them to find the true median.
m15-skewed-mean: key checks the skewed mean ✓ spot the gap mean far from median means skew or an outlier. ✓ report the median it stays at 14 even if the outlier grows to 800. ✓ investigate decide if the outlier is an error or a real case. mistake using the mean when an outlier is present. using mean with outliers misleads decisions. worked example worked values: 12, 13, 14, 15, 80 sum = 134, count = 5, mean = 134 / 5 = 26.8 four of the five values are 15 or below, so 26.8 describes nobody in this sample. statistic value describes the typical case? mean 26.8 no: pulled up by 80 median 14 yes: the middle value why it matters budgets, staffing and targets set from a skewed mean are set for a case that rarely happens. skewed mean mean vs median: outliers mislead ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice report the mean by default 12, 13, 14, 15, 80 gives 26.8 compare mean and median 26.8 vs 14 shows the skew ignore the extreme value one 80 drags the average up report the median: 14 the true typical value set targets from the mean fits almost no one in the data check why 80 is so high error or real case? result: misleading decision result: decision on the typical case mistake mean 26.8 describes none of the five values. best practice median 14 sits in the middle of the data. rule of thumb outlier present? use the median. report both if the gap matters. three fixes to apply 1 spot the gap mean far from median means skew or an outlier. 2 report the median it stays at 14 even if the outlier grows to 800. 3 investigate decide if the outlier is an error or a real case.
m15-balanced-median: key checks the balanced median ✓ sort first arrange values from lowest to highest. ✓ take the middle two values on each side of 14 in this sample. ✓ keep the outlier flag it instead of deleting it from the data. best practice report the median when extremes are present. median identifies the true typical patient. same sorted sample worked sorted: 12, 13, 14 , 15, 80 two values below, two above: the median is 14 . change 80 to 800 and the median is still 14. the median depends on position, not on how extreme the outer values are. show the mean as well when the gap between the two is the story. balanced median the median: the true typical value ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice take the middle of unsorted data wrong position, wrong value sort, then take the middle 12, 13, 14, 15, 80 gives 14 drop the outlier silently hides a possibly real case keep the outlier, note it 80 stays visible in the data report only one statistic reader cannot see the skew show median beside the mean gap tells the skew story result: wrong or hidden story result: honest typical value mistake the centre is only right once sorted. best practice median 14: two values below, two above. rule the median depends on position, not on how extreme the ends are. three fixes to apply 1 sort first arrange values from lowest to highest. 2 take the middle two values on each side of 14 in this sample. 3 keep the outlier flag it instead of deleting it from the data.
m15-position-formula: key checks median position formula ✓ sort order the list before counting positions. ✓ compute plug n into (n + 1) / 2 to get the position. ✓ look up return the value found at that position. formula median position = (n + 1) / 2 , where n is the number of values in the sorted list. goal find the true centre by completely neutralizing extreme outliers. n position meaning 5 (5 + 1) / 2 = 3 the 3rd value is the median 7 (7 + 1) / 2 = 4 the 4th value is the median 4 (4 + 1) / 2 = 2.5 halfway between the 2nd and 3rd values careful the formula gives a position, not the median itself. look up the value at that position in the sorted list. position formula median position: (n + 1) / 2 ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice treat the formula as the answer it gives a position, not a value sort the values first lowest to highest use n / 2 instead lands on the wrong item compute (n + 1) / 2 n = 5 gives position 3 apply it to unsorted data position means nothing yet read the value at that spot third value of 12..80 is 14 result: wrong median reported result: correct median mistake position 3 is not the same as the value 3. best practice position first, then look up the value. formula median position = (n + 1) / 2 then read the value there. three fixes to apply 1 sort order the list before counting positions. 2 compute plug n into (n + 1) / 2 to get the position. 3 look up return the value found at that position.
m15-sort-first: key checks fix 1: sort data first ✓ sort all values lowest to highest, no partial sorts. ✓ find the centre use the position formula on the sorted list. ✓ check with code compare your hand result to the .median() output. rule always arrange values from lowest to highest before locating the centre. worked raw: 15, 80, 12, 14, 13 position 3 of the raw list is 12, which is wrong. sorted: 12, 13, 14 , 15, 80 → position 3 is 14. # pandas sorts for you df['days'].median() # or by hand sorted(values) sort first sort first: the median needs order ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice pick the middle of raw rows 15, 80, 12, 14, 13 gives 12 sort lowest to highest 12, 13, 14, 15, 80 assume data arrives sorted exports are rarely ordered then locate the centre third value is 14 sort only part of the data middle shifts unpredictably let a tool do it pandas .median() sorts for you result: wrong median result: reliable median mistake order in the file is not value order. best practice always sort before you locate the centre. rule no sort, no median. order first, centre second. three fixes to apply 1 sort all values lowest to highest, no partial sorts. 2 find the centre use the position formula on the sorted list. 3 check with code compare your hand result to the .median() output.
m15-identify-skew: key checks fix 2: identify skew ✓ compare mean and median side by side. ✓ visualize sorted list or boxplot shows the extreme. ✓ decide median for skewed data; say why in your report. rule use the median instead of the mean whenever an extreme outlier is present. check what it tells you mean far from median the data is skewed or has an outlier sorted list or boxplot shows the extreme value directly mean close to median either statistic is fine our sample mean 26.8 vs median 14: a gap of 12.8 points to the outlier 80. then ask is 80 a data-entry error or a real case? check before you decide what to do with it. identify skew identify skew before you choose ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice choose the statistic by habit mean is not always right compare mean and median 26.8 vs 14: a gap of 12.8 never look at the spread outlier goes unnoticed look at a sorted list or boxplot see the extreme directly trust the mean-median gap blindly gap says look, not what to do use the median if skewed report both when the gap matters result: wrong summary statistic result: summary fits the data mistake habit picks the mean even when skewed. best practice choose the statistic after seeing the shape. rule of thumb extreme outlier present? use the median, not the mean. three fixes to apply 1 compare mean and median side by side. 2 visualize sorted list or boxplot shows the extreme. 3 decide median for skewed data; say why in your report.
m15-even-fix: key checks fix 3: even numbers fix ✓ count check if n is even or odd. ✓ take both middles position 2.5 means the 2nd and 3rd values. ✓ average add them, divide by 2 for the median. rule if two middle numbers exist, average them to find the true median. worked sorted: 12, 13 , 14 , 15 (n = 4) position = (4 + 1) / 2 = 2.5, between the 2nd and 3rd values median = (13 + 14) / 2 = 13.5 with an even count the median may not be a value that appears in the data. that is expected, not an error. even count even counts: average the two middles ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice pick one of the two middle values 13 or 14 for 12, 13, 14, 15 find position (n + 1) / 2 n = 4 gives position 2.5 round position 2.5 up or down throws away half the information take the 2nd and 3rd values 13 and 14 expect the median in the data 13.5 is a valid median average them (13 + 14) / 2 = 13.5 result: biased median result: correct median 13.5 mistake one middle value ignores the other. best practice even count: average the two middle numbers. rule two middle numbers exist? average them. three fixes to apply 1 count check if n is even or odd. 2 take both middles position 2.5 means the 2nd and 3rd values. 3 average add them, divide by 2 for the median.
m16-overview: positioning r is not a replacement for python. r's core strengths are statistical rigor, publication-grade visualization, and reproducible research . this module teaches the correct way to do ml in r — not "run a model in r," but "use r for statistical reasoning and visualization, use python for deployment." quick look r for ml: five stages and the artifact each one leaves behind enlarge r does the reasoning and the reporting explore profile the data before modelling skimr::skim() 1 model recipe + workflow + tuning tidymodels 2 visualise roc, errors, importance ggplot2 3 report numbers regenerate from code quarto render 4 hand off version and serve the model vetiver 5 data profile missingness, ranges, types fitted workflow one object, tested on folds figures publication-ready png / svg report.html or pdf / word, same source model api plumber, docker or python each stage ends with something you can open, check and hand to someone else. 1 explore first run skimr::skim(data) to see types, missing values and ranges. the output tells you what the recipe must fix. 2 model with tidymodels a recipe cleans, a model spec learns, a workflow bundles both, and resampling scores them honestly. 3 visualise the evidence plot the roc curve, residuals and importances with ggplot2. a picture of the error beats a single metric. 4 report from code a quarto document re-runs the analysis and rewrites every number and chart. no copy and paste into slides. 5 hand off to production vetiver versions the fitted workflow and can expose it as an api; python services can also consume it via a saved file or rest call. what it will look like who leads when in a typical project enlarge 0 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 week explore the data explore the data: week 0–1.5 r build and tune models build and tune models: week 1–4.5 r: tidymodels charts and diagnostics charts and diagnostics: week 3.5–5.5 r: ggplot2 report for stakeholders report for stakeholders: week 5–6.5 r: quarto serve the model serve the model: week 5.5–8 python / api monitor in production monitor in production: week 7–8 review illustrative schedule. r carries analysis and reporting; python or an api usually carries serving. your split will differ. run it, then check the result your first 10 minutes: install, attach, profile install.packages ( c ( "tidymodels" , "skimr" , "quarto" , "vetiver" )) library (tidymodels) # attaches the core packages tidymodels_prefer () # resolves name clashes in favour of tidymodels skimr:: skim (wine) # step 1: profile before you model what the console prints illustrative output: structure matches what r prints; m16-recipes: definition recipes uses step_* functions to define preprocessing pipelines. all steps "learn" on training data then apply to test data — automatically preventing data leakage. quick look a recipe learns from training data, then applies the same numbers everywhere enlarge one recipe, order matters raw rows na in sulphates, text in type type sulph ph red na 3.1 white 0.6 na 1 1. impute fill gaps first step_impute_bag() na -> 0.58 2 2. encode text to 0/1 columns step_dummy() type -> type_white 3 3. scale mean 0, sd 1 step_normalize() 9.4 -> -0.31 4 prep(train) learns means, levels, models from training rows only prep(wine_recipe) 5 bake(any data) applies the stored numbers to train, test or new data bake(prepped, test) 6 1 start from untidy rows missing values and text columns are normal. the recipe handles them; you do not edit the data by hand. 2 impute first fill gaps before anything depends on them. if missingness means something, add a flag column before imputing. 3 encode categories step_dummy() turns text levels into 0/1 columns the model can use. 4 scale last step_normalize() centres and scales using the training mean and sd, not the test data. 5 prep() learns once means, levels and imputation models are estimated from the training rows only. nothing from test data enters. 6 bake() applies everywhere the stored numbers transform train, test and future data wine_recipe <- recipe (quality_fct ~ ., data = train_data) %>% step_impute_bag ( all_predictors ()) %>% step_dummy ( all_nominal_predictors ()) %>% step_normalize ( all_numeric_predictors ()) common step_* functions function purpose step_normalize() standardization (mean 0, variance 1) step_dummy() one-hot encoding step_impute_bag() fill missing values with bagged trees step_pca() principal component analysis step_corr() remove highly correlated features why recipes matters order matters: impute first, then encode categories, then scale. when missingness itself carries meaning, keep a flag column before imputing so the model can still see it, instead of silently filling in a default value. leakage prevention recipes automatically learns preprocessing parameters on training folds, then applies them to validation/test folds. this is the core advantage of tidymodels over manual preprocessing. recipes recipes: prepare data without leakage ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice scale before splitting test rows shape the mean learn steps on training data prep() uses train only impute on the full dataset test info leaks into training apply the same steps to test bake() reuses the learned values repeat steps by hand later easy to forget or reorder order: impute, encode, scale keep a flag if missing matters result: scores look too good result: honest evaluation mistake honest-looking numbers that will not hold up. best practice same preparation for train and new data. rule learn every transform on the training data only. three fixes to apply 1 split first divide before you preprocess. 2 use step_* define each step in one recipe. 3 keep flags mark missing values when they carry meaning.
m16-workflows: definition workflows binds a recipe and a model spec into one object. calling fit() trains both preprocessing and model together. quick look one object carries preprocessing and model together enlarge recipe prepare features wine_recipe 1 model spec the algorithm and its settings rand_forest(trees=500) 2 workflow one object holds both workflow() %>% add_recipe() %>% add_model() 3 fit() trains recipe and model together fit(wine_wf, train) 4 predict() new rows get the same prep 5 tune_grid() fit_resamples() accepts the workflow directly 5 1 the recipe defines how raw columns become model inputs. it is attached, not run, until you fit. 2 the model spec defines the algorithm. swap this one piece to compare models. 3 the workflow holds both. because they travel together, training and prediction cannot disagree about preprocessing. 4 fit() trains both the recipe is prepped on the training data, then the model learns from the prepped data. 5 reuse it everywhere predict() , fit_resamples() and tune_grid() all take the same object. what it will look like compare models by changing only the model line enlarge 0.00 0.25 0.50 0.75 1.00 cv roc auc logistic regression: 0.81 0.81 logistic regression random forest: 0.86 0.86 random forest boosted trees: 0.87 0.87 boosted trees illustrative: seeded synthetic data. shapes are realistic; values are examples, not results from your data. run it, then check the result build the workflow and inspect it rf_spec <- rand_forest (trees = 500 ) %>% set_engine ( "ranger" ) %>% set_mode ( "classification" ) wine_wf <- workflow () %>% add_recipe (wine_recipe) %>% add_model (rf_spec) wine_wf # print it to check both parts are attached print(wine_wf) illustrative output: structure matches what r prints; numbers are examples. == workflow ======================================================= preprocessor: recipe model: rand_forest() -- preprocessor ------------------------------------------------------- 3 recipe steps * step_impute_bag() * step_dummy() * step_normalize() -- model -------------------------------------------------------------- random forest model specification (classification) main arguments: trees = 500 computational engine: ranger check: both a preprocessor and a model section appear. if the model section says "none", fit() will fail. swap the model with one line, keep everything else wine_wf %>% update_model ( logistic_reg ()) %>% fit (train_data) # logistic wine_wf %>% update_model ( boost_tree (trees = 500 ) %>% set_engine ( "xgboost" ) %>% set_mode ( "classification" )) %>% fit (train_data) # boosted what this solves for the business 01 training and prediction cannot drift the same bundle prepares data in both places, removing a classic source of silent errors. fewer silent bugs 02 cheap model comparison changing one component re-runs the whole pipeline fairly. minutes per candidate 03 ready for tuning and resampling the workflow plugs straight into tune_grid() , so settings are searched without extra glue. less code to maintain do this next wrap your recipe and model in a workflow done when: print(workflow) shows a preprocessor and a model section. fit and predict with the workflow only done when: no separate prep() or bake() call appears in the script. compare two models by update_model() done when: both scores sit in one table with the same folds. syntax library (tidymodels) # 1. define model (parsnip) rf_spec <- rand_forest (trees = 500 ) %>% set_engine ( "ranger" ) %>% set_mode ( "classification" ) # 2. define workflow wine_wf <- workflow () %>% add_recipe (wine_recipe) %>% add_model (rf_spec) # 3. train wine_fit <- wine_wf %>% fit (data = train_data) advantages one pipeline — preprocessing + model, no manual step-by-step reusable — swapping models requires only changing add_model() integrates with tune — pass directly to tune_grid() for hyperparameter search analogy a workflow plays the role of scikit-learn's pipeline: preprocessing and model travel together, and the whole object goes into cross-validation and tuning. workflows workflows: one object, no mismatch ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice fit recipe and model apart easy to apply different steps add_recipe + add_model one workflow object re-type steps for new data copy errors creep in fit() trains both parts prep and model together rebuild code to tune search setup is rewritten pass it to tune_grid() cross-validation just works result: train and test mismatch result: one reusable pipeline mistake pieces drift apart over time. best practice swap the model, keep the rest. rule bundle preprocessing and the model before you fit. three fixes to apply 1 bundle create one workflow(). 2 swap change only add_model(). 3 tune hand it to tune_grid().
m16-parsnip: definition parsnip uses one syntax to call any model. changing the model type means changing the model function, while the rest of the code stays the same. quick look a spec has three parts: type, engine and mode enlarge model type what kind of model rand_forest() 1 engine how it is computed set_engine("ranger") 2 mode which task set_mode("classification") 3 model spec a recipe for a model, not yet fitted 4 fit() / predict() the same calls for every spec fit(spec, y ~ ., train) 5 1 pick the model type names the family: logistic_reg() , rand_forest() , boost_tree() , svm_rbf() , ... 2 choose an engine the package that does the maths (glm, ranger, xgboost). swap it without changing your arguments. 3 set the mode classification or regression. some types support both, so say which. 4 you now hold a spec a description, not a trained model. printing it is free and shows what will happen. 5 same verbs for all fit() and predict() behave identically whichever model type sits inside. what it will look like argument names parsnip translates for you parsnip argument ranger randomforest what it controls mtry mtry mtry predictors tried at each split trees num.trees ntree number of trees min_n min.node.size nodesize smallest node that may split parsnip gives every engine the same argument names, then translates them for you. compare model families with the same recipe enlarge 0.00 0.25 0.50 0.75 1.00 cv roc auc logistic_reg glm: 0.81 0.81 logistic_reg glm rand_forest ranger: 0.86 0.86 rand_forest ranger boost_tree xgboost: 0.87 0.87 boost_tree xgboost illustrative: seeded synthetic data. shapes are realistic; values are examples, not results from your data. run it, then check the result inspect a spec before you fit it rf_spec <- rand_forest (trees = 500 ) %>% set_engine ( "ranger" ) %>% set_mode ( "classification" ) show_engines ( "rand_forest" ) # which engines exist for this model type translate (rf_spec) # the exact call parsnip will make show_engines() then translate() illustrative output: structure matches what r prints; numbers are examples. # a tibble: 3 x 2 engine mode <chr> <chr> 1 ranger classification 2 ranger regression 3 randomforest classification random forest model specification (classification) main arguments: trees = 500 computational engine: ranger model fit template: ranger::ranger(x = missing_arg(), y = missing_arg(), num.trees = 500, num.threads = 1, verbose = false, seed = sample.int(10^5, 1), probability = true) why this matters: trees = 500 became num.trees = 500 and probability = true was added for you. you never write engine syntax. what this solves for the business 01 compare many algorithms fairly one interface means every candidate gets the same data, folds and metrics. apples to apples 02 lower training cost for new analysts learn one syntax instead of one per package. faster onboarding 03 engine swaps without rewrites move from glm to glmnet or ranger to xgboost by changing one string. less rework do this next create three specs for one task done when: logistic, forest and boosted specs all print without error. run translate() on each done when: you can say what engine argument each parsnip argument became. fit all three on the same folds done when: one metric table lists the three models. core syntax library (parsnip) # logistic regression log_spec <- logistic_reg () %>% set_engine ( "glm" ) %>% set_mode ( "classification" ) # random forest (swap model = swap function) rf_spec <- rand_forest (trees = 500 ) %>% set_engine ( "ranger" ) %>% set_mode ( "classification" ) # xgboost xgb_spec <- boost_tree (trees = 1000 ) %>% set_engine ( "xgboost" ) %>% set_mode ( "classification" ) supported model range model type function linear regression linear_reg() logistic regression logistic_reg() decision tree decision_tree() random forest rand_forest() xgboost boost_tree() svm svm_rbf() knn nearest_neighbor() neural network mlp() naive bayes naive_bayes() (discrim package) lda discrim_linear() (discrim package) bart bart() because every model shares one interface, you can compare many algorithms (random forest, xgboost, svm, logistic regression, knn, neural network and more) with the same recipe and the same resamples. comparison parsnip gives many engines one consistent interface, much like scikit-learn's estimator api. parsnip parsnip: one interface for many models ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice learn each package's syntax glm, ranger, xgboost all differ pick a model function logistic_reg, rand_forest rewrite code to try a model slow, risky comparisons choose the engine set_engine("ranger") hard-code one engine locked into a single package set the mode regression or classification result: slow model comparison result: models swapped in one line mistake every new model means new code. best practice comparison takes minutes, not hours. rule describe the model once and let parsnip translate it. three fixes to apply 1 specify name the model type. 2 engine pick the package behind it. 3 mode state the problem type.
m16-yardstick: definition yardstick provides a consistent evaluation metric api. all metrics return the same tibble format for easy comparison. quick look one metric api, one tidy result enlarge accuracy share of all predictions correct (tp+tn) / all 1 precision of cases flagged, how many were real tp / (tp+fp) 2 recall of real cases, how many were found tp / (tp+fn) 3 roc_auc how well scores rank real above not-real 0.5 = coin, 1 = perfect 4 every metric returns one tidy tibble .metric .estimator .estimate 5 1 accuracy hides imbalance if 95% of rows are negative, a model that always says "negative" scores 95%. never report accuracy alone. 2 precision protects against false alarms raise it when a flagged case triggers expensive action (an audit, a call, a recall). 3 recall protects against misses raise it when missing a real case is costly (fraud, disease, churn of a top customer). 4 roc auc compares rankings threshold-free, so good for choosing between models. it does not tell you which cut-off to use. 5 one shape for all because every metric returns the same tibble, you can bind rows, plot with ggplot2 and compare models directly. what it will look like what a roc curve looks like enlarge 0.00 0.25 0.50 0.75 1.00 0.00 0.25 0.50 0.75 1.00 false positive rate (1 - specificity) true positive rate (recall) default cut-off: recall 69%, false alarms 23% illustrative: seeded synthetic data. shapes are realistic; values are examples, not results from your data. the marked point is one cut-off on the curve; moving the cut-off slides along it. numbers match the matrix and table below. the confusion matrix at the default cut-off enlarge predicted positive negative actual positive negative true positive: 540 540 true positive false negative: 237 237 false negative false positive: 398 398 false positive true negative: 1325 1,325 true negative precision 58% of flagged, how many real recall 69% of real, how many found accuracy 75% share correct overall f1 0.63 balance of the two illustrative: seeded synthetic data. shapes are realistic; values are examples, not results from your data. orange cells are the errors that cost money; decide which of the two matters more. run it, then check the result score a model with a metric set, then look at the errors library (tidymodels) preds <- predict (wine_fit, test_data, type = "prob" ) %>% bind_cols ( predict (wine_fit, test_data)) %>% bind_cols (test_data %>% select (quality_fct)) class_metrics <- metric_set (accuracy, precision, recall, roc_auc) class_metrics (preds, truth = quality_fct, estimate = .pred_class, .pred_good, event_level = "second" ) conf_mat (preds, truth = quality_fct, estimate = .pred_class) roc_curve (preds, truth = quality_fct, .pred_good, event_level = "second" ) %>% autoplot () metric tibble and confusion matrix illustrative output: structure matches what r prints; numbers are examples. # a tibble: 4 x 3 .metric .estimator .estimate <chr> <chr> <dbl> 1 accuracy binary 0.746 2 precision binary 0.576 3 recall binary 0.695 4 roc_auc binary 0.808 truth prediction bad good bad 1325 237 good 398 540 what this solves for the business 01 price the error, not the average precision and recall map to real costs (wasted outreach vs missed cases). choose the cut-off from those costs. decision-ready metrics 02 fair model comparison one metric set applied to every candidate stops "my model looks better" from depending on how it was scored. defensible selection 03 metrics that plot themselves tidy tibbles go straight into ggplot2 for stakeholder charts. less manual charting do this next define the metric set before modelling done when: a metric_set() is in the script and the primary metric is stated. write down the cost of a false alarm and a miss done when: the two costs appear in the readme with numbers or ranges. pick the cut-off from those costs done when: the chosen threshold and its confusion matrix are saved with the model. report accuracy only next to recall and precision done when: no results table lists accuracy by itself. core syntax library (yardstick) # predict predictions <- wine_fit %>% predict (new_data = test_data) %>% bind_cols (test_data) # metrics (returns tibble) predictions %>% metrics (truth = quality_fct, estimate = .pred_class) # multi-class confusion matrix predictions %>% conf_mat (truth = quality_fct, estimate = .pred_class) common metrics function metric accuracy() accuracy sens() / spec() sensitivity / specificity precision() / recall() precision / recall f_meas() f1 score roc_auc() roc-auc mn_log_loss() multi-class log loss advantage yardstick metrics handle multi-class problems and class weights. with resampling, collect_metrics() gives means and standard errors. returned tibbles plot directly with ggplot2. yardstick yardstick: score models the same way ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice report accuracy alone misleads on imbalanced classes use a metric set accuracy, recall, roc_auc write custom metric code different shapes, hard to join read one tidy tibble easy to compare and plot score on training data optimistic, not real score on held-out data test set or resamples result: misleading model scores result: fair, comparable scores mistake a good number that hides real errors. best practice same format for every model. rule pick metrics that match the cost of each mistake. three fixes to apply 1 metric set choose several metrics. 2 held out score unseen data only. 3 plot send the tibble to ggplot2.
m16-stacking: definition the tidymodels family supports stacking through the stacks package: predictions from multiple models become features fed into a meta-model (usually a regularized linear model). quick look stacking: models feed a meta-model that blends them enlarge decision tree candidate 1 1 svm candidate 2 1 random forest candidate 3 1 stacks() collect each candidate's out-of-fold predictions add_candidates() 2 blend_predictions() a lasso keeps useful members, drops the rest penalty tuned 3 fit_members() refit the kept members on all training data final_stack 4 1 candidates must save predictions use control_stack_resamples() so each model keeps its out-of-fold predictions. 2 predictions become features each candidate's out-of-fold prediction is a column. the meta-model learns from those columns. 3 a regularised blend picks members the lasso gives some members zero weight. fewer members means a lighter pipeline. 4 refit and ship only retained members are refit, so scoring cost depends on the survivors. what it will look like which members survive enlarge 0 0.2 0.4 0.6 0.8 blend weight (non-negative, from the lasso) random forest random forest: 0.62 0.62 svm svm: 0.31 0.31 decision tree decision tree: 0.00 0.00 dropped illustrative: seeded synthetic data. shapes are realistic; values are examples, not results from your data. how much the stack actually adds enlarge 0.000 0.250 0.500 0.750 1.000 cv roc auc decision tree: 0.824 0.824 decision tree svm: 0.881 0.881 svm random forest: 0.903 0.903 random forest stack: 0.906 0.906 stack +0.003 over the best single model illustrative: seeded synthetic data. shapes are realistic; values are examples, not results from your data. a lift this small rarely justifies the extra complexity. run it, then check the result build, blend and inspect a stack library (tidymodels); library (stacks) multi_wf <- workflow_set (preproc = list (wine_recipe), models = list (dt_spec, svm_spec, rf_spec)) multi_res <- multi_wf %>% workflow_map ( "fit_resamples" , resamples = folds, control = control_stack_resamples ()) multi_stack <- stacks () %>% add_candidates (multi_res) %>% blend_predictions () multi_stack # how many members survived? final_stack <- fit_members (multi_stack) print(multi_stack) illustrative output: structure matches what r prints; numbers are examples. -- a stacked ensemble model --------------------------------------- out of 3 possible candidate members, the ensemble retained 2. penalty: 0.01. mixture: 1. # a tibble: 2 x 3 member type weight <chr> <chr> <dbl> 1 rand_forest_1_1 rand_forest 0.62 2 svm_rbf_1_1 svm_rbf 0.31 decision rule: if the stack beats the best single model by less than about 1%, ship the single model. kaggle can run 50 models; production cannot. what this solves for the business 01 know when complexity pays measure the lift against the cost of maintaining several models. most of the time the answer is "ship the best single model". less technical debt 02 fewer moving parts in production the lasso drops weak members, so only models that earn their weight are deployed. lighter pipeline 03 explainability budget a single model can be explained to a regulator; a stack needs extra work. count that cost before you stack. audit effort do this next fit the best single model and record its score done when: one cv score is saved as the bar to beat. build the stack with the same folds done when: print(multi_stack) shows how many members were retained. compute the lift done when: the difference in score is written as a percentage next to the maintenance cost. apply the 1% rule done when: a one-line decision (ship single or ship stack) is recorded with the reason. syntax library (tidymodels) library (stacks) # 1. define multiple workflows multi_wf <- workflow_set ( preproc = list (wine_recipe), models = list (dt_spec, svm_spec, rf_spec) ) # 2. evaluate on resamples (keep predictions for stacking) multi_res <- multi_wf %>% workflow_map ( "fit_resamples" , resamples = folds, control = control_stack_resamples ()) # 3. blend the candidates multi_stack <- stacks () %>% add_candidates (multi_res) %>% blend_predictions () # 4. fit the chosen members final_stack <- multi_stack %>% fit_members () empirical result in many real projects the lift from stacking is small (for example a few thousandths of r²). the lift is often tiny, but the cost is a large drop in interpretability and a heavier pipeline to maintain. always weigh whether the small accuracy gain is worth that loss. rule of thumb if stacking lifts the metric by less than about 1%, ship the single best model. kaggle can use 50 models; production cannot. stacking stacking: only if the lift is worth it ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice stack by default heavier pipeline for little gain compare against a single model measure the real lift ignore interpretability hard to explain to others weigh gain vs explainability decide with the team add models until it stops more upkeep, more risk ship the simpler model unless the lift is large result: complex model, tiny gain result: justified complexity mistake complexity that no one can explain. best practice stack only when it pays for itself. rule of thumb under about 1% lift, ship the single best model. three fixes to apply 1 baseline always keep a simple model. 2 measure compare with resamples. 3 decide weigh lift against cost.
m16-mlr3-overview: definition mlr3 is r's framework for large-scale benchmarking and custom pipelines. more modular and flexible than tidymodels, but with a steeper learning curve. quick look mlr3 is built from swappable parts enlarge task the data plus the goal tsk("german_credit") 1 learner the algorithm lrn("classif.ranger") 2 resampling how to split rsmp("cv", folds = 5) 3 measure how to score msr("classif.auc") 4 resample() runs the learner on every split and scores it resample(task, learner, resampling) 5 resampleresult scores and predictions, per fold rr$aggregate(measure) 6 1 task holds data and target built-in tasks ( tsk("iris") ) or your own with as_task_classif(df, target = "y") . 2 learner is the algorithm over 100 learners share one interface: lrn("classif.rpart") , lrn("regr.ranger") , ... 3 resampling is the split rule cross-validation, bootstrap, holdout, repeated cv. it is an object, so you can reuse it for every learner. 4 measure is the score auc, accuracy, rmse, or your own. pass it only when you aggregate. 5 resample() joins them trains a clone of the learner on each training split and predicts on each test split. 6 resampleresult keeps everything per-fold scores, predictions and the warnings or errors, so nothing is hidden behind one average. what it will look like what resample() gives you back enlarge 0.000 0.250 0.500 0.750 1.000 auc fold 1: 0.791 0.791 fold 1 fold 2: 0.768 0.768 fold 2 fold 3: 0.802 0.802 fold 3 fold 4: 0.775 0.775 fold 4 fold 5: 0.794 0.794 fold 5 mean 0.786 illustrative: seeded synthetic data. shapes are realistic; values are examples, not results from your data. the r6 trap to avoid easy mistake with r6 objects ✗ copy a learner with = lrn2 = lrn1 points at the same object. setting a parameter on one changes the other. ✗ compare learners that share state results look different yet both used the last parameters you set. use $clone() ✓ make a real copy lrn2 = lrn1$clone() gives an independent learner you can change safely. ✓ build learners with lrn() each time calling lrn() again always returns a fresh object. run it, then check the result assemble the four parts and run them library (mlr3verse) task = tsk ( "german_credit" ) # 1000 rows, credit risk learner = lrn ( "classif.ranger" , predict_type = "prob" ) resampling = rsmp ( "cv" , folds = 5 ) measure = msr ( "classif.auc" ) rr = resample (task, learner, resampling) # the whole experiment rr$ score (measure)[, .(iteration, classif.auc)] # one row per fold rr$ aggregate (measure) # the mean per-fold scores and the mean illustrative output: structure matches what r prints; numbers are examples. iteration classif.auc 1: 1 0.791 2: 2 0.768 3: 3 0.802 4: 4 0.775 5: 5 0.794 classif.auc 0.786 check: five rows for five folds. if the spread between folds is large (here 0.768 to 0.802), quote the range, not only the mean. what this solves for the business 01 swap any part without rewriting change the learner, the split or the metric in one line. the experiment code stays identical. cheap what-ifs 02 per-fold evidence seeing every fold exposes unstable models that a single average would hide. fewer surprises in production 03 scales to large studies the same four objects drive a 4-model test or a 400-model benchmark. one pattern for all sizes do this next build a task from your own table done when: task$nrow and task$feature_names match your data. run one learner with 5-fold cv done when: rr$score() returns five rows and you record the mean and range. practise $clone() done when: you can show a case where = shares state and $clone() does not. core design built on r6 objects — object-oriented, reference semantics depends on data.table — better performance on large datasets modular — every component (task, learner, measure) independently swappable benchmarking-first — native support for large-scale model comparison mlr3verse meta-package install.packages("mlr3verse") installs mlr3 plus all important extension packages. relationship with tidymodels dimension tidymodels mlr3 learning curve gentle (tidyverse users) steeper (r6 + data.table) benchmarking adequate specialty documentation excellent good but more technical community size larger academic-focused choice guidance use tidymodels for daily ml. use mlr3 when comparing many models, running large-scale benchmarks, or building custom pipelines. mlr3 mlr3: build from swappable parts ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice treat mlr3 like tidymodels the objects work differently define a task and a learner data and algorithm as objects ignore reference semantics r6 objects change in place choose resampling and measure split and score on purpose use it for a quick one-off more set-up than needed clone objects before editing avoid surprise changes result: confusion and bugs result: flexible, scalable runs mistake familiar habits that do not apply. best practice every part can be replaced. rule think in objects: task, learner, resampling, measure. three fixes to apply 1 task wrap the data. 2 learner pick the algorithm. 3 measure choose the score.
m16-mlr3-benchmark: definition mlr3's benchmark feature lets you compare multiple models under the same resampling scheme, with automatic result aggregation. quick look same splits for everyone makes the comparison fair enlarge 3 tasks datasets a, b, c tsks(c("a","b","c")) 1 4 learners tree, forest, boosting, svm lrns(c("classif.rpart", ...)) 1 1 resampling 5-fold cv, shared by all rsmp("cv", folds = 5) 2 benchmark_grid() every task x every learner, same splits 3 x 4 = 12 experiments 3 benchmark() 12 x 5 folds = 60 model fits plan(multisession) 4 bmr$aggregate() one tidy table, one row per experiment autoplot(bmr) 5 1 pick tasks and learners list every dataset and every model you want compared. add or drop any without changing the rest. 2 one resampling for everyone all learners see exactly the same train/test splits, which is what makes the comparison fair. 3 the grid is the design benchmark_grid() builds the full experiment table before anything runs. check its row count first. 4 run in parallel set a future plan and the 60 fits spread over your cores. 5 aggregate and plot bmr$aggregate() gives means; autoplot(bmr) shows spread. read both. what it will look like the result as a heat map enlarge task a task b task c rpart rpart / task a: 0.80 0.80 rpart / task b: 0.78 0.78 rpart / task c: 0.83 0.83 ranger ranger / task a: 0.88 0.88 ranger / task b: 0.86 0.86 ranger / task c: 0.90 0.90 xgboost xgboost / task a: 0.89 0.89 xgboost / task b: 0.85 0.85 xgboost / task c: 0.91 0.91 svm svm / task a: 0.84 0.84 svm / task b: 0.82 0.82 svm / task c: 0.86 0.86 illustrative: seeded synthetic data. shapes are realistic; values are examples, not results from your data. outlined cells are best per task. spread matters as much as the mean enlarge 0.75 0.80 0.85 0.90 0.95 accuracy across 5 folds on task a (dot = mean, line = range) ranger ranger: 0.88 (0.85 to 0.91) 0.88 xgboost xgboost: 0.89 (0.84 to 0.93) 0.89 svm svm: 0.84 (0.81 to 0.87) 0.84 rpart rpart: 0.80 (0.75 to 0.85) 0.80 illustrative: seeded synthetic data. shapes are realistic; values are examples, not results from your data. overlapping ranges mean no clear winner. run it, then check the result run a benchmark and read the table library (mlr3verse) future:: plan ( "multisession" ) # use all cores tasks = tsks ( c ( "iris" , "sonar" , "wine" )) learners = lrns ( c ( "classif.rpart" , "classif.ranger" , "classif.xgboost" , "classif.svm" )) resampling = rsmp ( "cv" , folds = 5 ) design = benchmark_grid (tasks, learners, resampling) nrow (design) # 3 x 4 = 12 experiments bmr = benchmark (design) bmr$ aggregate ( msr ( "classif.acc" ))[, .(task_id, learner_id, classif.acc)] nrow(design) then the aggregated table illustrative output: structure matches what r prints; numbers are examples. [1] 12 task_id learner_id classif.acc 1: iris classif.rpart 0.940 2: iris classif.ranger 0.953 3: iris classif.xgboost 0.947 4: iris classif.svm 0.960 5: sonar classif.rpart 0.706 ... ... 12: wine classif.svm 0.978 read it: compare learners within a task, not across tasks. a learner that wins one task by 0.01 and loses another by 0.02 has no clear edge. what this solves for the business 01 model choice you can defend every candidate was tested on identical splits with one metric, so the winner is a result, not a preference. defensible selection 02 find the cheap model that is good enough seeing accuracy next to run time shows when a small model is enough. lower serving cost 03 reusable evaluation harness add a new learner or dataset and re-run the same design. last quarter's comparison stays comparable. less rework do this next list the tasks and learners to compare done when: a table of 3 or more learners and 1 or more tasks is in the project notes. print the grid size before running done when: nrow(design) times folds equals the fits you budgeted for. run and plot with spread done when: autoplot(bmr) is saved next to the aggregate table. write the decision done when: the chosen learner and the reason (score, range, cost) are recorded. syntax library (mlr3verse) # 1. define task task <- tsk ( "iris" ) # 2. define learners learners <- lrns ( "classif.rpart" , "classif.ranger" , "classif.xgboost" , "classif.svm" ) # 3. define resampling resampling <- rsmp ( "cv" , folds = 5 ) # 4. benchmark design <- benchmark_grid ( tasks = task, learners = learners, resamplings = resampling ) bmr <- benchmark (design) # 5. aggregate bmr$ aggregate () bmr$ aggregate (measures = msr ( "classif.acc" )) mlr3 benchmarking advantages parallelization — multi-core runs through the future package nested resampling — for hyperparameter tuning result objects — directly visualizable or exportable scale — built to compare many learners across many tasks scenario when you need to answer "which model is best for this problem" rather than "run a model," use mlr3's benchmark. benchmarking benchmark: compare under the same splits ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice each model uses its own split scores are not comparable benchmark_grid() sets the plan tasks, learners, resamplings compare one run only luck decides the winner run with one resampling same folds for every learner write a loop by hand slow and hard to extend aggregate() the results one table of scores result: unfair comparison result: fair, repeatable ranking mistake a winner picked by chance or by split. best practice every model faces the same test. rule same data, same splits, same metric for every model. three fixes to apply 1 grid build the design first. 2 parallel run in parallel with the future package. 3 aggregate summarise with one call.

values are examples, not results from your data. 1 title block from yaml title, author, date and theme come from the header, not from typing into a layout. 2 chunk options control the code #| echo: false hides code for executives;
