m12x-survival: the idea churn, failure and default are time-to-event questions: the answer is a date, not a yes or no. survival analysis models time until the event and keeps rows where it has not happened yet . those are censored : lasted at least 400 days, end unknown. censoring: c and e have not churned yet five customers, one year of observation a b c d e join churn event still active logistic regression sees only yes/no and must guess what to do with c and e when to use it timing is the decision — act at month 9 or at month 30. follow-up is uneven — last month's accounts cannot have churned at 12 months. the event happens once — first failure, first default. you want a curve — share still active at every horizon, not one number. why a classifier throws the clock away logistic regression needs time collapsed into a label like churned in 90 days . younger accounts have no honest label: drop them and you lose your newest customers, code them 0 and you assert a survival you never observed. day 3 and day 89 then look identical. kaplan-meier estimates the curve directly, counting censored rows up to the moment they leave view. cox adds covariates: exp(coef) is a hazard ratio, so 1.4 means that group hits the event at 1.4 times the rate at any instant, assuming only that the ratio holds over time. approach censored rows output logistic flag dropped or mislabelled one probability kaplan-meier counted to last contact curve, no drivers cox ph counted to last contact hazard ratio per driver weibull aft counted to last contact expected time to event from lifelines import kaplanmeierfitter, coxphfitter # churned = 1 if the event was seen, 0 if still active km = kaplanmeierfitter ().fit(df.tenure_days, df.churned) print(km.median_survival_time_) cols = ["tenure_days", "churned", "plan", "spend"] cox = coxphfitter ().fit(df[cols], duration_col="tenure_days", event_col="churned") cox.print_summary() # exp(coef) = hazard ratio cox.check_assumptions(df[cols]) cox.predict_survival_function(new_accounts) the caution censoring must be uninformative: rows deleted because they churned are missing events, not censored, and every curve turns optimistic. check proportional hazards before quoting a ratio, and remember a hazard ratio is a rate ratio, not a probability. survival analysis logistic throws the clock away ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice collapse time to a 0/1 label day 3 and day 89 look the same model time until the event kaplan-meier gives a curve drop accounts under 90 days your newest customers vanish keep censored rows censored they count to last contact code still-active as survived asserts a year nobody observed cox for the drivers exp(coef) is a hazard ratio result: the timing signal is lost result: when, not just whether mistake half the cohort is too young to have a label. best practice every row counts for the time it was watched. rule of thumb if the answer is a date, do not fit a yes/no model. three fixes to apply 1 censor it mark not-yet-churned as censored, never as zero. 2 plot km first curve by segment before you model anything. 3 check ph test proportional hazards before quoting ratios.
m12x-hierarchical: the idea business data is nested: weeks inside stores, visits inside patients. rows from one group resemble each other, which breaks the independence assumption. a mixed-effects model adds a random intercept per group — one shared slope plus a group offset, each offset shrunk toward zero when that group has little data. partial pooling sits between the two extremes pool everything one line for all stores fit each alone noisy on small stores partial pooling shrunk to the average small groups borrow strength from the overall average when to use it repeated measures — many rows per store, patient or region. very uneven group sizes — one store with 104 weeks, another with 9. many groups, few rows — 300 schools, far too many for 300 fits. the group is the question — how much variation sits between groups. why both obvious options fail complete pooling ignores the group, so 104 correlated weeks count as 104 independent facts and standard errors come out far too small. no pooling — a fit per group, or an unshrunk dummy each — gives the nine-week store a coefficient driven by noise that you act on because it looks dramatic. partial pooling is the correct answer, not a compromise: the model estimates a between-group and a within-group variance, then pulls each group toward the overall mean by an amount set by that ratio and the group's size. the icc , between over total variance, says how much grouping mattered. strategy small groups risk complete pooling absorbed into the mean errors far too small one fit per group fit to noise wild, unstable estimates unshrunk dummies fit to noise hundreds of thin terms random intercept pulled to the mean needs enough groups import statsmodels.formula.api as smf # one shared promo effect, one intercept offset per store fit = smf. mixedlm ("sales ~ promo + sq_ft", df, groups=df.store_id).fit() btw, wtn = float(fit.cov_re.iloc[0, 0]), float(fit.scale) print("icc", round(btw / (btw + wtn), 3)) print(fit.random_effects["s03"]) # shrunken offset # let the promo effect itself vary by store smf. mixedlm ("sales ~ promo", df, groups=df.store_id, re_formula="~promo").fit() rules of thumb you need enough groups , not just rows — with four or five stores use a fixed effect instead. scale continuous predictors before adding random slopes or the fit will not converge. a singular fit, group variance estimated at zero, says the grouping explains nothing. hierarchical models one model is wrong, 300 are worse ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice pool every store together store differences vanish random intercept per group shared slope plus an offset fit one model per store nine-week stores fit noise let partial pooling shrink small groups move inward dummy per group, no shrinkage hundreds of thin estimates report the icc variance share between groups result: confident and unstable result: borrowed strength mistake a nine-row store gets its own wild coefficient. best practice thin groups lean on the overall pattern. rule of thumb fewer rows per group means shrink harder. three fixes to apply 1 name the group declare store_id before you fit anything. 2 start simple random intercept first, slopes only if needed. 3 read the icc near zero means pooling was fine after all.
m12x-causal: the idea a predictive model answers what will happen ; a causal question asks what would happen if we intervened . a coefficient fitted for the first does not answer the second. a confounder drives both treatment and outcome; omit it and the estimate absorbs its effect. a confounder feeds both the cause and the effect store size confounder z ad spend treatment x sales outcome y adjust for z, or the x arrow absorbs its effect when to use it someone will act on it — if it moves a budget, it is a causal claim. no experiment was possible — the discount was not randomised. treatment was self-selected — opt-ins differ from the rest. you have a before and after — plus a group never treated. why a strong predictor is not an effect a predictive fit minimises error and will happily use a mediator sitting downstream of the outcome, or a collider caused by both. adding one improves prediction and corrupts the effect, so the control set comes from reasoning about what causes what, not from feature importance. propensity-score matching models the chance of treatment from pre-treatment covariates, then pairs each treated unit with an untreated one equally likely to be treated; what matters is the balance check afterwards. difference-in-differences instead compares the change in the treated group with the change in an untreated one, so anything hitting both cancels. design key assumption gives controls only all confounders seen adjusted association ps matching no hidden confounding effect on matched diff-in-diff parallel pre-trends effect on treated import pandas as pd, statsmodels.formula.api as smf from sklearn.linear_model import logisticregression from sklearn.neighbors import nearestneighbors # confounders must predate treatment ps = logisticregression ().fit(d[conf], d.treated) d["ps"] = ps.predict_proba(d[conf])[:, 1] t, c = d[d.treated == 1], d[d.treated == 0] _, i = nearestneighbors (1).fit(c[["ps"]]).kneighbors(t[["ps"]]) m = pd.concat([t, c.iloc[i.ravel()]]) print(m.groupby("treated")[conf].mean()) # balance first # did: the interaction term is the estimate did = smf. ols ("revenue ~ treated * post", panel).fit() print(did.params["treated:post"]) the caution matching only balances what you measured; it cannot fix a confounder you never recorded. never match on anything measured after treatment began, and never trust a diff-in-differences whose pre-trends were already diverging. causal estimates a strong predictor is not a cause ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice read coefficients as effects fitted to predict, not explain state the causal question treatment, outcome, controls add every available column mediators and colliders too match, then prove balance std diff small on every one compare treated to untreated the groups never matched difference-in-differences trend before, trend after result: a confounded number result: a defensible estimate mistake discount users already bought more anyway. best practice show parallel trends in the pre-period. rule of thumb no balance check means no causal claim. three fixes to apply 1 draw it first sketch what causes what, then pick controls. 2 check balance compare covariates after matching, before effects. 3 plot pre-trend both groups, before the change landed.
m12x-timeseries-reg: the idea when rows are ordered in time, yesterday carries information about today. you exploit that with lag and rolling features, and pay twice: residuals stop being independent, and a random split trains the model on the future. one rule fixes both — respect the ordering. split by time, never at random random split lets the model see the future time rolling origin keeps every test after its training 1 2 3 train test when to use it every row has a timestamp and nearby rows are related. the recent past predicts — demand, traffic, spend, sensors. you need drivers too — price and promotion beside the lags. the model runs forward — scored on data that did not exist yet. shift first, then backtest a lag is the target shifted back: lag_1 is yesterday, lag_7 last week's same weekday. a rolling window must end before the row it describes, so rolling(28).mean() on the raw column leaks — it includes today. shift, then roll. autocorrelation is the second cost: correlated residuals shrink standard errors, so a weak predictor looks significant, and a spike at lag 7 in the residual acf reveals a weekly pattern still unmodelled. a shuffled split then puts december in training and january in test. rolling-origin backtesting trains to a cut, tests the block just after, then moves the cut. split train window verdict random k-fold scattered, holds future leaks; score is fiction rolling, expanding everything to the cut honest; like retraining rolling, sliding recent window only use when old data is stale from sklearn.model_selection import timeseriessplit from sklearn.linear_model import ridge from statsmodels.graphics.tsaplots import plot_acf d = d.sort_values("date") d["lag_1"] = d.units.shift(1) d["lag_7"] = d.units.shift(7) d["roll_28"] = d.units.shift(1).rolling(28).mean() # shift first d = d.dropna() # each fold tests the 28 days after its training cut for tr, te in timeseriessplit (5, test_size=28).split(x): f = ridge ().fit(x.iloc[tr], y.iloc[tr]) print((y.iloc[te] - f.predict(x.iloc[te])).abs().mean()) plot_acf (y - f.predict(x), lags=40) the caution beyond one step ahead lag_1 does not exist at scoring time — you would feed the model its own prediction and errors compound. build features at the horizon you need, and match the training-to-test gap to your real reporting delay. time-structured regression a random split trains on the future ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice shuffle the rows, then split december teaches january sort by date, then build features end at t minus one rolling(28) on the raw column the target explains itself shift before you roll the window closes yesterday assume residuals independent autocorrelation shrinks ses backtest on rolling origin train past, test next block result: a score you cannot keep result: the score survives launch mistake error doubles the first week after launch. best practice each fold ends where the next one starts. rule of thumb never let a model see a later timestamp. three fixes to apply 1 sort first order by date before any feature is built. 2 shift then roll every window ends at t minus one. 3 rolling origin timeseriessplit, never a shuffled kfold.
m12x-bayesian: the idea a bayesian regression returns a distribution over coefficients, not one best fit. you state a prior — what is plausible before the data — the likelihood supplies the evidence, and the result is the posterior , summarised by a credible interval . prior and data combine into a posterior prior likelihood (data) posterior 95% credible interval the parameter is in here with 95% probability when to use it the sample is small — forty rows per channel, one pilot. you know something already — prior studies, physical limits. the decision needs a probability — the chance the effect is positive. uncertainty must travel — the estimate feeds a cost model. what the prior buys, what the interval means a weakly informative prior is a constraint, not a thumb on the scale: on standardised predictors a normal centred at zero with modest spread says enormous effects are unlikely. with plenty of data the likelihood dominates and the posterior lands where least squares did; with little data the prior rules out absurd values a flat fit would entertain, narrowing the interval and shrinking wild estimates toward zero. a 95% confidence interval describes the procedure: repeat the study and 95% of such intervals cover the truth. you may not say this one has a 95% chance of holding it. a 94% credible interval says exactly that. aspect frequentist bayesian result estimate plus error posterior per term interval about the procedure about this parameter prior knowledge not expressible stated, auditable small samples wide or unstable regularised by prior import bambi as bmb, arviz as az model = bmb. model ("uplift ~ channel + spend_z", df) # weakly informative: big effects allowed, not favoured model.set_priors({"channel": bmb. prior ("normal", mu=0, sigma=0.5)}) idata = model.fit(draws=2000, chains=4, random_seed=42) # r_hat near 1.00 or the chains did not converge print(az. summary (idata, hdi_prob=0.94)) # posterior probability the effect is positive draws = idata.posterior["channel"].values.ravel() print((draws > 0).mean()) practical notes always report the priors you used; an unstated prior is an unauditable assumption. check convergence first — r-hat near 1.00, no divergences, overlapping chains. then refit with a wider prior: if the conclusion flips, the data is too thin to support it. bayesian regression a credible interval answers the question ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice read a 95% ci as a chance that is not what it says weakly informative priors absurd values ruled out flat priors on forty rows intervals too wide to use keep the whole posterior a distribution per term report one point estimate the uncertainty disappears quote a credible interval 0.94 chance it is in here result: overstated precision result: honest on small samples mistake forty rows gave a huge interval nobody read. best practice you can also read the chance the effect helps. rule of thumb small samples: say what you assume up front. three fixes to apply 1 set a prior normal(0, 1) beats flat on scaled predictors. 2 check r-hat near 1.00 or the chains never converged. 3 show the interval report the range, not just the mean.
m12x-monitoring: the idea a model is not finished at launch; it starts decaying. monitoring watches three streams: the inputs arriving, the predictions going out, the outcomes coming back. the first two arrive at once, outcomes weeks later — so performance alone is too slow an alarm. watch inputs, predictions and outcomes together inputs feature drift predictions score shift outcomes true accuracy alert: inputs moved first when to use it anything scoring live traffic — an unmonitored model is risk. labels are delayed — defaults confirm themselves months later. upstream feeds change — a renamed column silently breaks a feature. the population shifts — a new market the model never saw. stability versus performance stability asks whether today's data looks like the training data. freeze a reference sample at launch, then compare each feature's live distribution against it — the population stability index is the usual summary. score drift applies the same test to the model's own output and is often the earliest signal, because it aggregates every input. performance asks whether the model is still right, and only matured rows can answer. drift without decay is common and no reason to act; decay without drift means the relationship changed, which retraining will not fix. stream watch action inputs drift, nulls, new levels fix the feed predictions score spread, approval rate investigate early outcomes auc, error, calibration retrain or roll back operations latency, fallback rate engineering fix import numpy as np def psi (ref, live, bins=10): e = np.quantile(ref, np.linspace(0, 1, bins + 1)) e[0], e[-1] = -np.inf, np.inf a = np.histogram(ref, e)[0] / len(ref) + 1e-6 b = np.histogram(live, e)[0] / len(live) + 1e-6 return float(((b - a) * np.log(b / a)).sum()) for col in features: print(col, round( psi (ref[col], live[col]), 3)) print( psi (ref_scores, live_scores)) # score drift m = live[live.label_ready] # outcomes only print( roc_auc_score (m.y, m.score)) the caution the psi bands usually quoted are a credit-scoring convention, not a law: calibrate thresholds against your own stable history. never score performance on immature rows, or you will mistake a reporting lag for sudden decay. agree the rollback trigger before launch. model monitoring a model decays quietly after launch ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice watch accuracy only labels arrive months late track inputs and scores both move before outcomes no input monitoring a renamed field goes unseen separate drift from decay drift alone is not damage retrain on every wobble you chase noise each week write the rollback rule threshold, owner, action result: silent failure for months result: you see it in week one mistake nulls jumped in week 6 and nobody looked. best practice input drift is the earliest warning there is. rule of thumb monitor what arrives now, not what arrives late. three fixes to apply 1 freeze a baseline keep the launch sample as the reference. 2 psi the inputs compare live bins to the frozen reference. 3 agree rollback set the trigger before you ever need it.
m13x-imbalance: the idea rarity is a property of the problem, not a fault in the model. on a one-in-five-hundred base rate, accuracy is dominated by the majority class and the 0.5 cutoff was never chosen for this problem. fix the metric, then the threshold, and only then the training rows. threshold before resampling predicted probability for each class stays churns 0.50 default tuned move the threshold first. resampling changes the probabilities themselves. when to use it the rare class is the point — fraud, churn, failure, default. accuracy looks great — compare it with the constant predictor. someone acts on the score — the operating point beats the ranking. you need the probability itself — exactly where resampling hurts. three levers, in this order metric first. roc flatters: its false-positive rate has the whole majority class in the denominator, while precision divides by what you flagged — so use average precision, whose baseline is the positive rate. threshold second , because fitting changes the model but thresholding changes only the decision, so sweep it on a holdout. resampling last , and know what it costs: a model trained on balanced data learns the probability under the resampled prior, so every output comes back too high. the ranking survives; the numbers do not. lever changes probabilities move the threshold the decision only untouched class weights the loss shifted up smote, oversampling the training rows distorted by the prior undersampling drops real rows distorted, same cause # 1. metric: always read it against the base rate print(y_val.mean(), average_precision_score (y_val, p_val)) # 2. threshold: sweep it, do not inherit 0.5 prec, rec, thr = precision_recall_curve (y_val, p_val) ok = rec[:-1] >= 0.70 # illustrative recall target cut = thr[ok][prec[:-1][ok].argmax()] print((p_val >= cut).mean()) # flag rate at the new cutoff # 3. resampling, if at all: in the pipeline, never before the split pipeline ([("smote", smote()), ("clf", clf)]).fit(x_tr, y_tr) the caution resampling outside the training fold puts rows interpolated from validation points into training: the cv score climbs and production does not follow. and anything downstream that multiplies your probability by a cost or a balance will overstate it. imbalanced learning done right move the threshold before the data ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice report accuracy on 1 pct base a constant model scores 99 pct pick the metric first: pr, ap baseline is the positive rate reach for smote first probabilities stop being honest sweep the cutoff on a holdout cheapest lever: only the rule resample before the cv split synthetic rows leak into folds weights before resampling keeps every real row in train result: great cv, useless alerts result: honest score, chosen cutoff mistake the 0.5 cutoff was never chosen for this problem. best practice if you resample, then recalibrate on clean data. rule of thumb fix the metric and cutoff before the training rows. three fixes to apply 1 metric first average precision, not accuracy. 2 sweep the cutoff choose it on validation, not at 0.5. 3 pipeline it smote inside each fold, never before.
m13x-conformal: the idea split conformal wraps any fitted model in a set with a coverage guarantee. score each point of a held-out calibration set by how badly the model missed, take a quantile of those scores, and widen every prediction by it. the set then covers the truth at least 1 - alpha of the time, assuming only exchangeability. one quantile of the calibration errors sets the interval calibration residuals, sorted smallest to largest 90% quantile q prediction ± q covers the truth 90% of the time when to use it someone acts on the uncertainty — a quoted range, a reserve. no honest interval of its own — boosting, forests, nets. you distrust the one it has — a linear interval needs assumptions. you would rather abstain — a two-label set says a human is needed. the quantile, and what it does not promise split three ways: train, calibrate, test. define a nonconformity score that is large when the model did badly, compute it on the calibration rows, and take the quantile at ceil((n + 1) * (1 - alpha)) / n ; that correction is not cosmetic, since the plain 1 - alpha quantile under-covers. for regression the score is abs(y - yhat) , so the interval is yhat plus or minus q ; for classification it is one minus the true label's probability, and the set is every label above 1 - q . the guarantee is marginal — true on average, not in every subgroup. method score width adapts split, regression absolute residual no — one width quantile (cqr) distance outside band yes split, classes 1 minus true-label prob. weakly group-conditional either, but per group per group alpha = 0.10 # target coverage 90 percent def conformal_q (s, alpha): n = len(s) # not plain 1 - alpha return np.quantile(s, np.ceil((n + 1) * (1 - alpha)) / n) # calibration rows: unseen in fit, tuning, early stopping q = conformal_q (np.abs(y_cal - model.predict(x_cal)), alpha) yh = model.predict(x_new) covered = (y_new >= yh - q) & (y_new <= yh + q) for g in np.unique(grp): # marginal hides slices print(g, covered[grp == g].mean()) the caution calibrating on data the model touched — including through early stopping or a hyperparameter search — makes the residuals too small and the intervals too narrow. and marginal coverage is no per-group promise, so print it per slice. conformal prediction intervals coverage you can actually promise ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice trust the model native interval rests on assumptions, not data hold out a calibration set never seen in fit or tuning calibrate on the training set residuals there are too small score, then take the quantile add the width to any model read 95 pct as per subgroup a marginal average hides slices check coverage per slice or calibrate within groups result: intervals too narrow result: a distribution-free bound mistake nominal 95 pct, real coverage much lower. best practice any model, any loss, one held-out set. rule of thumb coverage is earned on data the model never saw. three fixes to apply 1 split three ways train, calibrate, test. keep them apart. 2 use the quantile ceil((n+1)(1-a))/n of the scores. 3 check slices marginal coverage can hide a bad group.
m13x-skew: the idea skew is a feature with one name and two implementations: in training a batch job over a warehouse table, in serving a request handler hitting a different source in a different language. the heading matches, the numbers do not, nothing complains — and the model you evaluated is not the model you deployed. the same feature computed two ways training serving warehouse table live api call ≠ pandas groupby hand-written sql ≠ full history last 24 hours ≠ one shared transformation, called by both paths when to use it offline and online disagree — and no data looks obviously broken. training is batch, serving live — two runtimes, two implementations. a feature is a window aggregate — counts and rates over 7 or 30 days. before launch — the replay test below costs an afternoon. three different things all called skew implementation skew: two codebases differing in details nobody wrote down — a left join yields null where a dictionary lookup yields 0 , and one path counts thirty calendar days where the other counts thirty active ones. both suites pass, each asserting its own behaviour against its own fixtures. point-in-time skew: the training row used a value not knowable at the decision moment, such as a lifetime count from today's snapshot — this inflates offline metrics most. upstream lag: a producer changes a unit, and serving sees it before the training table is rebuilt. symptom likely cause fix online weaker implementation skew replay served vectors a feature too strong point-in-time leak as-of join on decision time serving 0, training null null handling one transform decides # features.py - the only definition, imported by both paths def build_features (events, as_of): e = events[events.event_ts <= as_of] # point-in-time correct w = e[e.event_ts > as_of - pd.timedelta(days=30)] return w.groupby("cust_id").size().fillna(0) # missing: once # serving: log the values scored, not just the inputs log.write({"id": rid, "ts": now, "features": f.to_dict()}) # ci, daily: replay the logged vectors through the training path for r in served_log: off = build_features (warehouse, as_of=r["ts"]) assert r["features"] == off.loc[r["cust_id"]].to_dict() the caution unit tests never find this: both suites pass, because the bug lives in the gap between them. log the served feature values and replay them. shared code, as-of joins and a daily replay are three separate defences. training-serving skew one feature, two definitions ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice sql in training, python live two codebases, one name one transform module, shared training and serving call it nulls defaulted differently missing becomes 0, not nan feature store, one definition as-of joins for training rows train on a value not yet known no point-in-time join log the served feature vector replay it through training result: offline great, online worse result: same value on both paths mistake the metric never moves. only the outcome does. best practice a replay test catches what unit tests miss. rule of thumb a feature has one definition, or it has none. three fixes to apply 1 share the code import one function in both paths. 2 log and replay compare served vectors to recomputed ones. 3 as-of join only values knowable at decision time.
m13x-drift: two problems covariate drift means p(x) moved while the learned relationship still holds. concept drift means p(y | x) itself changed. covariate drift may cost nothing; concept drift always costs something, and the two look identical on an input dashboard — so an alert is a reason to investigate, not to retrain. two different failures, two different fixes covariate drift inputs move relationship still holds often: refresh the data concept drift inputs look normal relationship changed must: retrain or rebuild only labels reveal concept drift, and labels arrive late when to use it the model is live and unwatched — the usual state. labels arrive late — a default at ninety days, a churn at renewal. the environment moves — pricing, a channel, a policy. you are asked how often to retrain — and want a real answer. monitor in tiers, because the signals arrive at different times tier one, immediate: schema, types, null rates, category vocabularies, ranges. it needs no labels, catches most real incidents, and a breach should page. tier two: input distributions, via psi per feature or a domain classifier whose auc says if the periods are distinguishable. tier three: the score distribution and flag rate at your cutoff, the cheapest warning before labels land. tier four, delayed: performance by cohort, once labels mature — and concept drift shows nowhere else. signal detects before labels schema, nulls broken pipelines yes — an incident psi, domain clf. covariate drift yes, alerts easily score, flag rate behaviour change yes — best proxy calibration concept drift no def psi (ref, live, bins=10, eps=1e-6): # bin edges from the reference period only, then fixed e = np.quantile(ref, np.linspace(0, 1, bins + 1)) e[0], e[-1] = -np.inf, np.inf r = np.histogram(ref, bins=e)[0] / len(ref) + eps l = np.histogram(live, bins=e)[0] / len(live) + eps return float(np.sum((l - r) * np.log(l / r))) def trigger (m): if m["breach"]: return "page_on_call" if m["pr_auc"] < m["floor"]: return "retrain_now" if m["max_psi"] > 0.25: return "investigate" return "scheduled" if m["due"] else "hold" the caution the 0.25 above is a credit-risk rule of thumb, not a derived threshold. test three hundred features every morning at the five-percent level and you get alerts every morning, after which nobody reads them. and if the model chose who got a label, retraining on them teaches the next one this one's blind spots. drift detection and retraining not all drift hurts the model ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice alert on every feature shift 300 tests, daily false alarms tier it: schema, inputs, score then performance when labels auto-retrain on a drift alert covariate shift is often fine separate covariate from concept only one moves p(y given x) wait for labels to notice labels land 90 days later watch proxies in the label gap flag rate, score distribution result: noise, then a silent miss result: alerts people still read mistake concept drift is invisible in the inputs alone. best practice a drift alert opens an investigation, not a job. rule of thumb monitor what you can see before labels arrive. three fixes to apply 1 tier the signals schema, inputs, scores, then performance. 2 pick a trigger cadence plus a guardrail beats drift alone. 3 mind feedback your model shaped the labels you retrain on.
m13x-cost: the idea a probability is not a decision. acting costs c_fp when the case turns out negative; not acting costs c_fn when it turns out positive. so act when (1 - p) * c_fp < p * c_fn , which rearranges to p > c_fp / (c_fp + c_fn) . that ratio, not 0.5 , is the threshold. the cost of each mistake sets the threshold true negative no cost false negative cost of missing false positive cost of acting true positive value gained predicted no predicted yes actually no actually yes act when p > c(false positive) / ( c(fp) + c(fn) ) when to use it the two errors differ in cost — which is nearly always true. someone can state the costs — pinning them down often beats the model. you are asked where the cutoff goes — the answer is about costs. value varies per case — a small claim and a large one share no cutoff. what the formula needs, and what overrides it with an illustrative review cost of eight dollars against an illustrative average loss of four hundred, the threshold is 8 / 408 , roughly 0.02 — a long way from 0.5 , which is why inherited defaults are so wrong on rare-event problems. one threshold is only right when both costs are the same for every case, so once loss depends on exposure, rank by p times the amount: 0.04 on a large balance can outrank 0.30 on a small one. and capacity usually binds first — if the rule flags nine hundred and the team reviews three hundred, rank and fill the queue. situation rule what you need unequal costs cutoff at the ratio costs, calibration benefits too compare four cells a signed-off matrix value varies rank by p times value per-case amounts fixed capacity rank, take top n capacity, recomputed # illustrative, and from the business owner - not from you c_fp, c_fn = 8.0, 400.0 thr = c_fp / (c_fp + c_fn) # only the ratio matters # an ev rule on a miscalibrated p is confidently wrong print( brier_score_loss (y_val, p_val)) # confirm the cutoff by sweeping the realised cost def cost (y, p, t): f = p >= t return (f & (y == 0)).sum() * c_fp + (~f & (y == 1)).sum() * c_fn # exposure varies, so rank; capacity, not ev, usually binds queue = np.argsort(-(p_val * exposure - c_fp))[:300] the caution do not invent the costs. a threshold built from numbers you made up is a guess wearing a formula, and harder to challenge than an honest guess because the arithmetic lends it authority. get the cells from whoever owns the consequence. cost-sensitive decisions a probability is not a decision ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice act on everything above 0.5 0.5 is a convention, not ev write the cost of fp and fn owners sign the numbers off treat fp and fn as equal they almost never cost alike cutoff = cfp / (cfp + cfn) act when acting wins on ev plug uncalibrated scores in wrong cutoff, stated boldly calibrate before you use p reliability curve, then brier result: a confidently wrong cutoff result: a cutoff that defends itself mistake the arithmetic is right. the inputs are not. best practice capacity-bound? rank by expected value instead. rule of thumb the cutoff comes from costs, not from 0.5. three fixes to apply 1 name the costs ask the owner. do not invent them. 2 calibrate an ev rule needs honest probabilities. 3 check capacity if ev flags more than you can review, rank.
m13x-governance: what it delivers months later, somebody asks which version made a decision, on what data, and who approved it. governance is the four artefacts that answer that: a model card , lineage back to source, a version pin , and an approval trail naming who signed. nothing ships without a named approver build model + card review data and fairness approve named owner signs deploy version pinned audit trail kept the card, the lineage and the sign-off are written before launch, not after when to use it it affects people — credit, hiring, housing. or money, or safety — pricing, reserves. two people will touch it — after a handover. you need to roll back — one you cannot rebuild is not one. the four artefacts, and who signs the model card states what the model is for and, explicitly, what it is not for, plus the data, the evaluation by subgroup, and an owner. emit it from the training run: a card written later from memory is a reconstruction, and reconstructions flatter. a version is reproducible only with five pins together — snapshot hash, commit, lockfile, parameters, artefact hash — and the data one is usually missed, because a query on a mutable table only looks like a specification. approval needs three distinct roles: the owner proposes, an independent reviewer validates, the business owner takes the risk. artefact question it answers minimum model card what is this not for? a page, from the job lineage what breaks upstream? tables per col. version pin can we rebuild it? 5 pins approval who took the risk signers, dates # emitted by the training run, from what the run actually used card = { "version": "churn-1.4.0", "intended_use": "rank open cases for review.", "not_for": ["auto-decline", "pricing: untested"], # all five pins, or the version cannot be rebuilt "pins": {"snapshot": file_hash (train_path), "artefact": file_hash (model_path), "lockfile": file_hash ("uv.lock"), "commit": git_sha (), "params": prm}, # left none by the job: a human fills these, or no promotion "approval": {"proposer": none, "reviewer": none, "owner": none}, } blockers = [k for k, v in card["approval"].items() if v is none] the point of it governance written after the fact is fiction, and everyone can tell. make it a build artefact: the job emits the card, the card carries the hashes, and the registry will not promote a version with empty approval fields. model governance and documentation who signed off, and on what evidence ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice card written after launch reconstructed from memory emit the card from the run written by the training job only the code is versioned data snapshot is not pinned pin data, code, env, params plus the artefact hash builder approves own model no independent review reviewer, then business owner legal when people are affected result: nobody can rerun it result: a decision you can audit mistake six months on, no one knows which data it saw. best practice lineage answers: which models use this table? rule of thumb if you cannot rerun it, you cannot defend it. three fixes to apply 1 automate the card emit it from training, not from a doc. 2 pin everything data hash, git sha, env, params, artefact. 3 set a review date approval expires. put it in the registry.

m16x-pipelines: the idea mlr3pipelines makes preprocessing a first-class operator — a pipeop — connects them into a graph , then wraps it with as_learner() . the result is a learner: one train, one predict, one parameter set covering every stage. quick look the graph architecture: what as_learner() packs into one object enlarge the graph: 7 pipeops wired together pca nothing patient table na values, mixed columns task 1 impute fill na with the column mean po("imputemean") 2 encode factors become numbers po("encode") 3 branch tuner picks one path per trial branch.selection 4 pca path compress numeric columns po("pca") rank. = 2 to 20 5 skip path pass data through as-is po("nop") 5 unbranch merge the two paths po("unbranch") 6 random forest the model lrn("classif.ranger") 6 graphlearner one object: train, predict, tune as_learner(graph) 7 resample() / tune refits every step per fold auto_tuner(...) 7 click a numbered pin or a card to link the diagram to its explanation. this is what glrn$graph$plot() draws in r, with the details added. 1 start with the raw task missing values and factor columns go in untouched. nothing is cleaned in a separate script, so nothing is estimated on all rows. 2 impute inside the graph po("imputemean") learns each column mean from the training rows of the current fold only , then applies it to the validation rows. 3 encode categories po("encode") turns factor columns into numeric ones (one-hot or treatment coding) so pca and the forest can read them. 4 branch = a tunable decision the preprocessing choice becomes a hyper-parameter: branch.selection is "pca" or "nothing" . the tuner tries both fairly. 5 two parallel paths pca compresses the numeric columns to pca.rank. components (2 to 20). po("nop") does nothing, which is what makes "no pca" a real option. 6 merge, then model po("unbranch") joins the paths; classif.ranger trains on whichever data arrived. its tuned values are mtry and min.node.size . 7 wrap it once as_learner(graph) makes the whole chain a single learner. resample() and auto_tuner() now refit every step in every fold. run it, then check the result 1. build the graph and wrap it as one learner "readmitted_30d" ) # chain the steps. ppl("branch") builds branch -> (pca | nop) -> unbranch for you. patient_graph = po ( "imputemean" ) %>>% # 1. fill na with column means po ( "encode" , method = m16x-performance: the idea measure, then fix what you measured. profile with profvis , vectorise, move big tables to data.table , parallelise with future , and reach for rcpp last. skipping to the end is how a day goes into c++ for a loop that should not exist. quick look measure, fix the hot line, measure again enlarge measure is it slow, or short of memory? profvis({ ... }) 1 find the hot line read time and allocation one line, usually 2 fix it in order cheapest fix first pre-allocate, vectorise 3 scale it big tables, many cores data.table, future 4 rcpp, last only a true sequential loop c++ for that line 5 re-measure did the number move? if not, back to step 1 bench::mark() 6 1 measure before touching anything profvis() for time and memory, bench::mark() to compare two versions. 2 read the hot line the slow line is rarely the one you suspect. look at the memory column as well as time. 3 pre-allocate and vectorise first cheapest fixes. growing a vector in a loop and row-by-row arithmetic are the two usual causes. 4 scale with data.table and future := updates in place, setkey() speeds joins, future spreads independent fits over cores. 5 rcpp only for a sequential loop if each step needs the previous result and no vector form exists, c++ for that one line. 6 re-measure after every fix if the number did not move, you fixed the wrong line. revert and look again. what it will look like same job, five ways (log scale) enlarge 0.01 s 0.1 s 1 s 10 s row loop with c(out, x) row loop with c(out, x): 38 s 38 s apply() by row apply() by row: 11 s 11 s (3x faster) vectorised base r vectorised base r: 0.09 s 0.09 s (422x faster) data.table data.table: 0.03 s 0.03 s (1,267x faster) rcpp rcpp: 0.02 s 0.02 s (1,900x faster) illustrative: seeded synthetic data. shapes are realistic; values are examples, not results from your data. times are examples for a row-wise calculation on a few million rows. why the loop gets worse as data grows enlarge 0 1 2 3 4 0 10,000 20,000 30,000 40,000 50,000 items in the loop seconds out <- c(out, x) in a loop: (5,000, 0.0375) out <- c(out, x) in a loop: (10,000, 0.15) out <- c(out, x) in a loop: (20,000, 0.6) out <- c(out, x) in a loop: (30,000, 1.35) out <- c(out, x) in a loop: (40,000, 2.4) out <- c(out, x) in a loop: (50,000, 3.75) pre-allocated vector: (5,000, 0.00125) pre-allocated vector: (10,000, 0.0025) pre-allocated vector: (20,000, 0.005) pre-allocated vector: (30,000, 0.0075) pre-allocated vector: (40,000, 0.01) pre-allocated vector: (50,000, 0.0125) out <- c(out, x) in a loop pre-allocated vector doubling the size quadruples the time illustrative: seeded synthetic data. shapes are realistic; values are examples, not results from your data. what a profile tells you line (profvis view) time memory verdict out <- c(out, sqrt(x[i])) 1,040 ms 1,580 mb hot: fix this for (i in seq_along(x)) 30 ms 0.1 mb leave alone score_portfolio(trades) 12 ms 2 mb leave alone what a profile lets you decide: one line carries almost all the time and nearly all the memory. run it, then check the result measure the classic waste, then confirm the fix library (profvis); library (bench); library (data.table); library (furrr) # 1. find the line, do not guess it profvis ({ scores <- score_portfolio (trades) }) # 2. the classic waste: reallocates on every pass slow <- function (x) { out <- c () for (i in seq_along (x)) out <- c (out, sqrt (x[i])); out } mark ( slow ( 1 : 20000 ), sqrt ( 1 : 20000 )) # the fix is one call # 3. big tables: key once, update in place setdt (trades); setkey (trades, account_id, trade_date) trades[, net := amount - fee] trades[, .(total = sum (net)), by = account_id] # 4. work across cores (mind the memory per worker) plan (multisession, workers = 4 ) fits <- future_map (splits, fit_one) bench::mark(): median time and memory allocated illustrative output: structure matches what r prints; numbers are examples. # a tibble: 2 x 6 expression min median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec` <bch:expr> <bch:tm> <bch:tm> <dbl> <bch:byt> <dbl> 1 slow(1:20000) 0.98s 1.04s 0.96 1.49gb 4.8 2 sqrt(1:20000) 54.3us 57.1us 16890. 78.2kb 0 check: the fixed version is orders of magnitude faster and allocates a fraction of the memory. if only one of the two moved, look again. what this solves for the business 01 jobs that fit the overnight window a scoring run that grew from 20 minutes to 4 hours is brought back under the batch window without buying a bigger server. no new hardware 02 engineering time spent on the right line profiling stops the day lost on c++ for a loop that should not exist. days saved 03 lower cloud bill for the same output a tuning job that finishes in a third of the time costs about a third as much on pay-per-hour compute. direct cost cut do this next profile your slowest script done when: a profvis view shows one or two lines with most of the time. fix the hot line and re-measure done when: bench::mark() shows both a faster median and lower mem_alloc . check memory before parallelising done when: object size times workers fits in ram, or the serial run is faster. when to use it a script that finished now does not — the data crossed a threshold. memory is the limit, not time — r copies on modify. work is independent — model fits, resamples, simulations. the algorithm is sequential — each step needs the previous. where the time actually goes almost always one of two habits. growing an object : out <- c(out, x) in a loop reallocates the whole vector every pass, so cost rises with the square of the length; pre-allocate. looping over rows for arithmetic a column already supports: the loop runs in the interpreter, the column form compiled. profvis() finds both; its allocation column matters as much as its timings. past that, := updates a table in place rather than copying it, and setkey() sorts once so joins use binary search. parallel backends are configured separately: set a plan, and code written against future uses it. symptom usual cause fix loop slows as it runs growing a vector pre-allocate row-wise apply interpreted per row operate on columns group-by on a huge table copying each change data.table , setkey() no vector form exists genuinely sequential rcpp , that one # 1. find the line, do not guess it profvis ({ scores <- score_portfolio(trades) }) # 2. the classic waste: reallocates on every pass slow <- function (x) { out <- c() for (i in seq_along(x)) out <- c(out, sqrt(x[i])); out } mark(slow(1:20000), sqrt(1:20000)) # the fix is one call # 3. big tables: key once, update in place setkey(dt, account_id, trade_date) dt[, net := amount - fee] dt[, .(total = sum(net)), by = account_id] # 4. work across cores plan(multisession, workers = 4) fits <- future_map(splits, fit_one) the caution each worker is a separate r process with its own copy of the data it touches, so four workers on a three-gigabyte object want twelve and can run slower than the serial version. never optimise a line profvis did not flag. performance in r profile first, then fix that one line ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice guess where the time goes optimise a line that is fast profvis() to find the line watch allocations, not time out = c(out, x) in a loop reallocates on every pass pre-allocate or vectorise whole columns, compiled code jump straight to rcpp c++ for a loop to delete data.table for large tables update in place, setkey once result: a day spent, same speed result: the hot line fixed only mistake the real cost was never the line you rewrote. best practice compare versions with bench::mark(), not a clock. rule of thumb never optimise a line profvis did not flag. three fixes to apply 1 measure profvis the job, then bench::mark the fix. 2 vectorise pre-allocate. operate on whole columns. 3 watch ram each worker copies the data it touches.
m7p-comprehensions: the idea a comprehension is a one-line loop that returns a collection . any loop whose whole body is result.append(...) is a list comprehension waiting to happen, and the same shape in braces builds a dict or a set instead. same result, one expression out = [] for r in rows: if r.ok: out.append(r.v) out = [r.v for r in rows if r.ok] append loop comprehension past two conditions or a nested loop, go back to the loop when to use it cleaning a header row — strip and lowercase every name at once. filtering a folder listing — keep the csvs, drop the lock files. building a lookup — code to label, out of two columns. de-duplicating — a set comprehension does it for free. the shape, and the readability limit read it left to right: [expression for item in source if condition] . the if at the end filters rows out , so the result is shorter. an if/else placed before the for is a different animal — it recodes every row and drops none. a comprehension cannot hold a try/except , so a step that might raise belongs in a small named function you call from inside it. the honest limit is one line of reading: with two nested for clauses, the plain loop is clearer. goal what you write you get transform rows [f(x) for x in xs] same length keep some rows [x for x in xs if ok(x)] shorter list build a lookup {k: v for k, v in pairs} dict unique values {x.strip() for x in xs} set raw = [" fund code ", "fy25 amount", " dept "] # clean every header in one pass cols = [c.strip().lower().replace(" ", "_") for c in raw] # filter: the if at the end, so the list gets shorter csvs = [f for f in names if f.endswith(".csv")] # recode: if/else in front, nothing is dropped band = ["high" if a > 50000 else "low" for a in amounts] # braces give a dict or a set label = {r["code"]: r["label"] for r in rows} practical notes if the body needs logging, a running total or error handling, write the loop — a comprehension computes one expression and nothing else. and a comprehension over a dataframe column is the wrong tool: a vectorised pandas operation is far faster. comprehensions five lines of append is one line ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice empty list, loop, append four lines to say one thing one expression, one line says what you want back nest two loops to be clever nobody can read line three put the filter in the if shorter list, visible rule hide a condition in the body the filter is invisible braces give dict or set lookups and unique values result: longer and harder to read result: the intent is the code mistake four lines of plumbing around one expression. best practice a set comprehension de-duplicates for free. rule of thumb if it needs decoding, write the plain loop. three fixes to apply 1 spot the append a loop that only appends is a comprehension. 2 filter at the end the if after the for drops rows. 3 stop at one line two for clauses means use a real loop.
m7p-fstrings: the idea an f-string is a literal prefixed with f whose braces are evaluated in place. after a colon inside the braces comes the format spec : thousands separators, decimal places, percentages, sign and alignment — what turns a raw float into a line a reader can scan. the format spec does the work value format spec output 1234567.891 {:,.0f} 1,234,568 0.0734 {:.1%} 7.3% 42 {:>8} 42 3.14159 {:.2f} 3.14 f"revenue: {total:,.0f}" puts the spec inside the braces when to use it any printed figure — 1284330.4567 is not a number anyone reads. a run log — row counts, file name and elapsed time on one line. a summary beside a table — totals and growth rates in prose. building file names — stamped with period and version. the spec is where the work happens inside the braces the pattern is value:[align][width][,][.precision][type] , and you rarely need all of it. a bare comma inserts thousands separators. .2f fixes two decimals. .1% multiplies by 100 and appends the sign, so a stored 0.0734 prints as 7.3% — never do that multiplication yourself as well. alignment is what makes a column legible: numbers right-aligned to a common width, labels left. against str(x) + " rows" , an f-string reads better and never raises the typeerror that concatenating a number produces. spec value renders as :, 1284330 1,284,330 :,.2f 1284330.456 1,284,330.46 :.1% 0.0734 7.3% :>12,.0f 48219 right-aligned in 12 :+,.0f -4200 -4,200, sign shown total, rate, rows = 1284330.456 , 0.0734 , 48219 # one expression per placeholder, spec after the colon print(f"spend {total:>14,.2f}") print(f"growth {rate:>14.1%}") print(f"rows {rows:>14,d}") # alignment turns a loop into a readable column for dept, amt in totals.items(): print(f"{dept:<22}{amt:>12,.0f}") # a trailing = prints the expression too print(f"{len(df)=}") name = f"fy25_spend_{month:02d}.csv" the caution formatting is display only — the stored value keeps every decimal, so figures rounded for a report will not re-add to the rounded total. round the data deliberately when the reader must be able to tot up the column. and never build sql by interpolation: pass parameters. f-strings concatenation is not a report ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice str(x) plus a space plus text typeerror waiting to happen f-string with a format spec separators and decimals print 1284330.4567 raw nobody reads that number use .1% for a rate it scales and labels it multiply by 100 yourself then add a percent sign too align to a fixed width numbers right, labels left result: unreadable, often wrong result: a line a reader can scan mistake columns of digits with nothing lining up. best practice one spec does commas, decimals and padding. rule of thumb format at the edge, never in the data. three fixes to apply 1 braces not plus f before the quote, then the value in braces. 2 comma for thousands a bare comma groups the digits for you. 3 align the column right-align numbers to one common width.
m7p-enumerate-zip: the idea three small tools remove the bookkeeping from loops. enumerate hands you the position with the item. zip walks two sequences in step. tuple unpacking names the pieces on the spot, so for code, amount in rows replaces row[0] . index and pairs without manual counters zip pairs them up and stops at the shorter one north south east west 120 98 143 — dropped for i, (region, value) in enumerate(zip(regions, values), start=1): when to use it reporting the row that failed — you need the position. numbering files you process — file 3 of 47, in the log. pairing headers with values — a column and a dtype list. two aligned lists — month labels against totals. the index you do not have to maintain a counter you increment yourself is one more thing to get wrong, and range(len(xs)) then forces you to index back into the list on every line. enumerate yields (position, item) pairs and takes a start , which is how you get 1-based numbering in a message a person reads. zip yields tuples across its inputs and stops at the shortest — no error, no warning, the tail of the longer sequence never appears. twelve headers against eleven values quietly give eleven pairs. task what you write note position and item enumerate(cols) counts from 0 human numbering enumerate(f, start=1) counts from 1 two lists in step zip(cols, dtypes) stops at shortest refuse ragged input zip(a, b, strict=true) raises # start=1 so the log reads the way a person counts for n, name in enumerate (files, start= 1 ): print(f"[{n}/{len(files)}] reading {name}") # pair headers with types, and refuse a ragged pair for col, dtype in zip (cols, dtypes, strict= true ): print(f"{col:<20}{dtype}") # zip_longest pads instead, keeping every month pairs = list ( zip_longest (months, totals, fillvalue= 0 )) # unpacking names the pieces, with a catch-all code, amount, *rest = ["fd-902", 48219 , "fas"] the caution silent truncation is the bug that costs you a day: zip drops the overflow without a murmur, so a missing column becomes a shifted report. assert the lengths match, or use strict=true . enumerate and zip zip truncates and says nothing ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice for i in range(len(xs)) then index back in twice enumerate for the index position and item together keep your own counter one more thing to get wrong start=1 for human counts file 3 of 47 in the log zip two ragged lists the overflow vanishes silently zip with strict=true raises on a length mismatch result: a quietly shifted report result: the mismatch raises mistake twelve headers, eleven values, eleven pairs. best practice unpack to name the pieces on the spot. rule of thumb check the lengths before you zip anything. three fixes to apply 1 drop the counter enumerate hands you the position already. 2 count from one pass start=1 so the log reads like a list. 3 use strict strict=true turns silence into an exception.
m7p-lambda-map: the idea a lambda is a nameless function of one expression: lambda r: r["amount"] is a function you hand to something else. map applies one to every item, filter keeps what it is true for. a comprehension usually says it more plainly. a pipeline a comprehension usually says better rows filter keep r.ok map take r.v result [r.v for r in rows if r.ok] says the same thing more plainly lambda earns its place as a key= argument: sorted(rows, key=lambda r: r.v) when to use it sorting records by a field — where a lambda earns its place. max, min and group keys — the same one-expression rule. a one-off transform — inside .map() on a column. reading other code — you meet all three either way. why the comprehension usually wins list(map(lambda x: x.strip(), names)) and [x.strip() for x in names] do the same thing; the second reads left to right and needs no list() wrapper, because map and filter return lazy iterators that look empty once consumed. a lambda is genuinely right as an argument : sorted , max and .map() want a tiny function and nothing else. once it needs a second line or a test, write def . need reach for why transform a list comprehension no wrapper needed filter a list comprehension + if condition visible sort by a field key=lambda the idiom logic you reuse def with a name testable # this is what lambda is for: a key argument top = sorted (rows, key= lambda r: r["amount"]) worst = min (rows, key= lambda r: r["margin"]) # two keys at once: return a tuple rows.sort(key= lambda r: (r["dept"], -r["amount"])) # same result, and the second is the one to write clean = list ( map ( lambda s: s.strip(), names)) clean = [s.strip() for s in names] # once it needs a name and a test, make it a def def to_cents (x): return round ( float (x) * 100 ) practical notes a lambda holds one expression — no assignment, no if statement, no try — and appears in a traceback only as <lambda> . never assign one to a variable to name it. lambda, map, filter a comprehension usually reads better ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice map and filter everywhere then a list() wrapper too comprehension to transform reads left to right assign a lambda to a name that is what def is for lambda only as a key= sorted, max, min, .map a lambda three clauses long no name, no test, no doc def once it needs a name testable and traceable result: harder to read and debug result: each tool where it fits mistake a traceback just says lambda and nothing more. best practice key=lambda r: r.amt is lambda at its best. rule of thumb longer than its line? give it a def. three fixes to apply 1 prefer brackets a comprehension beats map plus a wrapper. 2 keep key lambdas sorting by a field is the real use case. 3 name it to test it a def can be imported and tested on its own.
m7p-mutability: the idea assignment binds a name to an object; it never copies. b = a gives one list two names, so appending through either changes what both see. lists, dicts, sets and dataframes are mutable ; numbers, strings and tuples are not. every quiet corruption bug here starts there. assignment copies the name, not the data b = a b = a.copy() a b [1, 2, 3] one list, two names a b [1, 2, 3] [1, 2, 3] two lists def clean(rows, drop=[]) reuses that same list on every call when to use it before editing a shared list — a column list two functions hold. any helper taking a dict — new one back, or yours edited? nested config — a dict of lists needs more than a shallow copy. writing a default — a mutable default is a bug, always. shallow, deep, and the default created once a.copy() or a[:] makes a new outer container whose entries still point at the same inner objects . for a flat list of strings that is enough; for a dict of lists it is not, and editing an inner list still reaches through. copy.deepcopy rebuilds the whole tree. then the trap: a default argument is evaluated once , at definition, so def f(rows=[]) shares one list across every call that omits it. run it over twelve files and the twelfth call sees the first eleven. you write what you get safe to edit? b = a one object, two names no — both change b = a.copy() new outer, shared inners only if flat b = deepcopy(a) independent tree yes, slower d2 = df.copy() independent frame yes from copy import deepcopy keep = ["code", "amount"] also = keep # not a copy also.append("dept") # keep has three entries too cfg2 = deepcopy (cfg) # dict of lists: needs deep # the bug: one list shared by every call def load_bad (path, rows=[]): rows.append(path) return rows # the fix: none, then build it inside def load_ok (path, rows= none ): rows = [] if rows is none else rows the caution this corrupts analyses silently: no error, just totals that grow a little each run and a notebook that answers differently the second time you run the cell. make cleaning helpers return a new object rather than edit the one they were handed. mutability assignment binds a name, not a copy ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice b = a then edit b you just edited a as well copy() only a flat list nothing nested inside it copy() a dict of lists the inner lists are shared deepcopy for nested data a fully independent tree a list as a default value one list for every call default none, build inside a fresh list every call result: totals that creep each run result: the same answer twice mistake the twelfth call sees eleven earlier files. best practice helpers return a new object, never edit yours. rule of thumb never default to a list or a dict. three fixes to apply 1 copy on purpose df.copy() before you add any column. 2 go deep if nested deepcopy any dict that holds lists. 3 none as default build the container inside the function.
m7t-modules: the idea a module is just a .py file. import runs it once and gives you its names. that applies as much to the file you wrote yesterday as to pandas, so the cleaning function pasted into four notebooks belongs in cleaning.py beside them, imported in one line. put shared cleaning code in one file project/ helpers.py clean_jan.py clean_feb.py from helpers import clean_dates one definition, used everywhere from helpers import * you cannot tell what came from where when to use it the same fix in several notebooks — one definition, four users. column renames and type maps — constants nobody retypes. a notebook past a few hundred lines — move the plumbing out. handing work over — a reviewer reads a module, not a long cell. four import forms, and the one to avoid import pandas as pd keeps the namespace visible: every call says where it came from. from pathlib import path pulls in one or two unambiguous names. your own file works identically — put cleaning.py in the folder you launch the notebook from and import cleaning finds it. from cleaning import * is the habit to drop: it dumps every name into your namespace, so a reader cannot tell where clean came from and a later import can silently replace it. form you then write use when import pandas as pd pd.read_csv() the standard alias from pathlib import path path() one or two clear names import cleaning cleaning.strip(df) your own helpers from cleaning import * anything, invisibly never # ---- cleaning.py, next to the notebook ---- renames = {"fund code": "fund_code", "fy25 amount": "amount"} def strip_cols (df): """return df with tidy snake_case names.""" out = df.copy() out.columns = [c.strip().lower().replace(" ", "_") for c in out.columns] return out if __name__ == "__main__": print("runs directly, not on import") # m7t-regex: the idea a regular expression is a tiny pattern language for finding structure inside text. it earns its place on the fields nobody validated: a free-text reference holding an invoice number, a code with an optional prefix, a column where the fund identifier is buried in a sentence. learn four constructs, cover most jobs one pattern, three captures order inv-2026-0147 shipped 03/14 invoice date r"(inv-\d{4}-\d{4}).*?(\d{2}/\d{2})" \d a digit + one or more ? lazy, not greedy ( ) capture it when to use it extracting an embedded code — an account number in a note. validating a format — does every row match the pattern? cleaning inconsistently — several separators at once. splitting on a pattern — not on one fixed character. six constructs do most of the work you need \d for a digit, \w for a letter, digit or underscore, and \s for whitespace. you need the quantifiers: + one or more, * any number, ? optional, {2,4} a range. you need [a-z] for a character class, parentheses for the capture group — the piece you want back — and ^ and $ to anchor start and end. always write the pattern as a raw string , or the backslashes are eaten before the engine sees them. pattern matches analyst use \d+ one or more digits invoice or po number [a-z]{2,4}-\d+ prefix, dash, digits fund or account code (...) captures that part the piece you extract ^...$ the whole value format validation import re note = "transfer re fd-9021 / dept fas (approved)" # capture the code; none if it is simply not there m = re. search (r"([a-z]{2,4}-\d+)", note) code = m. group ( 1 ) if m else none # fullmatch validates the whole value, not just part ok = bool (re. fullmatch (r"[a-z]{2,4}-\d{4}", code)) # collapse any run of whitespace to one space tidy = re. sub (r"\s+", " ", note).strip() pat = re. compile (r"([a-z]{2,4})-(\d+)") # many rows df[["prefix", "num"]] = df.note.str. extract (pat) practical notes search finds the first match, findall all of them, sub replaces. if startswith , in or split will do, use them. keep a greedy .* out of the middle, and test on a known-bad row. regular expressions a pattern beats four str calls - sometimes ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice a regex for startswith str methods were clearer raw string every time an r before the quote pattern without the r backslashes eaten first capture only what you want parentheses mark the part a greedy any-run of text it swallows past the match fullmatch to validate anchored start to end result: matches too much, or none result: extraction you can trust mistake it passed on the rows you happened to test. best practice compile once when it runs over many rows. rule of thumb str methods first, regex when they fail. three fixes to apply 1 raw it prefix the pattern with an r, always. 2 capture the part parentheses around the piece you want back. 3 test a bad row run it against input you know should fail.
m7t-generators: the idea a list holds every value at once. a generator produces them one at a time, only when asked, and forgets each as it goes. swap the brackets of a comprehension for parentheses, or write yield instead of return , and a job that needed gigabytes of memory needs one row of it. stream the file instead of loading it list — loads everything generator — one at a time 2 gb file, 2 gb of memory one row held at a time a generator is used up after one pass: list() it if you need it twice when to use it a file larger than memory — stream it, keep what matches. summing over a big source — you never need the rows again. a pipeline of steps — read, parse, filter, one row at a time. stopping early — the first hundred bad rows. lazy, and therefore single-use a generator function looks ordinary except that yield hands a value out and pauses , resuming where it stopped on the next request. nothing runs until something iterates it, so building one costs nothing and the work happens as the consumer pulls. chain them and each row flows through the whole pipeline before the next is read — peak memory is one row, not one file. the cost is the one-pass rule: a generator is consumed . form memory reusable fh.readlines() whole file yes [x for x in fh] whole file yes (x for x in fh) one row no, one pass read_csv(chunksize=) one chunk no, one pass import csv def big_rows (path, dept): """yield matching rows; never holds the file.""" with open (path, newline="", encoding="utf-8") as fh: for row in csv. dictreader (fh): if row["dept"] == dept: yield row stream = big_rows ("all_txns.csv", "fas") # instant # a generator expression keeps the pipeline lazy too amounts = ( float (r["amount"]) for r in stream) print( sum (amounts)) # the file is read, once print( sum (amounts)) # 0 - it is exhausted the caution the one-pass gotcha is the whole topic: a second loop over a spent generator finds nothing and raises no error, so a total silently comes out as zero. len() does not work either. if a step needs the values twice, wrap it in list() . iterators, generators a file bigger than your memory ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice read all lines of 8 gb every row held at once yield one row at a time peak memory is one row build a list, then filter you pay for rows you drop parentheses, not brackets a lazy generator expression loop a generator twice the second pass finds nothing materialise only if reused deliberately, and once result: a crash, or a silent zero result: any size, one row deep mistake sum() ran twice and returned zero. best practice nothing runs until something iterates it. rule of thumb lazy means single-use. plan the second pass. three fixes to apply 1 yield the rows a generator function never holds the file. 2 swap the brackets parentheses make it lazy, brackets eager. 3 materialise once build a list only when two passes are needed.
m7t-typing-style: the idea a type hint records the contract of a function in its signature: what goes in, what comes out. pep 8 is the shared python style agreement — naming, indentation, import order. a formatter and a linter apply both automatically, so nobody argues about blank lines in review. the signature is the contract def clean(rows: list[str], drop: bool = true) -> dataframe: what goes in default value what comes out pep 8 the shared convention formatter rewrites layout for you linter flags the rest when to use it a helper someone else will call — the signature answers them. code you revisit in six months — you are the next reader. a shared module — hints plus a docstring beat a conversation. every repository — one formatter ends the style argument. what a hint does and does not do a signature reading (df: pd.dataframe, cols: list[str]) -> pd.dataframe tells the reader, and the editor, exactly what is expected;
