m7t-debugging: the idea a traceback is not noise, it is a report, and it reads bottom-up . the last line names the exception and what triggered it. above it sit the call frames, newest first — so you scan upward for the deepest line that is your file. the top of the block is merely where the chain started. read a traceback from the bottom up traceback (most recent call last): file "run.py", line 12, in <module> clean(df) file "helpers.py", line 40, in clean return row["total"] / row["qty"] zerodivisionerror: division by zero start here what broke then read up for the line that called it breakpoint() beats scattering print() when to use it every error, before changing anything — it usually names the fix. a cell that worked yesterday — read what changed. an error inside a library — find your own last line. a wrong answer, no error — where a debugger beats guessing. what each exception is really telling you a keyerror on a column name almost never means the column is absent; it means the name is not exactly that, so print list(df.columns) and look for trailing spaces or capitalisation. typeerror is the wrong kind of thing — very often a none where a number was expected. valueerror is the right type with an impossible value. attributeerror on nonetype means an earlier call returned nothing and you kept going. exception what it really means keyerror that exact name is not there — spelling, spaces typeerror wrong kind of object, often a none valueerror right type, impossible value filenotfounderror relative path, wrong working directory # traceback (most recent call last): # file "run.py", line 12 <- where it started # total = summarise(df) # file "cleaning.py", line 31 <- your last line # return df["amount"].sum() # keyerror: 'amount' <- read this first print( list (df.columns)) # "amount " has a trailing space def summarise (df): breakpoint () # pauses here: n p c q return df["amount"].sum() the caution do not read a traceback top-down and conclude the library is broken: the line you can fix is the lowest one in your own file. never paper over an error with a bare except , which hides typos as well as bad data. prefer breakpoint() to prints you forget to delete. tracebacks, debugging a traceback reads from the bottom up ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice read the top line only that is where it started last line names the error exception plus the value blame the library your own last line is lower find your deepest frame the lowest line you wrote scatter print calls then commit them by accident breakpoint() to inspect real values, nothing to undo result: hours on the wrong line result: the real cause, first try mistake keyerror on amount was a trailing space. best practice print the column list before anything else. rule of thumb bottom line first, then your lowest frame. three fixes to apply 1 bottom first the last line is the error and the value. 2 find your file scan up to the lowest frame you wrote. 3 use breakpoint a prompt beats prints you forget to remove.
proj-idea: the idea a vague idea names a topic : look at churn. a real question names a population, a measure, a comparison and a window — and could come back either way. until it could, there is nothing to find out. sharpen it until it can be answered "sales are down" not answerable which segment? getting closer did smb churn rise in q3? one period, one group a real question names a group, a period and a number you can check when to use it you have an itch, not a brief — something in the data feels wrong. you were handed a topic — look at retention, see what you find. you have three ideas and need to know which one is doable. before any tool opens — the question picks the data, not the reverse. four parts and two tests an answerable question carries a population (which rows), a measure with a unit, a comparison (last year, the other segment, a target) and a window (which dates). then two tests. the falsifiability test : write down the answer that would disappoint you — if you cannot, you are hunting a confirmation. the so-what test : name the decision that goes differently depending on the result. if every answer leads to the same action, the question is decoration. expect five versions; the first is always too big, and shrinking the population usually rescues it. vague idea what is missing sharper version look at churn population, window first-year accounts, 2025 are we efficient? a measure and a unit cost per request, by team study the survey a comparison score this year versus last improve the report a decision which pages nobody opened # prompt - sharpen a vague idea into three questions my rough idea: "[one or two sentences, as vague as it really is]" data i think i can get: [sources, grain, date range] who would act on it: [role]. time i have: [half-days] give me three candidate questions. for each one: 1. the population it covers and the time window 2. the single number that answers it, with its unit 3. the comparison that makes that number mean something 4. what changes if the answer is high, and if it is low 5. the one missing field that would kill the question rank them by how answerable they are with the data above, say which you would drop and why, and mark anything you assumed about my data as an assumption. do not propose a method yet. the caution a question you cannot lose is not a question. if you already know the answer and want a chart to prove it, say so out loud and reframe it as a measurement task — a legitimate job, just a different one. framing the question a topic is not a question ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice start from the data you have the question gets bent to fit name population and window which rows, which dates write a topic, call it a brief look at churn is not a question one measure, one comparison a number with a unit skip the decision it feeds nobody acts on the answer write the losing answer prove it could go either way result: a chart nobody uses result: a question you can lose mistake every answer leads to the same action. best practice if you cannot lose it, it is not a question. rule of thumb if no decision changes, it is decoration. three fixes to apply 1 add a window which dates, exactly, and which rows. 2 name the number one measure, one unit, one comparison. 3 find the decider who acts, and what they do differently.
proj-stakeholder: the idea every analysis has one reader who will act on it and several who will comment on it. name the first. the audience sets the format, the depth of the method section, and the precision you need — which is what tells you when to stop. name the decision before the method who decides head of sales what changes where we spend q4 by when board, 14 nov if no decision changes, the project is a report nobody needs when to use it right after the question — before you estimate anything. when the ask came down a chain — three people from the decision. when access needs approval — the data owner is a stakeholder too. when scope keeps moving — usually two readers wanting two things. four roles, not one person separate the decider who acts, the sponsor who clears your time, the data owner who grants access and knows the field-level traps, and the reviewer who checks the numbers first. one person can hold two roles, but an empty role is a risk worth naming early. then write the thing most people skip: what the decider does today without you. replacing a spreadsheet somebody already trusts is harder than filling a blank, and knowing which you are in tells you how much of the deliverable must explain the difference from the existing number. role what you need ask them decider the decision and its date what would change your mind? sponsor time and cover what does this push down? data owner access and warnings where is this field weak? reviewer a check before launch what will you compare it to? # template - stakeholder card, one per person, eight lines name and role : [name], [title] role here : [decider | sponsor | data owner | reviewer] decision it feeds : [the choice this analysis informs] needs it by : [date, or the meeting it must reach] uses today : [report, spreadsheet, vendor number, gut feel] would move if : [the finding that would actually change them] cost of wrong : [what breaks, who notices, how fast] wants it as : [one chart | one page | a deck | a live table] precision : [direction only | nearest 10% | exact figure] practical note if you cannot name a decider, you have a learning project rather than a business one. that is a fine thing to build — just label it that way, scope it to a weekend, and stop defending it as though a budget depended on it. audience and decision one reader acts, the rest comment ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice write for everyone at once nobody recognises themselves name the decider first format follows the reader assume the ask came from above three people from the decision separate the four roles decider, sponsor, owner, reviewer skip the data owner access arrives in week three ask what they use today replacing a trusted sheet result: a report with no reader result: the output fits the reader mistake two readers wanted two different projects. best practice precision needed is set by the decision. rule of thumb no decider means it is a learning project. three fixes to apply 1 write one card eight lines per person, no more than that. 2 ask the owner where is this field unreliable? proj-scope: the idea scope is defined by what you refuse. a written non-goal is a promise you can point at when someone asks for one more cut, and a written definition of done is the only thing that lets you finish rather than merely run out of time. three lists keep a project finishable in scope churn by segment 3 quarters one chart out of scope pricing new data pipeline forecasting later monthly refresh dashboard other regions "done" = the three in-scope items exist and someone has read them when to use it before the first query — scope written afterwards is a description. when the ask keeps growing — each new segment is a second project. when several people ordered it — their non-goals will disagree. when the deadline is fixed — then scope is the only adjustable thing. cut along an axis, not a corner scope on five axes: population , window , granularity , questions and output . shrinking one cleanly — one region instead of nine, monthly instead of daily — keeps the work defensible. doing all nine at half the care is the bad cut, because nobody can tell which parts to trust. everything you remove goes on a later list with one line of reasoning, so it reads as a decision rather than an oversight; that list is also the pitch for round two. then make done verifiable by somebody else: not understand churn but a one-page memo with a cohort table and three named drivers, each traced to a query. axis decide now bad cut to avoid population one segment, named all nine, none checked window two full years whatever the export gave questions two, in priority order six, all half-answered output one page plus appendix a dashboard to maintain # template - scope, non-goals and done in scope population : [rows included, and the filter that defines them] window : [start] to [end] granularity : [one row per ...] questions : [q1] then [q2] not in scope (this round) [item] - because [reason] - revisit when [trigger] [item] - because [reason] - revisit when [trigger] done means [artefact] exists, containing [specific contents], every number traceable to [script or query], reviewed by [name], delivered by [date]. not done is not failure if [the blocker you already know about] the caution a definition of done only you can judge is not one. if the test is it feels thorough, the project ends when you are tired. write a criterion your reviewer could tick off without asking what you meant by it. scope and done scope is what you refuse in writing ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice leave non-goals unwritten every new cut sounds small cut along one axis cleanly one region, done properly do all nine regions badly nobody knows what to trust write non-goals with reasons plus the revisit trigger define done as feels thorough it ends when you are tired make done a reviewer test a criterion they can tick result: creep, then no finish line result: you can finish and prove it mistake week three brought two more segments. best practice the later list is also your round-two pitch. rule of thumb shrink an axis, never the care taken. three fixes to apply 1 list non-goals three lines, each with a reason attached. 2 pick one axis narrow population or window, not both. 3 write done down a test your reviewer could tick off.
proj-feasibility: the idea three things get confused here: the data exists , you can access it, and it is usable at the grain you need. most projects that stall cleared the first gate and assumed the other two. test all three with a real extract before planning around a source. every source gets a verdict check access before you promise the analysis crm export have it ready billing db need access ask it support tickets no field for churn drop or proxy survey does not exist out of scope a project that needs data you cannot get is not a project yet when to use it straight after scoping — before estimating, before promising a date. any source you have not pulled — including one a colleague swears by. any join across systems — that is where quiet row loss happens. anything needing approval — access requests run on their own calendar. pull a hundred rows first per source, answer five things: who owns it, how you pull it, what one row is , which key joins it, and how far back it is trustworthy. then extract a sample. count rows, count distinct keys, count nulls in the fields the question depends on, and check the key is unique at the grain you assumed — a key that repeats turns an inner join into silent row multiplication. then give every source a verdict. a blocked source on day one is a re-scope; on day nine it is a cancelled project. gate the test if it fails exists someone names the table re-scope or collect it access you ran a query yourself request it today, in writing grain key unique as assumed aggregate before joining history window fully covered shorten the window # prompt - turn a question into a data feasibility check the question is: "[one sentence, population and window]" sources i think exist, one line each, in my own words: [name] | [system or owner] | [what i think it holds] | [how i would pull it] for each source give me one table row with: - the exact fields this question needs from it - what one row represents, as far as my description shows - the key it must join on, and what breaks if that key repeats - the one question to ask the owner before relying on it - a verdict: ready, needs access, needs workaround, blocked then list what a question like this normally needs that i have not mentioned. mark every statement about my systems as taken from my description or as a guess. do not invent table or field names: write a placeholder instead. the caution an assistant cannot see your warehouse. any table name, field name or row count it offers is a guess dressed as a fact — confirm each with your own query. and get access in writing: a verbal yes does not survive the person going on leave. data feasibility exists is not the same as usable ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice trust that the table exists nobody pulled it themselves pull a hundred rows first counts, nulls, distinct keys plan around pending access the request has its own queue check the key at your grain repeats mean aggregate first assume the join key is unique rows multiply in silence give each source a verdict ready, access, workaround result: blocked on day nine result: surprises land on day one mistake the field was null before 2023. best practice a blocked source early is just a re-scope. rule of thumb no extract run means no plan around it. three fixes to apply 1 run a select count rows and distinct keys before planning. 2 ask in writing a verbal yes dies with the person on leave. 3 verdict per source ready, needs access, workaround, blocked.
proj-brief: the idea the brief is the contract: one page, written before the first query, sent to everyone who could later change the ask. its job is not to describe the project but to make disagreement happen now , while changing your mind is still free. five sections, one page 1 question 2 decision 3 data 4 method 5 done 6 one page if it does not fit, 7 signed by the decider when to use it every project with a reader — if someone waits for it, write one. after feasibility — so the plan rests on sources you checked. when the ask came verbally — write it down and send it back. when you inherit half-done work — a brief surfaces what was assumed. one page, and it has to fit nine fields: question, decider and decision, scope, non-goals, sources with verdicts, method in a sentence, deliverable, date, risks. the page limit does real work — if it will not fit, the scope is too wide, not the format too small. write the method line in your reader's language: a brief nobody can read gets approved without being read. send it with a specific ask — reply yes, or the one thing that is wrong. a dated brief nobody objected to is the strongest thing you can hold up in week three. field length catches question one sentence two projects in disguise decision one line work nobody will act on non-goals three bullets the week-three creep sources one line each the source you cannot get # template - one-page project brief, version it and date it project : [short name] version : [v1] date : [yyyy-mm-dd] question : [population, measure, comparison, window] decider : [name] decides [decision] by [date] in scope : [population] | [window] | [grain] non-goals : [item] ; [item] ; [item] sources : [source] - [owner] - [ready | access | blocked] method : [one plain sentence a non-analyst would accept] deliverable : [artefact] to [audience] by [date] done means : [the checkable condition from your scope note] risks : [risk] - mitigation [action] reply with : yes, or the one thing that is wrong, by [date] practical note keep the brief in the project folder, not only in an email, and bump the version whenever scope moves. a dated v2 beside v1 records what changed and who asked. the one-page brief one page, sent before the first query ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice keep the brief in your head everyone remembers it differently nine fields, one page if it will not fit, re-scope write it after the work that is a description, not a limit write method in their words a reader can object to it describe method in jargon approved without being read ask for yes or one objection date it and version it result: the ask changes in week 3 result: disagreement happens early mistake no dated page to point back to. best practice changing your mind is still free now. rule of thumb if it will not fit a page, the scope is wrong. three fixes to apply 1 date and version v1, v2, kept side by side in docs. 2 send it back write the verbal ask down and confirm it. 3 name the risks two bullets you already expect to happen.
proj-plan: the idea a step is only a step if it produces something you can show: a file, a table, a chart, a note. analyse the data is a mood, not a step. each line gets an owner, an estimate and a named output, and nothing runs longer than a day. break it down, then add up the days estimate in days, not in hope 1d scope 3d get data 4d clean 3d analyse 2d write up start 13 days cleaning is usually the longest step. plan for it, do not discover it. when to use it once the brief is agreed — the plan turns it into days. when you owe a date — a date with no steps behind it is a wish. when you keep stalling — that means a step is still two steps. riskiest step first the spine is usually the same: get access, understand the data, build the measure, check it, communicate it. order within it is yours, and the rule is to pull the step that could kill the project as early as you can bear — the join that may not hold, the field that may be all null. learning that on day one costs a morning. estimate in half-days: under that is not worth a line, over a day you have not decomposed yet. keep one visible slack line instead of padding each estimate, and mark every step that waits on someone else. phase output that proves it is done risk it retires access sample extract saved to raw never getting the data understand row counts, nulls, key check wrong grain assumed build numbered script, output table unreproducible numbers check reconciliation to a known figure a wrong answer shipped communicate one page plus the chart good work nobody uses # template - step plan, one row per step, nothing over a day step | phase | output artefact | owner | half-days | blocked by 1 | access | [sample extract in raw/] | [you] | [1] | [owner reply] 2 | understand | [profile note, counts] | [you] | [1] | [step 1] 3 | build | [script + output table] | [you] | [2] | [step 2] 4 | check | [reconciliation note] | [name]| [1] | [step 3] 5 | communicate | [one-pager + chart] | [you] | [1] | [step 4] slack [2] # riskiest step first: [which, and what it proves] the caution do not let an assistant set your estimates. it cannot know how slow your access request is or how full your week is. ask it to decompose and to spot a missing step; keep the numbers yours. step plan a step without an artefact is a mood ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice write analyse the data no output, no finish one named output per step a file, table, chart or note pad every estimate quietly the plan stops being honest estimate in half-days over a day means decompose leave the risky step late it kills you on day eight riskiest step pulled forward a morning now, not a project result: a date with nothing behind result: a date you can defend mistake the join never held, and you found out late. best practice one visible slack line beats hidden padding. rule of thumb nothing on the list runs longer than one day. three fixes to apply 1 show the output name the artefact each step produces. 2 add a slack line buffer once, visibly, not per estimate. 3 mark dependencies flag every step that waits on someone.
proj-structure: the idea a folder layout is cheap memory. months later, without you, it answers where the data came from, which script made which number, and which file is the one to send. one rule carries most of the benefit: raw is read-only . decide the folders before the first file project/ └ data/raw/ └ data/clean/ └ notebooks/ └ src/ └ outputs/ └ readme.md two rules that save you later raw/ is read-only — never overwrite it every output is rebuildable from src/ name files so they sort: 2026-10-12_churn_v1.csv when to use it before the first download — retrofitting structure wastes an afternoon. any project you might repeat — monthly, quarterly, or next year. anything another person touches — including future you. anything you may defend — audit means re-run it in front of someone. three zones and a number keep raw for untouched extracts, interim for what a script produced on the way, outputs for what leaves the project. delete the last two and the scripts should rebuild both; that is the test of reproducibility. number scripts in run order — 01_extract , 02_clean , 03_measure — so the sequence is visible without a readme, and keep a five-line readme anyway. name files so they sort: dates as yyyy-mm-dd , lower case, underscores, no spaces, no final . version with v2 , never with final_v2_really. folder holds rule raw extracts as delivered read-only, never edited interim cleaned and joined tables disposable, rebuildable outputs charts, tables, the memo dated, nothing hand-typed src numbered scripts run in order, top to bottom # template - project folder manifest, fill the slots [project-slug]/ readme.md # question, sources, run order, owner docs/ brief_[v1].md # the one-page brief data_notes.md # per-source traps, as you find them prompts.md # prompts that worked, by stage raw/ [date]_[source].csv # never edited, never overwritten interim/ [step]_[what-it-is].parquet outputs/ [date]_[figure].png [date]_[memo]_[v1].pdf src/ 01 _extract_[source].py 02 _clean_[entity].py 03 _measure_[question].py practical note an assistant is genuinely good at this: hand it your question and sources and ask for a tree plus a readme skeleton. it costs nothing to check, because you see the whole answer at once — unlike a number, which looks the same either way. folders and naming raw is read-only, the rest rebuilds ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice edit the extract in place the original is gone raw, interim, outputs delete two and re-run final_v2_really.xlsx nobody knows which one number scripts in run order 01 extract, 02 clean one folder, forty files which script made this? sortable names, no spaces dates as yyyy-mm-dd result: numbers you cannot re-run result: reproducible by anyone mistake months later nobody can rebuild the table. best practice a five-line readme carries the rest. rule of thumb never edit a source extract in place. three fixes to apply 1 make raw read-only nothing writes there after the download. 2 number the scripts run order visible without a readme. 3 version with v2 never final, never final_really.
proj-ai-roles: the idea an assistant is strong at drafting structure, naming things, writing boilerplate, explaining an error and listing what you forgot. it is unreliable on facts, numbers, citations and anything it cannot check — so every figure and source it produces must be verified against your data or the original document before it reaches a deliverable. delegate the shape, verify the substance delegate to ai an outline or structure boilerplate and naming what you forgot verify yourself every number every source and quote the conclusion ai is confident whether or not it is right: check anything you will be asked to defend when to use it blank-page moments — an outline is faster to fix than to invent. stuck on an error — it reads a traceback and suggests what to test. before you submit — ask what a reviewer would attack, and what is missing. the test is whether you can check it delegate freely where the answer is self-evident on inspection : a folder tree is right or wrong in front of you, a function runs on your rows or does not. be strict where it is not — a number, a rate, a field name, a quoted source. those arrive fluent whether or not they are true, and a plausible wrong number is worse than none, because it survives review. so run its code on your own rows, treat a field name as a hypothesis to confirm with a query, and take every citation back to the document. two sentences earn their keep in any prompt: mark anything you are guessing , and use placeholders rather than invented names . task delegate? how you verify folder tree, readme yes, fully read it; it is all visible code, boilerplate yes run it; check counts and edges any number or rate no re-derive it from the data sources, citations no open the document and read it # prompt - review my plan for what i have forgotten you are reviewing an analytics project plan. here it is: [paste the brief and the step plan] what i know about my data, in my own words: [grain, row counts i checked, known gaps] do three things, in this order: 1. list the steps a plan like this usually has that mine lacks. 2. name the three assumptions that would hurt most if wrong, and for each the cheapest check i could run this week. 3. write the two questions a sceptical reviewer would ask. rules: do not estimate durations, that is my call. do not invent table names, field names or row counts - use placeholders and tell me what to look up. end with a list headed guesses holding anything you could not take from my text. the caution you own every number in the deliverable, whoever typed it. if you cannot name the query behind a figure and re-run it, remove it. the honest sentence when challenged is here is the query. delegate or verify delegate what you can check at a glance ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice paste its number into a deck fluent whether right or wrong delegate structure and code outlines, boilerplate, readme accept a field name as fact it cannot see your warehouse run every snippet on your rows check counts and edge cases let it set your estimates it does not know your week re-derive every figure from the data, by yourself result: a plausible wrong answer result: speed without fiction mistake a wrong number reads exactly like a right one. best practice ask it to mark anything it is guessing. rule of thumb you own every number, whoever typed it. three fixes to apply 1 ban invention no field names or figures - placeholders. 2 ask for guesses a list of what it could not take from you. 3 run the code on your own rows, then check the counts.
proj-prompts: the idea a prompt that worked once is an asset, and you keep it by writing it with slots instead of specifics. four parts do the work: the context you supply, the artefact you paste in, the output shape you demand, and the constraints that stop it inventing things. one prompt per stage, kept short scope "ask me 5 questions to narrow this" explore "what should i check in this data first?" analyse "critique my method and name the risks" write up "rewrite this for a non-technical reader" always end with: "what would make this wrong?" when to use it any task you will repeat — a monthly refresh, each new source. when answers come back shapeless — the shape was never specified. after a prompt lands well — save it that day or it is gone. demand a shape, forbid invention vague prompts return essays. naming the shape — a five-row table with these columns, three bullets of fifteen words, a numbered checklist — makes the answer usable and a bad answer obvious at a glance. constraints matter as much: say what not to do, and ask for an explicit guesses section at the end. keep the library in docs/prompts.md beside the work, one entry per stage, each with the prompt and how you had to fix its output last time. that fix note is the part that improves fastest. stage the prompt's job output shape to demand framing three candidate questions table: question, measure, decision feasibility per-source checklist one row per source, with a verdict building code and edge cases runnable function plus a test list delivering answer-first summary headline, three bullets, caveat # template - prompt skeleton, fill the four slots role and context i am [role] working on [one-line project]. the audience is [who], who will decide [decision]. stage: [framing | feasibility | building | checking | delivering] artefact [paste the brief, plan, schema, code or draft findings] output shape give me [a table with columns a, b, c | n bullets | a checklist], at most [length], ordered by [what matters most]. constraints do not invent [field names, figures, sources, dates]. use placeholders where you would need one, and say what to check. do not [estimate durations | propose a method | write prose]. end with a guesses list of anything not taken from my text. # saved as: docs/prompts.md -> [stage] -> [name] practical note paste the real artefact rather than describing it. a prompt holding your actual schema or error text gets a specific answer; one describing it from memory gets a generic answer built on whatever filled the gaps. prompt library demand a shape, forbid invention ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice ask an open question you get an essay back name the output shape a five-row table, three bullets describe your data from memory it fills the gaps itself paste the real artefact schema, error text, findings re-type the prompt each time the good one is lost keep docs/prompts.md one entry per stage result: shapeless, generic answers result: reusable and checkable mistake the gaps got filled with plausible invention. best practice note the fix you had to make last time. rule of thumb say the shape, and say what not to do. three fixes to apply 1 four slots context, artefact, shape, constraints. 2 paste it in the real schema beats your summary of it. 3 save it same day a prompt not written down is gone.
proj-checkpoints: the idea a checkpoint is a date agreed in advance when you show unfinished work and someone decides: continue, change, or stop. without them a project has one moment of feedback — the end — the most expensive place to learn the question had moved. four moments to stop and ask brief agreed? data in usable? first result believable? draft readable? if a checkpoint fails, change the plan — do not just work harder stopping at "good enough and defensible" is a skill when to use it anything over a week — put a checkpoint near its midpoint. anything exploratory — where the answer may be there is no effect. anything new to you — your estimates are weakest there. three honest reasons to stop stop when the question is answered to the precision the decision needs — if the decider acts the same way at eighteen percent as at twenty-two, the second decimal is someone else's money. stop when another day would not change the recommendation — test that by writing the recommendation now and asking what would reverse it. stop at the deadline, delivering what exists plus a note on what is missing; a dated partial answer beats a perfect one arriving after the decision. name the sentences that run projects past their value: just one more model. checkpoint what you show decision it forces after feasibility source verdicts, counts go, re-scope, or stop now first numbers ugly chart, the direction is this the right question? draft answer one page, caveats included enough, or one more cut? pre-delivery reconciliation to a known figure ship, or explain it # template - checkpoint log, one block each, written the same day checkpoint : [name] date : [yyyy-mm-dd] shown to : [names and roles] shown : [the artefact, however rough] best answer : [one sentence, as if you had to stop today] would flip it : [the finding that would reverse the advice] decision : [continue | re-scope | stop | pause for access] scope change : [what moved in or out, and who asked] next check : [date] and [what will be shown] # stopping rules, agreed at the first checkpoint: # precision: [direction | nearest 10% | exact] # deadline: [date] - ship what exists, name the gaps the caution never arrive at a checkpoint with nothing because the work is not presentable. an ugly chart on the agreed date is a checkpoint; a polished one a week late is a surprise, and surprises are what checkpoints prevent. checkpoints and stopping one feedback moment is the dear one ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice show nothing until it is done feedback arrives too late set dates in advance midpoint of anything long skip a check because it is ugly polish later is a surprise show the ugly chart on time continue, re-scope, or stop stop when you are tired or never, with one more model write the stopping rules precision needed, hard date result: value burned past the answer result: cheap course corrections mistake the question had moved two weeks earlier. best practice a dated partial answer beats a late perfect one. rule of thumb stop when another day changes nothing. three fixes to apply 1 book the dates at the start, not when you feel ready. 2 answer as if today one sentence, written at every check. 3 agree the precision direction, ten percent, or exact.
proj-deliver: the idea order the deliverable the way a decision-maker reads: the answer first, then the evidence , then the method , then the appendix. the chronological order you worked in is the worst order to present in, because the answer lands on the page nobody reaches. four things to hand over the answer one slide or paragraph the evidence charts and tables the method how, and its limits the files data, code, outputs lead with the answer. the method is support, not the headline. when to use it every time work leaves your folder — email, memo, deck or dashboard. when the reader is senior — assume the first paragraph only. when the result is awkward — no effect still needs a clear headline. one claim, one chart, one source write the headline as a finding, not a title: first-year accounts leave at twice the rate of the rest , never churn analysis results . then one chart per claim, each with its own takeaway sentence, and nothing in the pack that supports no claim. put the limitations in your own words before anyone finds them — a named weakness reads as competence, a discovered one as carelessness. every number must trace to a script you can re-run while someone watches. state the recommendation in the imperative, with an owner: we should consider is where analyses go to die. audience format lead with decider, busy one page, one chart the answer and the action committee short deck, appendix headline, then each claim analyst peer notebook plus readme method and known caveats recurring users table or dashboard definitions and refresh date # prompt - turn findings into an answer-first one-pager audience: [role], who decides [decision] on [date]. they currently believe [the existing number or assumption]. my findings, in my own words, each with the figure i verified: [finding 1 + the number + the query that produced it] [finding 2 ...] limitations: [list them, including what i could not check] draft a one-pager with exactly this structure: - headline: one sentence stating the finding, not the topic - so what: two bullets on what should happen, with an owner - evidence: one bullet per claim, each naming its figure - limitations: mine, in plain language, nothing softened - if you read one thing: a single line rules: use only the numbers i gave, exactly as written. do not round, rescale or add context i did not supply. if a sentence needs a number i did not give, write needs figure instead. the caution never present a number you cannot re-derive, and never let an assistant smooth your caveats into reassurance. read the final text against your limitation list: if a hedge got softer on the way through, put it back. packaging the result the answer goes first, not last ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice present in the order you work the answer lands on page nine headline the finding twice the rate in year one title the slide churn analysis a topic, not a finding one claim, one chart, one key each with its takeaway line let the reader find the flaw discovered reads as careless name your own limitations named reads as competence result: good work nobody acts on result: a decision gets made mistake senior readers stop after the first line. best practice recommend in the imperative, with an owner. rule of thumb if you cannot re-derive it, do not show it. three fixes to apply 1 finding, not topic write what you found, not what you studied. 2 one chart per claim each with its own takeaway sentence. 3 check the hedges nothing may get softer on the way through.
proj-retro: the idea the lasting asset is rarely the chart. it is what you now know about those sources, the prompts that worked, the gap between estimate and reality, and the code you can lift into the next project. write it down while you still remember, because none of it survives a week. three questions, fifteen minutes keep what worked change what slowed you drop what added nothing write it the day you finish: a template you reuse is worth more than a perfect one when to use it within a day of delivering — the data traps fade fastest. after anything that went badly — the dense lessons are there. before you hand it over — the notes are most of the handover. four things worth keeping data notes pay best per minute: this field is null before 2023, this key repeats for merged accounts. nobody else wrote that down and you will need it again. prompt entries go back to the library with a line on how you fixed the output. estimate versus actual , per step, is the only way estimating improves. reusable code means the two functions worth lifting, moved somewhere findable rather than left inside 03_measure.py . then name one thing to start and one to stop: two items you act on beat ten you file. keep where pays off when data notes docs/data_notes.md next time you touch it prompt entries docs/prompts.md same stage, next project estimate vs actual retro note you next quote a date reusable code a shared utils file the next extract or chart # template - project retro, twenty minutes, within a day project : [name] delivered : [date] verdict : [one line] answer : [the finding, one sentence] acted on : [what actually changed, or not yet] estimate vs actual (half-days) [step] : est [n] | actual [n] | why [one phrase] [step] : est [n] | actual [n] | why [one phrase] data notes (append to docs/data_notes.md) [source] : [the trap, in one reusable line] prompts that worked (append to docs/prompts.md) [stage] : [name] - fix needed: [what you corrected] [function or query worth reusing] -> moved to [where] next time start doing : [one imperative sentence] stop doing : [one imperative sentence] practical note this is the only item on the list that compounds. project two is faster for the data notes, project three for the prompt library, and by the fourth your estimates mean something — none of which happens if the retro slips. keeping the lessons the data notes are the real asset ✗ common mistake ✓ best practice close the folder and move on the gotchas fade in a week twenty minutes, same week before the detail fades keep the chart, lose the notes you relearn it next quarter notes, prompts, times, code the four things worth keeping file ten lessons, act on none a document, not a change one start, one stop two items you will act on result: project two is just as slow result: the next one is faster mistake nobody wrote down the repeating key trap. best practice by project four your estimates mean something. rule of thumb write it the day you deliver, or not at all. three fixes to apply 1 log the gotcha one line per source, reusable by anyone. 2 est vs actual per step, no excuses, no commentary. 3 lift the code move the two useful functions somewhere.

m27-pm-build: one table per subject, linked by program_id. start in a spreadsheet and move to a database when you need to. quick look tracker data model enlarge program program_id, name, sponsor, start, end one row per program 1 indicator indicator_id, program_id, formula, thresholds defined once 2 snapshot program_id, snapshot_date, scores, health, status one row per program per month 3 risk risk_id, program_id, l, i, score, owner re-scored monthly 4 benefit benefit_id, program_id, planned, forecast owner in the business 5 decision date, program_id, decision, decider, action append only 6 1 program the master list. every other table links to program_id, so a program is named once. 2 indicator definitions live here, not in slide notes. a change creates a new version. 3 snapshot one row per program per month. never overwrite; history is the trend. 4 risk current risk register with likelihood, impact and score. keep monthly copies if you want a risk trend. 5 benefit planned and forecast benefit per line, each with a business owner. 6 decision append-only. a decision is never edited; corrections are new rows. run it, then check the result create the tables and let the database score create table program ( program_id text primary key, name text not null , sponsor text, start_date date, end_date date); create table program_snapshot ( program_id text references program(program_id), snapshot_date date, schedule int, budget int, scope int, benefits int, risk int, -- 1 to 5 health decimal( 5 , 1 ), status text, primary key (program_id, snapshot_date)); -- weighted health score from the five 1-5 scores update program_snapshot set health = ( 25 *schedule + 20 *budget + 15 *scope + 25 *benefits + 15 *risk) / 5.0 ; update program_snapshot set status = case when health >= 75 and risk > 2 then 'green' when health >= 60 then 'amber' else 'red' end ; same rule as the scorecard tile. keeping the formula in one place stops different reports from disagreeing. the portfolio headline select status, count (*) as programs, round(avg(health), 1 ) as avg_health from program_snapshot where snapshot_date = date ' 2026 - 09 - 30 ' group by status order by avg_health desc; you should see illustrative output status programs avg_health green 3 83.0 amber 2 71.5 red 3 51.0 matches the example portfolio on the other tiles. no database? the same design in a spreadsheet sheet "snapshot" columns: a program_id | b snapshot_date | c..g scores | h health | i status h2: =sumproduct(c2:g2, weights!$b$ 2 :$f$ 2 )/ 5 i2: =if(h2>= 75 , if(g2<= 2 , "amber" , "green" ), if(h2>= 60 , "amber" , "red" )) sheet "dashboard" latest month: =max(snapshot!b:b) count of red: =countifs(snapshot!b:b, dashboard!b1, snapshot!i:i, "red" ) average health: =averageifs(snapshot!h:h, snapshot!b:b, dashboard!b1) trend line: pivot snapshot by month, average of health -> line chart data validation: scores 1 - 5 whole numbers;
